name: Abhayadatta
summary: Compiler of the Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti, the lives of the eighty-four siddhas (c. 11th–12th c.); often identified with Abhayadattaśrī of Campāraṇya.

name: Abhayadevasūri
summary: Pupil of Jineśvara, the 'commentator on nine Aṅgas' (navāṅgī-vṛttikāra) in the 1060s.

name: Abhayākaragupta
summary: Late Vikramaśīla master (c. 1100), author of the Munimatālaṃkāra, a summa of Madhyamaka doctrine, as well as tantric works.
alt_summary: U44 contribution: abbot of Vikramaśīla (d. c. 1125), author of the Vajrāvalī, Niṣpannayogāvalī and Āmnāyamañjarī, which standardized the maṇḍala and consecration rites of late Indian Vajrayāna.

name: Abhimanyu
summary: Named in the Gītā only as Saubhadra, the strong-armed son of Subhadrā, a great chariot-warrior who blows his conch (1.6, 1.18); identified as Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, from the epic.
notes: Saubhadra = Abhimanyu is the epic identification. Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6, 1.18.

name: Abhinanda (Gauḍa Abhinanda)
summary: Kashmiri author to whom the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is ascribed.

queries: Laghu Yoga Vasistha Gauda Abhinanda date
checks.note: The Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha's final colophon names 'gauḍamaṇḍalālaṅkāra śrīmad-abhinanda'. Wikipedia identifies him with Abhinanda of Kashmir, son of Jayanta Bhaṭṭa (9th-10th c.). Slaje argues that the Kashmiri Abhinanda and the Gauḍa Abhinanda of the colophon are distinct and a 10th-c. date is untenable, so the dating stays unsettled.

name: Abhinandananātha
summary: The fourth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the monkey. Parents: Saṃvara and Siddhārthā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fourth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: The central figure of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism: author of the Tantrāloka, Tantrasāra, Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa, Mālinīślokavārttika, the two commentaries on the Īśvarapratyabhijñā, the Paramārthasāra, Gītārthasaṅgraha, devotional hymns, and of the Abhinavabhāratī and Locana in aesthetics. He integrated Trika, Kula, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā under the four upāyas.

scholarly.text: c. 975-1025 CE; dated works: Kramastotra (Laukika 66, c. 990/91), Bhairavastava (68, c. 992/93), Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (90, c. 1014/15)

realization_account.text: The Tantrāloka describes one born of a union of parents absorbed in the Kaula state as 'yoginībhū', by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra himself (TĀ 29.162-163), a description the tradition applies to Abhinavagupta. Later Kashmiri tradition relates that he entered the Bhairava cave near Bīrwa with many disciples and did not return (oral legend; low confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Teacher ids tch:induraja and tch:bhatta-tauta (poetics, dramaturgy) belong to U31.

checks.note: Confirmed.

alt_summary: Author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.

U31 contribution: in the Abhinavabhāratī and the Locana he gave the classical account of rasa — the relish (carvaṇā) of a generalized emotion in the spectator's own consciousness, free of obstacles, at rest in itself (viśrānti), marked by wonder (camatkāra) — and defended śānta as a rasa whose stable basis is knowledge of the self; aesthetic rapture is akin to, not identical with, the bliss of the supreme.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni
summary: Companion of Śaunaka Kāpeya in the saṃvarga episode (ChU 4.3.5-7).

checks.note: Located: ChU 4.3.5-6.

name: Abhirāmi Paṭṭar
summary: 18th-c. Tamil devotee of the Goddess Abhirāmi of Tirukkaṭavūr and author of the Abhirāmi Antāti.

realization_account.text: Absorbed in the Goddess, he told the king that the day was full moon; to vindicate him the Goddess threw her earring into the sky, which shone as the moon.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Acalabhrātṛ
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether merit and demerit (puṇya, pāpa) exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Ācārya Bhikṣu (Bhīkhaṇjī)
summary: Founder (1726–1803) of the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth; he left the Sthānakavāsī order of Raghunāth in 1760 over monastic laxity and the definition of dharma, gave the order a single ācārya and a written code (maryādā), and wrote extensively in Rajasthani verse.

name: Acinta

realization_account.text: A poor woodcutter consumed by desire for wealth, taught to meditate on his longing as the sky. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 38): In objectless mahāmudrā the many deluded recollections are lost; by the light of gnosis-awareness whatever appears is seen as mahāmudrā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 38 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A poor woodcutter consumed by desire for wealth, taught to meditate on his longing as the sky.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Acyuta Piṣāraṭi
summary: Kerala astronomer, pupil of Jyeṣṭhadeva and teacher of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri (author of the Nārāyaṇīyam).

name: Acyutaprekṣa
summary: The ascetic at Uḍupi from whom Madhva took renunciation; the Sumadhvavijaya calls him Acyutapramati. In the tradition's account his ascetic line had come under the teaching of māyā, and he later accepted his disciple's doctrine.
notes: The earlier names of his line (the 'Haṃsa paramparā' back to Nārāyaṇa as Haṃsa and Brahmā) are not listed; see lin:dvaita notes.

name: Āḍhamalla
summary: Commentator on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā (Dīpikā).

name: Adhokṣaja Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Pejavara maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Ādinātha
summary: Śiva as the first Nāth and first teacher of yoga; the Haṭhapradīpikā opens with homage to Śrī Ādinātha 'by whom the knowledge of haṭha yoga was taught' (HYP 1.1), and Nāth lineages begin with him. In Nāth accounts he taught Matsyendra, who overheard or received the teaching he gave to Pārvatī.

realization_account.text: The supreme Lord himself; the source of the teaching.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U28 contribution: in the haṭha texts Ādinātha — Śiva as the first lord — is the revealer of haṭhavidyā (HYP 1.1), of the eighty-four postures (HYP 1.33), the ten mudrās (HYP 3.8, 3.128), 'a crore and a quarter' ways of laya (HYP 4.66; DYŚ 14: eight crore saṅketas), and of the Khecarīvidyā; the Jyotsnā says he taught haṭha to Girijā (Pārvatī).

name: Aditi Dākṣāyaṇī
summary: Named as one possible seer of RV 10.72 on the birth of the gods (Aditi born of Dakṣa and Dakṣa of Aditi).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: Aditi Dākṣāyaṇī as one alternative seer of 10.72; 10.72.4 located.

name: Āditya (the Sun as teacher)
summary: The Sun-god who instructs visitors to his world: Triśikhi (Triśikhibrāhmaṇa), Sāṅkṛti (Akṣi); in the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa Yājñavalkya goes to the solar world and is taught by the Person there (Nārāyaṇa).

queries: e-text name search: Āditya (the Sun as teacher)
checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of trisikhibrahmana, aksi, mandalabrahmana, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Ādityadāsa
summary: Father and teacher of Varāhamihira, from whom he received his knowledge (BJ 28.9).

name: Ādityanāth
summary: Present mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur (from 2014), also a political figure.
notes: Recorded only as head of the seat; no teachings attributed.

name: Ādivaṇ Śaṭhakopa Jīyar
summary: Founder of the Ahobila maṭha of the Vaṭakalai (traditionally 1398), who, the tradition says, received his renunciation from Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha of Ahobilam himself.

tradition.text: founded the Ahobila maṭha in 1398 CE

name: Advaita Ācārya
summary: Elder Vaiṣṇava scholar of Śāntipur whose prayers, the tradition says, called Caitanya down; one of the Pañca-tattva.

realization_account.text: Mahāviṣṇu and Sadāśiva combined; lived to a great age (tradition: 125 years).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Adzom Drukpa Natsok Rangdrol (a 'dzom 'brug pa)
summary: Dzogchen master and treasure revealer of Kham, disciple of Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Patrul Rinpoche.

name: Agasti (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 15 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Agastya
summary: In the Vīraśaiva tradition, the sage to whom Reṇuka taught the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi on the Malaya mountain (SSM 1.29; ch. 4–5).

checks.note: Headers: 'agastyo maitrāvaruṇiḥ' for 1.165(13–15)–1.190; 1.191 is also his per Sāyaṇa's attributes (the DharmicData header for 1.191 is a misprint). 1.179 dialogue confirmed; 'ubhau varṇau' in 1.179.6. Tamil Siddhar identification and scholarly doubt confirmed by web sources.
Located as described.
Lalitopākhyāna frame (Brahmāṇḍa 3.5), Kāśī Khaṇḍa 4.1.6.28-45, BhP 8.4.10 (the curse on Indradyumna) located.

notes: Contribution of U20 to a shared registry entity (Agastya is owned elsewhere).
alt_summary: U23 contribution: one of the twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā; the disciple of Hayagrīva to whom the Lalitā Sahasranāma and Triśatī are taught; husband of Lopāmudrā.

In the Tamil Siddha tradition, Akattiyar (Kuṟumuṉi, Kumpamuṉi) is the first and foremost of the Siddhars and the founder of Siddha medicine: sent south by Śiva to the Potiyil hills, he received Tamil from Śiva or Murukaṉ, composed the lost grammar Akattiyam, and is the author-authority of a large medical, alchemical and yogic corpus and of the vital-point (varmam) lore.

Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi, seer of RV 1.165–191; in 1.179 he answers his wife Lopāmudrā, reconciling long tapas with married life, and is said to have 'nourished both colours'. Born with Vasiṣṭha of Mitra-Varuṇa in the tradition; the Tamil tradition identifies him with the Siddhar Agastya (the Vedic contribution is recorded here).
In the Rāmāyaṇa the sage Agastya teaches Rāma the Āditya Hṛdaya before the final battle (Yuddhakāṇḍa 105/107).

In the Purāṇas the sage who, pilgrimaging with Lopāmudrā, receives the Lalitopākhyāna from Hayagrīva, and who in the Kāśī Khaṇḍa teaches Lopāmudrā the inner tīrthas (SkP 4.1.6.28-45); he also cursed Indradyumna to become the elephant Gajendra.
The seer whose star's heliacal rising (Agastyacāra, BS 12) is a saṃhitā topic, and the most cited author of the Tamil palm-leaf nāḍīs (the tradition's claim).
places: Anantaśayanam (Thiruvananthapuram) — samādhi in the popular list

realization_account.text: When all gods and sages gathered in the north for Śiva's wedding and the earth tilted, Śiva sent the diminutive Agastya south, where he balanced the world from the Potiyil hills; he is held to live there still as a Siddhar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_notes: U22 contribution (Tamil Siddha / Siddha medicine). Scholars do not assume the Vedic, epic and Tamil Agastyas are one person, and regard the Tamil medical works under his name as late. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.
Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Scholars do not assume the Vedic and Tamil Agastyas are one person.
U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Agastya's sister (mother of the Gaupāyanas)
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 10.60.6; named among the brahmavādinīs of the Bṛhaddevatā.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Aghamarṣaṇa Mādhucchandasa
summary: Seer of RV 10.190 (ṛta and satya born of tapas), the 'sin-effacing' verses recited at the bath.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'mādhucchandaso 'ghamarṣaṇaḥ'.

name: Aghoraśiva
summary: Twelfth-century Śaiva ācārya of Chidambaram (Āmardaka lineage — moderate confidence) whose ritual manual Kriyākramadyotikā (1157/58) and commentaries (on the Mṛgendravṛtti and six of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa treatises) fixed the dualist reading of the Siddhānta followed by South Indian temple priests.
notes: Corrected: his Aṣṭaprakaraṇa commentaries cover six treatises (not the Mokṣakārikā or Paramokṣanirāsakārikā).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Saiddhāntika ācārya of Cidambaram whose ritual manual (Kriyākramadyotikā, 1157/58) became the standard for Tamil Śaiva temple and domestic ritual; he also wrote commentaries on the Mṛgendravṛtti, the Sarvajñānottara and works of Sadyojyoti and Bhoja.

name: Agnibhūti
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether karma exists. Brother of Indrabhūti.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Agniveśa
summary: The first of Ātreya's disciples to compose a tantra (Ca Sū 1.32); he is the questioner throughout the Caraka Saṃhitā, whose text is 'the tantra made by Agniveśa and redacted by Caraka' (colophons).

name: Agradās
summary: Disciple of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī, seated at Raivāsā (16th c.), founder of the rasik mode of Rāma devotion and guru of Nābhādās, whom he commanded to write the Bhaktamāl.

name: Ahobala
summary: Author of the Saṅgītapārijāta.

name: Aitiśāyana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, e.g. for the prima facie view that only men are eligible for rites because of the masculine gender in 'svargakāmo yajeta' (MS 6.1.6) and at MS 3.2.43.

name: Aiyaṭikaḷ Kāṭavarkōṉ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pallava king who gave up the throne and went on pilgrimage, singing a veṇpā at each shrine (the Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā).

realization_account.text: A Pallava king who gave up the throne and went on pilgrimage, singing a veṇpā at each shrine (the Kṣēttirat Tiruveṇpā).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ajagaṇṇa
summary: Muktāyakka's brother, a hidden devotee whose death occasions her meeting with Allama.

name: Ajahn Chah Subhaddo
summary: Thai forest master (1918–1992) of Wat Nong Pah Pong in Ubon Ratchathani, who met Ajahn Mun briefly and founded a large lineage of monasteries including Wat Pah Nanachat for Western monks.
notes: A Mahānikāya monk, not Dhammayut.

name: Ajahn Fuang Jotiko
summary: Thai forest monk (1915–1986), pupil of Ajahn Lee and teacher of Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu.

name: Ajahn Lee Dhammadharo
summary: Thai forest master (1907–1961), pupil of Ajahn Mun, known for his systematic breath meditation (Keeping the Breath in Mind) and founder of Wat Asokaram.

name: Ajahn Maha Boowa Ñāṇasampanno
summary: Thai forest master (1913–2011) of Wat Pa Baan Taad, pupil and biographer of Ajahn Mun, who taught an energetic path of body contemplation and wisdom culminating in seeing through the radiant citta.

name: Ajahn Mun Bhūridatto

realization_account.text: His disciples' biographies say he attained arahantship in a cave in Chiang Mai province, after years of solitary practice and visions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Thai forest master (1870–1949) who revived the dhutaṅga wandering life in the forests of Isan and northern Thailand; teacher of nearly all later forest masters.

name: Ajahn Sao Kantasīlo
summary: Thai Dhammayut monk (1861–1941), austere meditation master and teacher of Ajahn Mun; with him the founder of the forest tradition.

name: Ajahn Sumedho
summary: American-born senior Western disciple of Ajahn Chah (b. 1934), founder of Chithurst and Amaravati monasteries in England.

name: Ajahn Thate Desaransi
summary: Thai forest master (1902–1994), pupil of Ajahn Mun, abbot of Wat Hin Mark Peng.

name: Ajaib Singh (Sant Ji)
summary: Disciple of Kirpal Singh, teacher at Sant Bani Ashram (77 RB, Rajasthan), associated with the English Anurāg Sāgar.

name: Ajātaśatru of Kāśī
summary: King of Kāśī who refutes Gārgya Bālāki's twelve (KauU: sixteen) identifications of brahman and teaches the self into which the sleeping person withdraws, from which all breaths, worlds and gods come forth like sparks (BAU 2.1; KauU 4). He notes it is against the natural order for a brahmin to come to a kṣatriya to learn brahman.
notes: Distinct from the Magadhan king of the Buddhist texts; id disambiguated.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 2.1.1-20 has twelve persons proposed (2.1.2–2.1.13) and at 2.1.15 'pratilomaṃ caitad yad brāhmaṇaḥ kṣatriyam upeyāt'. KauU 4.1-20 has sixteen (4.2–4.17). The text calls him 'kāśya', king of Kāśī.

name: Ajātasattu
summary: King of Magadha who killed his father Bimbisāra and later confessed to the Buddha (DN 2).

name: Ajita Kesakambalī
summary: One of the six famous teachers, named for his blanket of human hair. DN 2 reports his annihilationism: there is no gift, sacrifice or offering, no fruit of good and bad deeds, no this world or other world, no mother or father, no spontaneously born beings, no ascetic who has realized the other world; the person is made of the four great elements, which return to their masses at death, the faculties passing into space; fool and wise alike are annihilated at the body's breaking up.
alt_names: 阿夷陀翅舍欽婆羅 (Chinese, Dīrgha-āgama)

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: Doctrine reported_by_opponent. Later tradition and scholars treat him as a forerunner of the Lokāyata; no text links him to that school by lineage. SN 44.9 reports (surprisingly) that he too declared where his dead disciples were reborn.

name: Ajita (Pārāyana)
summary: One of the sixteen brahmin students of Bāvarī who questioned the Buddha in the Pārāyanavagga (Snp 5.2).

name: Ajitamitra
notes: The commentary is D4159 (catalog:Derge-Tengyur:D4159); author's name from memory.
summary: Author of the Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's Ratnāvalī preserved in Tibetan (Ratnāvalīṭīkā).

name: Ajitanātha
summary: The second Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the elephant. Parents: King Jitaśatru and Queen Vijayā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His cousin Sagara was the second world-emperor (cakravartin).

tradition.text: the second of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Ajogipa

realization_account.text: An idle son who would do nothing but lie in bed; a guru taught him to visualize a drop (like a mustard seed) at the tip of his nose while lying down, and he realized. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 26): By the true guru's instruction I meditated on a drop at the tip of the nose, the upper door; my mind steady in it, the object, the mustard-seed drop, was lost in emptiness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 26 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). An idle son who would do nothing but lie in bed; a guru taught him to visualize a drop (like a mustard seed) at the tip of his nose while lying down, and he realized.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The song confirms the story of the drop at the nose tip.

name: Akalaṅka

realization_account.text: Victory in debate over the Buddhists at Kāñcī, where Tārā spoke from behind a curtain until he exposed her (legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Digambara logician who gave Jain epistemology its classical form (the conventionally direct and truly direct perception; memory, recognition, reasoning, inference and scripture as indirect knowledge) and wrote the Tattvārtharājavārttika. The tradition tells that he studied in a Buddhist monastery in disguise with his brother Niṣkalaṅka, who was killed, and later defeated the Buddhists in debate at the court of Himaśītala at Kāñcī, where the goddess Tārā spoke behind a curtain.

name: Akampita
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether hell-beings exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Akao no Dōshū
summary: Lay follower of Rennyo from Etchū, remembered as an exemplary myōkōnin for his 'twenty-one resolutions' and austere devotion.

name: Akappēyc cittar
summary: Siddhar poet named from his refrain addressing 'akappēy', the demon that is one's own mind.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

name: Ākāśagarbha
summary: The bodhisattva 'womb of space', before whom bodhisattvas confess root downfalls (Ākāśagarbha-sūtra); his mantra-recitation (gumonji) was practiced by Kūkai.

name: Akhaṇḍānanda
summary: Author of the Tattvadīpana on the Vivaraṇa.

name: Akiñcana Dāsa
summary: Author of the Vivartavilāsa, which reads the Caitanya-caritāmṛta as Sahajiyā doctrine.

name: Akka Mahādēvi
summary: Akka Mahādēvi (Mahādēviyakka) of Uḍutaḍi, the woman saint who took Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna for her only husband, left a royal household, wandered clad only in her hair, was examined by Allama at Kalyāṇa and ended at Kadaḷi on Śrīśaila; her vacanas of bridal devotion and fearless renunciation are the tradition's great witness to women's spiritual equality.

realization_account.text: Devoted from childhood to Cennamallikārjuna, she refused (or left) the king Kauśika, renounced even clothing, was tested and acknowledged by Allama and the śaraṇas at Kalyāṇa, and attained union in the Kadaḷi forest of Śrīśaila.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Whether she was married to Kauśika differs between sources; recorded as the sources' variance.

name: Akkamma
summary: A woman vacanakāra of the śaraṇa circle whose vacanas are included in the modern collections of the women śaraṇas; details of her life are not recorded here.

name: Akkanāgamma
summary: Basava's sister (Nāgalāmbike), mother of Cennabasava and a vacanakāra.

name: Akṛtavraṇa
summary: One of Romaharṣaṇa's disciples in both lists (VP 3.6.17; BhP 12.7.5), of the Kāśyapa lineage (VP 3.6.18 counts 'Kāśyapa' among the makers of saṃhitās; BhP 12.7.7 calls Akṛtavraṇa a disciple of Rāma Jāmadagnya).

checks.note: VP 3.6.17-18 and BhP 12.7.5, 12.7.7 ('rāmaśiṣyo 'kṛtavraṇaḥ') located.

name: Akṣayamati
summary: The bodhisattva whose teaching on the inexhaustible qualities gives the Akṣayamatinirdeśa its name; in Lotus ch. 25 he asks about Avalokiteśvara.

name: Akṣobhya
summary: The 'Immovable' buddha of the eastern world Abhirati, who as a monk vowed never to feel anger.

name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva, pontiff after Mādhava Tīrtha, and teacher of Jayatīrtha. The Mādhva tradition records his debate with the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya on 'tat tvam asi', with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika declaring Akṣobhya the victor; the Advaita tradition does not accept this account.
notes: See dsp:tat-tvam-asi (historical_debates).

name: al-Bīrūnī
alt_names: Abū Rayḥān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Bīrūnī
summary: Khwārazmian scholar who learned Sanskrit in India and rendered a Pātañjala yoga text with a commentary into Arabic (Kitāb Pātanǧal). He was not a member of the tradition; he is listed under this lineage only as the translator of its text.

name: Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: Younger brother of Piḷḷai Lokācārya, author of the Ācārya Hṛdayam, which presents Nammāḻvār's Tiruvāymoḻi as the Tamil Veda.

name: Āḷāra Kālāma
summary: A teacher of the bodhisatta who taught the attainment of the sphere of nothingness and offered to share leadership of his community (MN 26, MN 36).
notes: Known only through Buddhist texts.

name: Alarka
summary: Youngest son of Madālasā and King Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva); raised as a king, he received his mother's ring-instruction and, when defeated in war, went to Dattātreya, learned yoga and renounced (MkP 25-44).

checks.note: Located as described.
MkP 25 (Madālasā's sons) and 38-43 located.

alt_summary: A royal sage who first sought to conquer the mind and senses with arrows and then learned that they are conquered only by yoga (Anugītā 14.30).

name: Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa
notes: Role: commentator. Date not established.
summary: Commentator on the Sātvata Saṃhitā.

name: Ālekhana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 6.5.17).

name: Allama Prabhu
summary: Allama Prabhu (Prabhudēva), the mystic of the void (śūnya, bayalu) whose enigmatic vacanas, signed Guhēśvara, test every attainment; in the Śūnyasampādane he presides over the Anubhava Maṇṭapa on the 'throne of the void' and examines Basava, Cennabasava, Siddharāma, Akka Mahādēvi, Muktāyakka and Gorakṣa.

realization_account.text: Harihara: a temple drummer of Baḷḷigāve who, grieving the death of Kāmalate, came upon a buried shrine where the yogi Animiṣa placed a liṅga in his hand and passed away, and he awoke. Cāmarasa: Śiva's own descent, unmoved by Māyā sent by Pārvatī, whose body passes untouched by Gorakṣa's sword. He ended in Kadaḷi at Śrīśaila, merging into the liṅga.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U28 contribution: HYP 1.8 names 'Allama' and 'Prabhudeva' among the Mahāsiddhas — possibly the Vīraśaiva saint Allama Prabhu counted twice under two names; identification not settled; the text says these Siddhas broke the staff of time by the power of haṭha and roam the universe (HYP 1.9).

name: Amalānanda
summary: Author of the Vedāntakalpataru on the Bhāmatī and of the Śāstradarpaṇa; 13th-century Advaitin at the Yādava court.

name: Amarnīti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.

realization_account.text: A merchant who gave loincloths to devotees; a loincloth left with him by Śiva disguised as a celibate vanished, and he offered its weight in cloth, then all his wealth — the scale balanced only when he, his wife and son climbed on it, and they were taken to Śiva's world.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ambapālī
summary: The courtesan of Vesālī who gave the Buddha her mango grove (DN 16) and later, as a nun, reflected on her ageing body (Thig 13.1).

name: Ambigara Cauḍayya
summary: The ferryman śaraṇa whose vacanas, signed with his own name, attack hypocrisy, ritualism and the pride of learning.

name: Amitābha / Amitāyus
summary: The buddha of Immeasurable Light and Life who presides over Sukhāvatī in the west; as the monk Dharmākara he made the vows (48 in T360) to receive all who call on him.
alt_names: Jin jippō mugekō nyorai 尽十方無碍光如来

realization_account.text: Awakened ten kalpas ago (Smaller & Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha)
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (as a figure of the sūtras)

notes: U43 contribution: in the Sanskrit Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha (GRETIL, Fujita) the vows number 47; Tanluan praises twelve names of his light; Shinran calls him the Tathāgata of Unhindered Light filling the ten directions; to Ryōnin he is said to have revealed the interfusing nenbutsu (1117).

name: Amitacākarar
summary: Jain prosodist, author of the Yāpparuṅkalam and Yāpparuṅkalakkārikai (11th c.).

name: Amitagati (II)
summary: Digambara author of the Yogasāraprābhṛta, the Subhāṣitaratnasaṃdoha and (by tradition) the Sāmāyikapāṭha.

name: Amoghavajra
summary: Esoteric master and translator (705-774) in Tang China who re-translated the Humane Kings sūtra and the Adhyardhaśatikā and many dhāraṇī texts.
alt_summary: U44 contribution: disciple of Vajrabodhi (705–774), translator of the first part of the Tattvasaṃgraha and of many kriyā texts into Chinese.

name: Amṛtānandanātha Sarasvatī (of Devīpuram)
summary: 20th-c. Śrīvidyā teacher who founded the Devīpuram temple in Andhra with a walk-in Śrī Meru, and taught Śrīvidyā worship widely, including to women and non-Brahmins.

name: Amṛtacandra
summary: The great Digambara commentator on Kundakunda (Ātmakhyāti on the Samayasāra, Tattvapradīpikā on the Pravacanasāra, Samayavyākhyā on the Pañcāstikāya), author of the Samayasāra-kalaśa verses, the lay-conduct Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya and the Tattvārthasāra.
alt_summary: Digambara commentator whose Ātmakhyāti (with its kalaśa verses) made Kundakunda's Samayasāra the charter of the niścaya-centred path; also author of the Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya and commentaries on the Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya.

name: Amṛtānanda
summary: Disciple of Puṇyānanda, author of the Dīpikā on the Yoginīhṛdaya (and, by tradition, the Saubhāgyasudhodaya); he explains Tripurā as the fusion of light and self-awareness.

name: Amyé Zhab Ngawang Kunga Sönam
summary: Sakya throne-holder and prolific historian of the Khön family, the Lamdre and the Sakya tantric cycles.
notes: Included as the historian of the Sakya; details recalled with low confidence.

name: Anagārika Munindra
summary: Indian Bengali Barua lay teacher (1915–2003) trained with Mahāsi Sayadaw, who taught at Bodh Gaya and influenced the first Western insight teachers.

name: Anand Swarup (Sahabji Maharaj)
summary: Founder of the Dayalbagh colony at Agra (1915), joining Radhasoami practice with industry, education and community life.

name: Ānanda
summary: Named in MN 118:1 among the well-known senior disciples present at Sāvatthī.

checks.note: Level not raised (entities are not promoted by the spot-check). By code: every linked id resolves in data/ or these shards; no restricted flag; no modern/psychological/health wording found. Content not read line by line by J.

alt_summary: The Buddha's cousin and personal attendant for twenty-five years, foremost in learning, memory, attentiveness and service; interceded for women's going forth (Cv 10.1); recited the Dhamma at the First Council; many suttas are his teaching (MN 52, MN 108, SN 22.83, AN 4.170).
In the Chan account the second patriarch, who received the Dharma from Mahākāśyapa (the 'knock down the flagpole' exchange, Wumenguan case 22). (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)

realization_account.text: Attained arahantship during the night before the First Council, as he was lying down, before his head reached the pillow (Cullavagga 11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)
alt_notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 2.

name: Ānanda (author of the Mūlaṭīkā)
summary: The elder credited with the root sub-commentary on the Abhidhamma commentaries.

name: Ānanda (father of Somānanda)
summary: Son of Aruṇāditya and father of Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.120).
notes: Id disambiguated from tch:ananda (the Buddha's attendant).

name: Ānanda (lay disciple)
summary: A householder of Vāṇijagrāma, the first of the ten lay disciples of the Upāsakadaśā, who took the twelve lay vows and the eleven pratimās, gained clairvoyance (avadhi-jñāna) and died in peace; when Gautama doubted the extent of his clairvoyance, Mahāvīra sent Gautama to apologize to the layman.

name: Ānandabhaṭṭa (Bhaṭṭānanda)
summary: Author of the Vijñānakaumudī on the Vijñāna Bhairava; its opening honours Somānanda, Bhūtirāja, Utpala, Lakṣmaṇagupta and Abhinavagupta.

name: Ānandabodha (Bhaṭṭāraka)
summary: Dialectical Advaitin, author of the Nyāyamakaranda (and the Nyāyadīpāvalī and Pramāṇamālā).

name: Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Tātparyaprakāśa commentary on the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

evidence: local:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/vedAnta/valmiki/ and unknown_Anandabodhendra/ (Yogavāsiṣṭha vulgate with Tātparyaprakāśa, Nirṇaya Sāgara ed.; Muktabodha M00335-M00339, M00345)
checks.note: The Tātparyaprakāśa's final colophon names Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī and dates completion to Śaka 1766 (c. 1844 CE); Dasgupta puts him in the 19th c. The entry gives no dating; one could be added: 19th c., c. 1844.

name: Ānandagarbha
summary: Great exegete of the yoga tantras (c. 9th c.), author of the Tattvālokakarī on the Tattvasaṃgraha and of works on the Sarvadurgatipariśodhana.

name: Ānandaghana
summary: Śvetāmbara (Tapā Gaccha) monk who became a wandering mystic poet; author of the Covīsī hymns to the Tīrthaṅkaras and of the Bahottarī padas. He sings the soul's love for the Jina, dismisses sectarian dispute and treats the six darśanas as limbs of the Jina. The tradition identifies him with the monk Lābhānanda, says he lived and died at Meṛtā, and that Yaśovijaya sought him out and praised him.

name: Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna)
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on many of Śaṅkara's works, including the Gītābhāṣya.

checks.note: Confirmed (13th c.; = Ānandajñāna).

alt_summary: 13th-century glossator of nearly all of Śaṅkara's commentaries (Nyāyanirṇaya on the BSBh; ṭīkās on the Upaniṣad and Gītā bhāṣyas) and of Sureśvara's Vārttika; his glosses name Bhartṛprapañca as the opponent refuted there.

name: Ānandavardhana
summary: Kashmiri poet-theorist, author of the Dhvanyāloka, who established suggestion (dhvani) as the soul of poetry and rasa-dhvani as its highest form; he named śānta the principal rasa of the Mahābhārata.

name: Anaṅgapa

realization_account.text: A handsome man vain of his looks, taught to see the body as illusory. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 81): Saṃsāra has no essence; in this rainbow-like body, by ignorance, clinging and pride, one holds poison as bliss; when the poison-disease of clinging is cleansed, saṃsāra itself is the dharmakāya.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 81 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A handsome man vain of his looks, taught to see the body as illusory.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Anaṅgavajra
summary: Author of the Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi; disciple of Padmavajra per the siddhi-text lineage.

name: Ananta Daivajña
summary: Astrologer of a family settled at Kāśī, father of Nīlakaṇṭha and Rāma Daivajña (MC 1.2 names Rāma as Ananta's son).

name: Anantadās
summary: Rāmānandī hagiographer (disciple in the line of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī) who wrote the Paracaīs of Kabīr, Raidās, Pīpā, Nāmdev and others.

name: Anantadeva (author of the Padacandrikā)
summary: Author of the Padacandrikā, a short commentary on the Yoga Sūtra dedicated to Śiva.
notes: Whether he is identical with other authors named Anantadeva (e.g. the 17th-c. Mīmāṃsaka) is not established here; id disambiguated for that reason.

name: Anantāḻvāṉ
summary: Disciple of Rāmānuja sent to Tirumala to maintain a flower garden for Veṅkaṭeśvara.

name: Anantānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples, through whom the Galtā line (Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī) descends.

name: Anantanātha
summary: The fourteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the falcon (śyena) in Śvetāmbara lists; the porcupine in Digambara lists. Parents: Siṃhasena and Suyaśā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fourteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Anantārya
summary: Author of the Sanskrit hagiography Prapannāmṛtam (Anantācārya; distinct from Prativādi Bhayaṅkaram Aṇṇaṉ).

name: Anantaśaktipāda
summary: Commentator on the Vātūlanāthasūtra.

name: Anasūyā
summary: Ascetic wife of the sage Atri, honoured for her austerities, who teaches Sītā the dharma of the devoted wife (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Anāthapiṇḍika
summary: The merchant Sudatta of Sāvatthī who bought Jeta's Grove for the Saṅgha; foremost lay donor; instructed on his deathbed by Sāriputta (MN 143).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Anavamadarśī (Saṅgharāja)
summary: Sri Lankan monk to whom the Daivajñakāmadhenu, a Sanskrit manual of jyotiṣa, is ascribed.

name: Āṉāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.

realization_account.text: A cowherd who played the five-syllable mantra on his flute; Śiva appeared and took him to his world with his music.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Āṇṭāḷ
summary: The woman among the Āḻvārs: author of the Tiruppāvai, the thirty verses of the Mārkaḻi vow sung across South India, and the Nācciyār Tirumoḻi of bridal longing for Kṛṣṇa. She wore the Lord's garland before offering it and vowed to marry only the Lord; the tradition says she was wedded to Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam.
alt_names: Cūṭikkoṭutta Nācciyār ('the lady who gave after wearing')

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE (astronomical readings of Tiruppāvai 13 give dates in the 8th–9th c.)

realization_account.text: Found as an infant under a tulasī plant in Periyāḻvār's garden; as a girl she wore the garlands meant for the Lord and looked at herself in a well to see if she was a fit bride. Her father, discovering this, did not offer that garland; the Lord told him in a dream that he wanted only garlands she had worn. Refusing any mortal bridegroom, she was taken in bridal procession to Śrīraṅgam at the Lord's command and entered the image of Raṅganātha.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Held to be Bhūdevī (the Earth) descended; hence some lists omit her from the Āḻvārs as not a human soul. Some modern scholars have suggested Periyāḻvār composed in her name; the tradition rejects this.

name: Aṅgir
summary: Link in the Muṇḍaka's line: received brahmavidyā from Atharvan and taught Satyavāha Bhāradvāja (MuU 1.1.2).

checks.note: Located: MuU 1.1.2 ('atharvā tāṃ purovācāṅgire brahmavidyām').

name: Aṅgiras (teacher of Śaunaka)
summary: Teacher of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: answers Śaunaka's question 'by knowing what is all this known?' with the higher and lower knowledge (MuU 1.1.3-5); 'this truth the seer Aṅgiras declared of old' (MuU 3.2.11).
notes: Whether tradition identifies him with the Ṛgvedic seer-family ancestor Aṅgiras is not asserted here.

queries: Atharvangirasah Atharvaveda atharvan auspicious bhesaja angiras hostile abhicara
checks.note: Confirmed: the AV's oldest name Atharvāṅgirasaḥ (AVŚ 10.7.20); auspicious/appeasing portions ascribed to the Atharvans, the terrible to the Aṅgirases.
Located: MuU 1.1.3-5 (Śaunaka approaches Aṅgiras) and 3.2.11 ('tad etat satyam ṛṣir aṅgirāḥ purovāca').

alt_summary: Eponymous ancestor of the Āṅgirasa priests; the Atharvaveda is 'the Atharvans and the Aṅgirases' (Atharvāṅgirasaḥ), the aṅgiras hymns being traditionally the fierce (ābhicārika) and the atharvan hymns the auspicious (bheṣaja) portion.
alt_notes: The division of the Atharvaveda into atharvan (auspicious) and āṅgirasa (fierce) portions is a traditional and scholarly account recalled with moderate confidence. The Aṅgiras who teaches Śaunaka in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad is a separate figure in U03's scope.

name: Aṅgulimāla
summary: A murderer who wore a garland of fingers, stopped by the Buddha ('I have stopped, you stop'), who went forth and became an arahant; his act of truth for a woman in labour is used as a paritta (MN 86; Thag 16.8).

name: Animiṣayya
summary: The 'unblinking' yogi who, in Harihara's account, placed the liṅga in Allama's hand in a buried shrine and passed away, awakening him.

name: Aniruddha (Sāṃkhya commentator)
summary: Author of the earliest known commentary (vṛtti) on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra.

name: Aniruddhadeva
summary: Founder of the Māyāmarā (Moāmoriyā) sattra in the Kāla saṃhati line, whose followers later rose against the Ahom state.

name: Annamācārya (Tāḷḷapāka Annamayya)
summary: Telugu singer-saint of Tirumala (1408–1503 by tradition), a Śrīvaiṣṇava initiate, who composed thousands of saṅkīrtanas to Veṅkaṭeśvara preserved on copper plates.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: the Telugu singer-saint of Tirumala whose thousands of saṅkīrtanas to Veṅkaṭeśvara are among the earliest compositions in the pallavi–caraṇa song form.

name: Annambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkasaṅgraha and its Dīpikā, the most widely used primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, written 'for the easy understanding of beginners'; tradition makes him a scholar from the Andhra country who worked in Vārāṇasī.

name: Anurādha
summary: A monk questioned by wanderers about the Tathāgata after death (SN 22.86; SN 44.2).

name: Anuruddha
summary: Named in MN 118:1 among the well-known senior disciples present at Sāvatthī.

checks.note: Level not raised (entities are not promoted by the spot-check). By code: every linked id resolves in data/ or these shards; no restricted flag; no modern/psychological/health wording found. Content not read line by line by J.

alt_summary: The Buddha's Sakyan cousin, foremost in the divine eye; practised with Nandiya and Kimbila (MN 31, MN 128); his eight thoughts of a great person (AN 8.30); present at the Buddha's parinibbāna (DN 16) and, by commentarial account, entrusted with the Aṅguttara.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists). Distinct from the later Abhidhamma author tch:anuruddha-acariya.

name: Anuruddha (ācariya)

scholarly.text: c. 10th–12th c. (contested; estimates range from the 8th to the 12th c.)

summary: Author of the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha, the Nāmarūpapariccheda and (perhaps) the Paramatthavinicchaya.

name: Āpadeva
summary: Son of Anantadeva; author of the Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa ('Āpadevī'), a standard introduction to Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā that dedicates dharma to Govinda.

name: Apālā Ātreyī
summary: ṛṣikā of RV 8.91: a maiden who found soma on her way to the water, offered it to Indra and was freed by him of a skin affliction.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'ātreyī apālā'; 8.91.1–7 read (see tea:rgveda:8.91).

name: Apāntaratamas
summary: Born of Nārāyaṇa's word, the teacher of the Vedas (vedācārya), called by some Prācīnagarbha; Vyāsa says he himself was Apāntaratamas in a former birth (12.337.38–61).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Aparājitasūri
summary: Author of the Vijayodayā commentary on the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā, generally regarded as a Yāpanīya.

name: Aparakuśika
summary: Number 10 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Aparārka (Aparāditya)
summary: Śilāhāra king and commentator on Yājñavalkya.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry. The Śilāhāra king and commentator on Yājñavalkya is confirmed. Wikipedia puts Aparāditya I's reign at 1170–1197 CE, later than the entry's 1100–1150; still 12th c. Partial.

name: Āpastamba
summary: Founder (sūtrakāra) of the Āpastamba branch of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda, to whom its whole Kalpasūtra is ascribed.

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE for the Dharmasūtra (estimates vary)

checks.note: Confirmed: eponymous sūtrakāra of the Āpastamba branch; the whole Kalpasūtra (30 praśnas) is ascribed to him. The Dharmasūtra date agrees with Olivelle and Kane (see src:apastamba-dharmasutra).

name: Appaṇṇācārya
summary: Disciple of Rāghavendra Tīrtha to whom the tradition ascribes the Rāghavendra-stotra recited by devotees.

name: Appar (Tirunāvukkaracar)
summary: One of the three Tēvāram poets (Tirumuṟai 4–6), a former Jain monk (Tarumacēṉar) who returned to Śaivism; exemplar of the servant's path (dāsa-mārga, caryā); famed for temple service (clearing the temple grounds) and hymns of defiance and surrender.

tradition.text: lived to 81 (tradition)

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of the Pallava Mahendravarman I (r. c. 600–630)

realization_account.text: Raised a Śaiva and cared for by his sister Tilakavati, he became a Jain monk; struck by an incurable colic he returned to Tilakavati at Tiruvatikai, received the sacred ash, and sang his first hymn, and the pain left him. The Jain-influenced Pallava king had him shut in a lime-kiln, fed poison, trampled by an elephant and thrown into the sea tied to a stone; he survived each by singing Śiva's names, floated ashore, and the king turned Śaiva. He died at Tiruppukalūr merging with Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Appayya Dīkṣita
summary: 16th-c. polymath of Adaippalam (Tamil country) who revived Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Vedānta in the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā while holding Advaita as final (Śivādvaitanirṇaya).

realization_account.text: Tradition says the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā was written under the patronage of Cinna Bomma of Vellore.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Polymath of Tamil Nadu, author of the Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha, the Kalpataruparimala (completing the Bhāmatī chain), the Nyāyarakṣāmaṇi, works in Mīmāṃsā and poetics, and the Śivārkamaṇidīpikā on Śrīkaṇṭha's Śaiva Vedānta; an Advaitin devoted to Śiva.
For Mīmāṃsā: author of the Vidhirasāyana (on the kinds of injunction) and the Upakramaparākrama (on the priority of the opening statement), among other works.

name: Appūti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, without having met Appar, named his sons, water-sheds and alms-houses after him; when Appar visited, a son died of snakebite and the parents hid it to feed their guest; Appar sang and the boy revived.

name: Aranātha
summary: The eighteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the nandyāvarta diagram in Śvetāmbara lists; the fish in Digambara lists. Parents: Sudarśana and Devī (Mitrā). Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the seventh world-emperor.

tradition.text: the eighteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Arcaṭa
summary: Commentator on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu.

name: Ārdraka (Ārdrakakumāra)
summary: A prince, in the tradition from a distant land, who became a monk of Mahāvīra and on his way to him debated Gośāla, Buddhists, brāhmaṇas, Vedāntin (ekadaṇḍin) ascetics and elephant-killing hermits (Sūtrakṛtāṅga 2.6).

name: Arivāṭṭāya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He offered red rice, greens and tender mango daily; impoverished and faint, he stumbled and the offering fell into a crack in the earth, and he began to cut his throat with a sickle (arivāḷ) — Śiva's hand rose from the crack to stop him.

name: Arjuna (Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The third Pāṇḍava, the archer, whose refusal to fight his kinsmen occasions the Gītā; he declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and takes refuge in him (2.7), receives the divine eye and the vision of the universal form (11.8ff), and after the war asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the teaching (Anugītā 14.16).

alt_summary: Son of Pāṇḍu and Kuntī, bearer of the bow Gāṇḍīva and the conch Devadatta (1.15, 1.30); the disciple of the Gītā. In ch. 1–3 he sees his kin in both armies, is overcome by compassion and despondency, argues against the battle and says he will not fight (1.28–2.9), declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple (2.7), and asks about the one of steady wisdom (2.54), why action is urged if understanding is superior (3.1–2), and what drives a person to sin (3.36).

The addressee of BhG 4–6 (so called by the vocatives Pārtha, Kaunteya, Bhārata, Parantapa, Mahābāho, Dhanañjaya, Pāṇḍava, Kurusattama, Kurunandana). He receives the ancient yoga as the Lord's devotee and friend (4.3); he asks how the Lord could have taught Vivasvat (4.4), which is better, renunciation or yoga (5.1), how the restless mind can be steadied (6.33–34), and what becomes of one who falls from yoga (6.37–39).
In BhG 7–9 the addressee; he asks the seven questions of 8.1–2 (Brahman, adhyātma, karma, adhibhūta, adhidaiva, adhiyajña, knowing the Lord at death) and is told to remember Kṛṣṇa and fight (8.7).

In BhG 10–12 he acknowledges Kṛṣṇa as the supreme brahman (10.12), asks to hear his manifestations and to see his sovereign form (10.16–18, 11.3–4), receives the divine eye, describes and praises the universal form in fear and wonder (11.15–46), asks forgiveness for past familiarity (11.41–42), and asks which worshippers know yoga best (12.1); named by the Lord among his manifestations ('Dhanañjaya among the Pāṇḍavas', 10.37).

Kṛṣṇa's disciple and interlocutor in the Bhagavad Gītā. In chapters 13–15 he asks about prakṛti and puruṣa, the field and its knower, knowledge and the knowable (13.1, in editions with that verse) and about the marks, conduct and means of the one beyond the guṇas (14.21); he is addressed as Kaunteya, Bhārata, Bharatarṣabha, Mahābāhu, Anagha, Pāṇḍava and Kurunandana.

name: Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga
summary: Questions Yājñavalkya on the eight graspers and over-graspers and on what remains of a person at death; they go aside and speak of karma (BAU 3.2).

checks.note: Located: BĀU 3.2.1-13 ('jāratkārava ārtabhāgaḥ'; 'karma haiva tad ūcatuḥ', 3.2.13).

name: Aruḷāḷa Perumāḷ Emperumāṉār
summary: Formerly the Advaita renouncer Yajñamūrti who, the tradition says, debated Rāmānuja for eighteen days, conceded, and became his disciple; author of the Tamil Jñānasāram and Prameyasāram.

name: Ārumuka Nāvalar
summary: Jaffna Śaiva reformer and scholar: prose catechisms of Śaiva Siddhānta, printed editions of Tamil Śaiva texts, schools, and polemic against Christian missionaries.

name: Aruṇadatta
summary: Author of the Sarvāṅgasundarā on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya.

name: Aruṇāditya
summary: Son of Varṣāditya in Somānanda's lineage (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.119).

name: Aruṇanti Civācāriyār
summary: Author of the Civañāṉa Cittiyār and Irupā Irupatu; a learned brahmin, family preceptor of Meykaṇṭār's father, who became Meykaṇṭār's chief disciple.

name: Ārya Vimuktisena
summary: Earliest known commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.

name: Āryabhaṭa
summary: Author of the Āryabhaṭīya, written when he was 23 in the year 3600 of the Kali age (499 CE) and honoured at Kusumapura. He taught the equal quarters of the yuga, the rotation of the earth (the boat simile), eclipses by the earth's shadow and the moon, and an alphabetic numeral notation; he opens by bowing to Ka, the supreme Brahman, and says his knowledge came by Brahmā's grace. His school (āryapakṣa) dominated South India and Kerala; Brahmagupta criticized him for departing from the smṛti.

name: Āryadeva
alt_names: Kāṇadeva / Āryadeva (Jiana Tipo 迦那提婆)

realization_account.text: The Chinese Life tells that he offered his own eye to a great statue of Maheśvara, defeated the teachers of other schools in debate, and was killed by a disciple of a defeated opponent, whom he forgave while dying, teaching that there is no one who kills and no one who is killed. Tibetan accounts make him the adopted son of a Sinhalese king, born from a lotus, who defeated the Śaiva debater Mātṛceṭa at Nālandā and converted him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The tantric works under this name (e.g. Caryāmelāpakapradīpa) are by a later Āryadeva (scholarly account).
summary: Nāgārjuna's principal disciple, author of the Four Hundred Verses (Catuḥśataka), which joins the bodhisattva's practice to the refutation of permanent entities, the self and extreme views.
alt_summary: Fifteenth patriarch in the Chan list, 'the one-eyed Deva'. (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)
alt_notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 15.

name: Āryadeva the Brahmin (bram ze Ārya de ba)
summary: An Indian master to whom the Chöd tradition attributes the Grand Poem on the Perfection of Wisdom; treated as an Indian source of Chöd. Distinct from Nāgārjuna's disciple Āryadeva in most accounts (identity uncertain).

name: Karṇaripa (Āryadeva)

realization_account.text: Born from a lotus in Siṃhala, disciple of Nāgārjuna at Nālandā; gave one of his eyes to a woman (or tree-goddess) who asked for it — hence 'the one-eyed'; defeated non-Buddhist debaters; the tradition identifies him with the Madhyamaka Āryadeva and the author of the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 18): All buddhas of the three times are one in essence; realized, that is one's own mind by nature; wishing to realize it, leave it uncontrived just as it is; habituated to it, yoga becomes manifest.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 18 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Born from a lotus in Siṃhala, disciple of Nāgārjuna at Nālandā; gave one of his eyes to a woman (or tree-goddess) who asked for it — hence 'the one-eyed'; defeated non-Buddhist debaters; the tradition identifies him with the Madhyamaka Āryadeva and the author of the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Āryarakṣita
summary: Elder credited with dividing the teaching into four anuyogas (conduct, narrative, calculation, substance) and with the Anuyogadvāra; the Trairāśika schism of Rohagupta and the Goṣṭhāmāhila schism are placed in his time.

name: Āryarakṣitasūri (founder of the Añcala Gaccha)
summary: 12th-c. founder of the Añcala (Vidhipakṣa) Gaccha; not the ancient Āryarakṣita.

name: Siṃha / Āryasiṃha (Shizi 師子)

name: Āryaśūra
summary: Indian poet, author of the Jātakamālā, one of the six Kadam texts.

name: Paṇḍita Āśādhara
summary: Digambara lay scholar of Malwa, author of the Sāgāra- and Anagāra-dharmāmṛta.

name: Asahara Saichi
summary: Clog-maker of Iwami counted among the myōkōnin, who wrote thousands of verses of the joy and wretchedness of the self embraced by Amida ('Namu Amida Butsu').

name: Asaṅga

tradition.text: lived 150 years (Tibetan histories); prophesied in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa

realization_account.text: Born in Puruṣapura as eldest of three brothers of a brahmin (Kauśika) family, he first ordained in the Mahīśāsaka (Paramārtha's account); dissatisfied with his understanding of emptiness, he meditated for twelve years in a cave, leaving three times in despair and each time turning back at a sign of perseverance; when compassion for a maggot-ridden dog finally opened his vision, Maitreya appeared and taught him in Tuṣita. He then converted his brother Vasubandhu.

summary: Founder, with his half-brother Vasubandhu, of the Yogācāra school: author of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha and Abhidharmasamuccaya and, for the Tibetans, compiler of the Yogācārabhūmi and receiver of the Maitreya texts; in Tibetan tradition the founder of the 'lineage of vast conduct'.

name: Āśmarathya
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra on a ritual detail of the new-moon rite (MS 6.5.16); also cited in the Brahma Sūtra.
alt_summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.20; 1.2.29): the self's identity with Brahman is stated in view of the promise that by knowing one all is known — later read as an early difference-and-non-difference view.

Early Vedāntin named in the Brahma Sūtras (1.2.29; 1.4.20). On the self and Brahman he held that the Upaniṣads' promise ('by knowing one, all is known') indicates non-difference; Śaṅkara glosses his view as difference-and-non-difference, like sparks and fire.
notes: Known only from the Brahma Sūtra and its commentators.

name: Asoka
summary: Maurya emperor whose edicts promote Dhamma and name Buddhist texts (Bairāṭ/Bhabru edict); in the Theravāda chronicles patron of the Third Council and father of Mahinda and Saṅghamittā.

tradition.text: consecrated 218 years after the parinibbāna

alt_summary: U33 contribution: Maurya emperor whose edicts pair brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas, urge honour to all sects, name the Ājīvikas among the orders cared for, and who dedicated caves in the Barābar hills to the Ājīvikas. Buddhist legend (Divyāvadāna) also says an Ājīvika at his father's court foretold his kingship.

name: Assaji
summary: One of the five monks; his bearing on alms round drew Sāriputta, to whom he spoke the verse 'ye dhammā hetuppabhavā' (Vin Mv 1.23).

name: Assalāyana

name: Aṣṭāvakra

name: Āśudhīra

His dispassion arose from the presence of the supreme sage (Yuktidīpikā on SK 43).

summary: Kapila's disciple and Pañcaśikha's teacher (SK 70). The commentaries describe him as a brahmin of the Āsuri clan who renounced householder life after Kapila's repeated questioning. A person named Āsuri also appears in Vedic ritual literature; identity with the Sāṃkhya Āsuri is uncertain.

name: Aśvala

name: Āśvalāyana

summary: King of the Kekayas who teaches five great householders and Uddālaka Āruṇi the vaiśvānara self as a whole, correcting each one's partial view (ChU 5.11-18); he claims there is no thief, miser, drunkard, man without a sacred fire, ignorant or adulterer in his kingdom (ChU 5.11.5).

alt_summary: King who taught the Vaiśvānara self to brāhmaṇa householders led by Aruṇa Aupaveśi (ŚB 10.6.1; ChU 5.11–18).

name: Aśvatthāman
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the leaders of his (the Kaurava) army (1.8).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.8.

name: The Aśvins
summary: The twin physicians of the gods (Nāsatyas, Dasras), who learnt Āyurveda from Prajāpati and taught it to Indra; they rejoined the head of the sacrifice cut off by Rudra, restored Pūṣan's teeth, Bhaga's eyes and Indra's arm, cured the Moon of consumption and made the aged Cyavana young (Su Sū 1.17; Ca Ci 1.4.41-44; Bhāvaprakāśa Pūrva 1.8-13).

name: Atharvan
summary: Eldest son of Brahmā, who received brahmavidyā and passed it to Aṅgir (MuU 1.1.1-2).

Located: MuU 1.1.1-2.

Located as a speaker in the Atharvan Mahā Upaniṣad (e-text no. 115), in the Śāṇḍilya and in the Atharvaśikhā. A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

U04 contribution: teaches Śāṇḍilya the eight-limbed yoga and brahmavidyā (Śāṇḍilya) and teaches Pippalāda, Aṅgiras and Sanatkumāra the meditation on Oṃ (Atharvaśikhā); speaker of the short Mahā Upaniṣad.

name: Atipatta Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Head of a fishing community who released the first fish of every catch for Śiva; in lean days he caught only one fish and released it, and when a golden fish set with gems came into his net he released that too; Śiva appeared.

name: Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna
summary: Bengali prince-turned-monk, scholar of Vikramaśīla, who received bodhicitta and mind-training above all from Serlingpa (Dharmakīrti of Suvarṇadvīpa, with whom the tradition says he spent twelve years) and also from Dharmarakṣita and Maitrīyogin; invited to Tibet by the Ngari kings Yeshe Ö and Jangchub Ö, he arrived in 1042, wrote the Lamp for the Path at Tholing, met Dromtönpa and died at Nyethang in 1054; founder of the Kadam.
