Candragarbha (name as a prince, in the tradition's account)

realization_account.text: Tārā foretold that going to Tibet would shorten his life but greatly benefit beings; he went nonetheless. The Kadam regard him as holding the complete lineages of the profound view and the vast conduct.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: U40 and U44 also define tch:atisa; this is the Kadam contribution.
alt_summary: U40 contribution: Vikramaśīla master who held Candrakīrti's Madhyamaka to be the correct view and taught it in Tibet in the Satyadvayāvatāra and Madhyamakopadeśa.

U44 contribution: Bengali master of Vikramaśīla (982–1054) who received tantric teachings from many siddhas (Avadhūtipa, Ḍombi, Nāropa per accounts); in the Bodhipathapradīpa (vv. 64–67) he permits the master's consecration but, citing the Ādibuddha tantra, forbids the secret and wisdom consecrations to celibates.

name: Ācārya Ātmārām (Sthānakavāsī)
summary: Punjabi Sthānakavāsī scholar (1882–1962), first ācārya of the united Śramaṇa Saṅgha (1952), translator and commentator of Āgamas.

name: Vijayānandasūri (Ātmārām)
summary: Punjabi Sthānakavāsī monk (1837–1896) who became a Mūrtipūjaka and revived the Śvetāmbara image-worshipping order in Punjab; he sent Virchand Gandhi to the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions.

name: Ātmasukha
summary: Recalled as author of the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā on the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

checks.note: Colophon: 'uttamasukhapūjyapādaśiṣyaśrīmadātmasukhaviracitāyāṃ vāsiṣṭhacandrikāyām'. Ātmasukha is the author and the pupil of Uttamasukha; his existence is no longer merely recalled.

name: Ātreya (of the Brahma Sūtras)
summary: Early teacher cited in BS 3.4.44: the fruit of meditations connected with ritual goes to the sacrificer (as owner), against Auḍulomi's view that it goes to the priest.

name: Ātreya (Mīmāṃsā teacher)
notes: Disambiguated from other Ātreyas (e.g. of Āyurveda).
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: the fruit stated for a rite is real, not mere praise (MS 4.3.18); only the three higher varṇas are eligible because the setting-up of the fires names only them (MS 6.1.26).

name: Punarvasu Ātreya
summary: The teacher of the Caraka Saṃhitā: out of friendliness and compassion for all beings he taught Āyurveda to six disciples — Agniveśa, Bhela, Jatūkarṇa, Parāśara, Hārīta and Kṣārapāṇi (Ca Sū 1.30-31) — and in every chapter 'thus spoke the venerable Ātreya'. He presides over the debates of the sages and closes them (Sū 12.13, 25.26-29, 26.9).
places: Kāmpilya in Pañcāla, by the Gaṅgā (Ca Vi 3.3)
notes: Caraka has Ātreya learn from Bharadvāja (implied by Sū 1.26-30); the Bhāvaprakāśa has Ātreya go to Indra himself. Bhikṣu Ātreya of Ca Sū 25.24 is a different speaker. Whether Kṛṣṇātreya (a śālākya authority in later sources) is the same person is disputed.

name: Ātreya Rāmānuja
summary: Kiḍāmbi Appuḷḷār, maternal uncle and teacher of Vedānta Deśika, disciple of Naḍādūr Ammāḷ; the Nyāyakuliśa is attributed to him.

name: Atri
summary: Atri Bhauma, founder of the Ātreya family whose hymns form Ṛgveda book 5 (e.g. 5.85, Varuṇa's great māyā); one of the seven seers of RV 10.137. Later tradition makes him husband of Anasūyā and father of Dattātreya.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header 5.85 'bhaumo 'triḥ'; seer of 10.137.4. Book 5 = Ātreyas. Later tradition (husband of Anasūyā, father of Dattātreya) confirmed by web sources.
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, yajnavalkya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
alt_summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Samūrtārcanādhikaraṇa.
Vedic seer who questions Yājñavalkya about Avimukta and the sacred thread (Jābāla 2, 5; Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad); father of Dattātreya.

name: Atri (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 11 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Auḍulomi
summary: Early Vedāntin cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.21; 3.4.45; 4.4.6): the soul is different from Brahman while embodied and becomes one with it on departing — an early form of difference-and-non-difference.
alt_summary: Early Vedāntin named in the Brahma Sūtras (1.4.21; 3.4.45; 4.4.6): the individual self becomes one with Brahman when it departs (in liberation), being different while bound; the liberated self exists as pure consciousness alone.

name: Audumbarāyaṇa
summary: An early authority quoted in Yāska's Nirukta (1.1) for the view that speech is 'permanent only in the sense-faculty' (indriya-nitya), read by later grammarians as an early form of the doctrine that the word is grasped as a whole in the mind.

name: Āulcānd

tradition.text: appeared c. 1694 (tradition); departed in the later 18th c.

realization_account.text: Caitanya, who had disappeared at Puri, reappeared in Bengal as Āulcānd to reveal the secret sahaja religion to the poor and low-caste.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The mysterious founder of the Kartābhajā, who appeared as a youth in a betel garden at Ulā (Nadia), was held to be Caitanya returned, wandered with twenty-two disciples, and chose Rāmśaraṇ Pāl as his successor.

name: Aupadhenava
summary: One of Suśruta's fellow students who approached Divodāsa Dhanvantari for the teaching (Su Sū 1.3).
notes: Later commentators cite tantras under some of these names (Aupadhenava, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata) — recalled, not checked.

name: Aupamanyava
summary: Early etymologist cited by Yāska, e.g. for 'ṛṣi from seeing: he saw the hymns' (Nirukta 2.11).

checks.note: Text-located: Nir 2.11 'stomān dadarśety aupamanyavaḥ' (also cited at Nir 1.1).

name: Aurabhra
summary: One of Suśruta's fellow students who approached Divodāsa Dhanvantari for the teaching (Su Sū 1.3).
notes: Later commentators cite tantras under some of these names (Aupadhenava, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata) — recalled, not checked.

name: Avaidyanāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the later 20th century.

name: Avalokitavrata
summary: Author of the vast sub-commentary on Bhāviveka's Prajñāpradīpa, a principal source on the history of the early Madhyamaka commentators and their opponents.

name: Avalokiteśvara
summary: The bodhisattva who, coursing in the deep perfection of wisdom, sees the five aggregates as empty and speaks the teaching to Śāriputra (Heart Sūtra 2.2-2.8).

checks.note: Entity read against the teachings it rests on and their segments: faithful; level not raised by J.

alt_summary: The bodhisattva of compassion: in Lotus ch. 25 he rescues all who call his name from fire, water, bandits and bondage and takes whatever form will teach them (33 forms); he speaks the Heart Sūtra; in the Kāraṇḍavyūha he empties the hells and gives the six-syllable mantra; attendant of Amitābha in Sukhāvatī; in the Gaṇḍavyūha a spiritual friend on Mount Potalaka; in the Śūraṅgama his penetration through hearing is chosen as best. Guanyin, Kannon, Chenrezig.

realization_account.text: A great bodhisattva of the tenth ground, or a buddha of the past (Zhengfa Ming) appearing as a bodhisattva; his realization is the penetration of hearing into the self-nature (Śūraṅgama juan 6)
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (as a figure of the sūtras)

notes: Gender: male in Indian and Tibetan iconography; female forms (Guanyin) prevalent in East Asia from c. 10th c.

name: Āvaṭya
summary: Sage, 'bearer of a body' (tanudhara), who questions Jaigīṣavya in YBh 3.18 about whether the happiness of contentment too belongs to suffering.

name: Aviddhakarṇa
summary: Early Naiyāyika known only from citations in Buddhist works (Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha and Kamalaśīla's commentary), among them arguments for Īśvara.
notes: Known only through opponents' reports; details unverified.
alt_summary: An author cited several times in Kamalaśīla's Pañjikā, including a 'Tattvaṭīkā'; later sources name him as a commentator on the Bṛhaspati Sūtra, while other passages show him arguing as a Naiyāyika. His affiliation is disputed.
alt_notes: Kamalaśīla's citations checked locally (TSP lines on atoms, inference, the two means of knowledge); the Cārvāka affiliation is not confirmed by those passages.

name: Auvaiyār (of the Vināyakar akaval)
summary: The poetess to whom the Vināyakar akaval, a Siddha-revered hymn of the inner yoga, is ascribed; several Tamil poetesses of different centuries bear the name.

name: Ayampula
summary: An Ājīvika lay follower of Sāvatthī who, in Bhagavatī 15, comes to ask the dying Gosāla a question and is answered in his delirium.

name: Ayāsya Āṅgirasa
summary: Identified with the breath in the mouth, the essence (rasa) of the limbs, in the udgītha passages (BAU 1.3.8, 1.3.19; ChU 1.2.12).

checks.note: Confirmed despite the low confidence. BĀU 1.3.8 and 1.3.19 ('so 'yāsya āṅgiraso 'ṅgānāṃ hi rasaḥ') and ChU 1.2.12 ('etam u evāyāsyaṃ manyante') identify him with the breath in the mouth. He also appears as a link in the vaṃśa at BĀU 2.6.3 and 4.6.3 ('ayāsyād āṅgirasād ayāsya āṅgirasa ābhūtes tvāṣṭrāt'), which the entry could add.

name: Āydakki Lakkamma
summary: Mārayya's wife, a vacanakāra remembered for sending back rice gathered beyond the day's need, teaching that kāyaka and dāsōha exclude hoarding.

name: Āydakki Mārayya
summary: The śaraṇa who lived by gleaning rice grains fallen in the market; his vacana declares that kāyaka is Kailāsa.

name: Aḻukaṇṇi (Aḻukaṇic cittar)
summary: Siddhar poet of forty stanzas in veiled imagery of the root, the six supports and the ninety-six principles, addressed to 'my Kaṇṇammā'; he tells how the guru came, showed his own form and burnt the supports and letters.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Nothing is recalled of his life. The name means 'weeping-eyed'; whether the poet is a man or a woman is not settled here.

name: Bābājī Caitanya
summary: The guru who initiated Tukārām in a dream, giving the mantra 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'; Tukārām names his line through Rāghava Caitanya and Keśava Caitanya.

name: Bādarāyaṇa

tradition.text: identical with Vyāsa, end of Dvāpara

notes: The identification with Vyāsa (tch:vyasa) is the tradition's; Śaṅkara refers to the sūtrakāra as Vyāsa in places. Scholars treat them as distinct.
summary: Author (tradition) or final redactor (scholarly) of the Brahma Sūtras; he states his own view by name at several points (e.g. BS 1.3.33, 3.4.1, 4.4.7, 4.4.12) against Jaimini, Bādari and others.
alt_notes: Identified with Vyāsa in Vedānta tradition; Mīmāṃsā contribution only here.
alt_summary: Cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra as an authority: the injunction is valid 'in Bādarāyaṇa's view' because it depends on nothing else (MS 1.1.5); women are eligible for rites because the class is meant (MS 6.1.8); also MS 5.2.19, 10.8.44, 11.1.63. Author of the Brahma Sūtra.

name: Bādari
summary: Early Mīmāṃsā teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: holds that only substances, qualities and purificatory acts are subsidiaries (MS 3.1.3) and that the injunctions are for all four varṇas (MS 6.1.27, a view rejected); also cited at MS 8.3.6 and in the Brahma Sūtra.
alt_summary: Early teacher cited in the Brahma Sūtras (1.2.30; 3.1.11; 4.3.7; 4.4.10) and in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra: the path of the gods leads to the conditioned (kārya) Brahman; the liberated has no body.

name: Baḍiśa Dhāmārgava
summary: Speaker: how vāyu, formless and unstable, is provoked and pacified through the body's condition (Ca Sū 12.7); eight tastes (Sū 26.8); the hands and feet form first (Śā 6.21).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Badulā Padma Ātā
summary: Disciple of Mādhavadeva counted among the founders of the Nikā saṃhati.
notes: Name and role to verify.

name: Bahiṇābāī
summary: Brahmin woman saint (1628–1700) who took Tukārām as guru in a dream, bore her husband's anger, and wrote an autobiography in abhaṅgas and the image of the saints as one temple with Tukārām its pinnacle.

name: Bāhiya Dārucīriya
summary: A bark-clothed ascetic of Suppāraka who received the brief teaching 'in the seen only the seen' on the road and was at once liberated; foremost in quick understanding (Ud 1.10).

realization_account.text: Liberated on hearing the brief teaching; died soon after (Ud 1.10).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara)
summary: Son of Ṛṣabha, who defeated his elder brother Bharata in single combat for the kingdom, then renounced in the moment of victory and stood motionless in meditation (kāyotsarga) for a year until creepers grew over him. Śvetāmbaras say his omniscience was delayed by pride until his sisters Brāhmī and Sundarī told him to 'get down from the elephant'; Digambaras say a lingering thought that he stood on Bharata's land delayed it. For Digambaras the first of this era to attain liberation. His 58-foot image (981 CE) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is anointed in the twelve-yearly Mahāmastakābhiṣeka.

realization_account.text: He stood a full year in body-abandonment; when the last obstacle (pride, or the thought of his brother's land) fell away he attained omniscience.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bāïsā
summary: Woman disciple who cared for Cakradhar; figures often in the Līḷācaritra.

name: Baiyun Shouduan 白雲守端
summary: Heir of Yangqi, teacher of Wuzu Fayan.

name: Baizhang Huaihai 百丈懷海
summary: Heir of Mazu, credited by the tradition with founding independent Chan monasteries and the monastic rule; 'a day without work, a day without food'; his fox kōan.

name: Bakhnā
summary: Disciple of Dādū and poet of the Dādū Panth.

name: Bāl Gaṅgādhar Tilak
summary: Scholar and political leader whose Gītā Rahasya (1915) argues that the Gītā teaches action (karma-yoga) by the enlightened rather than renunciation.

checks.note: Confirmed; 1856–1920.

notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Balabhadra
summary: 17th-century compiler of the Horāratna and the Hāyanaratna on Tājika.

name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Orissan scholar trained in Madhva's school who joined the Gauḍīyas; wrote the Govinda-bhāṣya (the school's Brahma Sūtra commentary), Prameyaratnāvalī, Siddhāntaratna and Gītābhūṣaṇa, defending the Gauḍīyas at Jaipur.

queries: Baladeva Vidyabhushana Gita Bhushana Govinda Bhashya
checks.note: Confirmed (d. 1768).

alt_summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Gītābhūṣaṇa (and the Govinda-bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra).

name: Bālakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Prameyaratnārṇava is attributed.

name: Balarām Hāḍi
summary: Founder of the Balarāmī sect of Meherpur, of the Hāḍi caste, venerated by his followers as God (Hāḍirām).

name: Bālarāma Udāsīna
summary: Modern scholar of the Udāsīna order to whom the Vidvattoṣiṇī on the Tattvakaumudī is ascribed.

name: Bali
summary: In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (5.22-29), the asura king who remembers his father Virocana's teaching on the realm beyond the worlds, inquires, and attains self-knowledge while continuing to rule.

checks.note: Located as described.
MU 5.22.17 'virocanasuto baḍiḥ'; Virocana's teaching 5.22.43; Śukra 5.25-26.

alt_summary: The defeated Daitya king who tells Indra that Time takes and gives all, and bears his fall without grief (12.216–218).

name: Ballālasena
summary: Sena king of Bengal who began the Adbhutasāgara, a digest of omens (1168), completed by his son Lakṣmaṇasena.

name: Bālnāth
summary: Nāth yogī associated with Tilla Jogian (Gorakh Ṭillā) in the Salt Range; in Wāris Shāh's Hīr he gives Rāñjhā the split-ear initiation.
notes: Distinct from the Himachali folk deity Bābā Bālaknāth (U59), with whom he is sometimes confused.

name: Bāmākhepā (Vāmākṣepā)
summary: Śākta 'mad saint' of the Tārāpīṭh cremation ground in Birbhum, devotee of Tārā, who lived as a child of the Mother, disregarding rules of purity; remembered for his miracles and for teaching by paradox.

realization_account.text: Taught by the ascetic Kailāspati Bābā at Tārāpīṭh, he had the vision of Tārā in the cremation ground and thereafter treated her as his mother.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bamda Gelek Gyatso ('ba' mda' dge legs rgya mtsho)
summary: Jonang scholar of Amdo, a prolific writer on Kālacakra and other-emptiness in the surviving eastern tradition.

name: Banārsīdās

realization_account.text: After studying the guṇasthānas with Rūpcand he says his understanding became balanced and he held niścaya and vyavahāra together (Ardhakathānaka).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Śrīmāl merchant-poet of Jaunpur and Agra (1587–c. 1643), founder figure of the Adhyātma movement; author of the Samayasāra Nāṭaka and of the Ardhakathānaka, the first autobiography in Hindi. Born into a Śvetāmbara (Kharatara) family, he turned to the Digambara Samayasāra; by his own account he first fell into disregard of conduct and was restored to balance by Rūpcand Pāṇḍe's teaching of the guṇasthānas.

name: Bankā
summary: Cokhāmeḷā's brother-in-law, a Mahār devotee-poet of the same circle.

name: Bankei Yōtaku 盤珪永琢

realization_account.text: Gravely ill after years of austerities, he spat a mass of black phlegm against a wall and at that moment realized that all things are perfectly resolved in the Unborn (Bankei's own account in his sermons).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Rinzai master who, after years of harsh practice and illness, realized that all things are resolved in the Unborn and taught in plain Japanese that everyone has the unborn buddha-mind.

name: Baozhi 寶誌
summary: Wonder-working monk at the Liang court who, in the tradition's account, told Emperor Wu that Bodhidharma was Avalokiteśvara transmitting the buddha-mind seal (Biyan lu case 1).

name: Bāpudeva Śāstrī
summary: Professor of astronomy at the Sanskrit College, Benares; worked on almanac (pañcāṅga) reform and wrote Sanskrit works on astronomy.

name: Bari Lotsawa Rinchen Drak
summary: Translator and second abbot of Sakya, Sachen's guardian-teacher, under whom the young Sachen did the Mañjuśrī retreat in which he received Parting from the Four Attachments.

name: Barku Vārṣṇa
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is sight (BAU 4.1.4); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 4.1.4 (Barku Vārṣṇa: sight is brahman).

name: Barom Darma Wangchuk
summary: Disciple of Gampopa, founder of the Barom Kagyu.

name: Baḍu Caṇḍīdās
summary: Bengali poet of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtana; the name 'Caṇḍīdās' is shared by several poets whose lyrics Caitanya loved and the Sahajiyās later claimed.

name: Basava
summary: Basava (Basavaṇṇa, Basaveśvara), minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala in Kalyāṇa, the central figure of the twelfth-century śaraṇa movement; his vacanas, signed Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, teach devotion, humility before devotees, work as worship, sharing, and the equality of all who wear the liṅga.

realization_account.text: Born to a brāhmaṇa family, he refused the sacred-thread initiation, took refuge at Kūḍalasaṅgama where Śiva as Saṅgamadēva became his lord, and was sent to Kalyāṇa, where as treasurer and minister he served the devotees, gathered the śaraṇas and founded the Anubhava Maṇṭapa; after the upheaval that followed an intercaste marriage among the śaraṇas he returned to Kūḍalasaṅgama and became one with the liṅga there.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Parents in the hagiographies: Mādarasa and Mādalāmbike (moderate). In the Pañcācārya account he is a great devotee within an older stream; in the śaraṇa account the founder. A Jaina narrative of Bijjala's reign gives a hostile account of these events (low confidence).

name: Basiasita (Poshesiduo 婆舍斯多)
summary: Twenty-fifth patriarch in the Chan list; the three names after Siṃha are unique to the Chan lineage.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 25.

name: Bāṣkala
summary: Eponym of the Bāṣkala recension of the Ṛgveda, named in the Purāṇic accounts among the pupils in Paila's line.
notes: Position in the pupil lists recalled from memory (low).

checks.note: Located: Paila gives Saṃhitās 'indrapramitaye … bāṣkalāya ca' (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4.16), Bāṣkala divides his in four (3.4.17) — his place in Paila's line (low confidence in the entry) is confirmed; Bāṣkala śākhā named in the Caraṇavyūha.

name: Baso Chökyi Gyaltsen
summary: Holder of the Ganden oral lineage, Khedrup Je's brother (recalled).

name: Bassui Tokushō 拔隊得勝
summary: Rinzai master who taught asking 'who is the master of seeing and hearing?' with great doubt.

name: Baudhāyana
summary: Founder (sūtrakāra) of the Baudhāyana branch of the Taittirīya school; its Kalpasūtra is ascribed to him.

scholarly.text: Śrautasūtra among the oldest sūtras (mid-1st millennium BCE); Dharmasūtra core c. 2nd c. BCE

checks.note: Confirmed: the Baudhāyana sūtra corpus is ascribed to him and regarded as older than Āpastamba (Wikipedia).

name: Bāvrī Sāhibā
summary: Woman Sant of Delhi to whom the Bāvrī line of Sants (Yārī, Bullā, Gulāl, Bhīkhā) traces itself.

name: Geshe Ben Gungyal
summary: Former bandit turned Kadam hermit, remembered for counting his virtuous and non-virtuous thoughts with white and black pebbles and for scolding himself when afflictions arose.
notes: Known from lojong and lamrim anecdotes; dates not recorded.

name: Benchō
summary: Hōnen's disciple from Kyushu, founder of the Chinzei line, counted the second patriarch of Jōdo-shū.

name: Bengar Jampal Zangpo
summary: Karma Kagyu yogin (15th c.), author of the Dorje Chang Thungma lineage prayer; teacher of the 7th Karmapa by the usual account.

name: Beomnang 法朗

tradition.text: 7th c.

summary: Silla monk said to have received Chan from the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin — the tradition's earliest Korean Seon link.

name: Bhabā Pāglā
summary: Mystic singer-poet of Bengal (Kalna) whose songs to the Mother and the Man of the Heart are sung by Bāuls.

name: Bhaddā Kāpilānī
summary: Wife of Mahākassapa before their renunciation; foremost nun in recollection of past lives (Thig 4.1).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā
summary: Former Jain debater, ordained with the words 'Come, Bhaddā'; foremost nun in quick understanding (Thig 5.9).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Bhaddiya
summary: One of the group of five monks (pañcavaggiyā) to whom the first discourse was taught at Isipatana; became an arahant with the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (Vin Mv 1.6).

name: Bhāde
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 35.
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Bhadrabāhu (the śrutakevalin)
summary: The last 'scripture-omniscient' (śrutakevalin), who knew all fourteen Pūrvas. Śvetāmbaras say that during a twelve-year famine he withdrew to Nepal to practise the 'great breath' (mahāprāṇa) meditation and there taught the Pūrvas to Sthūlabhadra; they ascribe to him the Kalpa Sūtra, three Chedasūtras and the niryuktis. Digambaras say he foresaw the famine, led the saṅgha south to Karnataka with the Maurya emperor Candragupta as his disciple, and died by sallekhanā on Candragiri at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa; those who stayed in the north adopted clothes.

tradition.text: died 170 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (Śvetāmbara) / 162 years (Digambara); contemporary of Candragupta Maurya

notes: Scholars distinguish a later Bhadrabāhu (II) to whom the niryuktis may belong.
alt_summary: U35 contribution: the Śvetāmbara tradition ascribes the protective hymn Uvasaggaharaṃ to Bhadrabāhu (in the later legend, a brother of the astrologer Varāhamihira).

name: Bhadrabāhu II
summary: A later Bhadrabāhu to whom some scholars (and a late Śvetāmbara tradition, which makes him brother of the astronomer Varāhamihira) assign the niryuktis; his identity and date (c. 5th–6th c. CE) are uncertain.

name: Bhadrācala Rāmadās (Kañcarla Gopanna)
summary: 17th-c. Telugu revenue official of Golconda who spent state revenue on the Rāma temple at Bhadrācalam, was imprisoned, and — by tradition — freed when Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa paid the sultan in gold; author of the Dāśarathi Śatakam and kīrtanas.
notes: A tradition that Kabīr initiated him is chronologically impossible; recorded only as the tradition's account.

name: Pattirakiriyār (Bhadragiri)
summary: King of Ujjain turned renouncer and disciple of Paṭṭiṉattār; his 'Lament for true knowledge' asks, in 231 couplets, 'when will the day come' of renunciation, inner yoga and knowledge. The tradition identifies him with Bhartṛhari, king of Ujjain.

realization_account.text: Seeing the stake burn when Paṭṭiṉattār was wrongly condemned, and learning the truth about his court, the king renounced and followed him; living on alms at Tiruviṭaimarutūr, he was chided by his guru for keeping a begging-bowl and a dog ('a householder!'), cast both away, and attained release before his guru.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The identification with Bhartṛhari (tch:bhartrhari) is the tradition's; scholars do not accept it. Story recalled at low–moderate confidence.

name: Bhadrakāpya
summary: Speaker: there is one taste only, not other than water (Ca Sū 26.8); the person and disease arise from karma (Sū 25.18-19); the navel forms first (Śā 6.21).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Bhadrapa

realization_account.text: A proud brahmin obsessed with purity who was taught by a yogin to overcome his pride and disgust. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 24): Realizing the meaning of emptiness pacifies error; meditating on love perfects conduct; by habituation to the non-duality of the manifold, the adverse is realized as one taste, the fruit.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 24 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A proud brahmin obsessed with purity who was taught by a yogin to overcome his pride and disgust.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Bhadraśaunaka
summary: Speaker: the large intestine and anus form first, as the seat of wind (Ca Śā 6.21).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Bhāgodās (Bhagvān Dās)
summary: Disciple of Kabīr credited by the panth with compiling the Bījak.

name: Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām
summary: Aghora teacher of Varanasi who founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh (1961) and a leprosy service ashram, taught Aghora as naturalness, service and the rejection of caste and social evils, and travelled abroad; he died in 1992.

name: The Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī (Yogeśvarī)
summary: Wandering woman tantric adept who taught Ramakrishna the sixty-four tantric sādhanas at Dakshineswar (1861–63) and declared his states to be those of an incarnation, in the Ramakrishna tradition's account.
notes: Known from the Ramakrishna biographies (U52).
alt_summary: The woman tantric adept who guided Ramakrishna through the practices of the sixty-four tantras at Dakṣiṇeśvar.

name: Bhaiṣajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha (sangs rgyas sman bla)

realization_account.text: A buddha whose twelve vows (Bhaiṣajyaguru sūtra) include healing all beings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: In Sowa Rigpa the teacher of the Four Tantras: seated in the medicine city Tanaduk, he emanates the sage Rigpé Yeshe, who teaches, and Yilé Kyé, who requests. Physicians practise his sādhana and consecrate medicines in his name.
alt_summary: The Medicine Buddha of the eastern land of lapis, whose twelve vows heal body and mind.

name: Bhaiṣajyarāja
summary: The 'Medicine King' bodhisattva of the Lotus, who in a past life as Sarvasattvapriyadarśana burned his body as an offering to the buddha and the sūtra (Lotus ch. 23).

name: Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī
summary: Son of Bhaktivinoda; founder of the Gauḍīya Maṭha (1920s), who gave renunciation (sannyāsa) a missionary form and criticised premature esoteric practice and caste-based guru lineages.

name: A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
summary: Disciple of Bhaktisiddhānta; founder of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (1966), which spread the chanting of the Hare Kṛṣṇa mahāmantra worldwide.

name: Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura (Kedarnath Datta)
summary: Magistrate and writer who revived Gauḍīya learning in the 19th c. (Jaiva Dharma and many works) and identified Māyāpur as Caitanya's birthplace.

name: Bhalaha

realization_account.text: Not well recalled; identification by position only. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 39): Bliss, bliss — the bliss of no-thing; without clinging, the bliss of no-thing; knowing all imputations there, bliss; the secret that needs no accomplishing, bliss.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 39 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Not well recalled; identification by position only.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Bhāmaha
summary: Author of the Kāvyālaṅkāra, the earliest surviving independent treatise on poetics after Bharata; founder of the 'figure' (alaṅkāra) school.

name: Bhandepa

realization_account.text: A god (or wealthy man) who, envying a yogin's radiance, was taught the four immeasurables. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 32): Love without clinging is supreme; realizing the natural state is compassion; uncontaminated bliss is joy; all phenomena one taste is equanimity perfected.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 32 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A god (or wealthy man) who, envying a yogin's radiance, was taught the four immeasurables.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The song recasts the four immeasurables in terms of realization.

name: Bhānudās
summary: Eknāth's great-grandfather (tradition 1448–1513), said to have brought the image of Viṭṭhala back to Paṇḍharpūr from Vijayanagara.

name: Bharadvāja
summary: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the sage who, chosen by the assembly of sages in the Himalaya when disease obstructed austerity and study, went to Indra 'seeking long life', learnt the threefold Āyurveda (cause, sign, remedy), gained immeasurable life and taught it to the sages (Ca Sū 1.3-27).
notes: Distinct in this unit from Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja who speaks in Ca Sū 12, 26 and Śā 6 (tch:kumarasiras-bharadvaja); the objector of Ca Śā 3.4 is simply 'Bharadvāja'.

checks.note: Headers: 'bārhaspatyo bharadvājaḥ' for book 6 (6.9 Vaiśvānara); seer of 10.137.1.
Text-located: TB 3.10.11.3–5.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of ramatapani (uttara), tarasara, rudraksajabala, bhiksuka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.

alt_summary: Bharadvāja Bārhaspatya, founder of the family of Ṛgveda book 6, whose vision of the light set in the heart (6.9.5–6) is among the Veda's inner experiences; one of the seven seers of RV 10.137.
Seer who questions Bhṛgu in the Mokṣadharma (12.175–185), raising doubts about the existence of a living self in a body made of elements.
U02 contribution: in TB 3.10.11.3–5 he spends three lives as a Vedic student and is shown by Indra that the Vedas are endless, then taught the Sāvitra fire as 'all knowledge'.
Vedic seer who asks Yājñavalkya about the tāraka (Rāmottaratāpanī; Tārasāra) and is among the rudrākṣa-wearing sages (Rudrākṣajābāla); named among the kuṭīcaka renouncers (Bhikṣuka).
alt_notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Bhāradvāja (the student)
summary: Vāseṭṭha's companion in MN 98 / Snp 3.9 and DN 13.

name: Bharata (the first world-emperor)
summary: Eldest son of Ṛṣabha and first of the twelve world-emperors (cakravartin) of this era, after whom Bhāratavarṣa is named in Jain tradition. He conquered the six divisions of Bharata-kṣetra; Digambaras (Ādipurāṇa) say he created the brāhmaṇas from among the laity who avoided trampling sprouts; Śvetāmbaras tell that he attained omniscience while looking in a mirror in his palace, seeing the body's unreality when a ring fell from his finger.

name: Bharata Miśra
summary: Author of a Sphoṭasiddhi distinct from Maṇḍana's.

name: Bharata (Bharata Muni)
summary: The sage to whom the Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed: Brahmā taught him the Nāṭyaveda, which he performed with his hundred sons before the gods; his sons' mockery of the sages brought a curse, and drama was brought down to earth at King Nahuṣa's request (NŚ 1, 36).

tradition.text: Tretā age (NŚ 1)

scholarly.text: the name of the tradition to which the compiled Nāṭyaśāstra is ascribed

realization_account.text: Received the Nāṭyaveda from Brahmā, who composed it by yoga from the four Vedas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bharata (Rāma's brother)
summary: Rāma's brother, who refuses the throne and rules as Rāma's regent; Rāma's teachings on impermanence and kingship are addressed to him (2.100–105).

checks.note: Located as described.

notes: Disambiguated from Bharata Muni (tch:bharata-muni).

name: Bhāratcandra Rāy (Rāyguṇākar)
summary: Court poet of Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, author of the Annadāmaṅgala in praise of Annapūrṇā.

name: Bhāratītīrtha
summary: Śṛṅgeri pontiff of the 14th century, associate of Vidyāraṇya; credited with part of the Pañcadaśī, the Vaiyāsikanyāyamālā and (by some) the Dṛg-Dṛśya Viveka.

name: Bhārgava (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Bhārgava Vaidarbhi
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks how many deities support a being (PrU 2).

checks.note: AVŚ 11.4 header: '1–26 bhārgavo vaidarbhiḥ', deity prāṇa.
Located: PrU 1.1 and 2.1 (how many deities support a being).

alt_summary: The seer to whom the Prāṇa hymn of the Atharvaveda (AVŚ 11.4) is ascribed.
notes: Ascription taken from the hymn header of the local Atharvaveda text (checked).

name: Bhartṛhari
summary: The grammarian-philosopher, author of the Vākyapadīya, its Vṛtti (traditionally) and the Mahābhāṣyadīpikā. He taught that Brahman is the Word-principle appearing as the world, that all cognition is permeated by the word, that meaning is borne by the indivisible sphoṭa and grasped as pratibhā, and that grammar is a door to liberation. The later tradition often identifies him with the poet of the Śatakatraya; the Chinese pilgrim Yijing reports a Bhartṛhari who went back and forth between monastic and household life.

tradition.text: identified by later tradition with the royal poet Bhartṛhari, brother of Vikramāditya (legend)

name: Bhartṛhari (Bharthari, the Nāth king-yogī)
summary: King of Ujjain in Nāth legend who renounced his throne — in the best-known telling after the fruit of immortality he gave his queen returned to him through her lover — and became a disciple of Gorakh; founder of the Bharthari (Vairāg) panth; hero of sung sagas; counted among the Marathi nine Nāths. Tradition often identifies him with the poet of the three śatakas and with Bhartṛhari the grammarian.
notes: Distinct id from tch:bhartrhari (the grammarian of the Vākyapadīya, U31). The tradition's identification of the three is not accepted by scholars.

name: Bhartṛmitra
summary: Pre-Kumārila Mīmāṃsaka whom the Nyāyaratnākara names among those who had made Mīmāṃsā 'Lokāyata' (ŚV pratijñā 10) — by the commentators' account, by denying that obligatory and prohibited acts bear fruit. His work is lost.

name: Bhartṛprapañca
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin and commentator on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (and reportedly the Kaṭha) Upaniṣad; taught that Brahman is both one and many like the ocean and its waves, that the world is its real modification, and that liberation needs knowledge combined with works. Known only from his critics Śaṅkara, Sureśvara and Ānandagiri.

scholarly.text: before Śaṅkara (6th–7th c. CE or earlier)

notes: The list of eight 'states' (avasthā) of Brahman ascribed to him by Sureśvara is recalled with low confidence and not recorded as a teaching.
alt_notes: Views reported by opponents (reported_by_opponent).
alt_summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin who held difference-and-non-difference between Brahman and the world/selves and taught that liberation requires knowledge combined with works; known through Śaṅkara's and Sureśvara's refutations in their Bṛhadāraṇyaka commentaries.

name: Bharuci
summary: Ancient Vedāntin named by Rāmānuja among the earlier teachers; possibly the same as the Dharmaśāstra commentator Bhāruci (uncertain).

name: Bhāsarvajña
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyasāra and its auto-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, known for independent positions: only three means of knowledge, and liberation as the cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal bliss. A Śaiva of Pāśupata orientation.
notes: The Ratnaṭīkā on the Pāśupata Gaṇakārikā is also attributed to him (attribution recalled, not checked).
alt_summary: Naiyāyika author of the Nyāyasāra (with its self-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa) and a Pāśupata: the Ratnaṭīkā on the Gaṇakārikā is ascribed to him, and Dalal's edition ascribes the Gaṇakārikā verses to him too.

name: Bhāskara (Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, the Vedāntin)
summary: Author of the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya that is the classic statement of aupādhika bhedābheda: Brahman really transforms through its power; souls are its parts, distinguished by real adjuncts; liberation after death through knowledge combined with lifelong duty. He attacked Śaṅkara's māyāvāda as Mahāyāna Buddhism in Vedic dress; Vācaspati Miśra and later Advaitins answer him.
notes: Often described as a tridaṇḍin (Vaiṣṇava-style renouncer) — low confidence. Distinct from the mathematician Bhāskara and from Bhāskararāya.

checks.note: Least-sure item: a Bhedābheda Vedāntin (8th–9th c.) who held that knowledge and works combine and wrote a partly surviving Gītā commentary. The position given for him in dsp:gita-primary-teaching matches this.

alt_summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin credited with a Gītā commentary defending the combination of knowledge and works.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Bhāskara I
summary: Expositor of the Āryabhaṭa school: Mahābhāskarīya, Laghubhāskarīya and the commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya (629 CE).

name: Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya)
summary: Born Śaka 1036 (1114 CE), son and pupil of Maheśvara; author of the Siddhānta Śiromaṇi (1150) with Līlāvatī, Bījagaṇita, Grahagaṇita and Golādhyāya, and the Karaṇakutūhala (1183). He taught that the earth rests in space by its own power and has a power of attraction.

name: Bhāskara (author of the Śivasūtravārttika)
summary: Kashmiri teacher, 'son of Bhaṭṭa Divākara', who wrote the Śivasūtravārttika on the teaching received from Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa, giving an account of the Śiva Sūtra's revelation and lineage that differs from Kṣemarāja's.

scholarly.text: c. 10th-11th c. CE; relation to Kṣemarāja debated

notes: Id disambiguated from tch:bhaskara (the Bhedābheda Vedāntin) and tch:bhaskarakantha.

name: Bhāskarabhaṭṭa Borīkar
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (early 14th c.), author of two of the seven classic poems — the Śiśupāla-vadha and the Uddhava-gītā (Ekādaśa-skandha).

name: Bhāskarakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit, author of the Mokṣopāyaṭīkā and (outside U06) of the Bhāskarī commentary on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī.

checks.note: 18th-c. Kashmiri (Rājanaka) Bhāskarakaṇṭha, author of the Mokṣopāyaṭīkā and the Bhāskarī on the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī.

alt_summary: 18th-century Kashmiri scholar, author of the Bhāskarī on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and of a commentary on the Mokṣopāya (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); identified by many with the Rājānaka Bhāskara who rendered Lal Ded's vākhs into Sanskrit verse.
notes: Identification with the Lallāvākyāni translator is low confidence.

name: Bhāskararāya
summary: The great 18th-c. systematizer of Śrīvidyā (initiatory name Bhāsurānandanātha), disciple of Nṛsiṃhānandanātha: author of the Saubhāgyabhāskara on the Lalitā Sahasranāma, the Setubandha on the Vāmakeśvara Tantra, the Varivasyārahasya, the Guptavatī on the Devī Māhātmya and commentaries on the Tripurā, Bhāvanā and Kaula Upaniṣads; he read the Śākta tantras through Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta and defended their Vedic standing.
places: the Kāverī region of Tamil Nadu (by tradition, a village named after him)

realization_account.text: Remembered as a perfected upāsaka of Lalitā who performed great sacrifices and vanquished opponents in debate at Kāśī; his life is told in the Bhāskaravilāsa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Initiatory name and guru's name checked in the Varivasyārahasya colophon and the Saubhāgyabhāskara opening. Places and exact dates are from memory (low).

queries: Bhaskararaya commentaries Tripura Upanishad Bhavana Upanishad Kaula Upanishad
checks.note: Confirmed: Bhāskararāya commented on the Kaula, Tripurā and Bhāvanā Upaniṣads (Wikipedia). The Kaula commentary is printed in Tantrik Texts XI (1922), which has a local eBhāratī copy.
Web: Bhāskararāya Makhin (1690-1785), author of the Guptavatī.

alt_summary: In this unit: author of the Guptavatī commentary on the Devī Māhātmya (his Śrīvidyā works belong to U23).
U04 contribution: commented on the Tripurā, Bhāvanā and Kaula Upaniṣads.

name: Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Miśra
summary: Author of the Jñānayajña, commentary on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka.

queries: Bhatta Bhaskara Jnanayajna Taittiriya commentary date
checks.note: Existence and work (Jñānayajña on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa, Āraṇyaka; pre-Sāyaṇa) confirmed; the date 'c. 11th century' not confirmed by the sources found.
Low-confidence entry confirmed: the Jñānayajña bhāṣya covers the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka (editions; HathiTrust study). No date is asserted.

alt_summary: Commentator on the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka (Jñānayajña).

name: Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa
summary: Early commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra, known through Abhinavagupta's report: rasa is the stable emotion intensified (upacita) by the determinants, existing primarily in the character (Rāma) and secondarily in the actor who imitates him.
notes: His views are known only through opponents' reports (Abhinavabhāratī, Kāvyaprakāśa).

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa
summary: Author of the Stavacintāmaṇi, a hymn to Śiva quoted in Utpaladeva's commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi as the work of a 'former teacher' (pūrvaguru).

name: Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka
summary: Kashmiri theorist (Hṛdayadarpaṇa, lost) who held that rasa is neither produced, inferred nor suggested but 'enjoyed': poetic language 'makes present' (bhāvakatva) the situation in universal form and 'makes it enjoyable' (bhojakatva) in a state of rest in sattva, akin to tasting the supreme Brahman.
notes: Known through Abhinavagupta's and Mahimabhaṭṭa's reports.

name: Bhaṭṭa Tauta
summary: U31 contribution: Abhinavagupta's teacher in dramaturgy, author of the lost Kāvyakautuka.

name: Bhaṭṭadeva (Vaikuṇṭhanātha Bhāgavata Bhaṭṭācārya)
summary: Disciple of Dāmodaradeva (1558–1638) whose Kathā-Bhāgavata and Kathā-Gītā are the foundation of Assamese prose.

name: Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra
summary: Early commentator on the Caraka Saṃhitā (Carakanyāsa), known from fragments.

name: Bhaṭṭodbhaṭa (Udbhaṭa)
summary: A commentator on the Bṛhaspati Sūtra known from citations in later Nyāya and Jain works, who is said to have reinterpreted the sūtras (e.g. allowing more than perception).
notes: Recalled from modern studies of the fragments (citations in Cakradhara's Granthibhaṅga and Vādideva's Syādvādaratnākara); not verified.

name: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Siddhāntakaumudī and other Pāṇinian works.

checks.note: Confirmed: early 17th c., settled in Vārāṇasī before 1600 (Wikipedia). The entry's c. 1550–1630 is consistent.

alt_summary: U31 contribution: besides the Siddhāntakaumudī, author of the Vaiyākaraṇa-siddhānta-kārikās, the verse summary of grammatical philosophy that holds, on final analysis, that only the sentence-sphoṭa is real.

name: Bhaṭṭotpala
summary: The great commentator on Varāhamihira's works (Bṛhajjātaka, Bṛhat Saṃhitā, Laghujātaka, Yogayātrā) and on Pṛthuyaśas; his commentaries preserve many lost earlier texts.

name: Bhāva Bṛhaspati
summary: Pāśupata ācārya who, according to the Prabhāsa (Bhadrakālī) inscription of 1169 CE, became head of Somanātha and directed its restoration under the Caulukya king Kumārapāla.

name: Bhavabhaṭṭa
summary: Commentator on the Laghuśaṃvara (Cakrasaṃvarapañjikā/Vivṛti), c. 10th c.

name: Bhavabhūti
summary: Dramatist of the Uttararāmacarita, Mālatīmādhava and Mahāvīracarita; held that compassion (karuṇa) is the one rasa.

name: Bhavadāsa
summary: Commentator on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra before Kumārila, who mentions him (ŚV pratijñā 63); the Nyāyaratnākara reports that he split MS 1.1.4 into two sūtras. His work is lost.

name: Bhavadeva Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tautātitamatatilaka, an exposition of Kumārila's doctrine.

name: Bhavadeva Miśra
summary: Author of the Yuktabhavadeva (1623), which combines haṭha practice with the Pātañjala eight limbs.
notes: Distinct from the Mīmāṃsaka/Dharmaśāstra author Bhavadeva Bhaṭṭa (tch:bhavadeva-bhatta).

name: Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu; author of the Tattvayāthārthyadīpana on the Tattvasamāsa.
alt_summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu and author of a Dīpikā on the Yoga Sūtra that condenses his teacher's Vārttika.

name: Bhāvamiśra
summary: Author of the Bhāvaprakāśa, son of Laṭakana Miśra (colophons).

name: Bhāvānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Bhavānanda Siddhāntavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Bhavānandī sub-commentary on the Dīdhiti.

name: Bhavanātha
summary: Prābhākara author of the Nayaviveka.

name: Bhāviveka

realization_account.text: Xuanzang records that Bhāviveka, wishing to debate the Yogācāra master Dharmapāla and failing to meet him, resolved to wait for Maitreya to settle his doubts, recited a dhāraṇī before an image of Avalokiteśvara and entered a rock palace of the asuras to await Maitreya's coming.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Xuanzang's story from memory (moderate); the later works under the name Bhavya are assigned by scholars to other authors.
summary: Madhyamaka master who introduced Dignāga's formal inference into Madhyamaka, criticized Buddhapālita, and in the Madhyamakahṛdaya and Tarkajvālā surveyed and answered the Śrāvaka, Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta and Mīmāṃsā schools; regarded in Tibet as the founder of Svātantrika.
alt_summary: Madhyamaka master (U40). This unit records only the doxography of the eighteen schools ascribed to Bhavya in the Tibetan canon.

name: Bhela
summary: Disciple of Ātreya whose tantra was read out to the assembly (Ca Sū 1.31-33); the partly surviving Bhela Saṃhitā bears his name.

name: Bhīkhā Sāhib
summary: Sant of the Bāvrī line (Bhurkuḍā, Ghazipur) whose verses are printed in the Santbānī series.

name: Bhikṣana

alt_summary: Son of Varuṇa who asks his father to teach him brahman and, by repeated tapas, realizes in turn that food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss are brahman (TU 3.1-6: 'the knowledge of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa').
Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes several adhikāras on temple ritual (Kriyādhikāra, Khilādhikāra, Prakīrṇādhikāra and others).

Seer who recites Manu's teaching in the Manusmṛti (1.59–60), one of Manu's ten mind-born sons (1.35); as Bhṛgu Vāruṇi, son of Varuṇa, he journeys through the other world in ŚB 11.6.1 and JB 1.42–44 (and learns Brahman in TU 3).
Ancient seer who answers Bharadvāja on creation, the elements, the self, the varṇas and the āśramas (12.175–185).

name: Bhūriśravas
summary: Named in the Gītā only as Saumadatti, 'the son of Somadatta', among the leaders of Duryodhana's army (1.8); usually identified as Bhūriśravas.

name: Bhusuku

realization_account.text: A monk of Nālandā who did nothing but eat, sleep and stroll (bhu-su-ku); challenged to recite a text before the assembly he recited the Bodhicaryāvatāra and rose into the air; Abhayadatta identifies him with Śāntideva; also a poet of the Caryāgīti. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 41): Until one realizes oneself there is great difference between tastes, and saṃsāra and the buddhas are very different; at the time of realization saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are great bliss, like a jewel blazing in the ocean.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Bhuśuṇḍa
summary: The ancient crow living on a wish-fulfilling tree on a peak of Meru, who tells Vasiṣṭha how contemplation of the breath (prāṇa-cintā) made him outlive many world-ages (Mokṣopāya 6.14-27; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha). The Rāmcaritmānas's Kāk Bhuśuṇḍi is a related figure.

MU 6.14.6 wish-tree (kalpataru) on Meru; prāṇa contemplation 6.25-26; story closes 6.28 ('bhusuṇḍopākhyānaṃ samāptam').

realization_account.text: Resting in the Self through contemplation of the breath, he remains unaffected by the dissolutions of the worlds he has witnessed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Questioner in the Bṛhajjābāla (of Kālāgnirudra) and Bhasmajābāla (of Mahādeva) on sacred ash.

name: Bhūtabali
summary: Pupil of Dharasena who completed the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, including its sixth part the Mahābandha; the bhūtas (spirits) are said to have worshipped him, hence the name.

name: Bhūtirāja
summary: A Kashmiri Śaiva teacher named among Abhinavagupta's teachers and praised by Ānandabhaṭṭa (Vijñānakaumudī, opening) with Somānanda and Utpala among those who descended to restore the Śaiva teaching.
notes: Subject taught to Abhinavagupta not verified here.

name: Bihārinidev
summary: Ācārya of the ascetic Haridāsī line (late 16th – 17th c.), author of doctrinal verses (siddhānta) of the sampradāya.

name: Bījārām
summary: Disciple and successor of Kīnārām at Krīm Kuṇḍ (tradition).
notes: The full succession list of Krīm Kuṇḍ heads is not reproduced (gap); only names recalled with some confidence are given.

name: Bilvamaṅgala (Līlāśuka)
summary: Poet of the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta, revered by Caitanya; placed by the Vallabha tradition in Viṣṇusvāmin's line.

name: Bimbisāra
summary: King of Magadha, patron of the Buddha, donor of the Bamboo Grove; at his suggestion the uposatha was instituted (Vin Mv 2.1).

name: Bīrbhān
summary: Founder (1657) of the Satnāmīs of Narnaul, whose community rose against Aurangzeb in 1672.

name: Bodhāyana (the Vṛttikāra)
summary: Author of an extensive vṛtti on the Brahma Sūtras which Rāmānuja says earlier teachers abridged and which he follows; claimed as a precursor of Viśiṣṭādvaita.

name: Bodhendra Sarasvatī
summary: Head of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi maṭha in its own succession list, remembered as a propagator of repeating and singing the divine name (nāma-siddhānta) and as a source of the South Indian bhajana tradition.
notes: Works on the divine name are ascribed to him; titles not recorded here (uncertain).

name: Bodhibhadra
summary: Nālandā master, commentator on the Jñānasārasamuccaya, and one of Atiśa's teachers.

name: Bodhidharma (Putidamo 菩提達磨)

tradition.text: arrived 520 or 527 (Song accounts); died 536 or later, returned west with one sandal

realization_account.text: Heir of Prajñātāra in the 28-generation Indian line; brought the mind-seal east; 'wall-gazing Brahmin'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: First Chinese and twenty-eighth Indian patriarch of Chan. In the tradition's account a South Indian prince and disciple of Prajñātāra who came to China, told Emperor Wu of Liang that his merit was 'no merit' and the holy truth 'vast emptiness, nothing holy', sat facing a wall for nine years at Shaolin, and transmitted robe and Dharma to Huike. The earliest source (Xu gaoseng zhuan, 645) describes a South Indian brahmin teaching 'wall-gazing' and the four practices in the Northern Wei.

name: Bodhiruci (6th c.)
summary: North Indian monk in Luoyang (arrived 508) who translated the ten-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra, the Vajracchedikā, Vasubandhu's Daśabhūmika commentary and the Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa.
notes: Distinct from the Tang translator Bodhiruci (d. 727) who compiled the Ratnakūṭa (T310).
alt_notes: U43 contribution: translator of the Rebirth Treatise; in the tradition's account (Xu gaoseng zhuan; Shōshinge) he gave Tanluan the Contemplation Sūtra, telling him that no Daoist longevity compares with the Buddha's immeasurable life, whereupon Tanluan burned his Daoist scriptures.

name: Bodhya
summary: A tranquil sage who, questioned by King Nahuṣa, names six teachers: Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden (Mahābhārata 12.171.57-61).

Disciple of Kālāṅki Nātar; teacher of Pulippāṇi, Koṅkaṇar and Karuvūrār.
places: Palani — samādhi within the hill temple (tradition)

name: Bopadeva
summary: Author of the Mugdhabodha grammar.

name: Brahmā (as first teacher)
summary: The first of the gods, maker and protector of the world, who taught the knowledge of brahman to his eldest son Atharvan (MuU 1.1.1); the first link of teacher-lines (ChU 3.11.4, 8.15.1); in KauU 1.5-7 he questions the knower arriving in the brahma-world.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of kalisantarana, naradaparivrajaka, pasupatabrahma, sarabha, yogatattva, yogasikha, kaivalya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): the first knower of the Veda of life, who 'remembering' it taught it to Prajāpati (AHS Sū 1.3; Ca Sū 1.4; Su Sū 1.20); in the Suśruta he first made it in a hundred thousand verses and a thousand chapters, then divided it eightfold for short-lived men (Su Sū 1.6).

Seen by Arjuna within the universal form, 'seated on the lotus-seat' (BhG 11.15); in one construal of 11.37 the Lord is 'the first maker even of Brahmā', and in 11.39 he is called the great-grandsire (prapitāmaha).

U04 contribution: answers Nārada (Kalisantaraṇa, Nāradaparivrājaka 2), Vaiśravaṇa (Pāśupatabrahma), Paippalāda (Śarabha); taught by Viṣṇu (Yogatattva) and Śiva (Yogaśikhā); as Parameṣṭhin teaches Āśvalāyana (Kaivalya).

In jyotiṣa, Pitāmaha is the source of the Paitāmaha Siddhānta; Āryabhaṭa says his knowledge was raised from the ocean of true and false knowledge by Brahmā's grace (Āryabhaṭīya 4.49); Parāśara teaches the horā 'as heard from Brahmā's mouth' (BPHS 1.6); Brahmā granted Rāhu the boon of receiving the offerings made at eclipses (BS 5.14).

name: Brahmā Sahampati
summary: The Great Brahmā who implored the newly awakened Buddha to teach (SN 6.1; MN 26; Vin Mv 1.5) and spoke verses at the parinibbāna (DN 16).

name: Brahmadatta
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara (or early) Vedāntin reported to have held that the knowledge from the Upaniṣads must be meditated upon throughout life (knowledge as an injunction to meditation) and that the individual self is not eternal; known through reports by Sureśvara and Yāmuna.

name: Brahmagupta
summary: Son of Jiṣṇu, astronomer of Bhillamāla; author of the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628, at age 30) and the Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665). He upheld the smṛti's yuga proportions and the stationary earth against Āryabhaṭa; founder figure of the Brāhma school.

name: Brahmānanda Giri
summary: Sixteenth-century Bengali Śākta teacher and author of the Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī and (traditionally) the Tārārahasya; remembered as the guru of Pūrṇānanda.

name: Brahmānanda (author of the Jyotsnā)
summary: Author of the Jyotsnā, the standard Sanskrit commentary on the Haṭhapradīpikā. He names Meruśāstrin as the prompter of his work and reads haṭha through Pātañjala yoga and Advaita: haṭha = union of sun and moon (prāṇa and apāna); rājayoga = asamprajñāta samādhi.
notes: Not the Advaitin Gauḍa Brahmānanda Sarasvatī (tch:brahmananda-sarasvati).

name: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Advaita scholar who wrote the Laghucandrikā on Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi, answering the Mādhva Rāmācārya's Taraṅgiṇī.
alt_summary: Author of the Laghucandrikā ('Gauḍa-Brahmānandī') on the Advaitasiddhi and of the Nyāyaratnāvalī on the Siddhāntabindu.

name: Brahmanandin (Ṭaṅka)
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin, the 'Vākyakāra', author of the Vākya cited by Yāmuna, Rāmānuja and others.

name: Brahmaṇya Tīrtha
summary: The ascetic of Abbūr who gave renunciation to Vyāsatīrtha; the colophons of the Nyāyāmṛta name Vyāsatīrtha as his disciple.
notes: Discipleship stated in the Nyāyāmṛta colophons checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

name: Brahmatantra Svatantra Jīyar
summary: Disciple of Vedānta Deśika and first head of the Parakāla maṭha (later at Mysore) in the Vaṭakalai line.

name: Brāhmī
summary: Daughter of Ṛṣabha, to whom he taught writing — the Brāhmī script is named after her; she became a nun and head of the nuns in his community.

name: Bṛhadārya
summary: Number 14 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Bṛhadratha
summary: A king of the Ikṣvāku line who, having installed his son and renounced his kingdom, practised austerities in the forest and asked Śākāyanya about the self, lamenting the foulness of the body and the transience of all things (MaiU 1.2-4).

name: Bṛhaspati
summary: Named by the Lord as his manifestation, the chief of household priests (purodhas) (BhG 10.24).

alt_summary: U33 contribution: the Lokāyata is 'Bṛhaspati's doctrine'. The tradition's account makes him the preceptor of the gods who composed a deluding doctrine for the asuras (Maitrī Up. 7.9) and gave it to his disciple Cārvāka (Prabodhacandrodaya 2); the Bṛhaspati Sūtra, quoted as 'the venerable Bṛhaspati' by Jayarāśi, is ascribed to him, as are the anti-Vedic verses at the end of the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha's first chapter. The Arthaśāstra's 'Bārhaspatyas' (1.2.4) hold that only economics and government are sciences.
Preceptor of the gods who asks Yājñavalkya about Kurukṣetra/Avimukta (Jābāla 1; Rāmottaratāpanī).
Preceptor of the gods; he officiates at Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323) and questions Prajāpati Manu on the highest knowledge (12.194).
U02 contribution: the preceptor of the gods, to whom the Bṛhaspatismṛti is ascribed; in the Mahābhāṣya he teaches Indra words one by one. The Lokāyata tradition's Bṛhaspati is treated by U33.
notes: Scholars distinguish the Lokāyata author (if a person) from the Vedic deity; recorded under the registry id per the tradition's identification.

name: Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of the hymn on knowledge and speech (RV 10.71) and, with alternatives, of the hymn on the birth of the gods (10.72).

name: Bṛhaspati (Saiddhāntika)
summary: An early Siddhānta authority cited by later exegetes (Rāmakaṇṭha, Abhinavagupta) as pre-dating or contemporary with Sadyojyoti; his work is lost except in citations (a title Śivatanu(śāstra) is associated with him — low confidence).
notes: Distinct from the Vedic Bṛhaspati and from the Lokāyata founder of the same name.

name: Buddhabhadra
summary: Indian dhyāna master and translator (359-429) who with Faxian translated the six-fascicle Nirvāṇa Sūtra and alone the 60-fascicle Avataṃsaka (418-421) and the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra.
alt_summary: Kashmiri meditation master and translator (the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya with Faxian; also the Avataṃsaka).

name: Buddhadāsa Bhikkhu
summary: Thai reformist monk (1906–1993), founder of Suan Mokkh (1932), who taught voidness of self, present-moment dependent origination and mindfulness with breathing, and engaged in dialogue with other religions.

name: Buddhadatta
summary: Commentator and manual author from Uragapura (Uraiyūr) in the Cola country, said to have been a contemporary of Buddhaghosa; author of the Abhidhammāvatāra and the Vinayavinicchaya.

name: Buddhadeva
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: a dharma is called past, present or future relative to what precedes and follows it, as one woman is called daughter and mother (anyathānyathika, AKBh 5.26).

name: Buddhaghosa

tradition.text: came to Lanka in the reign of King Mahānāma (Cūḷavaṃsa)

places: Magadha (near the Bodhi tree, per Cūḷavaṃsa)

realization_account.text: The Cūḷavaṃsa tells that he was a brahmin versed in the Vedas, converted by the elder Revata, and that the gods twice hid his Visuddhimagga so that he wrote it three times, each copy identical — proof that he was fit to render the commentaries; the Burmese Buddhaghosuppatti adds further legends.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great 5th-century commentator of the Mahāvihāra, author of the Visuddhimagga and of the Pali commentaries on the Vinaya, the four Nikāyas and the Abhidhamma, which fixed Theravāda orthodoxy.

name: Buddhaguhya
summary: Indian master of the kriyā, caryā and yoga tantras (8th c.), author of commentaries on the Mahāvairocana and the Tattvasaṃgraha (Tantrārthāvatāra); invited to Tibet under Trisong Detsen but declined, sending a letter.
alt_summary: For the Nyingma, an 8th-c. Indian master of the Māyājāla cycle and commentator on the Guhyagarbha (low confidence on the Nyingma attributions).

name: Buddhaguptanātha
summary: An Indian yogin and traveller of the 16th century from whom Tāranātha received the seven instruction lineages and many siddha transmissions (the tradition's account).

name: Buddhajīva
summary: Kashmiri Mahīśāsaka monk who translated the Five-Part Vinaya (423–424).

name: Buddhajñānapāda

realization_account.text: After years of practice he had a vision of Mañjuśrī, who gave him the oral instruction on the two stages.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Jñānapāda school of the Guhyasamāja (late 8th c.); trained under Haribhadra in Prajñāpāramitā and had a vision of Mañjuśrī, who gave him the teaching (tradition); teacher of Dīpaṅkarabhadra; associated with the early years of Vikramaśīla under King Dharmapāla.
notes: Place names and teachers recalled with low confidence.

name: Buddhamitra
summary: Buddhist teacher of Vasubandhu according to Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu, which tells that he was defeated in debate by the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa before a king at Ayodhyā; Vasubandhu is said to have answered with his (lost) Paramārthasaptati.
notes: Lineage assignment follows the biography's setting; verify.

name: Buddhamitra (Fuduo Miduo 伏馱蜜多), ninth Chan patriarch
summary: Ninth patriarch in the Chan list; distinct entry from the Buddhamitra who taught Vasubandhu (tch:buddhamitra).
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 9.

name: Buḍḍhan (Vṛddhānanda)
summary: The old man who appeared to the boy Dādū and blessed him, counted as Dādū's guru; identified by some in the panth with Kabīr or with God.

name: Buddhanandi (Futuo Nanti 佛馱難提)
summary: Eighth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 8.

name: Buddhapālita

realization_account.text: Tāranātha relates that he studied Nāgārjuna's works under Saṃgharakṣita, attained realization through the practice of Mañjuśrī, and taught at Dantapurī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Tāranātha details from memory, low confidence.
summary: Commentator on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā whose method of drawing out the opponent's unwanted consequences was criticized by Bhāviveka and defended by Candrakīrti, and who is therefore counted as the first 'Prāsaṅgika'.

name: Buddhayaśas
summary: Kashmiri Dharmaguptaka master who recited the Four-Part Vinaya and the Dīrghāgama for translation.

name: Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

checks.note: Located: ChU 5.11.1 and 5.16 (water, the 'bladder'). He is also Janaka's interlocutor on the Gāyatrī at BĀU 5.14.8. In ŚB 10.6.1 the same group goes to Aśvapati (GRETIL ŚB 10.6.1.1).

name: Butön Rinchen Drub
summary: Scholar of Zhalu (a tradition often grouped with the Sakya), editor of the Tengyur canon, author of the History of Buddhism and major Kālacakra and tantra works; his lineages reached Tsongkhapa.
notes: Affiliation: Zhalu; grouped here with the Sakya for convenience.
alt_notes: Usually counted as founder of the Zhalu (Bulug) tradition; no separate lineage id used here.
alt_summary: Scholar of Zhalu, compiler of the Tibetan canon (Kangyur/Tengyur catalogues) and a leading Kālacakra master, contemporary of Dolpopa; his treatise on the tathāgatagarbha reads the buddha-nature teaching as of provisional meaning, against the other-emptiness reading.

name: B. V. Raman
summary: Bangalore astrologer and editor of The Astrological Magazine; wrote widely in English on horā and muhūrta and proposed his own ayanāṃśa.

name: Caikitāyana Dālbhya
summary: One of three experts on the udgītha who discuss the support of the sāman (ChU 1.8).

checks.note: Located: ChU 1.8.1-8.

name: Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya (Viśvambhara Miśra, Nimāi, Gaurāṅga, Mahāprabhu)
summary: Founder figure of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism: Navadvīpa scholar who after initiation at Gayā led nocturnal congregational chanting, took renunciation, travelled to south India and Vṛndāvana, and lived his last eighteen years at Purī absorbed in Rādhā's love for Kṛṣṇa. His only writing is the Śikṣāṣṭaka; his teaching was given to Rūpa, Sanātana, Rāmānanda and others and recorded by his biographers.

realization_account.text: Kṛṣṇa himself, appearing with the mood and golden complexion of Rādhā to taste her love (CC 1.1.5–6); the hidden (channa) avatāra and yuga-avatāra of Kali who inaugurated the chanting of the name; in his last years he passed through states of divine madness (divyonmāda); he disappeared at Purī in 1533 (accounts differ on how).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cākkiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Buddhist who became Śiva's devotee while keeping the Buddhist robe; the first day, seeing a liṅga, he threw a stone at it in ecstasy and made that his daily worship; one day he forgot and ran back without eating, and Śiva appeared to him.

realization_account.text: A Buddhist who became Śiva's devotee while keeping the Buddhist robe; the first day, seeing a liṅga, he threw a stone at it in ecstasy and made that his daily worship; one day he forgot and ran back without eating, and Śiva appeared to him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cakradhar Svāmī
summary: Founder of the Mahānubhāva panth (13th c.), held by his followers to be Parameśvara's fifth incarnation. By their account the Gujarati prince Haripāla of Bharuch died and Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ entered his body; receiving Govindaprabhu's grace at Ṛddhipur, he wandered Maharashtra teaching in Marathi, admitted women and all castes to renunciation, forbade the worship of the devatās, and, threatened by the Yādava court, departed to the north (c. 1274).

tradition.text: incarnation of Parameśvara; left for the north Śaka 1196 (1274)

realization_account.text: Parameśvara himself, one of the five Kṛṣṇas; entered the dead body of Haripāla; survived the executioner and left for the north.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cakrapāṇidatta
summary: Bengali physician, author of the Āyurvedadīpikā on Caraka, the Bhānumatī on Suśruta and the Cikitsāsaṅgraha (Cakradatta).

name: Caluki

realization_account.text: A drowsy man who could not stay awake; taught to meditate with his sleep. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 54): By long habituation to the true guru's instruction, earth and the other elements dissolve into awareness and self-appearance becomes mahāmudrā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 54 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A drowsy man who could not stay awake; taught to meditate with his sleep.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Cāmarasa
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet at the court of Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara, author of the Prabhuliṅgalīle on Allama Prabhu.

name: Camaripa

realization_account.text: A cobbler taught by a monk-yogin to treat his work — the leather, the awl, the thread — as the path, who realized while making shoes. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 14): This leather of conceptual signs, soaked in the vessel of vajra emptiness, is stretched and stitched by the experience of wisdom in the continuous abandoning of the eight worldly concerns; the maker of the shoe of the spontaneous dharmakāya is Camaripa, best of cobblers.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 14 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A cobbler taught by a monk-yogin to treat his work — the leather, the awl, the thread — as the path, who realized while making shoes.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Campaka

realization_account.text: A king of Campaka who delighted in the scent of flowers; taught to meditate on the flower's fragrance. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 60): For means and wisdom, which are like clear light, the stream of the guru-river pervades all; from the wish-granting tree of the innate the fruit, the three bodies, is self-clear and wholly complete.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 60 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A king of Campaka who delighted in the scent of flowers; taught to meditate on the flower's fragrance.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Tiruñāṉacampantar
summary: Child-saint and the most prolific Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 1–3); exemplar of the son's path (satputra-mārga, kriyā); champion of Śaivism against the Jains at Madurai.

tradition.text: lived sixteen years

scholarly.text: 7th c.; contemporary of Appar, the Pāṇṭiya Neṭumāṟaṉ and Ciṟuttoṇṭar (Vātāpi, 642)

places: Nallūr Perumaṇam (union with Śiva at his wedding)

realization_account.text: At three, left on the tank's edge at Cīkāḻi, he cried and Umā fed him the milk of divine knowledge in a golden cup; asked who had fed him, he sang his first hymn pointing to Śiva and Umā. He went on pilgrimage with the bard Tirunīlakaṇṭa Yāḻppāṇar, was invited to Madurai by the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār and the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, cured the king's fever with sacred ash, and won the fire and water ordeals against the Jains. At sixteen, at his wedding at Nallūr Perumaṇam, he entered a divine light with his bride and all the guests.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cāmuṇḍa (rasa author)
summary: Author to whom the Rasasaṃketakalikā is attributed.

name: Cāmuṇḍarāya
summary: Minister of the Western Gaṅga kings who erected the colossal image of Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa (c. 981 CE) and wrote the Kannada Cāmuṇḍarāya Purāṇa.

name: Caṇḍakāpāli
summary: The questioner of the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā, who goes to Gheraṇḍa's hut and asks about the yoga of the pot (ghaṭastha-yoga), the cause of knowledge of reality (GS 1.1–2). The name suggests a Kāpālika.

name: Candanā (Candanabālā)
summary: The first nun of Mahāvīra's community and head of its nuns (the Kalpa Sūtra gives 36,000 nuns under her). A princess of Campā sold into slavery, shackled and shaven by a jealous mistress, she fulfilled Mahāvīra's secret vow (abhigraha) by offering him boiled beans from a winnowing basket, ending his long fast; she later took initiation. Śvetāmbara stories tell that she attained omniscience after her pupil Mṛgāvatī did.
alt_names: Vasumatī (her birth name in some accounts)

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience when, asking forgiveness of her pupil Mṛgāvatī who had attained it first, she saw the humility of her disciple (Śvetāmbara account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Caṇḍīdās (the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās)

tradition.text: before Caitanya, who is said to have delighted in his songs; placed at Nānnur (Birbhum) or Chhātnā (Bankura)

scholarly.text: the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās padas are 16th–18th c.; distinct from Baḍu Caṇḍīdās of the Śrīkṛṣṇakīrtan

realization_account.text: A priest of Bāśulī, he loved the washerwoman Rāmī; Sahajiyā tradition makes their love the exemplary practice of prema.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The Bengali poet whom the Sahajiyās claim as their master: lover of the washerwoman Rāmī, singer of the love of man above all; one of several poets called Caṇḍīdās.
notes: The 'Caṇḍīdās problem': several poets used the name; U26 owns Caṇḍīdās as a Vaiṣṇava poet.

name: Candrācārya
summary: The teacher who, according to the closing verses of the Vākyapadīya's second book, recovered the tradition of the Mahābhāṣya from a mountain region and spread it widely after it had declined.
notes: Some identify him with the Buddhist grammarian Candragomin; the identification is doubtful.

name: Candragomin
summary: Lay Yogācāra master and grammarian (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa); Tibetan tradition tells of his long debate with Candrakīrti at Nālandā, Yogācāra against Madhyamaka, and of his devotion to Tārā and Avalokiteśvara.

checks.note: Confirmed: Buddhist grammarian, c. 5th c. CE (Wisdomlib), within the entry's range.

alt_summary: Buddhist lay scholar, author of the Cāndra grammar (his Buddhist works belong to other units).

name: Candragupta Maurya
summary: Founder of the Maurya empire. Digambara tradition (and inscriptions at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa) says he renounced, followed Bhadrabāhu south and died by sallekhanā on Candragiri; Hemacandra's Śvetāmbara account also makes him end his life as a Jain.

name: Candrakīrti

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories tell that he studied under Kamalabuddhi, a disciple of Buddhapālita, became abbot of Nālandā and debated the lay master Candragomin there for years; to show that things lack own-nature he milked a painted cow and distributed the milk to the monks.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly account: 7th c.; the tantric commentator of the same name (Pradīpoddyotana) is regarded by scholars as a later author.
summary: Author of the Prasannapadā and the Madhyamakāvatāra, who defended Buddhapālita's method against Bhāviveka, rejected autonomous inference and own-nature at every level, and became for Tibetan traditions the definitive interpreter of Nāgārjuna (the Prāsaṅgika).

name: Candrakīrti (the tantric)

tradition.text: the Madhyamaka master (tch:candrakirti)

summary: Author of the Pradīpoddyotana on the Guhyasamāja; the tradition identifies him with the Madhyamaka Candrakīrti, disciple of Nāgārjuna; scholars place him c. 9th–10th c.
notes: Homonym: tch:candrakirti (the Madhyamaka author, U40) is kept separate by the scholarly account; the tradition identifies them.

name: Candramati
summary: Author of the Daśapadārthaśāstra, a Vaiśeṣika treatise of ten categories preserved only in Xuanzang's Chinese translation.
notes: The alternative name form is recalled with low confidence.

name: Candrānanda
summary: Author of the Vṛtti on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra that transmits the older recension of the sūtras.

name: Candraprabha
summary: The eighth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the crescent moon. Parents: Mahāsena and Lakṣmaṇā. Born at Candrapurī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as white.

tradition.text: the eighth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Candraśekhara Bhāratī III
summary: Pontiff of Śṛṅgeri (1892–1954), revered in the tradition as a jīvanmukta given to long absorption.

name: Candraśekharendra Sarasvatī
summary: Pontiff of the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi pīṭha (1894–1994), teacher of Advaita and Vedic dharma.

name: Cāndsāi
summary: Muslim tailor who became Śaṅkaradeva's disciple, remembered as proof that refuge was open to all.

name: Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ
summary: Saint of Dvārakā counted third of the five Kṛṣṇas; by Mahānubhāva tradition his spirit entered the dead prince Haripāla, who became Cakradhar.
notes: Distinct from the Vārkarī yogī Cāṅgadev (tch:cangadeva-vatesvar).

name: Cāṅgadev (Cāṅgā Vaṭeśvar)
summary: A yogī said to have lived fourteen hundred years by yogic power, who came riding a tiger with a cobra for a whip to meet Jñāneśvar and found the siblings riding a moving wall; humbled, he took Muktābāī as guru. Jñāneśvar's Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī is addressed to him.
notes: Distinct from the Mahānubhāva Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ of Dvārakā (tch:cangadeva-raul).

name: Caṇṭēcura Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin boy who, tending the village cows, made a sand liṅga and bathed it with their milk; when his father kicked over the milk pots he struck at his father's legs with the staff, which became an axe; Śiva made him Caṇṭēcuran, chief of his attendants, heir to his leftover garlands and offerings.
