realization_account.text: A brahmin boy who, tending the village cows, made a sand liṅga and bathed it with their milk; when his father kicked over the milk pots he struck at his father's legs with the staff, which became an axe; Śiva made him Caṇṭēcuran, chief of his attendants, heir to his leftover garlands and offerings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Caoshan Benji 曹山本寂
summary: Heir of Dongshan and co-founder of the Caodong house; elaborated the five ranks as lord and minister.

name: Caraka
summary: The redactor (pratisaṃskartā) of Agniveśa's tantra: 'the redactor expands what is said briefly and condenses what is too long, and makes an old tantra new' (Ca Si 12.36-37). In the Bhāvaprakāśa he is a portion of the thousand-headed Śeṣa who came to earth 'like a spy' (cara) and was born as a sage's son; Cakrapāṇi salutes the lord of serpents who removed the faults of mind, speech and body by the Pātañjala, the Mahābhāṣya and Caraka's redaction.

tradition.text: an incarnation of Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa)

notes: A Buddhist narrative preserved in Chinese makes a physician Caraka attend King Kaniṣka; scholars differ on whether this is the redactor (scholarly hypothesis, recalled).

name: Carpaṭanātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Carpaṭi in HYP 1.6) to whom Hindi sayings are ascribed (Nāth Siddhoṁ kī Bāniyāṁ); in Chamba tradition the guru of the founder-king of Chamba; also named among alchemical siddhas; one of the Marathi nine Nāths (Carpaṭnāth).
alt_summary: U28 contribution: named among the Mahāsiddhas of HYP 1.6 (Carpaṭi); the text says these Siddhas broke the staff of time by the power of haṭha and roam the universe (HYP 1.9).

Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): cited as a rasa authority in the Rasaratnākara (Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.17: 'what the siddha Carpaṭi taught') and listed as 'Carvaṭi' among those liberated in life by a mercurial body (SDS Raseśvara 12).

name: Cārvāka (the eponymous teacher)
summary: The legendary disciple of Bṛhaspati after whom the school is named; in the Prabodhacandrodaya (Act 2) he is the servant of Great Delusion who spreads the Lokāyata through his pupils. Guṇaratna and others derive the name from 'chewing' (carv) — those who 'swallow' merit, demerit and the unseen — or from 'pleasing speech' (cāru-vāk).
notes: Distinct from tch:carvaka-raksasa of the Mahābhārata; the texts do not identify the two.

name: Cārvāka the rākṣasa (Mahābhārata)
summary: In MBh 12.39 a rākṣasa, friend of Duryodhana, who in the guise of a mendicant (a Sāṃkhya with tuft and triple staff) denounces Yudhiṣṭhira as a kinslayer before the assembled brāhmaṇas and is burnt by their 'hum'; Kṛṣṇa explains that he had won from Brahmā fearlessness from all beings except when he insulted brāhmaṇas. He teaches no doctrine; Duryodhana (9.63.38) calls him 'the wanderer skilled in speech'.
notes: Listed under lin:carvaka only because the school's name coincides; the epic makes no link.

name: Caṭaiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Cuntarar's father, an Ādiśaiva brahmin.

realization_account.text: Cuntarar's father, an Ādiśaiva brahmin.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cāṭila
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 5 (the bridge over the river of existence).
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Catrapa

realization_account.text: A beggar who carried a book (or umbrella) and was taught the Hevajra; low certainty on details. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 23): For the yogin whatever appears is instruction; seeing the unborn is the supreme master; for the childish there is the concept that grasps two, and from it the fruits of virtue and evil arise as two.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 23 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A beggar who carried a book (or umbrella) and was taught the Hevajra; low certainty on details.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Catti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut out the tongues of those who reviled Śiva's devotees.

realization_account.text: He cut out the tongues of those who reviled Śiva's devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Caturbhuja Ṭhākur
summary: Grandson of Śaṅkaradeva, with Puruṣottama a leader of the Puruṣa saṃhati.

name: Caturbhujdās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, son of Kumbhandās.

name: Cauraṅgīnātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Cauraṅgī in HYP 1.5): a prince whose hands and feet were cut off at a stepmother's false accusation and who was restored by the Nāth gurus — known in Punjab as Pūraṇ Bhagat and in Telugu as Sāraṅgadhara. The Prāṇ Saṅkalī is ascribed to him.

realization_account.text: Restored in body by the guru's grace after twelve years of practice (the tradition's story in its several versions).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U44 contribution (the siddha of the eighty-four): No. 10 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A prince falsely accused by his stepmother, whose hands and feet were cut off and who was left in the forest; Mīnapa taught him breath and meditation, Gorakṣa served him, and after twelve years his limbs were restored.
U28 contribution: named among the Mahāsiddhas of HYP 1.5 (Cauraṅgī); the text says these Siddhas broke the staff of time by the power of haṭha and roam the universe (HYP 1.9).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Cekitāna
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army (1.5).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.5.

name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Minister of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (Anapāyaṉ), author of the Periya Purāṇam, the twelfth Tirumuṟai.

realization_account.text: Seeing the king delight in the Jain epic Cīvakacintāmaṇi, he turned him to the lives of Śiva's devotees; at Chidambaram Śiva gave him the first word 'ulakelām' and he completed the work in a year.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cennabasava
summary: Cennabasava (Cennabasavaṇṇa), Basava's nephew, honoured as the master of ṣaṭsthala doctrine; his vacanas are signed Kūḍalacennasaṅgamadēva, and after the Kalyāṇa upheaval he led the śaraṇas with the vacana manuscripts to Uḷavi.

realization_account.text: Son of Basava's sister Akkanāgamma; the Śūnyasampādane has Allama acknowledge his knowledge of the sthalas, and he gives liṅga-initiation to Siddharāma; he attained union at Uḷavi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nampūtirippāṭ
summary: Kerala brahmin of the Cēnnās family — hereditary tantris of the Guruvāyūr temple — and author of the Tantrasamuccaya, the standard manual of Kerala temple ritual.

name: Cēntaṉār
summary: Poet of the Tiruvicaippā and of the benedictory Tiruppallāṇṭu (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cēra king who heard the anklets of Naṭarāja's dance at the end of his daily worship; friend of Cuntarar, he rode with him to Kailāsa on a horse into whose ear he whispered the five syllables, and recited his Ulā there.

realization_account.text: A Cēra king who heard the anklets of Naṭarāja's dance at the end of his daily worship; friend of Cuntarar, he rode with him to Kailāsa on a horse into whose ear he whispered the five syllables, and recited his Ulā there.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ceruttuṇai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut the nose of the Pallava queen who smelled a flower meant for Śiva in the temple at Tiruvārūr.

realization_account.text: He cut the nose of the Pallava queen who smelled a flower meant for Śiva in the temple at Tiruvārūr.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Changchub Dorje, the twelfth Karmapa
summary: Karmapa who travelled with the 8th Situ to Nepal and China and died young.

name: Changkya Rolpai Dorje
summary: Gelug scholar at the Qing court, organiser of the Mongolian translation of the Tengyur; author of a presentation of tenets and of the song 'Recognising the Mother' on the view.

name: Changlu Zongze
summary: Song Chan master, compiler of the Chanyuan qinggui (1103), who founded a Lotus assembly (Lianhua shenghui) for recitation; fifth successor of Huiyuan in Zongxiao's list. His simile of farming and banking for Chan and Pure Land is cited in the Lushan lianzong baojian preface.
notes: Shared with U42.
alt_summary: Yunmen-line master and Pure Land devotee who compiled the Chanyuan qinggui (1103) with the Zuochan yi.

name: Changsem Gyalwa Yeshe (byang sems rgyal ba ye shes)
summary: Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü's successor at Jonang in the Kālacakra lineage.

name: Channa
summary: The charioteer of the bodhisatta's renunciation, later an obstinate monk on whom the 'higher penalty' (brahmadaṇḍa) was imposed after the parinibbāna (DN 16; Cv 11.1.12).
notes: The Channa of SN 22.90 and MN 144 is identified with him by some commentaries; not asserted here.

name: Chapa Chökyi Senge
alt_names: phya pa chos kyi seng ge
summary: Abbot of Sangphu and leading early Tibetan epistemologist, credited with the Collected Topics debate method.

name: Chapaṭa (Saddhammajotipāla)
summary: Burmese monk who studied in Sri Lanka in the late 12th century and returned to Pagan; credited with the Saṅkhepavaṇṇanā on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

name: Charan Singh (Maharaj Charan Singh)
summary: Master at Beas 1951–1990, grandson of Sawan Singh, author of Die to Live and many discourses.

name: Caraṇdās

realization_account.text: As a boy he met the sage Śukadeva in the forest and received initiation; he then practised yoga and devotion for years before teaching.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Delhi Sant, founder of the Caraṇdāsī sampradāya, who joined nirguṇa teaching with Rādhā–Kṛṣṇa devotion and aṣṭāṅga yoga; his guru was Śukadeva, who appeared to him.

name: Chatral Sangye Dorje (bya bral sangs rgyas rdo rje)
summary: Renunciant Dzogchen master, disciple of Khenpo Ngakchung; lived in retreat in the Himalaya.

name: Chekawa Yeshe Dorje
summary: Kadam master who, moved by the line 'giving victory to others, taking defeat upon oneself' of the Eight Verses, trained under Sharawa and composed the Seven-Point Mind Training; the tradition tells that he taught mind training to lepers, who were cured.
alt_names: 'chad kha ba ye shes rdo rje

name: Chengawa Tsultrim Bar
summary: One of the 'three brothers' of the Kadam, Dromtönpa's attendant, source of the oral-instruction (man ngag) Kadam line.

name: Chengyuan
summary: Ascetic Pure Land teacher of Nanyue ('the pratyutpanna master of Nanyue'), teacher of Fazhao; third patriarch in the Fozu tongji list.

name: Che btsan skyes (Chetsen Kye)
summary: Translator named in the colophon of the Dupa Do as having translated it, with Dharmabodhi and Dānarakṣita, from the script of Bruzha.
notes: Name and role taken from the local colophon of Tōh 829.

name: Chetsün Senge Wangchuk (lce btsun seng ge dbang phyug)
summary: Heart-essence master of the 11th-12th c. who received the Vima Nyingthig, had visions of Vimalamitra, and by tradition attained the rainbow body; source of the Chetsün Nyingthig revealed later.

name: Chewu Jixing
summary: Qing Chan master who turned to Pure Land ('true mind for birth and death, arouse bodhicitta, deep faith and vow, hold the name'); twelfth patriarch in the later list.

name: Swami Chinmayananda
summary: Advaita teacher (1916–1993), disciple of Sivananda and Tapovan Maharaj, founder of the Chinmaya Mission, who taught the prasthāna-traya and prakaraṇas in English.

name: Chītsvāmī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a Caube of Mathurā.

name: Chödrak Gyatso, the seventh Karmapa
summary: Scholar Karmapa, author on pramāṇa (the Ocean of Texts on Reasoning).

name: Bodong Chogle Namgyal (bo dong phyogs las rnam rgyal)
summary: Disciple of Dolpopa who succeeded to the Jonang seat and was a prolific Kālacakra scholar.

name: Chögyal Phagpa Lodrö Gyaltsen
summary: Fifth of the five Sakya founders, Sakya Paṇḍita's nephew; imperial preceptor to Kublai Khan, who gave him authority over Tibet; created the 'Phags-pa script' for the Yuan empire and wrote the Explanation of the Knowable.
alt_names: 'gro mgon chos rgyal 'phags pa blo gros rgyal mtshan

name: Chögyam Trungpa
summary: Holder of the Surmang Kagyu and Nyingma lineages who taught in the West (from 1970) and founded Shambhala; recent.

name: Chokgyur Dechen Lingpa (mchog gyur bde chen gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer of the 19th c. whose treasures, many revealed with Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo, were codified by Jamgön Kongtrul (the Chokling Tersar).

name: Chöje Döndrub Rinchen
summary: Tsongkhapa's first teacher in Amdo, who ordained him as a novice and sent him to Central Tibet.

name: Chōsai
summary: Hōnen's disciple of the Kuhon-ji line, known for holding that the various practices are also vowed in the primal vow (shogyō hongan gi).

name: Chöying Dorje, the tenth Karmapa
summary: Painter and sculptor Karmapa who lived years in exile during the wars of the 1640s that brought the Fifth Dalai Lama's government to power.

name: Chuji 處寂
summary: Jingzhong master, teacher of Musang.

name: Cidānanda (Kapūrcand)
summary: Śvetāmbara mystic poet of the 19th c., author of the Cidānanda Bahottarī and (by tradition) a Svarodaya.

name: Cidghanānandanātha
summary: Name under which the Ṣaṭkarmasaṅgraha, a manual of cleansing acts, is transmitted.

name: Cilarāi (Śukladhvaja)
summary: Koch general, brother of Naranārāyaṇa and patron of Śaṅkaradeva, who sheltered him at court.

name: Cimin Huiri

realization_account.text: After travelling to India he prayed at Gandhāra and received a vision of Avalokiteśvara urging him to the Pure Land (as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tang pilgrim to India (702–719) who on his return taught Pure Land practice joined with precepts and study and criticised Chan teachers who rejected recitation as mere form.

name: Cinnambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkabhāṣāprakāśikā on Keśava Miśra's Tarkabhāṣā.

name: Ciṟappuli Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who fed devotees and performed sacrifices for Śiva.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who fed devotees and performed sacrifices for Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Citra Gāṅgyāyani
alt_names: Citra Gārgyāyaṇi (reading of the Advaita-Śāradā text)
summary: A king who, about to sacrifice, questions Śvetaketu on the closed place of the world, then teaches Āruṇi (who comes fuel in hand) the path to the world of brahman (KauU 1.1-7).

checks.note: Located: KauU 1.1. The Advaita-Śāradā text reads 'citro ha vai gārgyāyaṇiḥ', as the alternative name in the entry says.

name: Citsukha
summary: Dialectical Advaitin, author of the Tattvapradīpikā and of commentaries on the Khaṇḍana, the Brahmasiddhi and the Nyāyamakaranda; pupil of Jñānottama.

name: Citta the householder
summary: Householder of Macchikāsaṇḍa, a non-returner, foremost lay Dhamma teacher; his discussions with monks and with the Nigaṇṭha fill SN 41.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Civañāṉa Muṉivar
summary: Monk of the Tiruvāvaṭuturai ātīṉam, the classical scholastic of Tamil Siddhānta: the Civañāṉa Māpāṭiyam and Ciṟṟurai on the Civañāṉa Pōtam, a commentary on the Cittiyār, the first part of the Kāñci Purāṇam, grammatical works and a Tamil rendering of the Tarkasaṅgraha.

name: Ciyuan 慈遠
summary: Disciple of Kuoan who wrote the prose prefaces to the Ten Oxherding Pictures.

name: Ciyun Zunshi
summary: Song Tiantai master who composed Pure Land repentance liturgies and the widely used 'ten recitations' method for lay people each morning.

name: Cokhāmeḷā
summary: Mahār saint of Maṅgaḷveḍhe (d. c. 1338), disciple of Nāmdev, kept outside the temple by caste but devoted to Viṭṭhala; his abhaṅgas voice both love and the pain of exclusion ('the sugarcane is crooked, its juice is not'). He died when a wall he was building collapsed; Nāmdev carried the bones, which murmured 'Viṭṭhala', to Paṇḍharpūr, where his samādhi stands before the temple's gate.

name: Cōmāci Māṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who performed Vedic sacrifices dedicated to Śiva and was a friend of Cuntarar.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who performed Vedic sacrifices dedicated to Śiva and was a friend of Cuntarar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cūḍālā
summary: Queen of Mālava who attained self-knowledge by her own inquiry and powers through breath-discipline; unable to teach her husband Śikhidhvaja as herself, she came to him in the forest disguised as the young brāhmaṇa Kumbha and led him to realization (Mokṣopāya 6.81-114; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha).

checks.note: MU 6.81.12 'mālavānāṃ pure śrīmāñ śikhidhvaja' (queen of Mālava), cūḍālāprabodha 6.82, kumbha 6.90, madanikā 6.110.36.

realization_account.text: Through daily inquiry into what the self is she found the Self and 'shone' so that her husband remarked on her changed radiance (MU 6.82-83 'cūḍālā-prabodha', 'cūḍālātmalābha').
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cūḍāmaṇi Miśra
summary: Author to whom the Rasakāmadhenu is attributed.

name: Culla-Dhammapāla
summary: A later Dhammapāla to whom some attribute the Abhidhamma Anuṭīkā and the Saccasaṅkhepa.

name: Cunda the smith
summary: The smith of Pāvā who served the Buddha his last meal (DN 16); the teaching on purity of AN 10.176 was given to a Cunda the smith of Pāvā.

name: Cunda the novice
summary: Sāriputta's younger brother and attendant who brought his relics to the Buddha (SN 47.13).

name: Cuntaramūrtti (Cuntarar)
summary: Third Tēvāram poet (Tirumuṟai 7); exemplar of the friend's path (sakhā-mārga, yoga); author of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai, the list of devotees on which the cult of the sixty-three rests.

realization_account.text: An Ādiśaiva boy of Tirunāvalūr adopted by the chieftain Naracinka Muṉaiyaraiyar; on his wedding day an old brahmin produced a deed showing Cuntarar's grandfather had pledged his line as the brahmin's slaves; followed to Tiruveṇṇeynallūr, the old man vanished into the temple — Śiva himself — and Cuntarar sang 'Pittā' ('Madman!'). Śiva later acted as his messenger to his wife Paravai. With Cēramāṉ Perumāḷ he rode to Kailāsa on a white elephant sent by Śiva.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cūṛāmaṇi Nām (Muktāmaṇi Nām)
summary: Son of Dharamdās, first of the forty-two ācāryas (vaṃś) of the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth.

name: Dachuan Puji 大川普濟
summary: Compiler of the Wudeng huiyuan (1252).

name: Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa
summary: Seer who taught the honey-doctrine (madhu-vidyā) to the two Aśvins through a horse's head, as recounted with Ṛgvedic verses at BAU 2.5.16-19.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 2.5.16-19 ('idaṃ vai tan madhu dadhyaṅṅ ātharvaṇo 'śvibhyām uvāca'). The alternative name Dadhīci is in the quoted verse at 2.5.17 ('dadhīce 'śvyaṃ śiraḥ').

name: Dādū Dayāl

tradition.text: 1544–1603; found floating on the Sābarmatī by the Nāgar brahmin Lodīrām (panth account)

scholarly.text: 1544–1603, probably born into a Muslim cotton-carder family

realization_account.text: At eleven, an old man (Buḍḍhan, 'the old one'; some say Kabīr or God himself) appeared to him, gave him pān and blessed him; seven years later he appeared again and Dādū's realization was complete; he met the guru 'in the unseen' (gaib).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Cotton-carder (dhuniyā) saint of Rajasthan, founder of the Dādū Panth: taught remembrance of the one Rām of Hindu and Turk, impartiality (nipakh), the body as the true mosque and temple, and dying to self; met Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri (1585).

name: Dagmema
alt_names: bdag med ma (Tib., 'Nairātmyā', her name as Marpa's consort)

realization_account.text: She interceded for Milarepa and helped forge a letter so that Ngok Chöku Dorje would teach him; Marpa later said that without his permission the teaching could not bear fruit.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Marpa's wife, remembered in the Life of Milarepa for her compassion toward Milarepa during his ordeals; in some accounts she dissolves into Marpa at death.

name: Dahui Zonggao 大慧宗杲

realization_account.text: On hearing Yuanwu quote 'a warm breeze comes from the south, and the palace pavilion grows slightly cool' he had a breakthrough, later deepened on the case 'being and non-being are like wisteria clinging to a tree' (tradition's account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Heir of Yuanwu who systematised 'Chan of observing the phrase' (kanhua Chan): concentrate the great doubt on the critical phrase ('wu') throughout daily life until it shatters in awakening; denounced 'heretical silent-illumination Chan'. The tradition says he burned the Blue Cliff Record's printing blocks.

name: Dainichi Nōnin 大日能忍
summary: Self-awakened founder of the Daruma school who obtained a certificate by proxy from Zhuoan Deguang; criticised by Eisai.

name: Daityāri Ṭhākura
summary: Author of a verse life of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva.

name: Daivarāti Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā instructed by Yājñavalkya in the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306).

checks.note: Located as described.

notes: Whether he is the Upaniṣadic Janaka (tch:janaka) is not asserted.

name: Dakpo Tashi Namgyal
alt_names: dwags po bkra shis rnam rgyal
summary: Abbot of Daklha Gampo, scholar of the Dakpo Kagyu, author of Moonbeams of Mahāmudrā and of works on the Six Yogas and on tantra.

name: Dakṣa Prajāpati
summary: The Prajāpati who received Āyurveda from Brahmā and taught it to the Aśvins (Ca Sū 1.4; Su Sū 1.20; AHS Sū 1.3); the Bhāvaprakāśa names him Dakṣa.
notes: Caraka, Suśruta and Vāgbhaṭa say only 'Prajāpati'; Bhāvaprakāśa Pūrva 1.6 and the commentators say Dakṣa.

name: Dakṣiṇā Prājāpatyā
summary: Named (beside Divya Āṅgirasa) as ṛṣikā of the hymn in praise of the sacrificial gift, RV 10.107.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'divya āṅgirasaḥ, dakṣiṇā vā prājāpatyā'.

name: Thubten Gyatso, Thirteenth Dalai Lama
summary: Dalai Lama who reformed the monastic examinations and led Tibet through the early 20th century.

name: Tenzin Gyatso, Fourteenth Dalai Lama
summary: Present Dalai Lama (b. 1935); Gelug teacher of the lamrim, the Three Principal Aspects and mind training worldwide. (Entry owned by U52; U47 adds the lineage link.)

name: Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, the Great Fifth Dalai Lama
summary: Became ruler of Tibet in 1642 with the support of Güshri Khan, founding the Ganden Phodrang government; built the Potala; author of the Sacred Word of Mañjuśrī lamrim and many works; also a holder of Nyingma lineages.
alt_names: ngag dbang blo bzang rgya mtsho
alt_summary: Gelug ruler of Tibet who was also a Nyingma practitioner and visionary, recording pure-vision treasures (the Sangwa Gyachen) and patronizing Mindroling and Dorje Drak.

name: Kelsang Gyatso, Seventh Dalai Lama
summary: Scholar and poet of the Gelug, author of songs and commentaries on tantra and the lamrim.

name: Ḍalhaṇa
summary: Author of the Nibandhasaṅgraha on the Suśruta Saṃhitā.

name: Damei Fachang 大梅法常
summary: Heir of Mazu who awoke at 'this very mind is buddha' and kept to it when Mazu switched to 'neither mind nor buddha'; Mazu said 'the plum is ripe'.

name: Dāmodara Paṇḍita
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Dāmodara (author of the Saṅgītadarpaṇa)
summary: Author of the Saṅgītadarpaṇa.

name: Dāmodaradās Harsānī
summary: Vallabha's first disciple, initiated with brahmasambandha the morning after the Gokul revelation (tradition).

name: Dāmodaradeva
summary: Brahmin preacher (tradition 1488–1598), founder of the Brahma saṃhati; the Mahāpuruṣīyā account makes him Śaṅkaradeva's disciple, while his own followers (Dāmodarīyā) stress his independence.

name: Dampa Kunga (dam pa kun dga')
summary: Principal Tibetan disciple of Padampa Sangye at Dingri and holder of the later transmission of Pacification.

name: Daṇḍin
summary: Author of the Kāvyādarśa; also credited with the prose romance Daśakumāracarita.

name: Danxia Tianran 丹霞天然
summary: Studied with Mazu and Shitou; burned a wooden buddha for warmth — 'I am burning it for relics'.

name: Danxia Zichun 丹霞子淳
summary: Caodong master, teacher of Hongzhi and Zhenxie.

name: Danyuan Yingzhen 耽源應真
summary: Attendant of Huizhong who passed the 97 circle-figures to Yangshan (Rentian yanmu).

name: Dao'an
summary: Leading Chinese monk of the 4th c., cataloguer and organiser of monastic rules, teacher of Huiyuan; he himself vowed to be born in Maitreya's Tuṣita heaven.

name: Daochuo

realization_account.text: Tradition says that at Xuanzhong si, reading the inscription on Tanluan's deeds (609), he turned to the Pure Land at forty-eight, lectured on the Contemplation Sūtra some two hundred times and recited the name 70,000 times a day, counting with beans (Xu gaoseng zhuan; later accounts).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Master who in the Anle ji taught that in the last age of the Dharma the holy path can hardly be realised and only the Pure Land gate is passable; that Amitābha is a reward-body buddha; that ten continuous recitations suffice even for evil-doers. Popularised counting recitations (with beans or a rosary). Fourth of the seven Shinshū masters.
notes: Counting details (70,000; beans) are from biographies and recalled, low-moderate confidence.

name: Daojing
summary: Tang monk named with Shandao (善道) as compiler of the Nianfo jing (T1966).

name: Daosheng
summary: Chinese monk (c. 355-434), disciple of Kumārajīva, who taught that even icchantikas have buddha-nature and can become buddhas and that awakening is sudden, before the full Nirvāṇa Sūtra reached the south; expelled from the Jiankang saṅgha, he was vindicated when Dharmakṣema's version arrived containing that teaching.

realization_account.text: Chinese accounts say that on Tiger Hill the stones nodded when he preached that icchantikas have buddha-nature
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Daoxin 道信
summary: Fourth patriarch, who settled on Mount Shuangfeng (Huangmei) with a large community; taught 'guarding the one without moving' and the one-practice samādhi (Lengqie shizi ji). When a novice he asked Sengcan for liberation and was asked 'who binds you?'

name: Daoxuan
summary: Founder of the Nanshan Vinaya school on Mount Zhongnan, who made the Four-Part Vinaya the standard monastic code of China; also a historian (Xu gaoseng zhuan).
alt_summary: Vinaya master and historian, author of the Xu gaoseng zhuan with the earliest Bodhidharma and Huike biographies.

name: Daoyu 道育
summary: With Huike one of Bodhidharma's two disciples named in the Xu gaoseng zhuan.

name: Daoyuan 道原
summary: Compiler of the Jingde chuandeng lu (1004), in the Fayan line.

name: Dārā Shikoh
summary: Mughal prince (1615–1659) who with pandits translated some fifty Upaniṣads into Persian (Sirr-i Akbar, 1657).

queries: Sirr-i Akbar Dara Shikoh 1657 fifty Upanishads
checks.note: Confirmed: Mughal prince (1615-1659) who translated about fifty Upaniṣads into Persian (Sirr-i Akbar, 1657).

name: Dārikapa

realization_account.text: A king of Pāṭaliputra who, with his minister Ḍeṅgi, became Lūipa's disciple and served a temple courtesan for twelve years; a lineage holder of Lūipa's Cakrasaṃvara and a Caryāgīti poet. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 77): Great bliss is within oneself but unrealized, obscured by delusion; one who wants bliss and clarity should gather the accumulations of merit and gnosis; without the two accumulations, though one strives for a hundred lives, without a guru one will not realize great bliss.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 77 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A king of Pāṭaliputra who, with his minister Ḍeṅgi, became Lūipa's disciple and served a temple courtesan for twelve years; a lineage holder of Lūipa's Cakrasaṃvara and a Caryāgīti poet.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Dariyā Sāhib of Bihar
summary: Sant of Dharkandhā (Shahabad, Bihar), founder of a Dariyā panth, teacher of the Name and the inner regions.

name: Dariyāv Sāhib of Mārvāṛ
summary: Sant of Rain (Marwar), founder of the Rain seat of the Rāmsnehīs.

name: Darma Dode

realization_account.text: Knowing the transference into another body from his father, at death he transferred his consciousness into a pigeon and then into a brahmin boy's body in India (Tiphupa); after him the practice of grong 'jug is said to have ceased in Tibet.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Marpa's son and intended heir, who died young after a fall from a horse; by the tradition's account he used the practice of 'entering another's body' (grong 'jug), first entering a dead pigeon that flew to India and then the corpse of a young brahmin, who became Tiphupa.
notes: The claim that transference into another body ended with him is the tradition's account (low).

name: Darshan Singh
summary: Son of Kirpal Singh; founded the Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission (1974); Urdu poet.

name: Dāruka
summary: A gaṇa dear to Śiva, paired with Reṇuka among the pramathas; Reṇuka's leap over him in Śiva's assembly is the occasion of Reṇuka's descent (SSM 2.27; 3.67–77).
notes: In Pañcācārya yuga-lists Dāruka is also named among the ācāryas of an earlier age (low confidence).

name: Dattātreya
summary: Son of Atri and Anasūyā, counted the sixth avatāra in the Bhāgavata (1.3.11: he taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others); Yadu and the Haihayas gained yogic powers from him (2.7.4). The tradition identifies him with the unnamed avadhūta who teaches King Yadu his twenty-four teachers (Bhāgavata 11.7-9), and ascribes to him the Avadhūta Gītā and the Jīvanmukta Gītā. Revered as the ādiguru of the Datta tradition and in the Nāth lineages.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of darsana, avadhuta, jabala, bhiksuka, naradaparivrajaka, sandilya, dattatreya, in the roles the summary gives. Śāṇḍilya 3 (the e-text's ch. 3) gives the etymology: datta, and the son of Atri born of Anasūyā. A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

BhP 1.3.11 'ṣaṣṭham atrer apatyatvaṃ ... ānvīkṣikīm alarkāya prahlādādibhya ūcivān' verified. The Avadhūta Gītā 8.28 names 'dattātreyāvadhūta' as its maker. The identification with the avadhūta of BhP 11.7 is the tradition's, as the entry says.
BhP 1.3.11 (sixth; ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others) and MkP 38-43 (teaching to Alarka) located.

realization_account.text: Son of Atri and Anasūyā (a portion of Viṣṇu; in some accounts of the Trimūrti), the sixth avatāra who 'taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others' (BhP 1.3.11); an avadhūta who hid his yoga under outward impurity (MkP 16-19); in the Bhāgavata he tells of his twenty-four teachers (BhP 11.7-9, U06).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The avadhūta yogin of the Purāṇas whose teaching to Alarka (MkP 37-43) is the Mārkaṇḍeya's yoga: discrimination of self and body, posture, breath, dhāraṇā, obstacles, powers, Oṃ and the signs of death.

U28 contribution: the teacher of the Dattātreyayogaśāstra, sitting in padmāsana under a mango tree in the Naimiṣa forest when Sāṅkṛti comes to learn yoga (DYŚ 2–8); he teaches the four yogas and holds rājayoga the best.

Son of Atri and Anasūyā, regarded as a form of Viṣṇu (or of the trimūrti) who 'gave himself' (datta) to Atri; in the minor Upaniṣads he teaches Sāṅkṛti the eightfold yoga (Darśana) and the nature of the avadhūta (Avadhūta), is named among the paramahaṃsas who live with unmanifest marks (Jābāla 6, Bhikṣuka, Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86), and is the 'most manifest' form of Brahman in Śāṇḍilya 3.
U23 contribution: in the Tripurā Rahasya he teaches Paraśurāma the knowledge and worship of Tripurā; Śrīvidyā tradition links the Kalpasūtra to his teaching.
In the Mahānubhāva reckoning, the second of the five incarnations (pañca-kṛṣṇa) of Parameśvara, eternally present at Māhūr, whose grace descends to the later incarnations.

U21 contribution: in Marathi Nāth tradition Dattātreya instructs the Nāths (Navanātha Bhaktisāra) and appears with Gorakṣa (Gorakṣaguṭikā 1.24); Aghora regards him as ādiguru, who appeared to Kīnārām at Girnar and whose form was Bābā Kālūrām.
notes: U26 contribution (Mahānubhāva view) only.

name: Dattila
summary: Author of the Dattilam on gāndharva; named among Bharata's sons in the Nāṭyaśāstra and among music's authorities (ŚR 1.1.16).

name: Daulatrām (author of the Chahḍhālā)
summary: Hindi Digambara poet (1798–1866), author of the Chahḍhālā (1834).
notes: Distinct from the 18th-c. Daulatrām Kāslīvāl.

name: Dayābāī
summary: Woman Sant, disciple (and kinswoman) of Caraṇdās, author of the Dayā Bodh.

name: Dayānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Founder of the Ārya Samāj (1875); commented on the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda and wrote the Ṛgvedādibhāṣyabhūmikā, teaching that the Saṃhitās alone are revelation, that they teach one God under many names, and that Vedic study is open to all.

queries: Dayananda Saraswati 1824 1883 Arya Samaj founded 1875 Rigvedadi Bhashya Bhumika
checks.note: Confirmed: 1824–1883; founded the Ārya Samāj (Bombay, April 1875); Ṛgvedādibhāṣyabhūmikā 1876–78; commentaries on RV and YV.

name: Swami Dayananda Saraswati (Arsha Vidya)
summary: Advaita teacher (1930–2015) of the traditional method of teaching (sampradāya) through the texts; founder of the Arsha Vidya Gurukulam. Distinct from the 19th-c. founder of the Ārya Samāj.

name: Dayang Jingxuan 大陽警玄
summary: Caodong master who, having no heir, entrusted his robe to the Linji master Fushan Fayuan to pass to Touzi Yiqing.

name: Gao'an Dayu 高安大愚
summary: Heir of Guizong; at his words Linji awoke and exclaimed 'there isn't much to Huangbo's buddha-dharma'.

name: Dazhu Huihai 大珠慧海
summary: Heir of Mazu, author of the Dunwu rudao yaomen lun; 'I have no treasure — your own treasure house is complete'.

name: Deshan Xuanjian 德山宣鑒
summary: Diamond-Sūtra scholar who burned his commentaries after awakening when Longtan blew out his candle; known for the stick ('thirty blows').

name: Deshan Yuanmi 德山緣密
summary: Heir of Yunmen who divided his statement into the three phrases (Rentian yanmu).

name: Deshin Shekpa, the fifth Karmapa
summary: Invited by the Yongle emperor to Nanjing (1407); by the tradition's account the emperor, seeing the ḍākinī-woven crown above the Karmapa's head, had a material replica made — the black crown of the ceremony.

name: Desi Sangye Gyatso (sde srid sangs rgyas rgya mtsho)
summary: Regent of the Fifth Dalai Lama's government, scholar of medicine and astronomy; author of the Blue Beryl commentary, the Supplement to the Oral Instructions and the history of medicine (Khogbug); he commissioned the medical paintings and founded the Chakpori medical college in Lhasa (1696).

name: Deumar Geshe Tenzin Phuntsok (de'u dmar dge bshes bstan 'dzin phun tshogs)

scholarly.text: b. 1672 or 1673 (as recalled); active early 18th c.

summary: Eighteenth-century physician and author of the materia medica 'Crystal Mirror and Crystal Rosary'.

name: Devabodha
summary: Early commentator on the Mahābhārata (Jñānadīpikā).

checks.note: Least-sure item: the earliest extant Mahābhārata commentator (Jñānadīpikā), c. 11th c. Lineage "epic-teaching" is the unit's choice; his school is not established.

name: Devacandra (Kharatara Gaccha)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk-poet of the Kharatara Gaccha, author of philosophical Gujarati hymns (Covīsī), the Adhyātmagītā and the Nayacakrasāra.

name: Devacandra Sūri (teacher of Hemacandra)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk who initiated the boy Cāṅgadeva as Somacandra (later Hemacandra).
notes: Distinct from the 18th-c. Kharatara author Devacandra (tch:devacandra-kharatara).

name: Devācārya
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Brahma Sūtra commentary Siddhāntajāhnavī.

name: Devadatta
summary: The Buddha's cousin and monk who sought leadership of the Saṅgha, plotted against the Buddha with Ajātasattu, proposed five compulsory austerities and caused the first schism (Cv 7).

name: Devahūti
summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of the sage Kardama and mother of Kapila; the questioner of the Kapila Gītā, who asks for a devotion suited to her and attains liberation.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Questioner of the Kapila Gītā (3.25.7 ff.; her praise 3.33.1-8); standard Bhāgavata genealogy (daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama).
BhP 3.28-29 addressed to Devahūti located.

realization_account.text: Following her son's instruction she practised devotional yoga at Bindusaras, her body withered unnoticed, and she attained the Lord; the place became Siddhapada (Bhāgavata 3.33).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama and mother of Kapila, who asked her son for the path to liberation, received the Kapila Gītā and attained perfection through its yoga (BhP 3.25-33).

name: Devala (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. The Mahābhārata presents an Asita Devala as teacher of related doctrines; the identity is uncertain.

name: Devānampiya Tissa
summary: King of Laṅkā converted by Mahinda; founder of the Mahāvihāra at Anurādhapura (chronicle account).

name: Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Smṛticandrikā.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: author of the Smṛticandrikā, 13th c. (Wisdomlib; another estimate 1150–1200).

name: Dēvara Dāsimayya
summary: The weaver-saint (Jēḍara Dāsimayya) of Muddanūru, reckoned by the tradition among the earliest vacanakāras, before Basava; his vacanas, signed Rāmanātha, deny that the self is male or female.

tradition.text: before Basava

scholarly.text: 10th–11th c. (debated; some place him closer to Basava)

notes: Whether 'Dēvara' and 'Jēḍara' Dāsimayya are one person is debated.

name: Devarāja Yajvan
summary: Commentator on the Nighaṇṭu.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: author of the Nighaṇṭu-nirvacana (12th c., or before the 14th c.).

name: Devarddhigaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
summary: Presided over the council at Valabhī (980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa, i.e. 453 or 466 CE) at which the Śvetāmbara canon was written down, reconciling the Māthurī and Vālabhī recensions; some identify him with Devavācaka, author of the Nandī.

tradition.text: 980 or 993 years after the nirvāṇa

name: Devaśarman

tradition.text: A hundred years after the parinirvāṇa (Chinese tradition; low confidence)

summary: Author of the Vijñānakāya, one of the six 'feet' of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma, which refutes the denial of past and future and the doctrine of the person.
notes: Known only from later lists (from memory).
alt_summary: Early commentator on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā whose commentary is lost; known from Avalokitavrata's list of commentators.

name: Devasena
summary: Digambara author of the Darśanasāra (933), Ārādhanāsāra, Tattvasāra and Ālāpapaddhati.
alt_summary: Author of the Darśanasāra (933 CE) on the origin of sects, and of the Ārādhanāsāra, Tattvasāra, Ālāpapaddhati and (attributed) Bhāvasaṃgraha.

name: Devasvāmin
summary: Horā author named by Varāhamihira among those who taught longevity (BJ 7.7).
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.
alt_summary: Author of a bhāṣya on the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa.

name: Devavācaka
summary: Author of the Nandī Sūtra (c. 5th c. CE); sometimes identified with Devarddhigaṇi.

name: Devendrasūri
summary: Tapā Gaccha ācārya, author of the new Karmagranthas.
alt_summary: Pupil of Jagaccandra, author of the 'new' Karmagranthas on karma doctrine (13th c.).

name: Devendrabuddhi
summary: Dharmakīrti's disciple and first commentator on the Pramāṇavārttika; Tibetan tradition says Dharmakīrti rejected his first two drafts and accepted the third, saying that the literal sense was grasped but not the intent.

name: Devendragaṇi (Nemicandra)
summary: Author of the Sukhabodhā commentary on the Uttarādhyayana (1073), with its Prakrit narratives.

name: The Goddess (Devī)
summary: The supreme Goddess, appearing as Bhuvaneśvarī, who teaches Himālaya and the gods in the Devī Gītā (Devī Bhāgavata 7.31-40): she is consciousness, supreme Brahman, whose power is māyā.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Speaker of the Devī Gītā; Bhuvaneśvarī named at DBhP 7.31.50.

name: Dhahuli

realization_account.text: A rope-maker with blistered hands. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 70): Union-awareness, the treasury of jewels, the non-dual state, is not found by seeking; like a mind that has given up activity, as it is placed, so it is blissful.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 70 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A rope-maker with blistered hands.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Dhammadinnā
summary: Foremost nun among Dhamma teachers; her answers to Visākha in MN 44 were approved by the Buddha; verse at Thig 1.12.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Luang Por Dhammajayo
summary: Thai monk (b. 1944), co-founder (1970) and long-time abbot of Wat Phra Dhammakaya.

name: Dhammapāla

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE (contested; some place him later)

summary: Commentator of Badaratittha (near Kāñcīpuram in South India) who wrote the Paramatthadīpanī on seven Khuddaka books, the Visuddhimagga sub-commentary Paramatthamañjūsā and sub-commentaries on the Nikāya commentaries.
notes: Whether the Khuddaka commentator and the ṭīkā author are one person is debated by scholars.

name: Dhamupa (Dhāma?)

realization_account.text: Not identified with certainty: Tōh 2292's 'Dhamu' may be Abhayadatta's Dharmapa (36) or the Caryāgīti poet Dhāmapa. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 36): From duality comes the poison of ignorance, which constantly seizes arisen awareness; the light of the guru's speech clears the poison-disease of the delusion of appearance and existence.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 36 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Not identified with certainty: Tōh 2292's 'Dhamu' may be Abhayadatta's Dharmapa (36) or the Caryāgīti poet Dhāmapa.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Dhanañjaya
summary: Author of the Daśarūpaka at the court of Muñja of Mālava.

name: Dhanapati Sūri
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya.

checks.note: Least-sure item: exists as an Advaita sub-commentator on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya. Dates not firmly established; one academic source gives 1750–1850.

name: Dhanika
summary: Brother of Dhanañjaya and author of the Avaloka commentary on the Daśarūpaka.

name: Dhannā
summary: Jat farmer devotee of Rajasthan counted among Rāmānanda's disciples; the story of the stone that ate his offering; hymns in the Ādi Granth.
alt_summary: Jāṭ farmer of Rajasthan whose simple faith made God eat his offering and tend his field; counted Rāmānanda's disciple in the Bhaktamāl; hymns in the Sikh scripture (context).

name: Piḷḷai Uṟaṅgāvilli Dāsar
summary: Wrestler of Uṟaiyūr whom, the tradition says, Rāmānuja turned from infatuation with his wife's eyes to the eyes of Raṅganātha; an exemplar of devotion regardless of birth.

name: Dhanvantari (Divodāsa, king of Kāśī)
summary: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): 'I am Dhanvantari, the first god, remover of old age, disease and death for the immortals, come again to earth to teach the limb of surgery with the other limbs' (Su Sū 1.21). As King Divodāsa of Kāśī he taught Aupadhenava, Vaitaraṇa, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata, Karavīrya, Gopurarakṣita, Suśruta and others (Su Sū 1.3), having learnt Āyurveda from Indra (Su Sū 1.20); the Bhāvaprakāśa tells how Indra sent him to be born in Kāśī.
notes: Ca Śā 6.21 cites Dhanvantari's view that all limbs of the embryo form at once.
alt_summary: The physician of the gods, counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars in the popular list, with a samādhi place at Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil, the shrine of Śiva as the divine physician.
places: Vaitīsvaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list
alt_notes: U22 contribution; the Āyurvedic account belongs to U30. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Dharamdās

tradition.text: Kabīr's contemporary

scholarly.text: 16th c. (if historical); the Dharamdāsī texts in his name are later

summary: Wealthy merchant (of Bāndhavgaṛh) who became Kabīr's chief disciple; the Anurāg Sāgar is Kabīr's teaching to him; his line of forty-two generations of ācāryas leads the Dharamdāsī Kabīr Panth.

name: Dharasena
summary: Digambara teacher at the Candra cave of Girinagar (Girnār) who knew part of the Pūrvas; fearing the loss of scripture he summoned two monks, tested them with defective spells which they corrected, and taught them the Karmaprābhṛta, which they set down as the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama.

tradition.text: c. 683 years after the nirvāṇa

name: Dharma (the god; Yama Dharmarāja)
summary: The deity Dharma, father of Yudhiṣṭhira; he tests his son as the Yakṣa at the lake (3.297–298) and as the dog on the great departure (17.3); Vidura is his incarnation (1.100.28).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Dharmadāsa
summary: 17th-c. Sthānakavāsī founder-figure whose twenty-two disciples are said to have headed the 'twenty-two groups' (bāīs ṭolā).

name: Dharmadhvaja Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who claims to be liberated while ruling and is tested by the ascetic Sulabhā (12.308).

checks.note: Located as described (he names Pañcaśikha as his teacher in 12.308).

name: Dharmagupta
alt_names: Fahu 法護 / Tanwude 曇無德
summary: Eponymous founder of the Dharmaguptaka; Vasumitra says the school claimed Maudgalyāyana as its teacher.

name: Dharmakīrti

scholarly.text: c. 600–660 CE (older view c. 530–600; E. Frauwallner 600–660; H. Krasser argued for c. 550–610)

places: Trimalaya / Cūḍāmaṇi in the south (birthplace in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: Born to a brahmin family in the south, he mastered the Vedas and, disillusioned, took up Buddhism; to learn his opponents' doctrine he served in disguise in the household of the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila; he heard the Pramāṇasamuccaya from Īśvarasena, understood it better than his teacher, and with his permission composed the Pramāṇavārttika, defeating many opponents in debate; he died in Kaliṅga.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Bu ston; Tāranātha)

summary: The most influential Buddhist epistemologist, author of 'seven treatises on valid cognition': he grounded inference in necessary connection by identity or causality, recast exclusion, proved momentariness from causal efficacy, argued for rebirth and for the Buddha as a person of valid cognition, and refuted God and the authorless Veda; one of the Tibetan 'six ornaments'.
notes: The Kumārila service story is chronologically doubtful and is the tradition's.

name: Dharmakṣema
summary: Indian monk (385-433) in the Northern Liang capital Guzang who translated the 40-fascicle Mahāparinirvāṇa (421), the Golden Light, the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka, the Mahāmegha and the Upāsakaśīla.

name: Dharmamegha Āraṇya
summary: Successor of Hariharānanda Āraṇya at the Kāpil Maṭh, Madhupur (recalled; verify).

name: Dharmanandi
summary: Tokharian monk who recited the Ekottarikāgama for translation (384–385).

name: Dharmanātha
summary: Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the Dharamnāthī panth; tradition says he performed austerities on Dhinodhar hill in Kutch, where his seat remains.
alt_summary: The fifteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the thunderbolt (vajra). Parents: Bhānu and Suvratā. Born at Ratnapurī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fifteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Dharmapa

realization_account.text: Abhayadatta's 'eternal student' (a scholar who went blind?) or the Caryāgīti's Dhāmapa; identification uncertain. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 48): Into the vessel of the phenomena of appearance and existence pour the butter of bodhicitta; on the wick of the six consciousnesses kindle the fire of non-dual gnosis: the darkness of conceptual delusion is destroyed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 48 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Abhayadatta's 'eternal student' (a scholar who went blind?) or the Caryāgīti's Dhāmapa; identification uncertain.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Dharmapāla (Yogācāra)

scholarly.text: c. 530–561 CE (Xuanzang's report that he died young; dates debated)

summary: Nālandā master whose interpretation of the Thirty Verses — four divisions of cognition, both innate and newly perfumed seeds — Xuanzang adopted as orthodox in the Cheng weishi lun; teacher of Śīlabhadra.
notes: Not the same as the Pāli commentator Dhammapāla (tch:dhammapala) or the Bengal king Dharmapāla.

name: Dharmarāja Adhvarīndra
summary: Author of the Vedāntaparibhāṣā, manual of Advaita epistemology.

name: Dharmarakṣa
summary: Yuezhi-descended monk of Dunhuang (c. 233-310) who translated the Lotus (286), the 25,000-line Perfection of Wisdom (Guangzan, 286), the Lalitavistara, the Daśabhūmika and many others.

name: Dharmarakṣita (Atiśa's teacher)
summary: Indian master said to have given away his own flesh out of compassion; by tradition the author of the Wheel of Sharp Weapons and the Peacock's Neutralizing of Poison and a teacher of Atiśa in mind training.
notes: Distinct from other Dharmarakṣitas (translators); historicity uncertain.

name: Dharmasiṃha
summary: 17th-c. Sthānakavāsī founder-figure (Dariyāpurī sampradāya), author of vernacular glosses on the Āgamas.

name: Dharmaśrī
summary: Author of the Abhidharmahṛdaya, the first verse digest of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma.

name: Dharmatrāta
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: dharmas passing through the three times change their mode of being (bhāva) but not their substance, as a gold vessel broken and remade (AKBh 5.26). Yaśomitra credits an elder Dharmatrāta with arranging the Udānavarga; he is also counted among the Dārṣṭāntikas.

name: Dharmatrāta (author of the Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya)
summary: Gandhāran master who enlarged Dharmaśrī's Abhidharmahṛdaya with Vibhāṣā material; distinct from the Vibhāṣā master of the same name.

name: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā (dharmavyādha)
summary: A meat-seller who, living by his inherited work, serving his parents and speaking truth, teaches the brāhmaṇa Kauśika dharma, karma and liberation (3.198–206).

checks.note: Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text

alt_summary: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā who teaches the proud brāhmaṇa Kauśika the dharma of one's own station and of service to parents (Mahābhārata 3.198-206).

name: Dharmodgata
summary: The bodhisattva of the city Gandhavatī who teaches the perfection of wisdom to Sadāprarudita: the Tathāgatas neither come nor go, like a mirage (Aṣṭa ch. 31).
alt_names: Fashang 法上 / Tanwujie 曇無竭

name: Dharmottara
summary: Kashmiri(?) logician whose commentaries on the Nyāyabindu and Pramāṇaviniścaya shaped later Indian and early Tibetan epistemology; he stressed that a means of knowledge makes one attain (prāpaka) its object.

name: Dhelipa

realization_account.text: An oil-presser (teli) taught to press out concepts as he pressed oil; identification by name and position (low). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 62): One is buddha from the beginning; by the power of realization it is dharmatā; by the innate received in consecration, Vajradhara seals (all) with the unborn.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 62 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). An oil-presser (teli) taught to press out concepts as he pressed oil; identification by name and position (low).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Ḍheṇḍhaṇa
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 33 (the riddle song).
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Ḍeṅgipa

realization_account.text: A brahmin minister who, with his king (Dārikapa), became a disciple of Lūipa and was sold as a servant to a courtesan, threshing rice for twelve years; he realized in that service. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 31): If horses and elephants are like the ocean, there is great bliss; if monkeys and children are like drawings on water, they are concepts; if river, sun and medicine are alike they are not divided; by crest, eye and wheel the fruit is gained.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 31 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A brahmin minister who, with his king (Dārikapa), became a disciple of Lūipa and was sold as a servant to a courtesan, threshing rice for twelve years; he realized in that service.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The song's imagery is obscure to the unit; paraphrase is literal and tentative.

name: Dhobīpa

realization_account.text: A washerman taught to see his washing as the purification of mind. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 28): Though one washes it for a long time, charcoal does not turn white by nature; the nature, wholly pure emptiness, is pure; the guru's instruction is the best washer of the nature.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 28 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A washerman taught to see his washing as the purification of mind.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The washing imagery confirms the identification with Abhayadatta's washerman.

name: Dhokaripa

realization_account.text: A pot-bearer who carried a pot everywhere; taught to see it as the vessel of dharmadhātu. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 49): Into the vessel of the nature of dharmadhātu put the substance of awareness, the dharmakāya; the fruit of expanse and awareness together fortunate yogins realize by awareness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 49 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A pot-bearer who carried a pot everywhere; taught to see it as the vessel of dharmadhātu.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The vessel imagery fits the pot-bearer.

name: Dhṛṣṭadyumna
summary: Son of Drupada and Droṇa's intelligent disciple, who arrayed the Pāṇḍava army (1.3); blows his conch (1.17).
notes: Identified as the drupadaputra of 1.3 by the epic context. Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.3, 1.17.

name: Dhṛṣṭaketu
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army (1.5).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.5.

name: Dhṛtaka (Tiduojia 提多迦)
summary: Fifth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 5.

name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The blind Kuru king, father of Duryodhana; hearer of the Gītā through Sañjaya, of Vidura's counsel (5.33–40), Sanatsujāta's teaching (5.41–45) and Vidura's consolations (11.2–7); he later retires to the forest (Āśramavāsika).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Located as hearer of Vidura, Sanatsujāta and Sañjaya.

alt_summary: The king whose question to Sañjaya opens the text: what did my people and the sons of Pāṇḍu do at Kurukṣetra, the field of dharma? (1.1); addressed by Sañjaya as 'lord of the earth' and 'Bhārata'.
Addressed as 'king' by Sañjaya in the narration of the universal form (11.9); his sons are seen entering the mouths of the fierce form (11.26).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.1, 1.19, 1.20.

name: Dhruva
summary: Son of King Uttānapāda; slighted by his stepmother, he went to the forest as a child, was initiated by Nārada (BhP 4.8) - or taught by the seven sages (VP 1.11-12) - and by austere meditation on Vāsudeva won the vision of Viṣṇu and the eternal position of the pole-star (dhruva-sthāna).

checks.note: BhP 4.8.54 (Nārada's mantra) and VP 1.11.43-44 (Marīci, Atri and the sages instruct him) located.

name: Dhruvadās
summary: Rādhāvallabha poet-theologian (late 16th – 17th c.), author of the forty-two līlās (Bayālīs Līlā).

name: Dhūmapa

realization_account.text: Known only from Tōh 2292, in the position where Abhayadatta has Carpaṭi. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 64): The supreme vow of all mantra practitioners is not to cling to one's own realization; filled with the realization of innate mind — that is seeing all the buddhas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 64 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Known only from Tōh 2292, in the position where Abhayadatta has Carpaṭi.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Ḍhuṇḍhirāja
summary: Author of the Jātakābharaṇa.

name: Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha
summary: Author to whom a Rasendracintāmaṇi is attributed.

name: Dhuṇḍisuta Mālu (Narahari Mālu)
summary: Marathi author of the Navanātha Bhaktisāra.

name: Dīghajāṇu
summary: Byagghapajja, a Koliyan householder taught the four sources of welfare now and hereafter (AN 8.54).

name: Dignāga
places: Siṃhavakta near Kāñcī (birthplace in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories tell that he defeated the tīrthika Sudurjaya at Nālandā, and that while he was composing the Pramāṇasamuccaya in a cave, an opponent twice erased the opening verse he had written on the rock; when he considered abandoning the work for his own liberation, Mañjuśrī appeared and told him to compose it, promising to be his spiritual friend until awakening.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Bu ston; Tāranātha)

summary: Founder of the Buddhist pramāṇa school, pupil of Vasubandhu by tradition: the Pramāṇasamuccaya's two means of knowledge, perception free of construction, reflexive awareness, the triple mark of the reason and the exclusion theory of meaning; in Tibet one of the 'six ornaments'.

name: Digvijaynāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the mid-20th century.
notes: Listed only as a head of the Gorakhpur seat; succession Digvijaynāth → Avaidyanāth → Ādityanāth as commonly reported.

name: Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche Tashi Paljor (dil mgo mkhyen brtse)
summary: Nyingma master and treasure revealer, holder of the Longchen Nyingthig and Rimé lineages, later head of the Nyingma school; transmitted the Rinchen Terdzö many times.

name: Dinakara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Dinakarī, a commentary on Viśvanātha's Siddhāntamuktāvalī.

name: Dipa Ma
summary: Indian laywoman meditation master (Nani Bala Barua, 1911–1989), trained in the Mahāsi method, renowned for her attainments and her teaching of householders.

name: Dīpaṅkara
summary: The buddha of the distant past who predicted the future buddhahood of Śākyamuni (then the brahmin youth Sumedha / Megha); the Vajracchedikā says the Tathāgata received no dharma from him.
alt_summary: The Buddha at whose feet the ascetic Sumedha vowed to become a Buddha (Buddhavaṃsa 2), the first of the twenty-four Buddhas who predicted Gotama's Buddhahood.

name: Dīpaṅkarabhadra
summary: Disciple of Buddhajñānapāda and author of the Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi.

name: Dīrghatamas
summary: Dīrghatamas Aucathya (Māmateya), seer of RV 1.140–164, including the riddle hymn 1.164 (the two birds, the four quarters of speech, 'the One Being the inspired call by many names'), the Viṣṇu hymn 1.154 and the horse-sacrifice hymns 1.162–163. The tradition remembers him as born blind.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). 'Born blind' and 'father of Kakṣīvant' are traditional (Bṛhaddevatā/epic) reports recalled with moderate confidence.

checks.note: Headers: 'dīrghatamā aucathyaḥ' for 1.140–164. Born blind, son of Mamatā and Ucathya, father of Kakṣīvant — confirmed by web sources (Bṛhaddevatā story; Mahābhārata Ādi-parvan).

name: Do Khyentse Yeshe Dorje (mdo mkhyen brtse ye shes rdo rje)
summary: Mind-incarnation of Jigme Lingpa, a wild visionary yogin and teacher of Patrul Rinpoche.

name: Doḍḍayācārya
summary: Mahācārya of Ghaṭikāśatam, a Vaṭakalai polemicist who continued Deśika's attack on Advaita in the Caṇḍamāruta; the tradition sets him against Appayya Dīkṣita.

name: Eihei Dōgen 永平道元

realization_account.text: During sitting at Tiantong, Rujing rebuked a dozing monk: 'practising Chan is body and mind dropping off'; hearing this Dōgen awoke and Rujing confirmed 'body and mind dropped off; dropped-off body and mind' (Sōtō biographies; Rujing xu yulu).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Japanese Sōtō: trained in Tendai and under Myōzen, went to China (1223–1227), received Caodong transmission from Tiantong Rujing, taught just sitting as the enactment of original realization, founded Kōshōji and Eiheiji, and wrote the Shōbōgenzō, Fukanzazengi and monastic instructions.

name: Dōhara Kakkayya
summary: A leather-worker śaraṇa of 'untouchable' birth honoured among the devotees.

name: Dölpa Sherab Gyatso (Geshe Dölpa)
summary: Disciple of Potowa who compiled the Blue Compendium from his teacher's examples.

name: Dolpopa Sherab Gyaltsen (dol po pa shes rab rgyal mtshan)
places: Lhasa and central Tibet (teaching journey late in life)

realization_account.text: The Jonang account holds that the other-emptiness view dawned in Dolpopa's own experience through the six-branch yoga before he set it out in writing, and that he was an emanation of the Kalkī Puṇḍarīka, author of the Vimalaprabhā (emanation claim: low confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great systematizer of the Jonang and of the other-emptiness (gzhan stong) view. Born in Dolpo, he trained at Sakya, received the Kālacakra six-branch yoga at Jonang, became its abbot, built its great stūpa, oversaw a new translation of the Kālacakra tantra and Vimalaprabhā, and taught — in the Mountain Doctrine, the Fourth Council and many other works — that the ultimate, buddha-nature, is permanent and empty only of what is other than it. Known as 'the Omniscient One of Dolpo'.

name: Ḍombipa (Ḍombi Heruka)

realization_account.text: A king of Magadha, disciple of Virūpa, who took a low-caste ḍombī girl as his consort; banished, he lived with her in the forest for twelve years and returned riding a tigress, holding a snake as whip; author of Hevajra works and (traditionally) the Sahajasiddhi. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 4): As the power of an alchemical elixir turns iron into gold, the power of the precious consecration transforms the afflictions into non-dual gnosis.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 4 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A king of Magadha, disciple of Virūpa, who took a low-caste ḍombī girl as his consort; banished, he lived with her in the forest for twelve years and returned riding a tigress, holding a snake as whip; author of Hevajra works and (traditionally) the Sahajasiddhi.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Doṇa
summary: A brahmin who asked whether the Buddha was a god, gandhabba, yakkha or human (AN 4.36).

name: Donglin Changzong 東林常總
summary: Heir of Huanglong at Mount Lu, teacher of the poet Su Shi (Su Dongpo), whose awakening verse on the valley stream Dōgen cites.

name: Dongshan Liangjie 洞山良价

realization_account.text: Crossing a stream he saw his reflection and awoke, composing 'Do not seek it from others… I now go on alone and meet it everywhere; it now is me, I now am not it' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 15).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Co-founder of the Caodong house; heir of Yunyan; questioned the preaching of the insentient, awoke on seeing his reflection while crossing a stream, and taught the five ranks and the Precious Mirror Samādhi.

name: Dongshan Shouchu 洞山守初
summary: Heir of Yunmen; answered 'three pounds of flax' to 'what is buddha?' (Biyan lu 12; Wumenguan 18). Distinct from Dongshan Liangjie.

name: Dongyang Dehui 東陽德輝
summary: Abbot of Baizhangshan who compiled the imperial edition of the Pure Rules (1335–1338).

name: Dorje Lingpa (rdo rje gling pa)
summary: The third 'king' treasure revealer, who also revealed Bön treasures.

name: Dōshō
summary: Japanese monk who studied with Xuanzang and brought Hossō (Yogācāra) teaching to Japan.

name: Doui 道義
summary: Silla monk who received Hongzhou Chan from Xitang Zhizang and returned in 821; founder of the Gajisan school and regarded by the modern Jogye Order as its founder.

name: Doushuai Congyue 兜率從悅
summary: Huanglong-branch master who posed the 'three barriers of Doushuai' (Wumen guan case 47).

name: Drāhyāyaṇa
summary: Author by tradition of the Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda Śrautasūtra.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as the eponymous author of the Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra.

name: Jetsün Drakpa Gyaltsen
summary: Third of the five Sakya founders, a celibate lay practitioner (upāsaka), author of many Lamdre instructions (the Yellow Volume) and of the song on Parting from the Four Attachments; uncle and teacher of Sakya Paṇḍita.
alt_names: rje btsun grags pa rgyal mtshan

name: Dramiḍa (Draviḍācārya)
summary: Pre-Śaṅkara Vedāntin who commented on Brahmanandin's Vākya; cited by Rāmānuja as an authority.

name: Drapa Ngönshé (grwa pa mngon shes)
summary: Treasure revealer who, in the tradition's account, recovered the Four Tantras in 1038 from a pillar of the main temple at Samye.

name: the Draupadeyas (sons of Draupadī)
summary: The sons of Draupadī, named as a group among the great chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍava army (1.6) and the conch-blowers (1.18). Group entry.
notes: A group, not a single person; the Gītā does not name them individually. Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6, 1.18.

name: Draupadī (Kṛṣṇā, Pāñcālī)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Wife of the Pāṇḍavas; in the forest she questions divine justice and argues for human effort against Yudhiṣṭhira (3.28–33), and after the war urges him to rule (12.14).

checks.note: Located as described.

alt_summary: Mother of the Draupadeyas; named only through her sons' metronymic (1.6, 1.18).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6, 1.18.

name: Dṛḍhabala
summary: Born in the city of Pañcanada, he completed Caraka's redaction, a third of which was missing, by gleaning from many tantras seventeen chapters of the Cikitsā and the Kalpa and Siddhi sections (Ca Si 12.38-40).

name: Drenpa Namkha (dran pa nam mkha')
summary: Great Bön master of the 8th c., who by Bön tradition upheld Bön under Trisong Detsen and concealed texts; the commentator of the Sipai Dzöpuk; figures also in Nyingma accounts (low confidence on details).
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Drokmi Lotsawa Shākya Yeshe
summary: Tibetan translator who studied in India (at Vikramaśīla, with Śāntipa/Ratnākaraśānti among others) and received the Lamdre and the Hevajra cycle from Gayadhara; teacher of Khön Könchok Gyalpo and fountainhead of the Sakya Lamdre in Tibet.
alt_names: 'brog mi lo tsā ba shākya ye shes

name: Dromtönpa Gyalwai Jungne
summary: Lay disciple and chief successor of Atiśa, whom the tradition regards as an emanation of Avalokiteśvara; founded Reting monastery (1056/57) and shaped the Kadam; the Book of Kadam records his dialogues with Atiśa.

realization_account.text: Regarded as an emanation of Avalokiteśvara; the Son Teachings of the Book of Kadam recount his previous lives.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Droṇa
summary: The teacher (ācārya), 'best of the twice-born', to whom Duryodhana speaks (1.2–11) and whose disciple Dhṛṣṭadyumna arrayed the Pāṇḍava army (1.3); with Bhīṣma one whom Arjuna holds worthy of worship (1.25, 2.4).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

notes: That the ācārya of 1.2–11 is Droṇa is the epic context; Droṇa is named at 1.25 and 2.4. Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.2, 1.3, 1.7, 1.8, 1.25, 2.4.
alt_summary: Seen by Arjuna entering the mouths of the fierce form (BhG 11.26); named by the Lord among the warriors 'already slain by me' (11.34).

name: Dru Gyalwa Yungdrung ('bru rgyal ba g.yung drung)
summary: Bön master credited with the practice manual of the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü and with arranging the A-tri.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Drubchen Chökyi Dorje
summary: Mahāsiddha of the Ganden oral lineage, who the tradition says attained an immortal 'rainbow' body and taught Gyalwa Ensapa.

name: Drukpa Kunley (Kunga Legpa)
summary: The Drukpa 'divine madman' of Tibet and Bhutan, whose satirical songs and outrageous conduct are remembered as teaching.

name: Drupada
summary: A great chariot-warrior on the Pāṇḍava side (1.4), father of the army's arranger (1.3), who blows his conch (1.18).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.3, 1.4, 1.18.

name: Du Fei 杜朏
summary: Lay author of the Chuan fabao ji.

name: Duddu Śāh
summary: Disciple of Lalon and composer of Bāul songs; wrote a verse life of Lalon (low confidence).

name: Dudjom Lingpa (bdud 'joms gling pa)
summary: Visionary treasure revealer of Golok whose Dzogchen treasures include Refining Apparent Phenomena and Buddhahood Without Meditation; many of his disciples are said to have attained the rainbow body.

name: Dudjom Rinpoche Jigdral Yeshe Dorje (bdud 'joms 'jigs bral ye shes rdo rje)
summary: Reincarnation of Dudjom Lingpa, treasure revealer, historian of the Nyingma (Fundamentals and History), editor of the enlarged Kama, and the first head of the Nyingma school in exile.

name: Düdul Dorje, the thirteenth Karmapa
summary: Karmapa remembered for his affinity with animals.

name: Duggaḷe
summary: Wife of Dēvara Dāsimayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Dugu Pei 獨孤沛
summary: Recorder of Shenhui's Huatai debate.

name: Dukhaṇḍi

realization_account.text: A scavenger who stitched rags; taught the generation and completion stages. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 25): Meditate on the conventional generation stage and the ultimate completion stage in union as mahāmudrā: the fruit, the three bodies and gnosis, dawns.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 25 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A scavenger who stitched rags; taught the generation and completion stages.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Durga (Durgācārya)
summary: Commentator on the Nirukta; date uncertain.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: the commentator on the Nirukta; the commentary is dated before 1200 CE (Wisdomlib).

name: Durjayacandra
summary: Commentator on the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra (Kaumudī), c. 10th c.; teacher of Drokmi's circle per Tibetan accounts.

name: Durvāsas
summary: The celibate sage whom Śrīkaṇṭha commanded to preserve the Śaiva scripture; he created a mind-born son, Tryambakāditya, and transmitted the secrets to him (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.110-112). Later Kashmirian accounts (Tantrāloka 36; Jayaratha) speak of his three mind-born sons for the non-dual, dual and dual-non-dual teachings, and a 'half' Kaula line - hence the 'three and a half maṭhikās' (TĀ 4.266).
notes: The three-sons account (Tryambaka, Āmardaka, Śrīnātha, plus Ardhatryambaka) is from memory of TĀ 36 and Jayaratha; TĀ 4.266 itself names the Śrī-, Tryambaka-, Ardha- and Āmarda- maṭhikās (confirmed).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, naradaparivrajaka, gopalatapani (uttara), in the roles the summary gives. Durvāsas and the gopīs is in the Gopālottaratāpinī (e-text no. 99). A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U23 contribution: identified by the Śrīvidyā tradition with Krodhabhaṭṭāraka, the twelfth of the great worshippers of the vidyā; ascribed the Lalitāstavaratna (Āryādviśatī) and the Śaktimahimnastotra; Bhāskararāya quotes him.
Irascible sage named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86); in the Gopālottaratāpanī he teaches the gopīs.

name: Durvekamiśra
summary: Bengali commentator on Dharmottara and Arcaṭa.

name: Duryodhana
summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son, king of the Kaurava side (rājā, 1.2), who names the leading warriors of both armies to his teacher and urges that Bhīṣma be protected (1.2–11); Arjuna calls him the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra (1.23).

name: Düsum Khyenpa, the first Karmapa
alt_names: dus gsum mkhyen pa ('knower of the three times')

realization_account.text: He attained realization at fifty; the ḍākinīs are said to have woven a crown from their hair and offered it to him — the origin of the Karmapa's black crown.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Gampopa (after studying Madhyamaka and logic with Kadam teachers), founder of the Karma Kagyu and of the monasteries of Kampo Nenang, Karma Gön and Tsurphu; regarded as the first Karmapa.

name: Dyānatrāy
summary: Hindi Digambara poet of Agra and Delhi (c. 1676–1726), author of pūjās and adhyātma padas.

name: Dzongpa Kunga Namgyal
summary: Founder of Gongkar Dorjeden monastery and of the Dzong sub-school of the Sakya.

name: Eikū
summary: Tendai precept master of Kurodani and Hōnen's teacher, in the lineage of Ryōnin.

name: Myōan Eisai 明菴榮西 (Yōsai)
summary: Tendai monk who went to China twice (1168; 1187–1191), received the Huanglong Linji transmission from Xu'an Huaichang, founded Shōfukuji (Hakata) and Kenninji (Kyoto), wrote the Kōzen gokoku ron and Kissa yōjōki, and combined Zen with Tendai and esoteric practice and strict precepts.

name: Ēkānta Rāmayya
summary: The Śaiva devotee of Abalūr who, according to an inscription there, staked his head in a contest with the Jainas, cut it off, offered it to Śiva and received it back.

name: Eknāth
summary: Brahmin saint of Paiṭhaṇ (1533–1599), disciple of Janārdana Svāmī: corrected the Jñāneśvarī text (1584), wrote the Eknāthī Bhāgavat, the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, bhāruḍs and abhaṅgas, and lived as a householder of legendary patience — bathing again and again without anger when spat upon, pouring Gaṅgā water meant for Rāmeśvaram into a dying donkey's mouth, feeding Mahārs at his ancestors' rite. Kṛṣṇa is said to have served in his house as Śrīkhaṇḍyā.

realization_account.text: Received Datta's vision through Janārdana's grace; Kṛṣṇa served him as a household servant for twelve years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata (completed Vārāṇasī 1573).

alt_summary: In U06's texts: author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata, the Marathi commentary on the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata Book 11).

name: Ēkōrāmārādhya
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Kedāra pīṭha (Kedārnāth).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Rāmanātha liṅga at Drākṣārāma and seat name Vairāgya-siṃhāsana: low confidence.

name: Embār
summary: Rāmānuja's cousin Govinda, once a Śaiva at Kāḷahasti, brought back by Periya Tirumalai Nambi; Rāmānuja's successor at Śrīraṅgam and teacher of Parāśara Bhaṭṭar, in the line the Teṅkalai follow.

name: Emperor Wu of Liang (Liang Wudi 梁武帝)
summary: Buddhist emperor (r. 502–549) who, in the tradition's account, asked Bodhidharma about the merit of his temple-building and was told 'no merit'.

name: Ēṉātinātar Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A master of swordsmanship whose defeated rival Atisūraṉ smeared sacred ash on his forehead before their duel; seeing the ash, Ēṉātinātar lowered his guard and let himself be killed rather than strike a wearer of Śiva's sign.

name: Enni Ben'en 圓爾辨圓 (Shōichi kokushi)
summary: Heir of Wuzhun Shifan who founded Tōfukuji (Kyoto) and combined Zen with Tendai and esoteric teaching.

name: Eṟipatta Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He cut down the royal elephant that had scattered the flowers gathered for Śiva by the devotee Civakāmi Āṇṭār, and its keepers; the king Pukaḻccōḻar offered his own life in atonement and Eṟipattar tried to take his own, until Śiva intervened and restored all.

name: Eshinni
summary: Shinran's wife, whose letters to their daughter Kakushinni (found in 1921) record Shinran's conversion and her dream of Hōnen as Seishi and Shinran as Kannon.

name: Ēyarkōṉ Kalikkāma Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Angered that Cuntarar made the Lord his messenger to Paravai, he was struck by colic that only Cuntarar could cure; rather than be cured by him he tore out his own bowels; Cuntarar, arriving, was about to die with him, when Śiva revived Kalikkāmar and the two became friends.
