name: Fahai 法海
summary: Huineng's disciple, named as recorder of the Platform Sūtra.

name: Faru 法如
summary: Hongren's disciple at Shaolin, presented in early epitaphs and the Chuan fabao ji as his successor.

name: Faxian
summary: Chinese pilgrim who went to India in search of the Vinaya, obtained the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya at Pāṭaliputra and the Mahīśāsaka Vinaya and Āgama manuscripts in Sri Lanka, and translated the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya with Buddhabhadra.
alt_summary: Chinese pilgrim-monk (c. 337-422) who travelled to India and Sri Lanka and brought back the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya and the Mahāyāna Nirvāṇa Sūtra, translated with Buddhabhadra (T376, 418).

name: Fayan Wenyi 法眼文益
summary: Founder of the Fayan house in Nanjing; used Huayan categories; wrote the Ten Guidelines criticising faults of Chan teachers.

name: Fazhao

realization_account.text: Tradition tells of visions of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra on Wutai who told him that recollecting the Buddha is the supreme practice (as recalled from later biographies).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Creator of the five-tone (wuhui) chanting of the name, taught at court in Chang'an; the Zhulin si on Wutai is associated with him; fourth patriarch in both Song lists. Ennin brought his chant to Mt Hiei.

name: Feixi
summary: Tang monk of the Caotang si (Zige shan), author of the Treatise on the Jewel-King Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha.

name: Feiyin Tongrong 費隱通容
summary: Heir of Miyun, abbot of Wanfusi on Mount Huangbo, teacher of Yinyuan (Ingen).

name: Fengxue Yanzhao 風穴延沼
summary: Linji master who kept the line alive in the 10th c.

name: Fenyang Shanzhao 汾陽善昭
summary: Linji master who composed verses on old cases (songgu), a precursor of the kōan collections.

name: Fu Dashi 傅大士 (Fu Xi)
summary: Lay bodhisattva of the Liang honoured in Chan anecdotes and credited with verses such as the Xinwang ming (in Jingde chuandeng lu juan 30).

name: Furong Daokai 芙蓉道楷
summary: Caodong master known for austerity and refusal of imperial honours.

name: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: The most prolific Navadvīpa Naiyāyika: the Gādādharī on the Dīdhiti and many vāda treatises, including the Vyutpattivāda and Śaktivāda on verbal cognition.
notes: Teacher relation to Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa is the tradition's account (low confidence).

name: Gadādhara Paṇḍita
summary: Caitanya's lifelong companion at Navadvīpa and Purī, identified in the tradition with Rādhā's śakti; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Gāḍge Mahārāj
summary: Wandering kīrtankār and reformer (1876–1956) who used Vārkarī kīrtan and the chant 'Gopālā Gopālā Devakīnandan Gopālā' to preach cleanliness, education and the end of caste discrimination and animal sacrifice.

name: Gāgā Bhaṭṭa
notes: His role in Śivājī's coronation (1674) is well known; not a Mīmāṃsā teaching.
summary: Vārāṇasī scholar (Viśveśvara Bhaṭṭa) of the Bhaṭṭa family; author of the Bhāṭṭacintāmaṇi.

name: Gagan Harkarā
summary: Postal runner of Shilaidaha whose song 'āmi kothāy pāba tāre, āmār maner mānuṣ ye re' Rabindranath Tagore admired and whose tune he adapted.

name: Gahinīnāth
summary: Nāth yogī, disciple of Gorakṣanātha, who initiated Nivṛttināth in a cave on the Brahmagiri near Tryambakeśvar and charged him to spread devotion to Kṛṣṇa; through him the Vārkarī saints trace their Nāth initiation.

name: Gahinīnātha
summary: Nāth guru of Nivṛttināth in the Marathi tradition, counted among the nine Nāths (the Marathi list); tradition places his meeting with Nivṛtti at the Brahmagiri near Tryambakeśvar and a samādhi at Gahinīnāthgaḍ.

name: Gajasukumāla
summary: Younger brother of Kṛṣṇa who became a monk under Ariṣṭanemi; meditating in a cremation ground, he kept equanimity while the brāhmaṇa Somila placed burning coals in a clay rim on his head, and attained liberation that night (Antakṛddaśā).

name: Gambhīrnāth
summary: Nāth yogī of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, revered as a realised yogī in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

name: Gampopa Sönam Rinchen (Dakpo Lhaje)
alt_names: sgam po pa bsod nams rin chen
Candraprabhakumāra (identified by the tradition with the bodhisattva of the Samādhirāja Sūtra)

realization_account.text: Foretold in the Samādhirāja Sūtra (by the tradition's reading) as a physician-monk who would spread its teaching; he came to Milarepa already accomplished in Kadam meditation, reported his experiences, and was told they were neither good nor bad; Milarepa's parting instruction was to show his calloused seat from years of sitting.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Physician of Dakpo who, after his wife's death, became a Kadampa monk and then Milarepa's chief disciple; he joined the Kadam graded path with Milarepa's Mahāmudrā and Six Yogas, founded Daklha Gampo (1121) and wrote the Jewel Ornament of Liberation; all the Dakpo Kagyu schools descend from his disciples.
notes: His Kadam teachers (e.g. Geshe Nyukrumpa, Jayulwa) are not given ids here.

name: Gaṇaka Moggallāna
summary: A brahmin accountant who asked about gradual training (MN 107).

name: Gaṇeśa (Gajānana)
summary: The elephant-faced lord who, in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, teaches King Vareṇya the Gaṇeśa Gītā.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Gajānana, speaker of the Gaṇeśa Gītā ('śrīgajānana uvāca').

name: Gaṇeśa Daivajña
summary: Son and pupil of Keśava, of Nandigrāma; author of the Grahalāghava (1520), the basis of many almanacs.

name: Gaṇeśa (author of the Jātakālaṅkāra)
summary: Author of the Jātakālaṅkāra (1613); distinct from Gaṇeśa Daivajña.

name: Gaṅgādhara Kaviratna
summary: Bengali physician and scholar who edited and commented on the Caraka Saṃhitā (Jalpakalpataru).

name: Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Svārājyasiddhi.

name: Gaṅgāmbike
summary: Basava's wife, daughter of the minister Baladēva; a vacanakāra.

name: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya

scholarly.text: first half of the 14th c. CE

summary: Founder of Navya-Nyāya: his Tattvacintāmaṇi in four books on the four means of knowledge recast Nyāya in a precise technical language.

name: Gaofeng Yuanmiao 高峰原妙
summary: Yuan-dynasty master of rigorous huatou practice who taught the three essentials of great faith, great doubt and great determination.

name: Garab Dorje (Prahevajra)
summary: The first human teacher of the Great Perfection. Born in Oḍḍiyāna to a nun-princess by miraculous conception, he received all the tantras from Vajrasattva, taught the Dzogchen scriptures, and at his passing into light left his testament, the Three Statements that Hit the Vital Point, to Mañjuśrīmitra.

realization_account.text: Realized the Great Perfection from birth; dissolved his body into light and dropped his testament in a golden casket from the sky.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is hearing (BAU 4.1.5); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 4.1.5 (Gardabhīvipīta Bhāradvāja: hearing is brahman).

name: Garga (as teacher of saṃhitā)
summary: For jyotiṣa, the ancient sage whose saṃhitā on omens and lunar mansions (Vṛddhagargasaṃhitā) is the principal older source of Varāhamihira's saṃhitā; Varāhamihira says he will relate the portents that Garga taught to Atri (BS 45.1).
alt_summary: Sage cited in the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (NBS 17) for the definition of devotion as attachment to hearing the Lord's stories; named among the bhakti teachers (NBS 83). In the Purāṇas the family priest of the Yādavas who named Kṛṣṇa.

name: Garga Bhāradvāja
summary: Seer of RV 6.47, including 'Indra goes in many forms by his māyās' (6.47.18).

name: Garga (Pāśupata)
summary: The second of Lakulīśa's four disciples in the Purāṇic lists (Liṅga P. 1.24.131; Kūrma P. 1.51.26) and third in the Jain lists of eighteen tīrthakaras (as Gārgya); a Pāśupata line was traced to him.

name: Gārgī Vācaknavī
summary: Woman participant in the debate at Janaka's court: she questions Yājñavalkya on what the worlds are woven upon, is warned not to ask too much lest her head fall off (BAU 3.6), returns with two questions 'like two arrows', hears the teaching of the imperishable (akṣara) and declares that no one will defeat him (BAU 3.8).

summary: The woman to whom Yājñavalkya teaches the eight-limbed yoga in the Yoga Yājñavalkya; the text presents her as a learned woman (and, in some readings, as his wife). Her identity with the Upaniṣadic Gārgī Vācaknavī (tch:gargi-vacaknavi) is not settled.

name: Gārgya

name: Garībdās (son of Dādū)
summary: Dādū's elder son and first successor at Naraina.

name: Garuḍa

name: Garuḍavāhana Paṇḍita
summary: Author, by tradition a contemporary of Rāmānuja, of the Sanskrit Divyasūricaritam on the lives of the Āḻvārs and Rāmānuja.

name: Gasan Jitō 峨山慈棹
summary: Heir of Hakuin (via Gessen in some accounts) and teacher of Inzan and Takujū.

name: Gasan Jōseki 峨山韶碩
summary: Keizan's heir who spread Sōtō through his many disciples; said to have trained in the five ranks.

name: Gauḍapāda
summary: Traditional author of the Kārikā on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad; the text itself does not name its author. Its four prakaraṇas restate the Upaniṣad (ch.1), argue the unreality of dream and waking (ch.2), teach non-birth by the space analogy and give counsel on restraining the mind (ch.3), and argue non-origination and the firebrand image (ch.4).

alt_summary: Author of the Māṇḍūkya Kārikā; teacher of Govinda, Śaṅkara's teacher, and in the paramparā disciple of Śuka; first systematic exponent of non-origination (ajātivāda) and asparśa-yoga.

U09 contribution: a Gauḍapāda is named in the closing verse of the bhāṣya on SK 1–69. Whether he is the Advaita teacher Gauḍapāda (author of the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā, Śaṅkara's paramaguru) is disputed; many scholars regard them as different persons.
In U06's context: a commentary on the Uttara Gītā is ascribed to him (attribution doubtful).
U23 contribution: Śrīvidyā tradition ascribes to him the Subhagodaya and the Śrīvidyāratnasūtra and places him at the head of the line Gauḍapāda - Govinda - Śaṅkara as upāsakas of the Goddess.
alt_notes: Registry id used as mandated; if the merge keeps the two persons apart, the Sāṃkhya commentator should be split out (e.g., tch:gaudapada-samkhya).

name: Gauḍīya Śaṅkara
summary: Author of a commentary (vṛttikā) on Brahmānanda's Tārārahasya, as attributed in the Muktabodha catalogue.

name: Gaura Kiśora Dāsa Bābājī
summary: Renunciate bābājī of Navadvīpa, guru of Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī.

name: Gauraṇa
summary: Telugu poet, author of the Navanāthacaritramu.

name: Gautama Akṣapāda

tradition.text: an ancient ṛṣi

scholarly.text: the Nyāya Sūtra is usually dated c. 2nd–3rd c. CE; nothing is known of its author(s)

realization_account.text: Called 'the best of sages' (Nyāyavārttika maṅgala) and 'the supremely compassionate sage' who composed the śāstra wishing to lift the world sunk in the mire of pain (Vācaspati, Tātparyaṭīkā on NS 1.1.1).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The sage to whom the Nyāya Sūtra is attributed, the founder of Nyāya. The commentators call him the best of sages who taught the śāstra for the peace of the world.
notes: Popular legends explain 'Akṣapāda' ('eyes in the feet'); not recorded here because the versions could not be checked.

name: Gautama (author of the Dharmasūtra)
summary: The Gautama of the Gautama Dharmasūtra, cited by Baudhāyana (BDh 1.1.2.7) and assigned by Parāśara to the Tretā age; distinct from Gautama Akṣapāda of Nyāya.

checks.note: Text-located: BDh 1.1.2.7 'mithyaitad iti gautamaḥ'; ParSm 1.24 'tretāyāṃ gautamāḥ smṛtāḥ'.

name: Gautama (questioner of the Haṃsa)
summary: Sage who asks for the means to brahmavidyā in the Haṃsa Upaniṣad; Brahmavidyā 53 also addresses a Gautama. Identity with other Gautamas not asserted.

queries: e-text name search: Gautama (questioner of the Haṃsa)
checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of hamsa, brahmavidya, in the roles the summary gives. Also addressed as 'gautama' in Brahmavidyā 53 and Yogakuṇḍalī 1.3. The entry rightly declines to identify him with other Gautamas. A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Gautama Saṅghadeva
alt_names: Qutan Sengqietipo 瞿曇僧伽提婆
summary: Kashmiri translator of the Madhyamāgama (397–398) and of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma texts.

name: Gautamī
summary: An aged brāhmaṇī whose son dies of snakebite; she refuses the vengeance a hunter offers, and in the ensuing debate the serpent, Death and Time each disclaim the cause until karma is named (Anuśāsana 13.1).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Gāvbā
summary: Disciple of Eknāth credited with completing the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa after Eknāth's death.
notes: Name as recalled; verify.

name: Gayadāsa
summary: Commentator on the Suśruta Saṃhitā (Nyāyacandrikā), used by Ḍalhaṇa.

name: Gayadhara
summary: Indian (or Kashmiri) paṇḍita who came to Tibet and transmitted the complete Lamdre to Drokmi Lotsawa, according to the Sakya histories in exchange for a large payment of gold.
notes: Lineage position (after Avadhūtipa) recalled; dates low confidence.

name: Gayaśata (Jiayesheduo 伽耶舍多)
summary: Eighteenth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 18.

name: Genchi
summary: Hōnen's attendant in his last years, for whom the One-Sheet Document was written; his line (Shirahata/Murasakino) later merged into the Chinzei.

name: Gendün Drup
summary: Disciple of Tsongkhapa who founded Tashi Lhunpo (1447); recognised retrospectively as the First Dalai Lama.

name: Gendün Gyatso
summary: Recognised as Gendün Drup's reincarnation; abbot of Drepung and Sera; founded Chökhor Gyal monastery near Lhamo Latso; retrospectively the Second Dalai Lama.

name: Genshin
summary: Tendai scholar of Yokawa whose Ōjōyōshū (985) gathered scripture on loathing this defiled world and seeking the Pure Land, on contemplative and oral nenbutsu and on deathbed practice; he organised the Nijūgo zanmai-e, a society of twenty-five monks who vowed to help one another die in right mindfulness. Sixth of the seven Shinshū masters.

name: Getse Paṇḍita Gyurme Tsewang Chokdrub (dge rtse paNDi ta)
summary: Scholar of Katok who edited the Derge edition of the Nyingma Gyubum and wrote its catalogue.

name: Gewai Lodrö (translator)
summary: Tibetan translator who, with Atiśa, translated and edited the Lamp for the Path (colophon).
notes: Known from the Derge colophon of Tōh 3947 ('zhu chen gyi lo tsA ba dge ba'i blo gros'); identity otherwise unrecorded here.

name: Ghaṇṭāpa

realization_account.text: A royal monk-scholar of strict celibacy whom the king of Pāṭaliputra tried to shame by sending a young woman; he took her as consort and, when accused, the two rose into the sky as Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī; founder of the Ghaṇṭāpa lineage of Cakrasaṃvara (the five-deity body maṇḍala). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 52): The three — lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī — the guru blessed and bound; the three — self, mind and appearance — the wise make firm so that realization may arise.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 52 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A royal monk-scholar of strict celibacy whom the king of Pāṭaliputra tried to shame by sending a young woman; he took her as consort and, when accused, the two rose into the sky as Cakrasaṃvara and Vajravārāhī; founder of the Ghaṇṭāpa lineage of Cakrasaṃvara (the five-deity body maṇḍala).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Ghāsīdās
summary: Founder of the Satnāmī panth of Chhattisgarh among the Camārs: rejected images and caste, enjoined vegetarianism and abstinence, and taught the true name.

name: Gheraṇḍa
summary: The sage who, in his hut, teaches Caṇḍakāpāli the sevenfold 'yoga of the pot' in the Gheraṇḍa Saṃhitā (c. 1700). The text presents him as a Vaiṣṇava-leaning yogin; no historical information exists.

name: Ghora Āṅgirasa
summary: Teacher who taught Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī, the doctrine of the person as sacrifice and the three sayings to be taken as refuge at death (ChU 3.17.6).

queries: Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.6 Krishna Devakiputra Ghora Angirasa identification with Krishna of Bhagavad Gita
checks.note: Located: ChU 3.17.6 ('ghora āṅgirasaḥ kṛṣṇāya devakīputrāyoktvovāca').

name: Ghoṣā Kākṣīvatī
summary: Daughter of Kakṣīvant, ṛṣikā of RV 10.39–40 to the Aśvins; the tradition says she remained unmarried in her father's house through a skin disease until the Aśvins healed her.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The illness story is the commentarial account (moderate confidence).

name: Ghoṣaka
summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā: dharmas differ in the three times by their characteristic (lakṣaṇa) — a past dharma has the past characteristic without being dissociated from the future and present ones, as a man attached to one woman is not without attachment to others (AKBh 5.26). The Abhidharmāmṛtarasa is attributed to him.

name: Giridhara (Giridharajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: Later Śuddhādvaita author to whom the Śuddhādvaitamārtaṇḍa is attributed.

name: Girimānanda
summary: A sick monk to whom Ānanda recited the ten perceptions, after which he recovered (AN 10.60).

name: Gö Lotsawa Zhönnu Pel
summary: Tibetan scholar (1392-1481), author of the Blue Annals and of a commentary on the Ratnagotravibhāga linking it with Mahāmudrā.
alt_names: 'gos lo tsā ba gzhon nu dpal
'gos lo tsA ba gzhon nu dpal
alt_summary: Translator and historian, author of the Blue Annals and of a commentary on the Ratnagotravibhāga that presents it as a basis of Mahāmudrā; affiliated with the Karma Kagyu and others.

name: Gobhila
summary: Author by tradition of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda Gṛhyasūtra.

The tradition holds him immortal, appearing in every age; he rescues Matsyendra from the Kadalī kingdom, initiates Gopīcand, Bharthari and Pūraṇ Bhagat (Cauraṅgī), and in Vīraśaiva accounts meets Allama Prabhu. The Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur is his principal seat; Gorkha and the Gurkhas take their name from him.

tradition.text: immortal; appears in all four ages (tradition)

realization_account.text: Born by the power of Matsyendra's ash (vibhūti) — in the common north Indian and Marathi telling, the ash given to a childless woman was thrown on a dung-heap, and Matsyendra later called forth the boy from it; the Gorakṣaguṭikā gives a different origin. Perfected in body, deathless, master of all siddhis.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U28 contribution: the haṭha texts treat Gorakṣa as the great teacher of haṭha: HYP 1.4 names him with Matsyendra; HYP 1.61 quotes 'Gorakṣa's saying' on what to avoid; HYP 4.65 credits him with the worship of the inner sound (nādopāsana) even for the dull; the Vivekamārtaṇḍa, Yogabīja and (doubtfully) the Amanaska are ascribed to him.

alt_summary: In DN 22 the Blessed One (Bhagavā) teaches the monks at Kammāsadhamma among the Kurus the four establishments of mindfulness, with the four noble truths expanded.
In MN 10 the Blessed One (Bhagavā) is the speaker: staying among the Kurus at Kammāsadhamma, he addresses the monks and teaches the four establishments of mindfulness.

Siddhattha Gotama of the Sakyan clan, the Buddha of this age: after going forth and six years of striving he awakened under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā, taught the middle way and the four noble truths at Isipatana, founded the Saṅgha of monks and nuns, taught for forty-five years in the middle Ganges region and attained final nibbāna at Kusinārā at eighty. He calls himself the Tathāgata; the texts present him as the rediscoverer of an ancient path (SN 12.65) and the seventh Buddha of ninety-one aeons (DN 14).

tradition.text: born 623 BCE, awakened 588 BCE, parinibbāna 543 BCE (Theravāda Buddhist-era reckoning; Buddhist Era counted from 544/543 BCE)

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE; the parinibbāna is placed c. 486 BCE on the 'corrected long chronology' or c. 400 BCE (±20) on the 'short chronology' now preferred by many scholars

realization_account.text: After six years of striving and the rejection of self-mortification, he recalled the first jhāna, took food, entered the four jhānas and in the three watches of the night attained recollection of past lives, the divine eye and the destruction of the effluents with knowledge of the four truths; 'unshakeable is my liberation, this is my last birth' (MN 26, MN 36, MN 4; SN 56.11; Vin Mv 1.1).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Haribhadra Sūri

tradition.text: Śvetāmbara tradition: died 529 CE (Vīra 1055)

summary: Śvetāmbara ācārya and the great systematizer of Jain yoga (Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, Yogabindu, Yogaśataka, Yogaviṃśikā), doxographer of all the darśanas (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, Śāstravārtāsamuccaya) and polemicist. The tradition tells that he was a learned brahmin of Citrakūṭa who vowed to become the pupil of anyone whose words he could not understand; hearing the nun Yākinī recite a verse he could not explain, he took initiation and called himself 'Yākinī's spiritual son'. After his pupils Haṃsa and Paramahaṃsa were killed by Buddhists, his anger was calmed by his teacher; he is credited with 1,444 works, many signed with the word 'viraha' (separation).
notes: Several different authors named Haribhadra existed; the ascription of some of the 1,444 works is doubtful.

summary: Teacher who accepts Satyakāma Jābāla because 'no non-brahmin could speak thus' and initiates him (ChU 4.4.3-5).

checks.note: Located: ChU 4.4.3-5 ('naitad abrāhmaṇo vivaktum arhati').

name: Harihara (Kannada poet)
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet of Hampi who created the ragaḷe form for lives of the śaraṇas and of the ancient Śaiva devotees (purātanas), and wrote the Girijākalyāṇa.

name: Hariharānanda Āraṇya
summary: Renunciant who founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur as a monastery of Sāṃkhya-Yoga and lived much of his life in seclusion in a cave there; author of the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga Bhāṣya and of works on Sāṃkhya (e.g., Sāṃkhyatattvāloka), and of the commentary rendered in English as 'Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali'.
notes: Dates, titles and the Maṭh's founding recalled, not checked.
alt_summary: Sāṃkhya-Yoga monk who spent long years in retreat, founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur, and wrote the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga-bhāṣya and a Bengali exposition of Patañjali's Yoga later published in English.

name: Hariharānanda Bhāratī (Hariharānandanātha Tīrthasvāmī)
summary: Bengali Kaula avadhūta and commentator of the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra; associated with Rammohun Roy, who cited the Mahānirvāṇa. Some scholars suggest the Mahānirvāṇa was composed in his circle; the tradition regards it as revealed scripture.
notes: Attribution of the Mahānirvāṇa's composition to him is a scholarly hypothesis only; recorded as 'disputed'.

name: Harirāy (Harirāyajī)
summary: Puṣṭimārga scholar and poet, commentator (Bhāvaprakāś) on the Vārtā literature and author of many Sanskrit and Braj works.

name: Harirām Vyās
summary: Sanāḍhya brahmin of Orchhā (16th c.) who settled in Vṛndāvana; a poet of the pair's love associated with Hita Harivaṃśa (his affiliation is also claimed by other sampradāyas).

name: Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika of the 17th c., remembered as the teacher of Gadādhara.

name: Hariṣeṇa
summary: Author of the Bṛhatkathākośa (931–932 CE).

name: Harisvāmin
summary: Commentator on the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (partly surviving).

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: his commentary on the Śatapatha was completed in Kali 3740 = 638 CE, i.e. 7th c. (search summary; edition with Sāyaṇa and Harisvāmin).

name: Hārīta (disciple of Ātreya)
summary: One of Ātreya's six disciples, each of whom composed his own tantra and read it to Ātreya and the sages (Ca Sū 1.31-33).
notes: Whether this is the same person as the homonymous sage of other traditions is not settled; kept separate.

name: Hārīta (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Also named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Hārītaka
summary: Named among the paramahaṃsas in the Bhikṣuka and Yājñavalkya Upaniṣads.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of bhiksuka, yajnavalkya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Haritāyana
summary: U23 contribution: the narrator of the Tripurā Rahasya, called Sumedhas, who received the teaching through Paraśurāma.
alt_summary: Narrator of the Tripura Rahasya, conveying Dattātreya's teaching to Paraśurāma.

name: Harivarman
summary: Author of the Satyasiddhiśāstra; trained in the Sarvāstivāda but rejected many of its positions; his school affiliation is variously given as Sautrāntika or Bahuśrutīya.

name: Harivyāsadeva
summary: Disciple of Śrī Bhaṭṭa; author of the Mahāvāṇī (Braj songs of the eternal love-play in the sakhī mood) and the Siddhāntaratnāñjali; his disciples spread the school through twelve branches.

name: Hāsan Rājā
summary: Zamindar-poet of Sunamganj (Sylhet) whose mystic songs of detachment are sung with the Bāul repertoire.

name: Hastāmalaka
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara; in the tradition's account a seemingly dull boy who, asked 'who are you?', answered with the verses of the Hastāmalakīya, knowing the self as clearly as 'an āmalaka fruit in the hand'; first head of the Dvārakā (Śāradā) maṭha.

name: Hayagrīva
summary: U23 contribution: the teacher of Agastya who reveals the Lalitā Sahasranāma and the Triśatī.

checks.note: BhP 2.7.11 ('bhagavān hayaśīrṣa') and Lalitopākhyāna (Brahmāṇḍa 3.5 colophons, Hayagrīva-Agastya dialogue) located.

alt_summary: The horse-headed form of Viṣṇu (BhP 2.7.11), who in the Lalitopākhyāna is sent as a portion of Viṣṇu to teach Agastya the story and worship of Lalitā.

name: Helārāja
summary: Kashmiri commentator on the third book of the Vākyapadīya (Prakīrṇaprakāśa), who read Bhartṛhari's categories as ways the one Word-Brahman appears; he mentions his own lost commentary Śabdaprabhā and a work Vārttikonmeṣa.

name: Helin Xuansu 鶴林玄素
summary: Oxhead master.

name: Hemacandra

realization_account.text: He says the twelfth chapter of the Yogaśāstra sets out what is 'established by experience' (anubhavasiddha), beyond what he learned from scripture and the teacher.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Śvetāmbara polymath of Gujarat ('Kalikālasarvajña', the omniscient of the Kali age), teacher of king Kumārapāla, for whom he wrote the Yogaśāstra; also author of the Pramāṇamīmāṃsā, the Vītarāgastotra, the two Vyavacchedikā hymns, the Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacarita, and works on grammar and poetics. He declares that the last chapter of the Yogaśāstra rests on his own experience.

checks.note: Confirmed as the Śvetāmbara author of the Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana (post-Pāṇinian grammar survey). His other work belongs to other units.

alt_summary: Śvetāmbara polymath (1088/89–1172) at the Caulukya court of Siddharāja and Kumārapāla — here as author of the Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra and the Pariśiṣṭaparvan, the standard Śvetāmbara universal history and lives of the elders.
Śvetāmbara polymath; U02 adds only his grammar, the Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana.
U31 contribution: author of the Kāvyānuśāsana on poetics and teacher of Rāmacandra and Guṇacandra.
notes: His Yogaśāstra and philosophical works are covered by U35.

name: Hemādri
summary: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): author of the Āyurvedarasāyana commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya.
notes: Identified by scholars with the Yādava minister and author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi.

checks.note: Confirmed: chief minister of the Yādava kings 1259–1274 (Wikipedia 'Hemadpant').
Web: minister (prime minister c. 1259-1274) of the Yādava kings of Devagiri, author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi.

alt_summary: Minister of the Yādava king Rāmacandra and author of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi; in Mahānubhāva memory the court's leading opponent of Cakradhar.
Author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi, whose volumes on vows and gifts are the fullest compilation of Purāṇic vrata and dāna.
U25 contribution: minister of the Yādava kings who wrote the Kaivalyadīpikā commentary on his associate Vopadeva's Muktāphala.
Minister of the Yādava kings, author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi.
alt_notes: U26 contribution: his role as opponent is the Mahānubhāva account (reported by the opposing side).

name: Hemaprabha
summary: Jain author of the Trailokyaprakāśa (1248) on Tājika and horā.

name: Hemrāj Pāṇḍe
summary: Hindi prose commentator (bālāvabodha) on the Pravacanasāra and other Digambara works, in Banārsīdās's circle.

name: Himavat (Himālaya)
summary: King of the mountains and father of Pārvatī, who asks the Goddess for the yoga, devotion and knowledge that lead to her (Devī Gītā).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Asks for yoga with devotion and knowledge ('himālaya uvāca', Devī Gītā 7.32 opening).

name: Hiraṇyadāma

scholarly.text: early 9th c. (as narrated in an inscription of 1052 CE)

summary: Brahmin who, according to the Khmer Sdok Kak Thom inscription (1052 CE), performed rites for King Jayavarman II and taught four Vāma tantras — Vīṇāśikha, Nayottara, Sammoha and Śiraścheda — to the royal priest.

name: Hiraṇyagarbha
alt_names: Pitāmaha (Brahmā) as first teacher of yoga

realization_account.text: The first and most ancient teacher of yoga: 'Hiraṇyagarbha is the speaker of yoga, no other is ancient' (verse cited by Vijñānabhikṣu from the Yoga-Yājñavalkya, YV 1.1). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' in YS 1.1 as Patañjali's re-teaching of the yoga Hiraṇyagarbha taught; Nārāyaṇatīrtha: 'Pitāmaha taught yoga, then Śeṣa'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The tradition's founder of yoga. The Yoga commentators (Vācaspati, Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa) name Hiraṇyagarbha as the original teacher and treat Patañjali's śāstra as a re-teaching; the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya likewise pairs Kapila as the teacher of Sāṃkhya with Hiraṇyagarbha as the knower of yoga.
notes: The Mahābhārata reference (Nārāyaṇīya, c. MBh 12.337 CE) and a reported Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā passage on a Hairaṇyagarbha yoga śāstra are from memory and need checking.

checks.note: Located as described.

alt_summary: Named in the Nārāyaṇīya as the knower (vettā) of Yoga, 'none more ancient' (12.337.60).
alt_notes: U05's contribution; Hiraṇyagarbha as the tradition's founder of Yoga is also treated by U10.

name: Hiraṇyagarbha Prājāpatya
summary: The seer to whom the Anukramaṇī ascribes the Hiraṇyagarbha hymn (RV 10.121); the deity is Ka, i.e. Prajāpati.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Hiraṇyakeśin (Satyāṣāḍha)
summary: Sūtrakāra of the Hiraṇyakeśin branch of the Taittirīya school.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as the sūtrakāra of the Hiraṇyakeśin (Satyāṣāḍha) Kalpa of the Taittirīya school.

name: Hiraṇyākṣa Kauśika
summary: Speaker: the person and diseases arise from the six dhātus, as the first Sāṃkhyas taught (Ca Sū 25.14-15); four tastes (Sū 26.8).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Hiraṇyanābha Kausalya
summary: A prince of Kosala who asked Sukeśā about the person of sixteen parts; Sukeśā, not knowing, refused to answer falsely, since one who speaks untruth withers to the root (PrU 6.1).

checks.note: Located: PrU 6.1 ('hiraṇyanābhaḥ kausalyo rājaputraḥ … samūlo vā eṣa pariśuṣyati yo 'nṛtam abhivadati').

name: Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 1.31–35, including the Indra–Vṛtra hymn 1.32 ('I will proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra…').
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 'hiraṇyastūpa āṅgirasaḥ' for 1.31–35.

name: Hīravijayasūri
summary: Tapā Gaccha leader (1527–1596) who visited Akbar at Fatehpur Sikri (1582) and obtained edicts restricting animal slaughter during Paryuṣaṇa.

name: Hita Harivaṃśa
summary: Founder of the Rādhāvallabha sampradāya (tradition 1502–1552), born at Bād near Mathurā, who received his mantra from Rādhā herself, settled in Vṛndāvana and installed Rādhāvallabha (1535). Author of the Hita Caurāsī and, by his tradition's account, the Rādhā-sudhānidhi; the tradition regards him as the flute of Kṛṣṇa incarnate.

realization_account.text: Rādhā gave him the mantra in a dream (or vision); he is Kṛṣṇa's flute (vaṃśī) incarnate.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Hōmyō
summary: Monk credited with reviving the Yūzū nenbutsu at Dainenbutsu-ji in the 14th c.

name: Hōnen

realization_account.text: In 1175, reading in Shandao's commentary 'single-heartedly and exclusively recollecting the name of Amida ... this is called the rightly determined act, because it accords with the Buddha's vow', he abandoned other practices; Jōdo-shū holds that he attained nenbutsu samādhi (Sanmai hottokki) and regards him as a manifestation of Seishi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tendai monk who after some thirty years of study found in Shandao the exclusive practice of calling Amida's name, left Mt Hiei and taught it at Yoshimizu to people of every station; wrote the Senchakushū for Kujō Kanezane; was defrocked and exiled in 1207 after the Kōfukuji petition and an incident involving court ladies; returned to Kyoto in 1211 and died in 1212 leaving the One-Sheet Document. Founder of Jōdo-shū and seventh Shinshū master.

name: Hongcheok 洪陟
summary: Founder of the Silsangsan school, heir of Xitang Zhizang.

name: Hongren 弘忍
summary: Fifth patriarch at the East Mountain (Huangmei); taught guarding the original true mind (Xiuxin yao lun); in the Platform Sūtra he set the verse contest and secretly transmitted robe and Dharma to Huineng.

name: Hongzhi Zhengjue 宏智正覺
summary: Caodong abbot of Tiantong for thirty years; taught silent illumination (mozhao) and wrote verses on a hundred cases (basis of the Book of Equanimity); friend of Dahui despite their disagreement.

name: Hṛdayaśiva
summary: Compiler of a Prāyaścittasamuccaya of Śaiva expiatory rites.

name: Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Palimaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa. He is remembered as the copyist of the manuscript collection of Madhva's works (the Sarvamūla) and as author of the short Sampradāyapaddhati.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Huaigan

realization_account.text: A Faxiang scholar who doubted the nianfo; on Shandao's advice he practised for three years before attaining the samādhi and seeing the Buddha's golden form (Song gaoseng zhuan, as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Shandao and author of the Shi jingtu qunyi lun, answering Yogācāra objections to Pure Land doctrine and recommending loud recitation.

name: Huangbo Xiyun 黃檗希運
summary: Heir of Baizhang; taught the one mind and no-mind to Pei Xiu (Chuanxin fayao, Wanling lu); struck Linji three times when asked the meaning of the buddha-dharma.

name: Huanglong Huinan 黃龍慧南
summary: Founder of the Huanglong branch; posed the 'three barriers' (Buddha's hand, donkey's leg, birth-conditions).

name: Huiguang
summary: Chinese Vinaya and Dilun master, founder of the southern branch of the Dilun school.

name: Huijiao
summary: Liang-dynasty monk, compiler of the Biographies of Eminent Monks (Gaoseng zhuan).

name: Huike 慧可 (Shenguang)

realization_account.text: 'I have searched for the mind and cannot find it.' — 'I have pacified your mind for you.' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 3; Wumenguan case 41).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Second Chinese patriarch. In the tradition's account he stood in the snow and cut off his own arm to show his resolve, asked Bodhidharma to pacify his mind and was told 'bring me the mind'; the earliest biography (Xu gaoseng zhuan) says bandits cut off his arm and that Bodhidharma gave him the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra.

name: Huineng 惠能 / 慧能 (the Sixth Patriarch)

tradition.text: 638–713 (born 638, received the robe at 24, ordained at 39, taught 37 years — Platform Sūtra 13.18)

realization_account.text: On hearing 'one should produce a mind that abides nowhere' from the Diamond Sūtra he 'greatly awakened that all dharmas are not apart from the self-nature' and exclaimed that the self-nature is originally pure, unborn, complete, unmoving and able to produce all dharmas (Platform Sūtra 4.13).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Sixth and last patriarch. In the tradition's account an illiterate firewood seller from Lingnan who awoke on hearing the Diamond Sūtra, laboured pounding rice at Hongren's monastery, answered Shenxiu's verse with 'originally there is not a single thing', received robe and Dharma at night, hid among hunters for fifteen years, revealed himself at the wind-and-flag debate, and taught the sudden teaching at Caoxi; his body is preserved at Nanhua temple. Scholars see him as a historical but obscure southern teacher whose image was shaped by Shenhui and the Platform Sūtra.

name: Huitang Zuxin 晦堂祖心
summary: Heir of Huanglong.

name: Huiyan Zhizhao 晦巖智昭
summary: Compiler of the Rentian yanmu (1188).

name: Huiyuan of Lushan

realization_account.text: Over his thirty years on Lushan he saw the sage forms three times in the first eleven years without speaking of it; at the end, rising from samādhi, he saw Amitābha filling space with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and was told he would be born in seven days (Fozu tongji 26).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Disciple of Dao'an who settled on Lushan (Donglin si) and never again crossed the Tiger Stream; in 402 he and 123 companions vowed together before an image of Amitābha to be born in the West (Gaoseng zhuan). He practised the samādhi of recollecting the Buddha (pratyutpanna), corresponded with Kumārajīva on it, defended the monastic order's independence from the throne, and was made the first patriarch of the Lotus school by Song writers. The 'White Lotus Society' and its 'eighteen worthies' are later names and legends (scholarly account).

name: Hūṃkara
summary: Indian vidyādhara of the Eight Herukas transmission to whom the tantras of Yangdag (Viśuddha Heruka, enlightened mind) were entrusted; one of the eight vidyādharas.

name: Huqiu Shaolong 虎丘紹隆
summary: Heir of Yuanwu from whom most later Linji and Japanese Rinzai lines descend.

name: Hyecheol 慧哲
summary: Founder of the Dongnisan school, heir of Xitang Zhizang.

name: Hyesim 慧諶 (Jingak guksa)
summary: Jinul's successor at Suseonsa, who promoted ganhwa Seon and compiled the Seonmun yeomsong jip.

name: Hyujeong 休靜 (Seosan daesa)
summary: Joseon master who unified Seon and doctrinal study under ganhwa practice (Seon'ga gwigam) and led monk-soldiers against the Japanese invasion of 1592.

name: Icaiñāṉiyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Cuntarar's mother.

realization_account.text: Cuntarar's mother.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Iṭaikkāṭar
summary: Shepherd-Siddhar (iṭaiyar) whose songs address the herdsman, cattle and flute. The tradition tells that, foreseeing a twelve-year drought, he fed his flock on erukku leaves and stored grain in mud, and when the nine planets came to him he so charmed them that they shifted their places and the rains returned.
places: Tiruvaṇṇāmalai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Distinct from the Caṅkam poet Iṭaikkāṭaṉār. The planets legend and his discipleship to Bogar are recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Ikkyū Sōjun 一休宗純
summary: Daitokuji-line eccentric poet-monk who satirised formal Zen; author of the Kyōunshū.

name: Ikṣvāku
summary: First king of the solar dynasty, who received the yoga from Manu; thus the royal sages knew it until it was lost (BhG 4.1–2).

summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A farmer who fed devotees until he was destitute; on a night of heavy rain he gathered the newly sown paddy from his field and pulled up his roof-beams for firewood to feed a guest, who was Śiva.

name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
summary: Traditional author of the Cilappatikāram, a Cēra prince turned ascetic; his Jain affiliation is contested.

name: Indra (as student and teacher)
summary: Lord of the gods: lives 101 years as Prajāpati's student and alone goes beyond the body-self (ChU 8.7-12); in the Kena he meets Umā Haimavatī and first knows the yakṣa as brahman (Kena 3.11-4.3); teaches Pratardana 'I am breath, the intelligent self' (KauU 3).

checks.note: Located: ChU 8.7-12 (Maghavan, 101 years), Kena 3.11-4.3 (meets Umā; first knew it as brahman) and KauU 3.1-9 (teaches Pratardana).

alt_summary: Lineage contribution (Āyurveda): received Āyurveda from the Aśvins and taught it — to Bharadvāja, who came on behalf of the sages (Ca Sū 1.3-26); to Dhanvantari (Su Sū 1.20); to Ātreya and the other sages (AHS Sū 1.3; Bhāvaprakāśa); and he revealed the rejuvenating herbs of the Himalaya to the sages (Ca Ci 1.4.3-6).
Named by Kṛṣṇa, as Vāsava, among his manifestations: 'of the gods I am Vāsava' (Bhagavad Gītā 10.22).
U23 contribution: one of the twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā.

name: Indrabhūti

realization_account.text: King of Oḍḍiyāna (Sambhola), brother of Lakṣmīṅkarā, who practised while ruling and attained realization; author of the Jñānasiddhi. Several Indrabhūtis are distinguished in Tibetan histories (the king who received the Guhyasamāja from the Buddha, the siddha, and a 'younger' one). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 42): If the moments of time are not blessed, the yoga of outer and inner conduct does not reach completion; the nature of joy and bliss is no different from the buddhas; when clinging is released, the experience of the innate is supreme joy.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 42 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). King of Oḍḍiyāna (Sambhola), brother of Lakṣmīṅkarā, who practised while ruling and attained realization; author of the Jñānasiddhi. Several Indrabhūtis are distinguished in Tibetan histories (the king who received the Guhyasamāja from the Buddha, the siddha, and a 'younger' one).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Homonyms: the king of Oḍḍiyāna who received the Guhyasamāja from the Buddha, the siddha, and the adoptive father of Padmasambhava are distinguished in Tibetan histories; this entry does not settle their identity.

name: Indrabhūti Gautama
summary: The first and chief gaṇadhara of Mahāvīra, a brāhmaṇa of Gobbara near Rājagṛha, who came to refute him and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his doubt whether a soul exists. The questioner of the Bhagavatī and the addressee of 'Gautama, be not careless for a moment' (Uttarādhyayana 10). His attachment to his teacher delayed his omniscience, which he attained on the night of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (Śvetāmbara account) — remembered at Dīvālī; he is invoked for success and wealth ('Gautama-svāmī').

tradition.text: contemporary of Mahāvīra; liberated 12 years after him (Śvetāmbara)

realization_account.text: His love for Mahāvīra was the last bond; when he learned of Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa he grieved, reflected on the Jina's detachment, and attained omniscience that night.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U35 contribution: chief disciple (gaṇadhara) of Mahāvīra, to whom the Ṛṣimaṇḍala-stotra is traditionally ascribed; in the Gaṇadharavāda his doubt about the existence of the soul is resolved by Mahāvīra.

name: Indradyumna Bhāllaveya
summary: One of the five great householders and great Vedic scholars who asked 'what is our self, what is brahman?' and, with Uddālaka Āruṇi, went to Aśvapati Kaikeya; each had venerated only one part of the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11-17).

name: Ippen

summary: Wandering holy man who gave up home and possessions ('the saint who casts off'), distributed nenbutsu talismans to over 250,000 people and led dancing nenbutsu across Japan; before dying he burned his books, saying all the teachings of his life had become 'Namu Amida Butsu'. Founder of the Ji-shū.

name: Īśāna (Pāśupata tīrthakara)

name: Īśvara Purī

name: Iṭaṅkaḻi Nāyaṉār

Sage of Sāṃkhya-Yoga lore. The Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 3.18) records his dialogue with Āvaṭya about the suffering even in the highest births, and cites his view (on YS 2.55) that the highest sense-control is non-apprehension (of objects) through one-pointedness of mind. The Mahābhārata places him in stories with Asita Devala.

name: Jaimini

tradition.text: pupil of Vyāsa, to whom Vyāsa entrusted the Sāmaveda (Purāṇic account)

notes: The Purāṇic Jaimini (Sāmaveda transmitter, narrator of the Jaimini Aśvamedha) and the sūtrakāra are identified by tradition; the identity is not established historically. The astrological Jaimini Sūtras (src:jaimini-upadesa-sutra) are a separate attribution.
summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra. In the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra he is cited by name for positions (e.g. that actions too are subsidiaries, MS 3.1.4); the Brahma Sūtra reports his views on the fruit of action, on knowledge as subsidiary to rites and on the released self (BS 3.2.40, 3.4.2, 3.4.18, 4.3.12, 4.4.5).

checks.note: Located: 'sāmago jaiminiḥ kaviḥ' (Bhāgavata 1.4.21), Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4.9. The identification with the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra author is traditional; the entry correctly marks it as disputed.
Confirmed as the eponym of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school, whose Brāhmaṇa is extant. The other identifications are labelled as tradition.
VP 3.4.9 (Jaimini for the Sāmaveda) and MkP 1.1 located.

alt_summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra; cited by name in the Brahma Sūtras for views Bādarāyaṇa records and often corrects: that knowledge is subsidiary to ritual (BS 3.4.2), that the gods are not eligible for the honey-meditation (1.3.31), that the path of the gods leads to the supreme Brahman (4.3.12), that the liberated has Brahman's qualities (4.4.5) and a body (4.4.11). Tradition makes him a disciple of Vyāsa.

Vyāsa's pupil who received the Sāmaveda (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21); eponym of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda. The tradition identifies him with the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (the identification is disputed by scholars).

In the Purāṇas Vyāsa's disciple for the Sāmaveda (VP 3.4), and the questioner of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, who asks about the Mahābhārata's puzzles and then about birth, death and liberation. (His identity with the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra author is the traditional view.)

For jyotiṣa, the seer to whom the tradition ascribes the Upadeśa Sūtras of the Jaimini system (sign-aspects, cara-kārakas, cara-daśā), identified by the tradition with the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra; commentators say he composed it at Kāśī. Scholarly account: date and authorship uncertain.
U02 contribution: eponym of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda school whose Brāhmaṇa bears his name; tradition makes him the pupil of Vyāsa and the author of the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (U12).

summary: Co-founder of the Rimé movement. He presented the other-emptiness view as the Great Madhyamaka and revived the Shangpa, Chöd and Kālacakra instructions.

summary: Early Cakrasaṃvara commentator of Vikramaśīla (Cakrasaṃvarapañjikā), c. 9th–10th c.

name: Jayācārya (Jītmal)
summary: Fourth ācārya of the Terāpanth (1803–1881), who organized its institutions, instituted the annual festival of the code (Maryādā Mahotsava) and wrote a Rajasthani verse rendering of the Bhagavatī.

name: Jayadatta Sūri
summary: Author of the Aśvavaidyaka.

name: Jayadeva
summary: Sanskrit poet of the Gīta Govinda, the song-poem of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's love in separation and union, sung daily before Jagannātha at Purī and revered by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas and in the temple music of Odisha, Bengal, Kerala and the south.
places: Kenduli / Kindubilva (claimed by Bengal and by Odisha as Kenduli Sasan)

realization_account.text: Son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (the poem's closing verse). A wandering ascetic, he was given Padmāvatī in marriage by her father at Jagannātha's command. When he hesitated to write that Kṛṣṇa asked to place Rādhā's foot on his head, he went to bathe; Kṛṣṇa, in Jayadeva's form, came and wrote the line 'dehi pada-pallavam udāram' himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Birthplace disputed between Bengal (Kenduli, Birbhum), Odisha (Kenduli Sasan near Purī) and Mithilā. Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth (context only). Distinct from the later Jayadeva of the Candrāloka.

name: Jayāditya
summary: Co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti.

checks.note: Confirmed: co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti, 7th c. CE (Wikipedia; Wisdomlib).

name: Jayadratha
summary: Named by the Lord, with Droṇa, Bhīṣma and Karṇa, among the warriors 'already slain by me' whom Arjuna is to slay (BhG 11.34); in the epic he is the Kaurava ally, king of the Sindhus.

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

name: Jayamiśra
summary: Author of the Śarkarikā commentary on the Ślokavārttika.

name: Jayānanda

realization_account.text: A brahmin minister who fed crows secretly and was imprisoned; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 58): The samādhi of gnosis-awareness is without beginning and abides as the innate; realized as it is, it is certain; conceptual recollection itself is darkness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 58 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A brahmin minister who fed crows secretly and was imprisoned; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.
alt_summary: Author of a Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Jayānanda (Madhyamaka)

realization_account.text: Tibetan accounts record a debate between Jayānanda and the Tibetan logician Chapa Chökyi Senge on Candrakīrti's rejection of autonomous reasoning; the accounts differ on its outcome.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Kashmiri Madhyamaka scholar of the 12th century, author of the only Indian sub-commentary on the Madhyamakāvatāra, active in Tibet and among the Tanguts; distinct from the Bengali Vaiṣṇava poet Jayānanda (tch:jayananda).

name: Jayanandī
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 46.
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyamañjarī, the Nyāyakalikā and the drama Āgamaḍambara, set in the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman (r. 883–902). He defends the Veda and the Lord and examines the validity of the Āgamas.
notes: His son is usually identified as the poet Abhinanda (moderate confidence).

name: Jayantī
summary: A laywoman of Kauśāmbī, sister-in-law of King Śatānīka, whose questions to Mahāvīra (on sleep and wakefulness, strength and weakness, and whether all beings capable of liberation will be liberated) are recorded in the Bhagavatī (12.2); she later became a nun.

name: Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tattvopaplavasiṃha, the only complete surviving work of the Lokāyata current. He quotes 'the venerable Bṛhaspati' and argues that no definition of any means of knowledge can be made good, so that no principle — not even the four elements — can be established; worldly conduct proceeds without examination.

name: Jayaratha
summary: 13th-century Kashmiri scholar, son of Śṛṅgāraratha, author of the Viveka commentary on the whole Tantrāloka - the main source for many lost tantras and for the Mata and Krama - as well as a commentary on the Vāmakeśvarīmata (Śrīvidyā) and a work on poetics.

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE (under King Rājadeva, early 13th c.)

notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue role); U19 owns his exegesis.
alt_summary: Kashmirian commentator on the Tantrāloka whose Viveka preserves, from the lost Śrīkaṇṭhīya Saṃhitā, the catalogues of the 28 Siddhānta tantras and of the 64 Bhairava tantras.
U23 contribution: author of the Vivaraṇa on the Vāmakeśvarīmata, the Kashmiri commentary on the root Śrīvidyā tantra.

name: Jayasena (commentator on Kundakunda)
summary: Author of Tātparyavṛtti commentaries on Kundakunda's Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra and Pañcāstikāya, using a longer recension than Amṛtacandra's.
alt_summary: Digambara commentator on Kundakunda's works (Tātparyavṛtti).

name: Jayata (Sheyeduo 闍耶多)
summary: Twentieth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 20.

name: Jayatarāma
summary: Author of the Braj Bhāṣā Jogapradīpikā (1737), a vernacular haṭha compendium of eighty-four postures and twenty-four mudrās.
notes: Sectarian affiliation low confidence.

name: Jayatīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1365–1388 in maṭha lists

realization_account.text: The tradition identifies Jayatīrtha with the bull that carried Madhva's manuscripts, who listened to Madhva's teaching and was blessed to become its commentator; seeing the young horseman drink from a river without dismounting, like an animal, Akṣobhya Tīrtha asked what he had been in his past body, and the memory awakened him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great commentator (Ṭīkācārya) of the tradition: author of the Nyāyasudhā on the Anuvyākhyāna and the Tattvaprakāśikā on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, commentaries on the Gītā works, the Ṛgbhāṣya and all ten prakaraṇas, and the independent Pramāṇapaddhati and Vādāvalī. His commentaries fixed the scholastic form of Dvaita. In the tradition's account he had been a young cavalryman (Dhoṇḍo Raghunātha of Maṅgaḷavēḍhe) whom Akṣobhya Tīrtha awakened to his past birth.
notes: The location of his brindāvana (Malkheḍ, per the Uttarādi Maṭha; Nava Brindāvana, per another view) is disputed within the tradition — recorded at low confidence. The realization account is oral and hagiographic tradition; no textual source was checked for it.

checks.note: Both works confirmed.

alt_summary: Author of the Prameyadīpikā and Nyāyadīpikā on Madhva's Gītā works.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jejjaṭa
summary: Early commentator on the Caraka Saṃhitā (Nirantarapadavyākhyā), partly extant.

name: Jetsün Chökyi Gyaltsen
summary: Author of the textbooks (yig cha) of Sera Je and Ganden Jangtse colleges.

name: Jhālī Rānī of Chittor
summary: Queen of Chittor who, in the Ravidāsī and Rāmānandī hagiographies, became Ravidās's disciple and invited him to her court.

name: Jiacai
summary: Tang monk of the Hongfa si in Chang'an who systematised Daochuo's teaching in his Jingtu lun, including biographies of those born.

name: Jianzhen

realization_account.text: After five failed crossings and the loss of his sight he reached Japan, conferred the precepts at Tōdaiji and founded Tōshōdaiji.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Chinese Vinaya master who established formal ordination by the Four-Part Vinaya in Japan.
notes: Daoxuan listed as teacher in the lineage sense (Nanshan line), not personally.

name: Jiezhu
summary: Northern Song monk who compiled the Jingtu wangsheng zhuan.

name: Jigme Gyalwai Nyugu ('jigs med rgyal ba'i myu gu)
summary: Disciple of Jigme Lingpa and Patrul Rinpoche's root teacher, whose oral teaching of the preliminaries Patrul wrote down as the Words of My Perfect Teacher.

name: Jigme Lingpa (rig 'dzin 'jigs med gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer and Dzogchen master who, in three visions of Longchenpa during retreats at Samye Chimphu, received the Longchen Nyingthig; author of the Yönten Dzöd and the Yeshe Lama; at his inspiration the Derge royal house had the Nyingma Gyubum carved, edited by Getse Paṇḍita (moderate).

realization_account.text: Received the mind-transmission of Longchenpa's wisdom body in visions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: First Dodrupchen, Jigme Trinle Özer (rdo grub chen 'jigs med phrin las 'od zer)
summary: Principal disciple of Jigme Lingpa who spread the Longchen Nyingthig in eastern Tibet.
notes: Lived past 1800 but his formation and main activity began before; not flagged recent (decision logged).

name: Jigten Sumgön (Drikung Kyobpa Rinchen Pal)
alt_names: 'bri gung skyob pa rin chen dpal
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa, founder of the Drikung Kagyu at Drikung Thil (1179); teacher of the 'single intent' and the fivefold Mahāmudrā; sent large numbers of retreatants to Kailash, Lapchi and Tsari.

name: Jīmūtavāhana
summary: Bengali jurist, author of the Dāyabhāga.

checks.note: Confirmed: c. 1050–1150; the Kālaviveka was written soon after 1093 (Wikipedia). This is consistent with the entry's 1090–1200.

name: Jinabhadra Gaṇi Kṣamāśramaṇa
summary: Śvetāmbara scholastic, author of the Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya (with the Gaṇadharavāda) and, by tradition, the Dhyānaśataka; defender of the view that the omniscient's knowledge and perception occur in sequence.
alt_summary: Śvetāmbara scholastic (6th–7th c.) whose Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya systematized the doctrines of knowledge, standpoints and the gaṇadharas' debates; also author of the Jītakalpa.

name: Jinadāsagaṇi Mahattara
summary: 7th-c. author of cūrṇis on the Niśītha, Āvaśyaka, Nandī and other canonical texts.

name: Jinadattasūri
summary: Kharatara ācārya (1075–1154), the first 'Dādāguru', credited with converting many Rajput and other clans to Jainism.

name: Jinakuśalasūri
summary: Kharatara ācārya (1280–1332), one of the four Dādāgurus, venerated at dādābāḍī shrines.

name: Jinamitra
summary: Kashmiri paṇḍita in Tibet (late 8th-9th c.) who co-translated many sūtras and the Mahāvyutpatti terminology.

name: Jinaprabha Sūri
summary: Kharatara Gaccha ācārya, author of the Vividhatīrthakalpa and of works on the Sūrimantra; the tradition tells of his wonders at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq.
alt_summary: 14th-c. Kharatara monk at the court of Muhammad bin Tughluq, author of the Vividhatīrthakalpa and of ritual and hymn literature.

name: Jinaputra
summary: Yogācāra commentator, one of the ten masters of the Cheng weishi lun; credited in Tibet with the Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya.

name: Jinasena (author of the Ādipurāṇa)
summary: Pupil of Vīrasena, preceptor of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I; completed the Jayadhavalā (837 CE) and wrote the Ādipurāṇa, which defines Jain householder rites and the Jain brāhmaṇa; also the Pārśvābhyudaya.
alt_summary: Digambara ācārya, author of the Ādipurāṇa (U35 cites its argument against a creator).

name: Jinasena of the Punnāṭa saṅgha
summary: Author of the Harivaṃśapurāṇa (783 CE); distinct from the author of the Ādipurāṇa.

name: Jinavallabhasūri
summary: Kharatara reformer (d. 1110) who continued the campaign against temple-dwelling monks.

name: Jinendrabuddhi
summary: Commentator on Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, whose Viśālāmalavatī preserves much of Dignāga's Sanskrit.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: a Buddhist grammarian of the 8th c. (Nyāsa c. 800–850), matching the entry's 8th–9th c.

alt_summary: Author of the Nyāsa on the Kāśikāvṛtti (a Buddhist, by most accounts).

name: Jineśvarasūri
summary: 11th-c. reformer who defeated the temple-dwelling monks in debate at the Caulukya court of Aṇahilapāṭaka (1024), winning the right of forest-dwelling (vasativāsī) monks to reside in the city; founder-figure of the Kharatara Gaccha.

name: Jingjue 淨覺
summary: Northern-school author of the Lengqie shizi ji.

name: Jingshan Faqin 徑山法欽
summary: Oxhead master honoured at court; the tradition says Danxia and others visited him.

name: Jingying Huiyuan
summary: Sui scholar-monk (not the Huiyuan of Lushan) whose commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra ranked the nine grades by the attainments of sages and ordinary beings; Shandao's commentary argues against this reading.

name: Jinul 知訥 (Bojo)

realization_account.text: Three awakenings through texts rather than a living teacher: reading the Platform Sūtra (the self-nature is not defiled by the senses), Li Tongxuan's Huayan commentary, and Dahui's records (freedom from lingering obstruction).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Goryeo reformer of Seon: founded the Samādhi and Prajñā Community (Suseonsa, later Songgwangsa); taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation, tracing back the radiance to the empty and calm numinous awareness, the balanced cultivation of samādhi and prajñā, harmony with Huayan, and the hwadu as a shortcut.

name: Jitāri
summary: Buddhist logician and doxographer (Sugatamatavibhaṅga), classed by Tibetan doxographers among the false-aspectarian Yogācāra-Madhyamaka; one of Atiśa's teachers.
alt_summary: Logician of Bengal, by tradition a teacher of Atiśa, author of short manuals of logic and of works on exclusion and universals.

name: Jitvan Śailini
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is speech (BAU 4.1.2); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 4.1.2 ('abravīn me jitvā śailinir vāg vai brahmeti'). 'Jitvan' is the stem of 'jitvā'.

name: Jīva Gosvāmī
summary: Nephew and disciple of Rūpa and Sanātana; the systematic theologian of the school (Ṣaṭ Sandarbha, Sarvasaṃvādinī, Kramasandarbha), grammarian (Harināmāmṛtavyākaraṇa), poet (Gopālacampū) and commentator; leader of the Vṛndāvana community after the elder Gosvāmīs.

name: Jīvaka Komārabhacca
summary: Physician to King Bimbisāra and the Saṅgha; brought Ajātasattu to the Buddha (DN 2); MN 55 addressed to him.

name: Jīvaśarman
summary: An earlier horā teacher whose own views on longevity (BJ 7.9) and royal yogas (BJ 11.1) Varāhamihira reports.
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Bhaṭṭāraka Jñānabhūṣaṇa
summary: Digambara bhaṭṭāraka, author of the Tattvajñānataraṅgiṇī.

name: Jñānagarbha
summary: Author of the Satyadvayavibhaṅga on the two truths; student of Śrīgupta and teacher of Śāntarakṣita in the Tibetan lineage.

name: Jñānānanda Paramahaṃsa
summary: Author of the Kaulāvalīnirṇaya, a digest of Kaula practice.

name: Jñānanetra (Śivānanda)
summary: Regarded as the founder of the Krama in Kashmir, who received the teaching from the goddess (in Oḍḍiyāna, in the tradition's account) and passed it to three female disciples.
notes: Names of the female disciples (Keyūravatī, Madanikā, Kalyāṇikā) recalled from secondary literature - gap.

name: Jñānaprakāśa
summary: Saiddhāntika author (described as resident of Śālivāṭipura) of a Pauṣkara commentary and of a collection on the greatness and authority of the Śaiva Āgamas.

name: Jñānaśiva
summary: Author of the Jñānaratnāvalī, a compendium of Siddhānta ritual.

name: Jñānaśrīmitra
summary: Vikramaśīla scholar (by tradition one of its 'gate-keepers') whose works on momentariness, exclusion, God and the reality of cognition's images mark the height of late Indian Buddhist philosophy.

name: Jñānasūtra
summary: Disciple of Śrī Siṃha and teacher of Vimalamitra in the instruction-series lineage; his testament is the Four Ways of Leaving as It Is.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Marathi saint-philosopher (Jñānadev, Jñānobā), second of the four siblings, disciple of his brother Nivṛttināth in the Nāth line. At about fifteen he spoke the Jñāneśvarī at Nevāse (1290), then the Amṛtānubhava, the Cāṅgadeva Pāsaṣṭī, the Haripāṭh and abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala; he founded the Vārkarī saint-tradition with Nāmdev, travelled with him, and at twenty-one entered living samādhi (sañjīvana samādhi) at Āḷandī.

tradition.text: 1275–1296; samādhi on Kārtika vadya 13, Śaka 1218

realization_account.text: Realized from boyhood by his guru's grace; made a buffalo recite the Veda at Paiṭhaṇ, rode a moving wall to meet Cāṅgadev, and entered living samādhi at Āḷandī where he is believed still present.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Confirmed (Nāth and Vārkarī lineages).

alt_summary: U21 contribution: in the Nāth line through Nivṛttināth; the Jñāneśvarī names the Nāth sequence of teachers at its close and calls the swallowing of the body by the body the secret of the Nāth signal (6.291).
Author of the Jñāneśvarī, the Marathi verse commentary on the Gītā (1290).
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Jñānottama
summary: Advaitin, teacher of Citsukha, author of a commentary (Candrikā) on the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi.

name: Jogipa

realization_account.text: A low-caste man sent by Śavaripa on pilgrimage to the twenty-four sacred sites, reciting the mantra as he walked. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 53): By habituation to a mind subtle and clear like the flame of a lamp, all things stable and moving dissolve into dharmadhātu.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 53 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A low-caste man sent by Śavaripa on pilgrimage to the twenty-four sacred sites, reciting the mantra as he walked.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Jōkei
summary: Hossō (Faxiang) monk and reformer, devoted to Maitreya, Kannon and Śākyamuni, who drafted the Kōfukuji petition of 1205 against the exclusive nenbutsu.

name: Jonang Lotsawa Lodrö Pal (jo nang lo tsA ba blo gros dpal)
summary: Translator in Dolpopa's circle who, with Mati Paṇchen, prepared the Jonang translation of the Kālacakra tantra and the Vimalaprabhā.

name: Juefan Huihong 覺範慧洪
summary: Huanglong-branch scholar-poet who championed 'lettered Chan' (wenzi Chan).

name: Juhū Brahmajāyā
summary: ṛṣikā (with Ūrdhvanābhā Brāhma as alternative) of RV 10.109 on the restoration of the brahmin's wife.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'juhūr brahmajāyā, brāhmaḥ ūrdhvanābhā vā'.

name: Jūkaku
summary: Kakunyo's son who compiled Shinran's letters as the Mattōshō (1333).

name: Julian P. Johnson
summary: American surgeon and disciple of Sawan Singh, author of The Path of the Masters (1939).

name: Juzhi 俱胝 (One-Finger Juzhi)
summary: Answered every question by raising one finger ('one-finger Chan' received from Tianlong), cut off a boy's imitating finger (Wumenguan case 3).

name: Jyeṣṭhadeva
summary: Author of the Malayalam Yuktibhāṣā setting out the demonstrations of the Kerala school.

name: Kabandhī Kātyāyana
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks whence creatures are born (PrU 1).

checks.note: Located: PrU 1.1 and 1.3 (whence creatures are born).

name: Kabīr

tradition.text: 1398–1518 (a life of 120 years); in the Kabīr Panth, Kabīr appeared as an infant on a lotus in Lahartārā tank and was found by the weavers Nīrū and Nīmā

scholarly.text: c. 1440–1518 on the common view; Ch. Vaudeville argued 1398–1448

realization_account.text: Initiated by Rāmānanda, who stumbled on him lying on the steps of the Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ before dawn and uttered 'Rām' (Rāmānandī and popular account); in the Kabīr Panth he needs no guru, being the Sat Puruṣ himself, and accepts Rāmānanda only to model discipleship. At his death at Maghar his Hindu and Muslim followers disputed his body; under the shroud they found only flowers, which they divided for a samādhi and a tomb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Weaver (julāhā) poet-saint of Banaras, raised in a Muslim weaver household, the most influential of the Sants: he taught love of the formless Rām through the Name and the true guru, mocked the formalism of paṇḍit and mullā, yogī and ascetic, rejected caste, idols and pilgrimage, and spoke of the natural state (sahaj) and of dying while alive. His words survive in three recensions (the eastern Bījak, the Rajasthani Granthāvalī/Pañcvāṇī, the Punjabi Ādi Granth) and in a vast oral corpus; the Kabīr Panth reveres him as the incarnate True Being.
notes: Relation to Rāmānanda is disputed (dsp:kabir-guru-ramananda). Encounters with Sikandar Lodī and with Gorakhnāth are legendary.

name: Kaccānagotta
summary: A monk who asked what right view is (SN 12.15).

name: Kaṭuveḷic cittar
summary: Siddhar poet of the 'Joy-song' (Āṉantak kaḷippu), whose refrain 'do no sin, O mind' and whose image of the mendicant breaking his hard-won pot are among the best-known Siddhar lines.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The name is read as 'the one of the vast (fierce) open space'; no life story is recalled.

name: Kahola Kauṣītakeya
summary: Asks Yājñavalkya the same question as Uṣasta and is told of the self beyond hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age and death, knowing which brahmins renounce the three desires (BAU 3.5.1).

checks.note: Located: BĀU 3.5.1 ('kaholaḥ kauṣītakeyaḥ'; 'putraiṣaṇāyāś ca vittaiṣaṇāyāś ca lokaiṣaṇāyāś ca vyutthāya').

name: Kailāspati Bābā
summary: Ascetic of the Tārāpīṭh cremation ground remembered as the teacher of Bāmākhepā.

name: Kairāta
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Kaivalyāśrama
summary: A renunciant commentator on the Saundaryalaharī (Saubhāgyavardhinī).

name: Kaiyadeva
summary: Author of the Kaiyadeva Nighaṇṭu.

name: Kaiyaṭa
summary: Kashmiri author of the Pradīpa on the Mahābhāṣya.

checks.note: Confirmed: Kashmir, 11th c. (Wisdomlib).

alt_summary: U31 contribution: Kashmiri author of the Pradīpa on the Mahābhāṣya, who reads Patañjali through Bhartṛhari and transmits the sphoṭa doctrine and the Word-monism to the later grammarians.

name: Kākacaṇḍīśvara
summary: Named among the authorities of rasa (Rasaratnasamuccaya 1.6); the Kākacaṇḍīśvarīmata bears his name.

name: Kākapucuṇṭar (Kākabhuśuṇḍa)
summary: The crow-sage, counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha the long-lived crow Bhuśuṇḍa teaches breath-contemplation.
notes: Siddhar-list membership recalled at low confidence.

name: Kakṣīvant
summary: Kakṣīvant Dairghatamasa Auśija, seer of RV 1.116–126 (hymns to the Aśvins and gift-praises); father of the ṛṣikā Ghoṣā.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 'kakṣīvān dairghatamasa auśijaḥ' for 1.116–126; Ghoṣā is 'Kākṣīvatī' (10.39–40 header), confirming the father–daughter relation.

name: Kakuan 覺晏
summary: Nōnin's successor, teacher of Ejō.

name: Kakunyo
summary: Shinran's great-grandson who made the Ōtani mausoleum into the temple Honganji and claimed for it the orthodox transmission (Shinran–Nyoshin–Kakunyo); author of the Godenshō.

name: Kakusandha
summary: The fourth of the seven Buddhas of DN 14, the first of this fortunate aeon.

name: Kakushinni
summary: Shinran's youngest daughter who cared for him in Kyoto and established the Ōtani mausoleum (1272), the origin of the Honganji, as its caretaker.

name: Kālacakrapāda
summary: The name of the Indian masters (an elder and a younger) credited with bringing the Kālacakra from Śambhala to India in the early 11th c. and teaching it at Nālandā/Vikramaśīla; Tibetan histories connect them with Cilupa and Piṇḍo; details differ by account.

name: Kālāgnirudra
summary: Rudra as 'fire of time': teaches Sanatkumāra the tripuṇḍra (Kālāgnirudra) and Bhusuṇḍa the sacred ash (Bṛhajjābāla); rudrākṣa beads arise from his tears (Rudrākṣajābāla).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of kalagnirudra, brhajjabala, rudraksajabala, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Kālaka (Kālakācārya)
summary: Elder remembered in the Kālakācāryakathā: to free his sister, the nun Sarasvatī, abducted by King Gardabhilla of Ujjayinī, he brought the Śaka kings; he also moved the Paryuṣaṇa (Saṃvatsarī) from the fifth to the fourth of Bhādrapada at the request of King Sātavāhana, a date the Tapā Gaccha keeps.

tradition.text: c. 1st c. BCE

name: Kalakala

realization_account.text: A man who talked incessantly and was shunned; taught to hear all speech as echo. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 68): In the centre of the pure sky of dharmadhātu the thunder of the unborn resounds; all the deluded phenomena of appearance and existence are the beautiful fruit, the three bodies and gnosis.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 68 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A man who talked incessantly and was shunned; taught to hear all speech as echo.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kālāṅki nātar
summary: Siddhar named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage; later tradition makes him the guru of Bogar.
notes: TM 69 (checked locally) names 'Kālāṅki'; the guru-of-Bogar link is the later tradition's.

name: Kalapa

realization_account.text: A handsome man thought mad by the people; taught to use his condition as the path. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 27): These beings have been deluded since beginningless time, and so the whole world is uneven; the nectar medicine of the guru's instruction burns the diseases of delusion in a single instant.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 27 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A handsome man thought mad by the people; taught to use his condition as the path.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kaḻaṟciṅka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pallava king whose queen smelled a flower fallen from the temple's flower-hall at Tiruvārūr; after Ceruttuṇaiyār had cut her nose, the king cut off the hand that had picked up the flower.

realization_account.text: A Pallava king whose queen smelled a flower fallen from the temple's flower-hall at Tiruvārūr; after Ceruttuṇaiyār had cut her nose, the king cut off the hand that had picked up the flower.

name: Kālīcaraṇa
summary: Commentator (Ṭīkā) on the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa and the Pādukāpañcaka, whose commentary Arthur Avalon translated in The Serpent Power.

name: Kālidāsa
summary: The classical poet; Śākta tradition holds that he gained his genius by the Goddess's (Kālī's) grace and ascribes to him the Śyāmalā Daṇḍaka and other hymns.

realization_account.text: An unlettered man who became the greatest poet when the Goddess wrote on his tongue.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: U23 records only the Śākta attributions and legend.

name: Kālidāsa (as ascribed author of the Uttarakālāmṛta)
summary: The Kālidāsa to whom the Uttarakālāmṛta is ascribed; the tradition sometimes identifies him with the poet (doubtful), as it also ascribes to 'Kālidāsa' the Jyotirvidābharaṇa.

name: Kalikkampa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who washed devotees' feet; when his wife hesitated to pour water for one who had once been their servant, he cut off her hand.

realization_account.text: A merchant who washed devotees' feet; when his wife hesitated to pour water for one who had once been their servant, he cut off her hand.
