name: Kaliya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. An oil-presser who kept the temple lamps burning; ruined, he tried to fill the lamps with his own blood, and Śiva stopped him.

realization_account.text: An oil-presser who kept the temple lamps burning; ruined, he tried to fill the lamps with his own blood, and Śiva stopped him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa
summary: Vasugupta's disciple, author of the Spandavṛtti and - according to Bhāskara, Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhagavadutpala - of the Spandakārikā itself; his lost Tattvārthacintāmaṇi commented on the last part of the Śiva Sūtra.

scholarly.text: fl. under King Avantivarman (855-883 CE) according to the Rājataraṅgiṇī (5.66)

name: Kallinātha
summary: Commentator on the Saṅgītaratnākara (Kalānidhi) at the Vijayanagara court.

name: Kālūrām
summary: Aghora ascetic of Varanasi, guru of Kīnārām, regarded in the tradition as Dattātreya himself; the Krīm Kuṇḍ seat is associated with him.

realization_account.text: A form of Dattātreya (tradition).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kalyāṇ Svāmī
summary: Rāmdās's principal disciple and scribe of the Dāsbodh.

name: Kalyāṇavarman
summary: Author of the Sārāvalī, a large compendium of horā; described as a king of Vyāghrataṭī (low confidence).

name: Kamāl
summary: Kabīr's son (or adopted son) in the legends, himself a devotee to whom some verses are ascribed; the proverb 'Kabīr's line sank when the son Kamāl was born' is quoted against him.

name: Kamalabuddhi
summary: In Tibetan accounts a disciple of Buddhapālita and teacher of Candrakīrti.

name: Kamalākānta Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta poet and sādhaka of Ambikā-Kālnā, later at Burdwan under Mahārāja Tejcandra; author of Śyāmā-saṅgīt to Kālī and Umā in the line of Rāmprasād, and of the Sādhaka-rañjana on tantric yoga.

realization_account.text: The Mahārāja of Burdwan became his disciple after he showed that the Goddess answered his call.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Nirṇayasindhu, of the Bhaṭṭa family of Vārāṇasī.

checks.note: Confirmed: the Nirṇayasindhu was composed in 1612 (Wisdomlib). The Vārāṇasī Bhaṭṭa family is standard.

name: Kamalākara (astronomer)
summary: Astronomer of Kāśī, author of the Siddhāntatattvaviveka (1658) in defence of the Saura school; distinct from Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa of the Nirṇayasindhu.

name: Kamalamuṉi
summary: Siddhar of the popular list, with a samādhi place at Tiruvārūr; no works or teachings are recalled here.
places: Tiruvārūr — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kamalaśīla

tradition.text: debated at Samye in the reign of Trisong Detsen

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories (the sBa bzhed and later) tell that he was invited on Śāntarakṣita's instruction, debated Moheyan before the king at Samye, was declared victor so that the gradual path of the six perfections became the norm in Tibet, wrote the Bhāvanākramas at the king's request, and was later murdered.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Samye debate date c. 792–794 in scholarly reconstructions; the Chinese Dunhuang sources give Moheyan's side as victorious.
summary: Śāntarakṣita's disciple, author of the Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, the Madhyamakāloka and the three Bhāvanākramas, who defended the gradual path at the Samye debate against the Chan master Moheyan.
alt_summary: Śāntarakṣita's disciple, commentator on the Tattvasaṃgraha and author of the Bhāvanākramas, which quote the Laṅkāvatāra's four-stage entry through mind-only.
alt_notes: Contribution of U41 (pramāṇa and Yogācāra side).

name: Kambala (Kambalapāda, Lvabapa)

realization_account.text: A prince who became a monk and then a yogin wearing only a black woollen blanket; he defeated a band of witches (ḍākinīs) who stole it; teacher of Indrabhūti, author of the Navaślokī and a Cakrasaṃvara commentary; named in Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa as the source of dream yoga (as La ba pa). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 30): In the deep and vast ocean full of jewels the nāga kings enjoy themselves marvellously; likewise all appearances and sounds are primordially the dharmakāya, and for those with realization the enjoyment is marvellous.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 30 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A prince who became a monk and then a yogin wearing only a black woollen blanket; he defeated a band of witches (ḍākinīs) who stole it; teacher of Indrabhūti, author of the Navaślokī and a Cakrasaṃvara commentary; named in Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa as the source of dream yoga (as La ba pa).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Tōh 2292 reads 'ka ma la'; the position (30) fits Abhayadatta's Kambala.

name: Kambalāśvatara
summary: A Lokāyata author quoted by Śāntarakṣita: 'cognition arises from the body alone, sustained by the in- and out-breaths' (Tattvasaṅgraha 1864); Kamalaśīla calls this 'the sūtra: kāyād eva'.

name: Kāmeśvarasūri
summary: Commentator on the Saundaryalaharī (Aruṇāmodinī), as remembered here.

name: Kampaṉ
summary: Tamil poet of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), the great devotional retelling of Rāma's story; by tradition he also sang the Caṭakōpar Antāti in praise of Nammāḻvār so that his Rāmāyaṇa would be accepted at Śrīraṅgam.
notes: Not an Āḻvār; placed under lin:alvar as the lineage of Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional poetry. Tradition: at the Rāmāyaṇa's first recital at Śrīraṅgam the Narasiṃha image roared approval.

name: Kamparipa

realization_account.text: A blacksmith taught to visualize his forge within: the channels as bellows and the fire of gnosis. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 45): On the hearth of natural form, on the charcoal of recollection, awareness and concepts, blowing the bellows of lalanā and rasanā and kindling the fire of gnosis in the avadhūtī, the concepts of the three poisons are forged into the dharmakāya; realizing this, Kampari was freed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 45 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A blacksmith taught to visualize his forge within: the channels as bellows and the fire of gnosis.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Smith imagery confirms the identification.

name: Kamta Prasad Sinha (Sarkar Sahab)
summary: Agra-line guru of Ghazipur, predecessor of Anand Swarup in the Dayalbagh succession.

name: Kāmukāyana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 11.1.56, 11.1.61).

name: Kaṇāda

tradition.text: an ancient ṛṣi

scholarly.text: the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra core is usually dated around the turn of the era (estimates vary widely)

summary: The sage to whom the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is attributed, founder of Vaiśeṣika; Praśastapāda salutes him after Īśvara. His names Kaṇabhuj / Kaṇabhakṣa ('grain-eater') are traditionally explained by his living on gleaned grains; Buddhist and Jain sources call the school Aulūkya after his name Ulūka.

name: Kanakhalā
alt_names: nA ga ka la ka (Tōh 2292 spelling)

realization_account.text: The younger of the two headless sisters (see Mekhalā). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 67): Putting on the great armour, with jewel-like courage, launching the boat of one's own mind, one surely enters the interior of the picture.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 67 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). The younger of the two headless sisters (see Mekhalā).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Tōh 2292 reads 'nA ga ka la ka'; identified with Kanakhalā by position (low). The song's meaning is obscure.

name: Kaṇampulla Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poor man who sold kaṇampul grass to buy oil for temple lamps; when he could not sell it he burned the grass itself, and when that ran out he set fire to his own hair.

realization_account.text: A poor man who sold kaṇampul grass to buy oil for temple lamps; when he could not sell it he burned the grass itself, and when that ran out he set fire to his own hair.

name: Kaṇanātha Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin of Cīkāḻi who served in the temple and trained others in its service; devoted to Campantar.

realization_account.text: A brahmin of Cīkāḻi who served in the temple and trained others in its service; devoted to Campantar.

name: Kāṅgāl Harināth (Harināth Majumdar)
summary: Journalist of Kumarkhali (Grāmbārtā Prakāśikā) and composer of Bāul-style songs as 'Phikir Cāṃd'; acquainted with Lalon.

name: Kāṇhapa (Kṛṣṇācārya)

realization_account.text: A monk-yogin of Somapura, disciple of Jālandhara, of great powers and great pride; the lives tell of his pride being humbled and of his death by a woman's curse; author of the Yogaratnamālā, of dohās and of many Caryāgīti songs. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 17): As a chariot lacking one wheel cannot go even when pulled, so, though one strives in giving and the other perfections, without a guru there is no supreme siddhi; as vultures of perfect strength with spread wings cut through the sky, fortunate yogins who have taken the instruction of consecration to heart are blissful.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: U44 contribution (the siddha of the eighty-four): No. 17 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A monk-yogin of Somapura, disciple of Jālandhara, of great powers and great pride; the lives tell of his pride being humbled and of his death by a woman's curse; author of the Yogaratnamālā, of dohās and of many Caryāgīti songs.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.
alt_summary: U21 contribution: in Nāth tradition Kānipā/Kānupā is Jālandhara's disciple (Bengali saga) and, as Kānifnāth, one of the Marathi nine Nāths, with a samādhi shrine at Madhi (Ahilyanagar/Ahmednagar district). Whether this Nāth figure is the same as the Buddhist siddha Kāṇha / Kṛṣṇācārya is not settled.
alt_notes: Registry id for the Buddhist mahāsiddha Kāṇha (U44). Identification with the Nāth Kānipā is the tradition's (shared siddha lists) and is disputed; HYP 1.7 'Kānerī' may or may not be the same figure.

name: Kānhopātrā
summary: Daughter of a courtesan of Maṅgaḷveḍhe (15th c.) who refused a king's summons and died at the Paṇḍharpūr temple, where she is the only saint with a memorial inside the precinct; her abhaṅgas plead for Viṭṭhala's protection.

name: Kaṇikaṇṇaṉ
summary: Disciple of Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār whose banishment from Kāñcī occasioned the story of the Lord who rolled up his serpent-bed and followed them.

realization_account.text: He refused to sing the Pallava king's praises, saying his tongue was for the Lord alone, and was banished.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kaṇimētāviyār
summary: Jain poet, author of the Ēlāti and the Tiṇaimālai Nūṟṟaimpatu.

name: Kañcamalaiyaṉ
summary: Named in TM 69 among Tirumūlar's disciples in the mantra-lineage.
notes: Checked in the local TM e-text (69); nothing further recalled.

name: Kaṅkālayogin
summary: Author to whom the Rasādhyāya is attributed.

name: Kaṅkaṇa

realization_account.text: A king who meditated on the light of the jewel of his bracelet (kaṅkaṇa) as the light of mind. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 29): From the wish-fulfilling jewel of thought the colour of experience arises; by the power of conduct all needs and wishes come; it is accomplished by those who have equal taste.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 29 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A king who meditated on the light of the jewel of his bracelet (kaṅkaṇa) as the light of mind.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kaṅkaripa

realization_account.text: A householder of low caste whose beloved wife died; grieving in the cremation ground, he was taught by a yogin to see her as the ḍākinī, empty and self-appearing, and realized mahāmudrā. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 7): As in empty space, the form free of one and of two — the self-appearing gnosis consort — is beyond example and beyond all conventions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 7 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A householder of low caste whose beloved wife died; grieving in the cremation ground, he was taught by a yogin to see her as the ḍākinī, empty and self-appearing, and realized mahāmudrā.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kāṅkāyana, the physician of Bāhlīka
summary: Speaker: the opposite of the provoking factors pacifies vāyu (Ca Sū 12.6); tastes are innumerable (Sū 26.8); the heart forms first, as the seat of consciousness (Śā 6.21); Prajāpati is the creator of the person and of disease (Sū 25.23).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Kaṇṇappa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A hunter who worshipped the liṅga of Kāḷahasti with meat he had tasted, water carried in his mouth and flowers from his hair, to the dismay of the temple priest Civakōcariyār; when blood flowed from the liṅga's eye he plucked out his own eye and set it there; when the other eye bled he placed his foot on it to mark the spot and began to cut out his second eye — Śiva stopped his hand crying 'Stay, Kaṇṇappa!' and took him to his side.

name: Kantali

realization_account.text: A ragman or tailor who pricked his finger; taught to see needle, thread and cloth as the path. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 69): With the needle of the true guru and the thread of compassion I stitched the three realms into a garment: wondrous yogin of cloth!
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 69 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A ragman or tailor who pricked his finger; taught to see needle, thread and cloth as the path.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Needle-and-thread imagery fits the tailor.

name: Kaṇṭarātittar
summary: Cōḻa king (Gaṇḍarāditya, r. c. 950–957) and poet of a Tiruvicaippā hymn to Naṭarāja at Chidambaram.

name: Kaṇva
summary: Kaṇva Ghaura, seer of RV 1.36–43 (incl. 1.43 to Rudra 'lord of songs, lord of sacrifice, with the healing jalāṣa'); eponym of the Kāṇva family whose hymns fill most of book 8.

summary: Heir of Daitō, founder of Myōshinji.

name: Kapālakuruṇṭaka
summary: Name to which the Haṭhābhyāsapaddhati is ascribed in its manuscripts (recalled).

name: Kapālapa

realization_account.text: A father whose sons had died; he carried a skull in his grief and was taught by Kāṇha to meditate on the skull and bone ornaments as symbols. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 72): All things are the non-dual Vajradhara; ornaments, the skull and the rest are adventitious; the delusion of grasping 'I', too, is not found when one searches for it oneself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 72 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A father whose sons had died; he carried a skull in his grief and was taught by Kāṇha to meditate on the skull and bone ornaments as symbols.

name: Kapardin
summary: Ancient Vedāntin named by Rāmānuja among the earlier teachers.

name: Kāpaṭika Bhāradvāja
summary: A sixteen-year-old brahmin student who questioned the Buddha on preserving and awakening to truth (MN 95).

name: Kapila

tradition.text: born at the beginning of creation endowed with virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power (Gauḍapāda on SK 1, 43); in the Purāṇic account an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 3)

realization_account.text: Born with innate (sāṃsiddhika) virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; seeing the world sunk in blind darkness, out of compassion he taught the knowledge of the twenty-five principles to Āsuri. A saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya calls him the first knower who, assuming a created mind (nirmāṇacitta), out of compassion taught the doctrine to the inquiring Āsuri.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Sāṃkhya in the tradition's account: the 'supreme sage' (SK 69) who gave the teaching to Āsuri out of compassion (SK 70). Gauḍapāda counts him among Brahmā's seven mind-born sons; the Māṭhara Vṛtti and the Purāṇas make him an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti. The Sāṃkhya Sūtra and the Tattvasamāsa are ascribed to him; the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Kapila Gītā) preserve further teachings in his name.

alt_summary: In U06's texts: the avatāra Kapila, son of Kardama and Devahūti, who teaches his mother a devotional Sāṃkhya (Kapila Gītā, Bhāgavata 3.25-33). The Bhāgavata identifies him with the founder of Sāṃkhya ('tattva-saṅkhyātā', 3.24-25); some later authors distinguish the two Kapilas.

The Mokṣadharma names Kapila, the supreme seer, as the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60); Nārāyaṇa says the Sāṃkhya teachers call him Kapila (12.326.64); 'among the perfected I am the sage Kapila' (BhG 10.26); in a dialogue Kapila tells Syūmaraśmi that he does not censure the Vedas but that the āśramas' duties have one aim (12.260–262).
In the Bhāgavata the avatāra-teacher of Sāṃkhya, eight-limbed yoga directed to the Lord's form (BhP 3.28) and devotion; a mahājana (6.3.20).

U28 contribution: the Dattātreyayogaśāstra says 'Kapila and the others' practised haṭha (the mudrās), whereas 'Yājñavalkya and others' knew the eight-limbed yoga (DYŚ 26–27, 119); both give the same fruit.
Named by the Lord as his manifestation among the perfected ones (siddha): 'the sage Kapila' (BhG 10.26).

Lineage contribution of lin:upanisadic: SU 5.2 speaks of 'the seer Kapila (or: the tawny seer) born in the beginning, whom he filled with knowledge'. Later tradition reads this as the Sāṃkhya founder, others as Hiraṇyagarbha; the Upaniṣad does not say which.
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).
alt_notes: Whether this Kapila is the founder of Sāṃkhya is not stated by the text.

name: Kapilāṇḍa
summary: Number 8 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Kapimala (Jiapimoluo 迦毘摩羅)
summary: Thirteenth patriarch in the Chan list, said to have converted Nāgārjuna.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 13.

name: Kāpya
summary: Speaker: Soma within kapha does good and ill in the body (Ca Sū 12.12).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant's wife who gave one of two mangoes to a hungry devotee; when her husband asked for the second, she prayed and a mango appeared; frightened, he left her and remarried. She asked Śiva to take her beauty and give her the form of a ghoul (pēy), climbed Kailāsa on her hands, and was greeted by Śiva as 'Mother' (Ammai); she asked for no rebirth — or, if born again, never to forget him — and to sing at his feet as he dances, which she does at Tiruvālaṅkāṭu.

realization_account.text: A merchant's wife who gave one of two mangoes to a hungry devotee; when her husband asked for the second, she prayed and a mango appeared; frightened, he left her and remarried. summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poet who used the rewards for his verses to build and serve temples.

name: Karṇa

name: Karṇakagomin

name: Kārṣṇājini

name: Kāśīrāma Vaidya
summary: Commentator on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā (Gūḍhārthadīpikā).

alt_summary: The ancient ritualist and phonetician to whom the Sarvānukramaṇī of the Ṛgveda, the Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya and the Śrauta Sūtra of the White Yajurveda are ascribed; the tradition often identifies him with Kātyāyana the critic of Pāṇini (disputed).

name: Kātyāyanī

summary: Author of the Jñānaprasthāna, the root text of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma; the Vaibhāṣikas held that he gathered the Buddha's scattered Abhidharma teachings into a treatise.

tradition.text: 978/990–1127/1139 (a life of about 150 years in the tradition's reckoning)

scholarly.text: 11th–12th c.; the traditional life-span is not accepted by modern historians

realization_account.text: He met Niguma in a charnel ground (Sosaling), where she appeared in the sky as a dark-skinned ḍākinī; she taught him in dreams and waking, and bade that the teachings pass to one disciple at a time for seven generations.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tibetan yogin, first trained in Bön and Dzogchen, who travelled to India and Nepal, received the six dharmas and the Amulet Mahāmudrā from Niguma and teachings from Sukhasiddhi, Maitrīpa and others, and founded the Shangpa Kagyu with its seat at Zhong-zhong in Shang.

name: Kiḍāmbi Āccāṉ
summary: Disciple of Rāmānuja who, the tradition says, cooked for him when attempts were made to poison his food; ancestor of the Kiḍāmbi family of teachers in Deśika's line.

name: Kīlhadās
summary: Disciple of Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī who succeeded at Galtā; associated with the ascetic and yogic (tapasvī) branch.

name: Kīnārām
summary: Founder of the present Aghora lineage at Krīm Kuṇḍ (Kīnārām Sthal), Varanasi. Tradition: born at Rāmgaṛh (Chandauli), he was first initiated by the Vaiṣṇava Śivarām, then received Aghora from Bābā Kālūrām, whom he recognised as Dattātreya (after a vision at Girnar); he wandered to Hiṅglāj and elsewhere, founded monasteries and wrote Hindi works — Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī.

tradition.text: 1601–1771 (Vikrama 1658 birth; lived about 170 years)

realization_account.text: Received Aghora-dīkṣā from Kālūrām (Dattātreya); famed for miracles and for compassion to the poor; lived about 170 years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Registry id. The dates are the tradition's; no independent confirmation checked.

name: Kinnari Bommayya
summary: A śaraṇa remembered as a player of the kinnari lute.

name: Kirapala

realization_account.text: A conquering king who repented after seeing the grief of the women of a sacked city. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 73): Until realization one is bound by the concepts of self and other; when realization comes, self and other are not established; so what is called 'buddha' is one's own (nature): hold that, free of elaboration, uncontrived, in its own place.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 73 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A conquering king who repented after seeing the grief of the women of a sacked city.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kirpal Singh
summary: Disciple of Sawan Singh who founded Ruhani Satsang in Delhi (1951) and taught widely in the West; author of Naam or Word and The Crown of Life.

name: Kisa Saṅkicca
summary: The second of the three Ājīvika leaders named in AN 6.57, MN 36 and MN 76.

name: Kisāgotamī
summary: Foremost nun in wearing coarse robes; her verses tell of the deaths of her family and her attainment of the deathless (Thig 10.1); the mustard-seed story is commentarial.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Kiyozawa Manshi
summary: Ōtani-ha priest and philosopher who led a reform of the order and taught 'spiritual activism' (seishinshugi), reliance on the Tathāgata as the foundation of the self.

name: Kōcceṅkaṭ Cōḻa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. In a former birth a spider that wove a canopy over the liṅga at Tiruvāṉaikkā and fought an elephant that also worshipped there, both dying; reborn as a Cōḻa king, he built many 'elevated temples' (māṭakkōyil) that elephants cannot climb.

realization_account.text: In a former birth a spider that wove a canopy over the liṅga at Tiruvāṉaikkā and fought an elephant that also worshipped there, both dying; reborn as a Cōḻa king, he built many 'elevated temples' (māṭakkōyil) that elephants cannot climb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kohala
summary: Ancient authority on drama, music and dance, named in the Nāṭyaśāstra's list of Bharata's sons and cited by Abhinavagupta and Śārṅgadeva; his works are lost.

name: Kokilipa

realization_account.text: A pleasure-loving king who, disturbed by the song of the cuckoo (kokila), was taught to meditate on sound. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 80): Giving up activity is the instruction; being without clinging and craving is the realization; the bliss of no-thing is the meditation; when there is nothing to accomplish, that is the supreme fruit.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 80 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A pleasure-loving king who, disturbed by the song of the cuckoo (kokila), was taught to meditate on sound.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Koṇāgamana
summary: The fifth of the seven Buddhas of DN 14.

name: Könchok Jigme Wangpo
summary: Second Jamyang Shepa of Labrang, author of the Precious Garland of Tenets.

name: Aññāsi Koṇḍañña
summary: The first of the five monks; the first to understand the first discourse ('whatever is subject to arising is subject to cessation', SN 56.11), hence 'Koṇḍañña who has understood'; foremost in seniority.

realization_account.text: The Dhamma-eye arose in him during the first discourse; he became an arahant with the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta (SN 56.11; SN 22.59; Vin Mv 1.6).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Koṅkaṇar
summary: Siddhar and alchemist, in the tradition a disciple of Bogar. A popular story tells that he burnt a crane with his glance and was then rebuked by a devoted housewife who had kept him waiting: 'Did you take me for the crane, Koṅkaṇa?' — sending him to learn from her and from Tiruvaḷḷuvar.
places: Tirupati — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The crane story (kokkeṉṟu niṉaittāyō koṅkaṇavā) is recalled with moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kōrakkar
summary: Siddhar of the popular list whom the tradition identifies with Gorakṣanātha: born from the sacred ash that Maccamuṉi gave a childless woman, who threw it away, until a boy came forth from where it fell. Herbal and alchemical works are ascribed to him; his samādhi is placed at Poyyūr (Vaṭakku Poykainallūr) near Nākappaṭṭiṉam.
places: Vaṭakku Poykainallūr (Poyyūr) — samādhi in the popular list

name: Kōsai
summary: Hōnen's disciple associated with the 'one-calling' teaching (ichinengi): birth is settled in a single moment of faith, one calling; his line (Ichinen-gi) died out.

name: Koṭali

realization_account.text: A peasant digging a mountainside with a hoe whom Śāntipa taught to dig the mountain of mind; he realized before his teacher did. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 44): All pleasure and pain arise from mind; by the guru's instruction dig the mountain of mind; the wise may dig mountains of earth but will not gain innate great bliss; ordinary knowing awakens in the centre of the heart and in the six collections bliss is unbroken; all imputations are meaningless causes of suffering; rest in the innate state beyond meditation and non-meditation.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 44 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A peasant digging a mountainside with a hoe whom Śāntipa taught to dig the mountain of mind; he realized before his teacher did.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Uses the term tha mal shes pa ('ordinary knowing').

name: Kōṭpuli Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cōḻa general who stored paddy for the temple before going to war; returning to find that his kinsmen had eaten it in a famine, he put them to death; Śiva appeared and took them all to his world.

realization_account.text: A Cōḻa general who stored paddy for the temple before going to war; returning to find that his kinsmen had eaten it in a famine, he put them to death; Śiva appeared and took them all to his world.

name: Koun Ejō 孤雲懷奘
summary: Former Daruma-school monk who became Dōgen's heir and second abbot of Eiheiji; recorded the Shōbōgenzō zuimonki.

name: Kriyāśakti
summary: Kālāmukha teacher remembered as preceptor (rājaguru) at the early Vijayanagara court and of the minister Mādhava; among the last prominent Kālāmukhas (identification of his order moderate-low).

name: Kṛpa
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the leaders of his (the Kaurava) army, 'victorious in battle' (1.8).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.8.

name: Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga; his departure from the world is taken to begin the Kali yuga (traditionally 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: The tradition regards him as the Lord (Bhagavān) himself born as Vasudeva's son; in the Gītā he speaks as unborn and imperishable, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6), and the Nārāyaṇīya presents him as a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Vasudeva and Devakī, prince of the Vṛṣṇis, Arjuna's charioteer and teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā and the Anugītā. In the Gītā he speaks as the Lord who descends age after age (4.6–8), is the source of all (10.8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (ch. 11); the Nārāyaṇīya names his birth at Mathurā among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.82). In the Anuśāsana he learns the thousand names of Śiva from Upamanyu (13.14–17).

Role as teacher of the Gītā and Anugītā (14.16.11), his manifestation at Mathurā (12.326.82) and the Upamanyu episode (13.14–17) located. Tradition-only dating as entered.

checks.note: Speaker of the Uddhava Gītā (BhP 11.7.1 ff.); legendary. The Uttara Gītā ascription is traditional (see src:uttara-gita).

notes: Historicity recorded as 'legendary' in the scholarly sense only; the tradition holds him to be the Lord incarnate.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: speaker of the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.7-29), in which he gives Uddhava his final teaching before leaving the world, and of the Uttara Gītā; he quotes the Kāma Gītā (Mahābhārata 14.13).

In Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's charioteer, who blows the conch Pāñcajanya (1.15), stations the chariot between the armies (1.24–25) and, from 2.2, teaches Arjuna ('śrī bhagavān uvāca'): the imperishable embodied self, svadharma, buddhi-yoga and action without claim on fruits, the person of steady wisdom, sacrifice and loka-saṃgraha, and desire as the enemy. He says he declared the twofold commitment of old (3.3), says he acts though he has nothing to gain (3.22–24), and asks Arjuna to resign all actions to him (3.30).

In BhG 7–9 the speaker (śrī bhagavān), who names himself Vāsudeva (7.19) and is addressed by Arjuna as Puruṣottama and Madhusūdana (8.1–2); he teaches himself as the source and dissolution of the world, the adhiyajña in the body, the one to be remembered at death, and the recipient of all worship.

In BhG 4–6 the speaker (śrī bhagavān), addressed as Kṛṣṇa (5.1, 6.34, 6.37, 6.39) and Madhusūdana (6.33). He says he first taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat (4.1), knows all his many births (4.5), and, unborn and lord of beings, comes into being by his own māyā age after age to establish dharma (4.6–8); he is enjoyer of sacrifices, great lord of all worlds and friend of all beings (5.29), the object of the meditator's thought (6.14), and the one whose faithful worshipper is the most yoked yogin (6.47).

In BhG 10–12 the Blessed Lord who declares himself the origin of all and names his manifestations — among them 'Vāsudeva among the Vṛṣṇis' (10.37); he gives Arjuna a divine eye and shows his universal form, declares himself Time (11.32), resumes his gentle human form (11.50–51) and teaches devotion and the marks of the devotee dear to him (ch. 12).

Speaker of the Bhagavad Gītā as the Blessed Lord (śrī bhagavān). In chapters 13–15 he teaches the field and its knower, the three guṇas and the highest person, and speaks of himself as the knower of the field in all fields (13.3), the seed-giving father of all forms (14.4), the foundation of brahman (14.27), the one seated in the heart of all and known by all the Vedas (15.15), and puruṣottama (15.18). Arjuna addresses him as Keśava (13.1) and Prabhu (14.21).

name: Kṛṣṇa Devakīputra
summary: 'Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī', pupil of Ghora Āṅgirasa, who on hearing the teaching became free from thirst (ChU 3.17.6).
notes: Later tradition, and some scholars, identify him with Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva of the Gītā (tch:krsna); the Upaniṣad says only 'Kṛṣṇa, son of Devakī'. Kept as a separate id; identification not asserted.

queries: Chandogya Upanishad 3.17.6 Krishna Devakiputra Ghora Angirasa identification with Krishna of Bhagavad Gita
checks.note: Located: ChU 3.17.6 ('apipāsa eva sa babhūva'). Web sources show that identifying him with the Kṛṣṇa of the Gītā is debated, as the entry says.

name: Kṛṣṇa Mitra
summary: Ācārya named in the colophon of the Sāṃkhya treatise Tattvamīmāṃsā (with his father's and grandfather's names; the e-text reading of the father's name is garbled).

name: Kṛṣṇa Yajvan
summary: Author of the Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā, an elementary manual.

name: Kṛṣṇadās Adhikārī
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet and manager (adhikārī) of Śrīnāthjī's temple.

name: Kṛṣṇadās Payahārī
summary: Rāmānandī ascetic ('who lives on milk'), disciple of Anantānanda, who established the seat at Galtā near Jaipur — by tradition after defeating the Nāth yogīs there; guru of Agradās and Kīlhadās.

name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta, the Govindalīlāmṛta and the Sāraṅgaraṅgadā commentary on the Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta; wrote in Vṛndāvana in old age from the accounts of Raghunātha Dāsa and Svarūpa's notes.

name: Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa
summary: Bengali tantric scholar of Navadvīpa, compiler of the Tantrasāra (Bṛhattantrasāra), the standard Bengali digest of tantric worship, which sets out the meditation and worship of Dakṣiṇakālī. Bengali tradition credits him with fixing the popular form of Dakṣiṇakālī and with introducing the worship of Kālī in clay images in the household.

tradition.text: A contemporary (some say a fellow student) of Caitanya

realization_account.text: Bengali legend: praying to know the form in which Kālī should be worshipped, he was told to adopt the first form he saw at dawn; he saw a dark village woman plastering a wall, her hair loose, who bit her tongue in embarrassment on seeing him — the pose of Dakṣiṇakālī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The legend is oral/popular; the Tantrasāra itself quotes the Kālī Tantra's older meditation verse (tea:tantrasara-krsnananda:2.syama-dhyana).

name: K. S. Krishnamurti
summary: Founder of the Krishnamurti Paddhati (KP), which subdivides each nakṣatra by the proportions of the Viṃśottarī periods into 'sub-lords'.

name: Kṣārapāṇi
summary: One of Ātreya's six disciples, each of whom composed his own tantra and read it to Ātreya and the sages (Ca Sū 1.31-33).
notes: Whether this is the same person as the homonymous sage of other traditions is not settled; kept separate.

name: Kṣemarāja
summary: Abhinavagupta's foremost disciple; author of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya and of commentaries that fused Spanda and Pratyabhijñā and read the Bhairava tantras non-dually: Śivasūtravimarśinī, Spandanirṇaya, Spandasandoha, Svacchandoddyota, Netroddyota, Vijñānabhairavoddyota (incomplete), Stavacintāmaṇivṛtti, Śivastotrāvalīvivṛti, Parāprāveśikā.

name: Kṣemendra
summary: Kashmiri polymath, pupil of Abhinavagupta, author of the Aucityavicāracarcā on propriety.

name: Kṣetrayya
summary: Telugu composer of padams to Muvvagopāla in which the devotee speaks as a woman in love; a basis of the dance repertoire.

name: Kṣitigarbha
summary: The bodhisattva of the earth-womb who vowed not to become a buddha until the hells are empty; protector of the dead, children and travellers in East Asia (Dizang, Jizō).

name: Kubir Gõsāi
summary: Poet of the Sāhebdhanī sect whose songs in the Sahajiyā-Bāul idiom are sung in Nadia.

name: Kucipa

realization_account.text: A farmer with a goitre on his neck whom Nāgārjuna taught to visualize the growth enlarging and then to see it as empty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 35): Where the innate is concerned, if one strains, a thorn arises; if one lets go without clinging, that is the supreme meditation; by the light of the guru's speech the extremes of existence and non-existence are not found; what is not found is seen; realizing that is the supreme meaning.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 35 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A farmer with a goitre on his neck whom Nāgārjuna taught to visualize the growth enlarging and then to see it as empty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The comparison 'like an elephant's eye' in the song is not understood.

name: Kuṭampai (Kutampaic cittar)
summary: Siddhar named from the refrain of his thirty-two couplets, addressed to a girl wearing kuṭampai ear-ornaments; for the realized, he asks, what need of mantra, seals, yoga, rejuvenation or hymns?
places: Māyavaram (Mayiladuthurai) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Kuiji
summary: Xuanzang's principal disciple and systematizer of Faxiang, counted its first patriarch; author of the great commentaries on the Cheng weishi lun and the Nyāyapraveśa and champion of the five-gotra doctrine.

name: Kujō Kanezane
summary: Regent and diarist (Gyokuyō) who received precepts from Hōnen and at whose request the Senchakushū was written (1198).

name: Kukkuripa

realization_account.text: A brahmin yogin who, on pilgrimage, rescued a starving bitch and practised in a cave with her; invited to Indra's heaven he returned for the dog, who was revealed as a ḍākinī; associated with the Mahāmāyā tantra and poet of Caryāgīti songs; in Tibetan accounts one of Marpa's teachers. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 34): Worship of buddhas and the like brings no benefit; where there is desire and striving there is no buddha; the glory of experience is the true guru's blessing; the fortunate have it within themselves yet do not see it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 34 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A brahmin yogin who, on pilgrimage, rescued a starving bitch and practised in a cave with her; invited to Indra's heaven he returned for the dog, who was revealed as a ḍākinī; associated with the Mahāmāyā tantra and poet of Caryāgīti songs; in Tibetan accounts one of Marpa's teachers.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Kulacciṟai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Minister of the Pāṇṭiya king Neṭumāṟaṉ who, with the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār, invited Campantar to Madurai and served devotees of every birth.

realization_account.text: Minister of the Pāṇṭiya king Neṭumāṟaṉ who, with the queen Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār, invited Campantar to Madurai and served devotees of every birth.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kuladatta
summary: Author of the Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā (11th–12th c.).

name: Kulaśekhara Āḻvār
summary: Cēra king of Kerala who renounced his throne for the company of devotees at Śrīraṅgam; author of the Tamil Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi and (by tradition) the Sanskrit Mukundamālā. His hymns ask to be born even as a fish or a step at Tiruvēṅkaṭam and cling to the Lord 'as a child pushed away by its mother still cries for her'.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE (identification with the Cēra Kulaśekhara of Mahodayapuram is debated)

realization_account.text: So absorbed was the king in hearing the Rāmāyaṇa that when the reciter told of Rāma fighting Khara's fourteen thousand demons alone, he ordered his army to march to Rāma's aid. His ministers, resenting the devotees who thronged his court, accused them of stealing a jewel; he put his hand into a pot containing a cobra, declaring that the devotees could not steal, and was unharmed. He gave up his kingdom to live among devotees at Śrīraṅgam.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the Kaustubha gem in the tradition's list (moderate). The threshold of the Tirupati sanctum is called 'Kulaśekharaṉ paṭi' after Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 4.9.

name: Kullūka Bhaṭṭa
summary: Bengali commentator on Manu whose text and numbering became the vulgate.

checks.note: The Bengali commentator whose text underlies the vulgate is confirmed. His date is disputed (Wisdomlib: 12th c.; other literature 13th–15th c., as the entry has), so it is only partly confirmed.

name: Kumagai Naozane
summary: Warrior of the Genpei war who became Hōnen's disciple as the monk Rensei; his vow to be born in the highest grade is recorded.

name: Kumāra Kassapa
summary: U33 contribution: the monk who refutes Pāyāsi's materialism with fourteen similes (DN 23).

name: Kumāra Varadācārya
summary: Son and disciple of Vedānta Deśika (Nayinārācārya), author of the Adhikaraṇacintāmaṇi and continuer of his father's line.

name: Rigdzin Kumārādza (rig 'dzin ku mA rA dza)
summary: Wandering Heart-essence master, Longchenpa's root teacher, who lived with his disciples in continual encampments.

name: Kumārajīva
summary: Kuchean monk-translator (344-413 or 350-409) in Chang'an, whose Chinese versions of the Lotus, Vimalakīrti, Diamond, Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha, Large and Small Perfection of Wisdom, Śūraṅgamasamādhi, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and the Dazhidu lun became standard in East Asia.
notes: Also referenced by other units; contribution here: sūtra translations.
alt_summary: U40 contribution: Kuchean translator (d. c. 409/413 CE) whose Chinese versions of the Madhyamaka treatises (Zhong lun, Shiermen lun, Bai lun, Da zhidu lun) founded East Asian Madhyamaka.
The great Kuchean translator (344–413 or 350–409). This unit records his translations of the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya and of the Satyasiddhiśāstra; his Madhyamaka and Mahāyāna work belongs to other units.
alt_notes: U43 contribution: translator of the Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha (T366) and the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā (T1521); answered Huiyuan's questions on the pratyutpanna samādhi.

name: Kumārakassapa
summary: An elder, foremost in variegated speech, who answered Pāyāsi's denial of the other world with similes (DN 23); the Vammika Sutta (MN 23) was addressed to him.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Kumāralāta
summary: Called by Xuanzang the 'original master' (founder) of the Sautrāntika; author of the Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti, a collection of illustrative stories.

name: Kumāraśiras Bharadvāja
summary: Speaker in the assemblies: vāyu is provoked by the repeated use of what shares its qualities (Ca Sū 12.5); there are five tastes — earthy, watery, fiery, airy and spatial (Sū 26.8); the head forms first in the embryo, as the seat of the senses (Śā 6.21).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Kumārata (Jiumoluoduo 鳩摩羅多)
summary: Nineteenth patriarch in the Chan list; sometimes linked by scholars with the Sautrāntika Kumāralāta (tch:kumaralata), not identified here.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 19.

name: Kumārila Bhaṭṭa

tradition.text: older contemporary of Śaṅkara, whom he met at Prayāga at the end of his life (Śaṅkaradigvijaya)

realization_account.text: Hagiographies of Śaṅkara (e.g. the Śaṅkaradigvijaya ascribed to Mādhava-Vidyāraṇya) present Kumārila as an incarnation of Skanda sent to restore the Vedic path; they tell that he studied among Buddhists, survived a fall from a height by the truth of the Veda, and later entered a husk-fire at Prayāga as expiation, where Śaṅkara met him and was sent on to Maṇḍana Miśra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Hagiographic details are from memory and are not in Kumārila's works (low confidence). The teacher–pupil link with Prabhākara is a Bhāṭṭa legend; its historicity is doubted.
summary: Founder of the Bhāṭṭa school: author of the Ślokavārttika, Tantravārttika and Ṭupṭīkā on Śabara, and a lost Bṛhaṭṭīkā. He defended the authorless Veda and intrinsic validity against Buddhists, rejected omniscience in matters of dharma, a creator and a total dissolution, and set out a path to release through avoidance of desire-prompted and prohibited acts.

name: Kumaripa

realization_account.text: A potter taught to see the wheel and kiln as the path. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 63): By the wheel of karma consistent with its cause the many songs and dances of existence are made; by the fire of gnosis-awareness every stain of delusion is burned.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 63 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A potter taught to see the wheel and kiln as the path.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Tōh 2292 reads 'kaM pa la'; the wheel-and-fire imagery fits Abhayadatta's potter (63).

name: Kumbhakarṇa (Rāṇā Kumbhā)
summary: Mahārāṇā of Mewar, author of the Saṅgītarāja and a commentary on the Gītagovinda.

name: Kumbhakarṇa (Mahārāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar)
summary: Rājput king and musicologist who wrote the Rasikapriyā commentary on the Gīta Govinda.

name: Kumbhandās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, a farmer of Jamunāvato near Govardhana; the tradition remembers his refusal of the imperial court ('what have saints to do with Sīkrī?').

name: Kumudavalli
summary: Wife of Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār in the hagiographies, who made his taking the Vaiṣṇava marks and daily feeding of devotees the condition of their marriage — the occasion of his turning to God.

name: Kundakunda
summary: The most revered Digambara ācārya, author of the Samayasāra, Pravacanasāra, Niyamasāra, Pañcāstikāyasāra, the Aṣṭapāhuḍa and the Bārasa Aṇuvekkhā (tradition credits him with eighty-four pāhuḍas). He taught the pure self from the standpoint of ultimate reality (niścaya) and the conventional standpoint (vyavahāra) as its teaching device, and upheld monastic nudity against clothed renunciation. The Mūla Saṅgha calls itself his lineage (Kundakundānvaya); Tamil Jains identify him with Elācārya, to whom they ascribe the Tirukkuṟaḷ.

tradition.text: 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE (Digambara paṭṭāvalīs)

realization_account.text: He travelled by magical power to the living Tīrthaṅkara Sīmandhara in Videha and heard the teaching directly (Devasena's Darśanasāra; later Digambara legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jetsün Kunga Drolchok (rje btsun kun dga' grol mchog)
summary: Sixteenth-century Jonang master, compiler of the hundred and eight Jonang instructions (khrid brgya); Tāranātha was recognized as his rebirth.

name: Kūṇika (Ajātaśatru)
summary: King of Magadha, son of Śreṇika, who visits Mahāvīra in state in the Aupapātika and wars against Ceṭaka of Vaiśālī in the Nirayāvalikā.

name: Kuṅkiliyakkalaya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He burned kuṅkiliyam incense before Śiva, sold all he had for it, and spent even his wife's marriage badge on incense; at Tiruppaṉantāḷ he straightened the leaning liṅga by pulling with a rope tied to his own neck.

realization_account.text: He burned kuṅkiliyam incense before Śiva, sold all he had for it, and spent even his wife's marriage badge on incense; at Tiruppaṉantāḷ he straightened the leaning liṅga by pulling with a rope tied to his own neck.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Künpang Thukje Tsöndrü (kun spangs thugs rje brtson 'grus)
summary: Founder of the Jonang hermitage in the Jomonang valley (c. 1294); a Kālacakra adept who is said to have received and unified seventeen transmission lines of the six-branch yoga, from which the Jonang takes its name and practice lineage.

name: Kuntaka
summary: Author of the Vakroktijīvita: striking, oblique expression (vakrokti) is the life of poetry.

name: Kunthunātha
summary: The seventeenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the goat. Parents: Sūra (Sūrasena) and Śrī. Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the sixth world-emperor.

tradition.text: the seventeenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Kuntī
summary: Named in chapters 1–3 only through her sons: Yudhiṣṭhira as kuntīputra (1.16) and Arjuna as Kaunteya (1.27 and passim) and Pārtha (son of Pṛthā).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.16, 1.27.

name: Kuntibhoja
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army (1.5).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.5.

name: Kuoan Shiyuan 廓庵師遠
summary: Song master (Liangshan) of the Yangqi line who composed the Ten Oxherding Pictures and verses.

name: Kūrakulottama Dāsar
summary: Disciple of Piḷḷai Lokācārya who, the tradition says, preserved and passed on his teacher's doctrine to Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai.

name: Kūreśa
summary: Rāmānuja's foremost disciple and scribe, the father of Parāśara Bhaṭṭar and author of the Pañcastava. The tradition says he memorized the Bodhāyana Vṛtti in Kashmir for Rāmānuja and was blinded by a Cōḻa king for refusing to affirm Śiva's supremacy.

name: Kūṟṟuva Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain who conquered many lands and wished to be crowned at Chidambaram; refused by the Tillai priests, who crown only Cōḻas, he prayed, and Śiva placed his feet on his head as his crown.

realization_account.text: A chieftain who conquered many lands and wished to be crowned at Chidambaram; refused by the Tillai priests, who crown only Cōḻas, he prayed, and Śiva placed his feet on his head as his crown.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kurukai Kāvalappaṉ
summary: Disciple of Nāthamuni to whom, the tradition says, the teaching of yoga (yogarahasya) was entrusted; Yāmuna was directed to him but arrived after his death.

name: Kuśa Sāṅkṛtyāyana
summary: Opened the debate on vāyu by naming its six qualities (Ca Sū 12.4).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Kuśika

tradition.text: first disciple of the incarnate Lord

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (ten generations before Uditācārya, 380 CE)

summary: The first of Lakulīśa's four disciples (Liṅga P. 1.24.131; Kūrma P. 1.51.26). Kauṇḍinya tells that Kuśika, prompted by Rudra, approached the Lord at Ujjayinī, declared his birth, lineage, learning and freedom from debts, and asked whether there is a final and absolute removal of all suffering - the question the Pāśupata Sūtra answers. The Mathurā inscription of 380 CE counts its donor as tenth in succession from Kuśika.

name: Kutsa Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 1.94–98 and 1.101–115, including the Rudra hymn 1.114 and 1.115.1 ('Sūrya is the self of what moves and what stands'); the Atharvaveda hymn to the highest Brahman (AVŚ 10.8) is also ascribed to Kutsa.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 'kutsa āṅgirasaḥ' for 1.94–98 and 1.101–115 (1.99 Kaśyapa, 1.100 Vārṣāgiras); AVŚ 10.8 header: seer Kutsa, deity ātman.

name: Kūya
alt_names: Ichi no hijiri 市聖 (saint of the marketplace)
summary: Wandering holy man (hijiri) who recited Amida's name in the streets and markets of Kyoto, dug wells, built bridges and buried the unclaimed dead; the statue at Rokuharamitsu-ji shows six small Amidas issuing from his mouth. Ippen took him as his model ('casting off').

name: Kyergangpa Chökyi Senge
alt_names: skyer sgang pa chos kyi seng ge
summary: Third of the Shangpa 'seven jewels', disciple of Mokchokpa.

name: Kyotön Sönam Lama (skyo ston bsod nams bla ma)
summary: Machig Labdrön's principal teacher, who gave her empowerment and instruction; a holder of Padampa Sangye's teachings.

name: Laba Aindra
summary: Seer of RV 10.119, the soma-exalted self-praise with the refrain 'have I not drunk of the soma?'; the Anukramaṇī gives its deity as ātman (Indra).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'aindro labaḥ', deity 'ātmā (indraḥ)'.

name: Lābukāyana
summary: Early teacher cited in the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra (MS 6.7.37; spelled Lāvukāyana in one edition).

name: Lachen Gongpa Rabsal
alt_names: bla chen dgongs pa rab gsal
summary: Tibetan monk in Amdo who preserved the monastic ordination after the persecution of Langdarma; source of the 'lower Vinaya' (smad 'dul) lineage.

name: Lagadha
summary: The 'great-souled' teacher whose knowledge of time the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa sets out (v. 2); known only from that text.

checks.note: Text-located at ṚVJ 2: 'kālajñānaṃ pravakṣyāmi lagadhasya mahātmanaḥ'. Known only from this text (Wikipedia).

name: Laghubhaṭṭāraka
summary: Kashmiri author to whom the Laghustava (Laghustuti) to Tripurā is ascribed.

name: Lakkaṇṇa Daṇḍēśa
summary: Minister of Dēvarāya II and author of the Kannada Śivatattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Lakṣmaṇa
summary: Rāma's brother: recipient of Rāma's teaching on māyā, knowledge and devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.4) and of the Rāma Gītā (7.5); in the Rāmcaritmānas he himself teaches Guha (the Lakṣmaṇa Gītā).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: AR 3.4 (Rāma to Lakṣmaṇa), AR 7.5 (Rāma Gītā), RCM Ayodhyā 92-93 (to Guha).

name: Lakṣmaṇa Deśika
notes: His identification with Abhinavagupta's teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta is sometimes proposed; not accepted here.
summary: Author of the Śāradātilaka, a manual of mantra-śāstra widely used as an authority, including in Kerala.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: author of the Śāradātilaka; details of his life, date and teachers are uncertain.

name: Lakṣmaṇagupta
summary: Disciple of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta's teacher in the Pratyabhijñā; no works survive.

name: Lakṣmīdhara

scholarly.text: 12th c. CE, minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra

summary: Author of the Kṛtyakalpataru, the digest that systematised Purāṇic teaching on vows, gifts, tīrthas and śrāddha.

checks.note: Confirmed: courtier of the Gāhaḍavāla Govindacandra (r. c. 1114–1155), matching the entry.
Web: minister of peace and war of Govindacandra of Kannauj (r. c. 1114-1155), who composed the Kṛtyakalpataru at the king's request.

alt_summary: Minister of the Gāhaḍavāla king Govindacandra, author of the Kṛtyakalpataru.

name: Lakṣmīdhara Kavi
summary: Author of the Advaitamakaranda.

name: Lakṣmīṅkarā

realization_account.text: Princess of Oḍḍiyāna, sister of Indrabhūti, promised in marriage to a king of Laṅkāpurī; she refused, feigned madness, lived in the cremation grounds and attained mahāmudrā; she taught the king's sweeper (who became a siddha); author of the Advayasiddhi; originator of a lineage of the 'headless' Vajrayoginī. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 82): First, the intelligent generate realization; second, they meditate undistractedly on the natural state; then, when experience has arisen, they practise conduct with care.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 82 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Princess of Oḍḍiyāna, sister of Indrabhūti, promised in marriage to a king of Laṅkāpurī; she refused, feigned madness, lived in the cremation grounds and attained mahāmudrā; she taught the king's sweeper (who became a siddha); author of the Advayasiddhi; originator of a lineage of the 'headless' Vajrayoginī.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Tōh 2292's 'nI lak+Sha na' at position 82 is taken as Lakṣmīṅkarā (low). The song states a sequence of view, meditation and conduct.

name: Lakulīśa

tradition.text: the 28th and last of Śiva's yoga-teacher incarnations of the Vaivasvata manvantara, in the age when Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva and Vyāsa Dvaipāyana are born (Liṅga P. 1.24.125-131; Kūrma P. 1.51.9-10)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. CE (reckoned back ten teacher-generations from the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE); some scholars say 1st–2nd c.

places: Kāyāvarohaṇa / Kāyāvataraṇa / Kāyārohaṇa (Karvan, near Vadodara, Gujarat)

realization_account.text: Not a human who became realized but the Lord himself: seeing an abandoned corpse in a cremation ground, Śiva entered it by yogic power and became the brahmacārin Lakulī at the siddha-field called Kāyāvatāra (Liṅga P. 1.24.127-130); Kauṇḍinya says the Lord, in human form, took a brahmin's body, descended at Kāyāvataraṇa and walked to Ujjayinī, where he taught Kuśika; the Kāravaṇa-māhātmya says Śiva was born to Viśvarūpa and Sudarśanā, and after the infant died Śiva entered the body and later merged into the Brahmeśvara liṅga at Kāyāvarohaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Lakulīśa, 'Lord with the club', is regarded as the incarnation of Śiva who founded the Pāśupata observance and taught the Pāśupata Sūtra, and the first of the Pāśupata tīrthakaras. His images show him seated, holding a club and a citron, often ithyphallic; the Liṅga Purāṇa (1.76.38-39) prescribes his image surrounded by disciples, hand raised in exposition. Kauṇḍinya does not use the name Lakulīśa; he speaks of 'the Lord' who descended at Kāyāvataraṇa.

name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī, Lallā)
summary: 14th-century Kashmiri yoginī whose vākhs, in the idiom of non-dual Śaivism and yoga, speak of seeking Śiva far and finding him at home in her own body, of breath-practice lighting the lamp of knowledge, and of the indifference of the realized to sectarian names.

realization_account.text: Tradition holds that she left an unhappy married life to wander as an ascetic, dancing unclothed after her teacher's single instruction to turn from the outer to the inner; she is also revered by Kashmiri Muslims (as Lallā Ārifa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Her teacher is named in tradition as Siddha Śrīkaṇṭha (Sed Bayu) - low confidence, not given as an id.

name: Lalitavajra
summary: Siddha of Oḍḍiyāna credited with bringing the Vajrabhairava tantra from the ḍākinī land (tradition).

name: Lalla
summary: Author of the Śiṣyadhīvṛddhida in the Āryabhaṭa school.

name: Lallujī Muni (Laghurāj Svāmī)
summary: Sthānakavāsī monk (1856–1936) who became Śrīmad Rājacandra's disciple and founded the Agas ashram.

name: Lalon Fakir (Lālan Sāṃi)

tradition.text: his followers say he lived 116 years; birth variously 1772 or 1774

scholarly.text: died 17 October 1890 at Cheuṛiyā; birth unknown (c. 1770s by most reports)

realization_account.text: Abandoned by his companions on a pilgrimage when he fell ill with smallpox, he was nursed by a Muslim household and met his guru Sirāj Sāṃi; his caste of birth (Hindu Kāyastha or Muslim) was lost and he himself refused to name it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The greatest Bāul master, of Cheuṛiyā near Kushtia: his songs of the unknown bird in the body's cage, the Man of the Heart, the mirror-city, the futility of caste and creed and the worship of the human are the classic Bāul teaching. His disciples ('Lalon's fakirs') keep his ākhṛā and festival.
notes: Birth, origin (Hindu or Muslim) and the details of the smallpox story are disputed; flagged recent because his life extends to 1890.

name: Lama Zhang (Zhang Yudrakpa Tsöndrü Drakpa)
alt_names: zhang g.yu brag pa brtson 'grus grags pa
summary: Founder of the Tsalpa Kagyu and of Tshal Gungthang; disciple of Gomtsul; author of the Ultimate Supreme Path of Mahāmudrā; also a political figure in the Lhasa region.

name: Langri Tangpa Dorje Senge
summary: Kadam master, disciple of Potowa, founder of Langtang monastery (1093) and author of the Eight Verses of Mind Training; the tradition says his face was always sad from contemplating the suffering of beings.
alt_names: glang ri thang pa rdo rje seng ge

name: Lanxi Daolong 蘭溪道隆 (Rankei Dōryū)
summary: Chinese master who came to Japan (1246) and founded Kenchōji in Kamakura, introducing strict Song-style monastic Zen.

name: Lao'an (Hui'an 慧安)
summary: Long-lived disciple of Hongren honoured by Empress Wu.

name: Lāṭyāyana
summary: Author by tradition of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda Śrautasūtra.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as the eponymous author of the Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtra.

name: Laugākṣi Bhāskara
summary: Author of the Arthasaṅgraha, a beginner's primer of Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā closely following Āpadeva, and of the Tarkakaumudī (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika).
alt_summary: Author of the Tarkakaumudī (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) and of the Arthasaṅgraha, a Mīmāṃsā primer.

name: Lavjī Ṛṣi
summary: 17th-c. reformer from the Loṅkā yatis of Surat, one of the founders of the Sthānakavāsī order, associated with the constant wearing of the mouth-cloth.

name: Layman Pang (Pang Yun 龐蘊)
summary: Lay practitioner who studied with Shitou and Mazu; 'supernatural power and wondrous function: carrying water and hauling firewood'.

name: Ledi Sayadaw
summary: Burmese scholar-monk (1846–1923) who wrote more than a hundred works in Pali and Burmese, founded the Ledi forest monastery near Monywa, and taught insight meditation and the Abhidhamma to laypeople — the source of the U Ba Khin – Goenka lineage.
notes: Ordination name given as U Ñāṇa / Ñāṇadhaja (moderate confidence).

name: Lhatsün Rinchen Namgyal
alt_names: lha btsun rin chen rnam rgyal
summary: Disciple of Tsangnyön Heruka, author of a Life of Nāropa and editor of Kagyu texts.

name: Lhodrak Drubchen Namkha Gyaltsen
summary: Nyingma and Kadam visionary of Lhodrak who, in the Gelug account, transmitted the Kadam lamrim lineages to Tsongkhapa and received visions of Vajrapāṇi.

name: Li Zunxu 李遵勗
summary: Lay official who compiled the Tiansheng guangdeng lu (1036).

name: Līlā
summary: Queen who, grieving for her husband Padma, is taught by the goddess Sarasvatī (Jñapti) and shown in consciousness-body the worlds of her husband's past and future lives (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 3.15-60).

checks.note: MU 3.15.19 King Padma; the goddess Jñapti Sarasvatī 3.16.30, 3.17.7.

name: Līlapa

realization_account.text: A king who would not give up his throne and pleasures; a guru taught him to meditate while seated on his lion throne, taking the jewel of his ring (or his royal ease) as the object, and he attained realization in the midst of royal life. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 2): In the hermitage of the four immeasurables the king of yogins is like a lion, his head adorned with a turquoise five-braided mane, bearing the yogin's insignia of the five families; as the lion's ten claws tear the flesh and bones of elephants, the yogin's ten perfections tear apart concepts, the adverse side; realizing thus, Līla was freed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 2 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A king who would not give up his throne and pleasures; a guru taught him to meditate while seated on his lion throne, taking the jewel of his ring (or his royal ease) as the object, and he attained realization in the midst of royal life.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Lingje Repa Pema Dorje
alt_names: gling rje ras pa padma rdo rje
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa, a wandering yogin-poet and the teacher of Tsangpa Gyare; forerunner of the Drukpa.

name: Lingyun Zhiqin 靈雲志勤

realization_account.text: 'Since once seeing the peach blossoms, until now I have had no more doubt' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Awoke on seeing peach blossoms after thirty years of seeking; Guishan confirmed him: 'one who awakens through conditions never regresses'.

name: Linji Yixuan 臨濟義玄

realization_account.text: Three times he asked Huangbo the great meaning of the buddha-dharma and three times was struck; sent to Dayu and told Huangbo had been 'grandmotherly', he awoke and said 'there isn't much to Huangbo's buddha-dharma' (Linji lu, record of pilgrimage).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Linji house in Zhenzhou (Hebei); heir of Huangbo. Taught the true person of no rank, independence from all names, 'be master wherever you are', and used the shout; his sayings are the Linji lu.

name: Liu Yimin
summary: Lay scholar of Pengcheng who joined Huiyuan on Lushan and wrote the text of the vow of 402 made by 123 persons before the image of Amitābha (Gaoseng zhuan).

name: Locana Dāsa
summary: Author of the Bengali Caitanya Maṅgala.

name: Lochen Dharmaśrī (lo chen dharma shrI)
summary: Terdak Lingpa's brother, great scholar of Mindroling, commentator on the Guhyagarbha and on the three vows; killed in the Dzungar persecution of 1717-18.

name: Loden Nyingpo (blo ldan snying po)
summary: Bön master through whom the Zijid, the long biography of Tönpa Shenrab, was transmitted.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Lokakṣema
summary: Kuṣāṇa monk in Luoyang (active c. 167-186) who made the first Chinese translations of Mahāyāna sūtras: the 8,000-line Perfection of Wisdom (Daoxing, 179), the Pratyutpanna-samādhi, the Akṣobhyavyūha, the Kāśyapaparivarta, the Śūraṅgamasamādhi (lost) and others.
notes: works = translations.

name: Lokanātha Gosvāmī
summary: Early associate of Caitanya in Vṛndāvana and Narottama's initiating guru.

name: Lokasāraṅga Muni
summary: Priest of the Śrīraṅgam temple who, at the Lord's command, carried Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār on his shoulders into the sanctum.

realization_account.text: Having struck the bard who stood in his path, he saw blood on the Lord's image and was told to carry the devotee in himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Lolimbarāja
summary: Poet-physician, author of the Vaidyajīvana.

name: Lakṣmīdhara (Lolla Lakṣmīdhara)
summary: Commentator on the Saundaryalaharī (the Lakṣmīdharā) and on the Subhagodaya; the classical exponent of the Samaya school, who restricts worship to the inner space, teaches the fivefold equality of Śiva and Śakti, and rejects the sixty-four tantras and Kaula practice as outside the Vedic path.

scholarly.text: c. early 16th c. CE; associated with the court of Pratāparudra Gajapati of Orissa

notes: Distinct from Lakṣmīdhara Bhaṭṭa, author of the Kṛtyakalpataru (tch:laksmidhara in U02/U07), and from Lakṣmīdhara Kavi of the Advaitamakaranda (tch:laksmidhara-kavi), though some identify him with the latter. name: Longchenpa (Longchen Rabjam Drime Özer)

realization_account.text: Reached the final vision of the exhaustion of phenomena; at his death the earth shook and relics appeared.

name: Lūipa

realization_account.text: A prince (of Oḍḍiyāna in some accounts) who left his kingdom, and on a ḍākinī's rebuke for his remaining pride lived twelve years on the Ganges bank in Bengal eating the fish entrails thrown away by fishermen; attained mahāmudrā; converted King Dārika and his minister Ḍeṅgi; root guru of the Cakrasaṃvara lineage that bears his name and poet of the first Caryāgīti song. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 1): As honey smeared on the nose of an untamed wild dog makes it bite in all directions, the guru's instruction given to the dull and unfit burns their own mind-stream; the fortunate who realize the unborn destroy concepts at the mere meeting with appearances, as a sword tied to the trunk of a steady, maddened elephant routs an army.

name: Machig Labdrön (ma gcig lab sgron)

realization_account.text: She is an emanation of the Great Mother Prajñāpāramitā and of Tārā; in her previous life she was an Indian paṇḍita (named Mönlam Drub in the accounts, low confidence) whose consciousness passed to Tibet; she attained realization while reading the chapter on māras in the Perfection of Wisdom; Indian scholars who came to test her accepted her teaching and carried Chöd to India.

summary: Tibetan woman master (11th–12th c.) who founded the Chöd practice lineage. A gifted reciter of the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras, she realized their meaning while reading, received instructions from Kyotön Sönam Lama and from Padampa Sangye, married the Indian yogin Thöpa Bhadra, raised children who became lineage holders, and taught at Zangri Khangmar. Her Great Bundle of Precepts is the root text of Chöd.

name: Madālasā

summary: A woman teacher of self-knowledge in the Mārkaṇḍeya. Her lullaby opens 'śuddho 'si re tāta, na te 'sti nāma' in the checked e-text (MkP 25.11); the popular verse 'śuddho 'si buddho 'si nirañjano 'si ...' recited under her name was not found there.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: A brāhmaṇa of Tirukkōḷūr who, while at Ayodhyā on pilgrimage, saw a light in the southern sky, followed it to Kurukūr and found the silent Nammāḻvār under the tamarind; tested him with a riddle, received his answer, and served him for the rest of his life.

name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī

name: Madhva

tradition.text: the tradition's own reckoning: born when 4,300 years of the Kali age had passed (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 32.120 = c. 1199 CE) and lived 79 years (to c. 1278); a second traditional reckoning, widely used by the maṭhas, gives 1238–1317

scholarly.text: c. 1238–1317 CE (B. N. K. Sharma, from the epigraphic dates of his disciple Narahari Tīrtha, 1264–1293); some earlier scholars followed 1197/1199–1276/1278

realization_account.text: Madhva is the third avatāra of Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), after Hanumān and Bhīma — he says so himself at the end of the Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya (32.162, 32.166) and of the Anuvyākhyāna (4.4.15), reading the Balitthā hymn (Ṛgveda 1.141) as naming Vāyu's three forms; Bhīma was reborn as a brāhmaṇa when 4,300 years of Kali had passed to proclaim the truth about Hari hidden by the daityas (MBTN 32.120). The Sumadhvavijaya tells of boyhood feats, renunciation and naming (4.33, 5.1–2), journeys to Badarī where he met Vyāsa and received his teaching, and closes with the gods hailing him as Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva and showering him with flowers (16.57–58). The tradition holds that he passed from human sight at Uḍupi while expounding the Aitareya Upaniṣad and dwells with Vyāsa at Badarī; the day is kept as Madhva-navamī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda). Born at Pājaka near Uḍupi to Madhyageha Bhaṭṭa, he took renunciation as a boy from Acyutaprekṣa, receiving the name Pūrṇaprajña (Pūrṇabodha), and was installed as master of Vedānta with the name Ānandatīrtha; he signs his works 'Madhva'. He toured India debating, twice went to Badarī, installed the image of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi and founded the eight Uḍupi maṭhas, and wrote thirty-seven works (the Sarvamūla) on the Brahmasūtras, the Gītā, ten Upaniṣads, the Ṛgveda, the epics and Purāṇas, ten polemical and doctrinal treatises, hymns and ritual manuals. He taught that Viṣṇu alone is independent, that the five differences are real and eternal, that souls are graded by nature, and that liberation comes by Viṣṇu's grace through knowledge and devotion.
notes: Scholarly and traditional dates are given in 'dating'. The Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa image is said in the tradition to have come ashore in a block of gopīcandana clay from a ship — not verified in this pass. His mother's name (Vedavatī in later tradition) was not found in the Sumadhvavijaya e-text by a simple search.
