name: Mahāvīra (Vardhamāna)
summary: The twenty-fourth and last Tīrthaṅkara of this era, emblem the lion. Born Vardhamāna to Siddhārtha of the Jñātṛ (Nāya) clan and Triśalā at Kuṇḍagrāma near Vaiśālī; renounced at thirty; for twelve and a half years practised severe austerities in silence, enduring hardships and attacks (Ācārāṅga 1.9); attained omniscience; taught for thirty years, founding the fourfold community with eleven gaṇadharas headed by Indrabhūti Gautama; attained nirvāṇa at Pāvā aged seventy-two. Śvetāmbaras add that his embryo was transferred from the brāhmaṇī Devānandā to Triśalā, that his mother saw fourteen dreams (sixteen for Digambaras), and that he married Yaśodā and had a daughter, Priyadarśanā; Digambaras deny the transfer and the marriage. Known in the Pali canon as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

tradition.text: 599–527 BCE (the commonly used traditional reckoning: nirvāṇa 470 years before the Vikrama era; some Digambara reckonings differ)

scholarly.text: 6th–5th c. BCE; the nirvāṇa is variously dated by scholars between c. 527 and c. 425 BCE

realization_account.text: In the thirteenth year of his ascetic life, on the tenth of the bright half of Vaiśākha, outside Jṛmbhikagrāma on the bank of the Ṛjupālikā, under a śāla tree, squatting in the milking posture in the heat of the sun after a two-and-a-half-day fast without water, in deep (pure) meditation, he attained the infinite, supreme, unobstructed, complete and full knowledge and perception called kevala; at Pāvā, in his seventy-second year, he passed to nirvāṇa, freed from all suffering.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: U33 contribution: in the Pali canon he appears as Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta (Aggivessana), one of the six famous teachers; DN 2 reports his teaching as the 'fourfold restraint' (cātuyāma-saṃvara), a report that differs from the Jain canon's own account (five great vows; the fourfold restraint is Pārśva's, Uttarādhyayana 23). The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra 15 makes him Gosāla's teacher and opponent.

name: Mahāvīrācārya
summary: Jain mathematician, author of the Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha under the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa.

name: Maheśacandra Nyāyaratna
summary: Calcutta Sanskrit scholar (principal of the Sanskrit College), author of the Navyanyāyabhāṣāpradīpa, a guide to the technical terms of Navya-Nyāya.

name: Maheśvarānanda
summary: South Indian (Cola country) teacher of the Krama (Mahārtha) around 1300, disciple of Mahāprakāśa; author of the Prakrit Mahārthamañjarī with the Sanskrit Parimala, synthesizing Krama, Pratyabhijñā and Śrīvidyā.
notes: Teacher's name Mahāprakāśa and alias Gorakṣa from memory (low).
alt_summary: U23 contribution: his Mahārthamañjarī and its commentary show the Krama teaching of the Cola country interwoven with Śrīvidyā worship.

name: Mahidāsa Aitareya
summary: The seer to whom the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka are ascribed.

realization_account.text: Son of Itarā, slighted by his father, he was favoured by the Earth goddess and received the Brāhmaṇa (Sāyaṇa's introduction); the Chāndogya says he lived 116 years by his knowledge (ChU 3.16.7).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Text-located: ChU 3.16.7 'mahidāsa aitareyaḥ … sa ha ṣoḍaśaṃ varṣaśatam ajīvat' (116 years). Books 1–3 of the AA are ascribed to him (Hindupedia). The Itarā story (from Sāyaṇa's introduction) was not checked locally.

Located: ChU 3.16.7 ('mahidāsa aitareyaḥ … sa ha ṣoḍaśaṃ varṣaśatam ajīvat', i.e. 116 years). The tradition that he is the seer of the Aitareya texts fits Wikipedia's account of the Aitareya Upaniṣad.

alt_summary: Knowing the person as sacrifice, he said to sickness 'why do you afflict me? I shall not die of this' and lived 116 years (ChU 3.16.7); the tradition regards him as the seer of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Āraṇyaka.

name: Mahīdhara
summary: Vārāṇasī scholar who wrote the Vedadīpa on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā; the same Mahīdhara compiled the tantric manual Mantramahodadhi.

checks.note: Confirmed: 16th-c. Vārāṇasī scholar; Vedadīpa on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā; Mantramahodadhi (c. 1588/1589) — same author, as the entry says.

alt_summary: U31 contribution: compiler of the Mantramahodadhi (1589) with its commentary Naukā.
Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 16.
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Mahimabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Vyaktiviveka, which reduces suggestion to inference.

name: Mahinda
summary: Son of Asoka and pupil of Moggaliputta Tissa who, by the chronicles, brought the Dhamma to Laṅkā, converting King Devānampiya Tissa at Mihintale, and founded the Mahāvihāra tradition; the commentaries were held to have been brought by him.

tradition.text: arrived in Laṅkā 236 years after the parinibbāna

notes: Dīpavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa account.

name: Mahipa

realization_account.text: A wrestler proud of his strength, taught to wrestle with his pride. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 37): The pride of ignorance obscures the wish-fulfilling jewel of non-conception; in wishing to act, needs and wishes arise; it is accomplished by those who have equal taste.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 37 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A wrestler proud of his strength, taught to wrestle with his pride.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Mahīpati
summary: Brahmin hagiographer of Tāharābād (1715–1790), author of the Bhaktavijaya, Santalīlāmṛta and Bhaktalīlāmṛta, through which the Vārkarī saints' lives are told.

name: Maitreya
summary: Sage who goes to Kailāsa and is taught by Mahādeva that the body is a temple and the jīva is Śiva (Maitreya Upaniṣad 2). Distinct from Yājñavalkya's wife Maitreyī.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of maitreya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Maitreya (the bodhisattva, future buddha)
summary: The bodhisattva who will be the next buddha, now in Tuṣita: in the Lotus he asks the questions that open the sūtra and receives the revelation of the Buddha's lifespan; in the Gaṇḍavyūha he opens the tower of Vairocana to Sudhana; in the Śālistamba he teaches dependent origination; in the Saṃdhinirmocana (ch. 8) he asks about calm and insight. Tibetan tradition makes him the teacher of Asaṅga and source of the five Maitreya treatises.
notes: Distinct from tch:maitreya (the Upaniṣadic sage). Same figure as tch:metteyya (U36, Pali form) — dedupe candidate for the merge. The treatise-author 'Maitreyanātha' of the scholarly account is tch:maitreyanatha.

name: Maitreya (in Caraka's assembly)
summary: Objected that medicine is ineffective, since some treated patients die and some untreated recover (Ca Sū 10.4); answered by Ātreya.
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Maitreya (sage)
summary: The sage who questions Parāśara in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (VP 1.1.1-11) and who, in the Bhāgavata's third and fourth books, instructs Vidura on creation and the Lord's deeds. Not the Buddhist Maitreya.

checks.note: VP 1.1.1-11 (Maitreya questions Parāśara) located; Maitreya instructing Vidura in BhP 3 (e.g. 3.11.1 'maitreya uvāca') located.

alt_summary: In the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra, the sage who approaches Parāśara with folded hands and asks for the horā, best of the three branches of jyotiṣa (BPHS 1.1–3).

name: Maitreyanātha

tradition.text: the bodhisattva Maitreya, regent of the Buddha, residing in the Tuṣita heaven

scholarly.text: if a human teacher, c. 4th c. CE; many scholars treat 'Maitreya' as a name under which Asaṅga's circle transmitted texts

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that the author is the bodhisattva Maitreya (tch:maitreya-bodhisattva), who appeared to Asaṅga after twelve years of fruitless meditation — first as a wounded dog whose maggots Asaṅga, moved by compassion, tried to remove with his tongue — and took him to Tuṣita, where he taught him the five treatises.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The name under which the five 'Dharmas of Maitreya' (Tibetan list) and, in Chinese tradition, the Yogācārabhūmi are transmitted; for the tradition, the future buddha Maitreya teaching Asaṅga.
notes: Whether a historical human teacher named Maitreya(nātha) existed is a scholarly question (Ui Hakuju argued yes; others treat the name as a pious attribution). The registry id is used for the author; the bodhisattva is tch:maitreya-bodhisattva (U39).

name: Maitreyī
summary: One of Yājñavalkya's two wives, described as a discusser of brahman (brahmavādinī, BAU 4.5.1); when he is about to leave the household she refuses wealth that cannot make her immortal and receives the teaching on the self (BAU 2.4, 4.5).

checks.note: Located: BĀU 2.4.1-3 and 4.5.1 ('tayor ha maitreyī brahmavādinī babhūva').

name: Maitrīpa (Advayavajra)
summary: U44 contribution: Indian scholar-siddha (c. 1007–1085), disciple of Śavaripa (and in some accounts of Nāropa), said to have been expelled from Vikramaśīla for keeping wine and a consort; author of the some twenty-one short works of the Advayavajrasaṃgraha (amanasikāra, the four seals, the Tattvaratnāvalī) and of a Vajrayoginī sādhana lineage; teacher of Marpa and of Vajrapāṇi and Sahajavajra.
alt_summary: U40 contribution: author of the Tattvaratnāvalī, whose doxography divides Madhyamaka into the illusion-like non-dualists and the proponents of the non-foundation of all dharmas, the latter being his own view.
Indian mahāsiddha and scholar (c. 1007–1085) credited in Tibet with recovering two Maitreya texts.

realization_account.text: Tibetan tradition holds that Maitrīpa rediscovered the Dharmadharmatāvibhāga and the Ratnagotravibhāga, hidden in a stūpa, after a vision of Maitreya.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Contribution of U41; U44/U46 own the entry.

name: Maitrīyogin (Kusalī the Younger)
summary: Indian master of love and compassion from whom, in the Kadam account, Atiśa received a lineage of mind training; the tradition tells that he took on the wound of a beaten dog.

name: Makkhali Gosāla
summary: Leader of the Ājīvikas. DN 2 reports his doctrine of purification through transmigration: there is no cause for the defilement or purification of beings, no human effort; all beings are shaped by destiny, circumstance and nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva) and, fool and wise alike, make an end of suffering after 8,400,000 great aeons, like a ball of string unwinding. AN 3.137 calls his doctrine the worst of all. The Jain Bhagavatī Sūtra (15) tells his birth in a cowshed, six years as Mahāvīra's companion, his claim to be a Jina, the confrontation at Sāvatthī, and his death in delirium followed by repentance; the Jain Isibhāsiyāiṃ (11) nevertheless records a saying of 'the arhat seer Maṅkhaliputta'.

tradition.text: (Jain) died at Sāvatthī sixteen years before Mahāvīra

realization_account.text: (Ājīvika claim, as reported by the Jains) Gosāla declared himself a Jina and the last tīrthaṅkara of this age; (Jain account) he confessed on his deathbed that he was Mahāvīra's disciple and not a Jina, and will attain liberation only after many births.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (reported by an opponent)

notes: The name: Jain sources derive 'Gosāla' from his birth in a cowshed (gośālā) and 'Maṅkhaliputta' from his father Maṅkhali, a maṅkha (picture-showman); Buddhaghosa derives 'Makkhali' from 'don't stumble' (mā khali) — both are the traditions' etymologies.

name: Malayagiri
summary: 12th-c. Śvetāmbara commentator on many Upāṅgas, the Nandī, the Chedasūtras and the karma texts; contemporary of Hemacandra.

name: Mallavādin
summary: Śvetāmbara dialectician, author of the Dvādaśāranayacakra; the tradition says he defeated the Buddhists in debate at Valabhī.

name: Mallikā
summary: Queen of Kosala; her dialogue with Pasenadi on whether anyone is dearer than oneself led to Ud 5.1.

name: Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya
summary: Andhra Śaiva teacher contemporary with Basava, founder figure of the Ārādhya Śaivas and subject of Pālkuriki Sōmanātha's Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra.

name: Mallinātha (Mallī)
summary: The nineteenth Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the water-jar (kalaśa), born at Mithilā to King Kumbha and Queen Prabhāvatī, attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. In the Śvetāmbara account (Jñātādharmakathā 1.8) Mallī was a princess who, courted by six kings (her companions in a former life), showed them a hollow golden image of herself filled daily with food that rotted within, to teach the impurity of the body, and then renounced with them; a woman Tīrthaṅkara is counted among the ten 'wonders' (accheras) of this era. In the Digambara account Mallinātha was a man.

tradition.text: the nineteenth Jina of this era

realization_account.text: Śvetāmbara: Mallī attained omniscience on the very day of her renunciation; her female birth resulted from a slight deceit in her past life as King Mahābala, who secretly undertook more fasts than his companions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: gender set to 'unknown' because the traditions disagree: female (Śvetāmbara, Yāpanīya-compatible), male (Digambara).

name: Malliṣeṇa (author of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa)
summary: Digambara ācārya of Karnataka ('poet-emperor of two languages'), author of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa and other mantra works.

name: Malliṣeṇa (author of the Syādvādamañjarī)
summary: Śvetāmbara monk of the Nāgendra-gaccha, author of the Syādvādamañjarī (1292).
notes: Distinct from the Digambara Malliṣeṇa of the Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa.

name: Malūkdās
summary: Sant of Kaṛā (near Allahabad), known for trust in providence ('Malūkdās says: Rām is the giver of all') and for teaching the inner Rām beyond sect.

name: Māluṅkyaputta
summary: The monk who demanded answers to the undeclared questions (MN 63) and who, in old age, received the 'in the seen only the seen' teaching (SN 35.95).

name: Mammaṭa
summary: Kashmiri author of the Kāvyaprakāśa, the most influential synthesis of poetics along the lines of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta.

name: Maṇakkāl Nambi
summary: Disciple of Uyyakkoṇḍār who, the tradition says, drew Yāmuna back from kingship to the teaching, by bringing him greens daily until admitted, and then leading him to Raṅganātha.

name: Māṉakkañcāṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.

realization_account.text: A general who, when Śiva came as a Māvratī ascetic on his daughter's wedding day and asked for her hair, cut it off at once and gave it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṇakkuṭavar
summary: Author of the oldest surviving Kuṟaḷ commentary; his own affiliation (some say Jain) is uncertain.

name: Mānatuṅga

realization_account.text: The chains fell away one by one as he sang the Bhaktāmara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author of the Bhaktāmara-stotra; the tradition says that when a king (Bhoja or Harṣa in different versions) had him bound in forty-four (or forty-eight) chains, each verse of the hymn broke one.

name: Maṉavācakaṅkaṭantār
summary: Disciple of Meykaṇṭār from Tiruvatikai, author of the Uṇmai Viḷakkam.

name: Maṇavāḷa Māmuni
summary: The last of the great Teṅkalai teachers: disciple of Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai, commentator on Piḷḷai Lokācārya's works and the Ācārya Hṛdayam, author of the Upadēśa Ratnamālai and Yatirājaviṃśati, and founder of the eight 'elephants' (aṣṭadiggaja) among his disciples; the Teṅkalai regard him as Rāmānuja returned.

realization_account.text: After he expounded the Īṭu for a year before Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam (1432 in the tradition's reckoning), the Lord appeared as a child and recited the verse 'śrīśaileśa-dayāpātram', taking him as his own teacher.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mānaveda
summary: Zamorin prince-poet of Calicut who wrote the Kṛṣṇagīti on the model of the Gīta Govinda, basis of the Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam of Guruvāyūr.

name: Maṇḍana Miśra

realization_account.text: In Śaṅkara's hagiographies Maṇḍana, a ritualist householder, debates Śaṅkara with his wife Ubhaya-Bhāratī as judge, is defeated, takes sannyāsa and becomes Sureśvara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The identification with Sureśvara is traditional and disputed by modern scholarship.
summary: Mīmāṃsaka of the Bhāṭṭa line (by tradition Kumārila's pupil): author of the Vidhiviveka (injunction means 'being a means to the desired'), Bhāvanāviveka, Vibhramaviveka, Mīmāṃsānukramaṇī, the Sphoṭasiddhi (defending sphoṭa) and the Advaita Brahmasiddhi.
alt_summary: Mīmāṃsaka and Advaitin, author of the Brahmasiddhi (and of the Mīmāṃsā works Vidhiviveka and Bhāvanāviveka, the Vibhramaviveka and the grammatical Sphoṭasiddhi); held avidyā to reside in the jīvas, the need for prasaṅkhyāna after verbal knowledge, and a helpful role for works; in the tradition's account defeated by Śaṅkara at Māhiṣmatī and became Sureśvara.
U31 contribution: author of the Sphoṭasiddhi, the classic defence of the sphoṭa against Kumārila; his Brahmasiddhi is sympathetic to the word-brahman.

name: Mandāravā
summary: Indian princess of Zahor, consort of Padmasambhava, with whom he attained the vidyādhara level of immortality in the Māratika cave; a long-life deity in Nyingma practice.

name: Maṇḍika (Maṇḍita)
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt concerned bondage and liberation.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Mangong Wolmyeon 滿空月面
summary: Heir of Gyeongheo, influential teacher of ganhwa Seon in the 20th c.

name: Mangu Ram Mugowalia
summary: Founder of the Ād Dharm movement in Punjab (1925), which declared the Ravidāsī Dalits a distinct religious community.

name: Maṇibhadrā

realization_account.text: A young wife of a householder who received instruction from Kukkuripa and practised secretly for a year while keeping house; when she broke her water pot on the way home she realized, and later flew into the sky. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 65): When one is without concepts, the many concepts follow sound; therefore the nature becomes manifest: whatever appears is that nature itself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 65 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A young wife of a householder who received instruction from Kukkuripa and practised secretly for a year while keeping house; when she broke her water pot on the way home she realized, and later flew into the sky.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The second line is uncertain.

name: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra
summary: Pre-Gaṅgeśa Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyaratna.

name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumuṟai 8); the fourth samayācārya, exemplar of the true path (san-mārga, jñāna). Not among the sixty-three.

tradition.text: placed before the Tēvāram poets by much of the tradition

realization_account.text: Chief minister of the Pāṇṭiya king (named Arimarttaṉa in later accounts), sent with treasure to buy horses, he met Śiva as a guru under a kuruntha tree at Tirupperunturai, received initiation and spent the treasure on a temple. Imprisoned, he was saved when Śiva turned foxes into horses (which became foxes again), and when Śiva, hired as a labourer by the old woman Vanti to repair the Vaikai embankment, received the king's blow that struck every creature. At Chidambaram he defeated Buddhists from Laṅkā in debate; Śiva, as a brahmin, wrote down the Tiruvācakam and signed it; asked its meaning, he pointed to Naṭarāja and merged in him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: His absence from Cuntarar's list is used by scholars to date him after Cuntarar.

name: Māṇikyanandi
summary: Digambara logician, author of the Parīkṣāmukha.

name: Maniruddin Śāh
summary: Disciple of Lalon (low confidence).

name: Maṇittha
summary: An earlier authority on longevity named by Varāhamihira with Maya, the Yavanas and Śaktipūrva (BJ 7.1).
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Mañjula (Muñjāla)
summary: Author of the Laghumānasa (932 CE); later authors credit him with a theory of the motion of the solstices (ayana-calana).

name: Mañjuśrī
summary: The bodhisattva of wisdom, 'ever-youthful' (kumārabhūta): visits Vimalakīrti and asks about non-duality; sends Sudhana on his pilgrimage and receives him at its end; teaches the Saptaśatikā; in the Lotus recalls the past buddha Candrasūryapradīpa and brings forth the nāga princess; in the Śūraṅgama chooses Avalokiteśvara's method.

realization_account.text: A bodhisattva who in the Śūraṅgamasamādhi-sūtra is revealed to have been a buddha in the past; Wutaishan in China is his abode (Chinese tradition).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (as a figure of the sūtras)

name: Mañjuśrīmitra
summary: Indian scholar who came to debate Garab Dorje, was defeated, became his disciple for many years, and arranged the Dzogchen teachings into three series (mind, space, instruction); author of the Gold Refined from Ore (Tōh 2591).

realization_account.text: Received Garab Dorje's testament; his own testament was the Six Meditation Experiences.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mañjuśrīyaśas
summary: First kalkin king of Śambhala who united the castes into one vajra family and composed the abridged Kālacakra (Laghutantra), by the tradition's account.

name: Maṅkaiyarkkaraciyār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The Cōḻa princess who became queen of Neṭumāṟaṉ and, with the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, brought Campantar to Madurai to restore Śaivism.

realization_account.text: The Cōḻa princess who became queen of Neṭumāṟaṉ and, with the minister Kulacciṟaiyār, brought Campantar to Madurai to restore Śaivism.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Maṅki
summary: A man who, after losing his young bulls, renounces desire and speaks the Maṅki Gītā (12.171).

evidence: local:DharmicData MBh CE 12.171.4-8 (his young bulls, damya), 12.171.25
checks.note: Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: MBh CE 12.171.4-54; a Maṅki is also taught by Vasiṣṭha in MU 6.180-183 (colophons maṅkivasiṣṭhasamāgama ... maṅkinirvāṇa).

alt_summary: Singer of the Maṅki Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.171), who renounced desire after his efforts at wealth failed. A Maṅki is also taught by Vasiṣṭha in the Mokṣopāya's Nirvāṇa book (MU 6.180-183; identity of the two not asserted).

name: Manmatha (Kāma)
summary: The god of love, one of the twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā; the Kādi form of the vidyā is called after him (Kāmarāja-vidyā). In the Lalitopākhyāna he is burned by Śiva and revived by Lalitā.

name: Manorathanandin
summary: Author of the only complete Sanskrit commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika.

name: Manorhita (Monaluo 摩拏羅)
summary: Twenty-second patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 22.

name: Manthānabhairava
summary: Named among the rasa authorities in the Rasaratnasamuccaya (1.6); the Ānandakanda is attributed to him in some accounts.

name: Mantreśvara
summary: Author of the Phaladīpikā; South Indian (tradition places him in the Tamil country). Dates uncertain.

name: Manu Svāyambhuva
summary: The first Manu, son of the self-existent, who received dharma from Svayambhū and taught it; his teaching is recited in the Manusmṛti by Bhṛgu. Parāśara assigns Manu's dharma to the Kṛta age.

tradition.text: the first Manu, at the beginning of creation

evidence: text:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/6_sastra/4_dharma/smrti/manu-smrti_plain_text.md (GRETIL, Kullūka vulgate numbering; M = Medhātithi numbering)
checks.note: Text-located: MDh 1.58–60 (Manu received the śāstra from the Self-existent and has Bhṛgu recite it), 1.61 (Svāyambhuva Manu), and ParSm 1.24 (Manu's dharmas for the Kṛta age).

name: Manu Vaivasvata
summary: Son of Vivasvat, who received the yoga from him and passed it to Ikṣvāku (BhG 4.1).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch04-06): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Headers: 'manur vaivasvataḥ' for 8.27–31 (8.29 alternatively Kaśyapa Mārīca).
Text-located: the flood and fish story ŚB 1.8.1.1–10 (the offering from which Iḍā arises, 1.8.1.7–10), and 'manur vaivasvato rājā' at ŚB 13.4.3.3.
Located: ChU 3.11.4 and 8.15.1 ('prajāpatir manave manuḥ prajābhyaḥ') and BĀU 1.4.10 ('ahaṃ manur abhavam').
Located as described.

notes: Distinguished from Svāyambhuva Manu, to whom the Manusmṛti is ascribed.
alt_summary: Son of Vivasvant, ancestor of humankind, seer of RV 8.27–31. (Distinct in the tradition from Manu Svāyambhuva of the Manusmṛti.)
Bhagavad Gītā 4.1: Vivasvat told the yoga to Manu, and Manu told it to Ikṣvāku. The text says only 'Manu'; commentators identify him as Vivasvat's son.
Lineage contribution of lin:upanisadic: link in the teacher-lines Brahmā -> Prajāpati -> Manu -> creatures (ChU 3.11.4, 8.15.1); Vāmadeva says 'I was Manu' (BAU 1.4.10).
The present (seventh) Manu, son of Vivasvat; in ŚB 1.8.1 he saves a fish that later tows his ship over the flood, and his offering gives rise to Iḍā.
alt_notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

name: Manulāl Miśra
summary: Kartābhajā Mahāśay and author of the Sahajatattva-prakāśa (early 20th c.).

name: Manuṣyaka
summary: Number 9 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Manzan Dōhaku 卍山道白
summary: Tokugawa reformer who restored face-to-face, one-teacher dharma transmission (isshi inshō) in Sōtō.

name: Mao Ziyuan

realization_account.text: In samādhi he awakened on hearing a crow's call (Lushan lianzong baojian).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Song monk of Kunshan, trained in Tiantai calming and contemplation, who founded lay repentance halls (Lianzong chantang) teaching the five precepts confirmed by five recitations of Amitābha's name and the 'perfect interfusion of the four lands'; summoned by the retired emperor in 1166 and given the title Cizhao zongzhu (Lushan lianzong baojian).

name: Maṟaimalai Aṭikaḷ
summary: Tamil scholar and Śaiva Siddhānta advocate, leader of the 'pure Tamil' movement; argued for an early date of Māṇikkavācakar and led the 1921 fixing of the Tiruvaḷḷuvar era.

name: Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar
summary: Disciple of Aruṇanti and guru of Umāpati Civācāriyār; third of the four teachers of the outer lineage. No Meykaṇṭa treatise is his.

realization_account.text: Seeing the Chidambaram priest Umāpati carried in a palanquin with a torch in daylight, he called out 'a day-blind man riding a dead log'; stung, Umāpati followed him and became his disciple, eating food from his hand, for which the Tillai priests excluded him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Details of his caste and the palanquin story are given at low confidence (they come from later hagiography).

name: Mārīca Kaśyapa
summary: The teacher of children's medicine whose instruction to Vṛddha Jīvaka forms the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā; in Ca Śā 6.21 'Mārīci Kaśyapa' holds that the order of the embryo's limbs cannot be known, being beyond perception.

name: Marīci
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Vimānārcanakalpa.

name: Marīci (in Caraka's assembly)
summary: Speaker: fire within pitta, provoked or unprovoked, does good and ill in the body (Ca Sū 12.11).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Maritoṇṭadārya
summary: Author of the Tattvapradīpikā commentary on the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi and of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā.

name: Mārkaṇḍeya
summary: The long-lived sage who instructs the Pāṇḍavas in the forest (3.180–221): on karma, the ages and the dissolution — in which he saw the worlds within the body of a divine child on a banyan branch (3.186.81–91) — the devoted wife and the righteous meat-seller.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of daksinamurti, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.
MkP 1.1 (Jaimini questions Mārkaṇḍeya), 81.1 (narrates the eighth Manu's story), BhP 12.9 located.

realization_account.text: The long-lived sage who, by Nara-Nārāyaṇa's boon, witnessed an illusory deluge and saw the Lord as an infant lying on a banyan leaf, entering and leaving the child's body (BhP 12.8-10).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The ever-young sage in whose name the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is told; he directs Jaimini to the wise birds and narrates the Devī Māhātmya as the story of the eighth Manu.
Long-lived sage whom Śaunaka and others ask, in the Dakṣiṇāmūrti Upaniṣad, how he lives in bliss; he answers with the knowledge of Śiva as Dakṣiṇāmūrti.

name: Marpa Chökyi Lodrö (Marpa the Translator)
alt_names: mar pa chos kyi blo gros

tradition.text: 1012–1097 (the usual Tibetan reckoning)

realization_account.text: After years of study and gold-gathering journeys, Marpa received the complete transmissions from Nāropa; when Nāropa manifested Hevajra's maṇḍala Marpa prostrated to the deity rather than to his guru, and Nāropa foretold that his family line would scatter while his Dharma lineage would flourish through his disciples, like a river. He tested and trained Milarepa with harsh ordeals before giving him the instructions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tibetan layman, farmer and translator of Lhodrak who travelled to India (three times by the usual account) and studied with Nāropa, Maitrīpa, Kukkuripa and others; he brought the Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Guhyasamāja and Mahāmāyā tantras, the six dharmas and Mahāmudrā to Tibet and is the Tibetan founder of the Kagyu.
notes: His translations appear with Nāropa as co-translator in the colophons of Tōh 2304, 2330, 2337, 2338 (read locally). Drogmi's role as his first teacher is from the Life (moderate).

name: Martsang Sherab Senge (Marpa Drubthob)
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa, founder of the Martsang Kagyu.

name: Marudevī
summary: Mother of Ṛṣabha; in the Śvetāmbara account the first soul of this era to attain liberation, reaching omniscience and nirvāṇa on elephant-back as she saw her son's samavasaraṇa.

name: Maruḷārādhya (Maruḷasiddha)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Ujjayinī pīṭha (Ujjaini, Kūḍligi taluk, Karnataka).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Seat name Saddharma-siṃhāsana (low confidence).

name: Maskarin
summary: Commentator on the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as the author of the extant Maskaribhāṣya on Gautama. The date is uncertain, as the entry says.

name: Mastnāth
summary: 18th-century Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the monastery at Asthal Bohar near Rohtak (Haryana).

name: Mataṅga
summary: Author of the Bṛhaddeśī, the first to define rāga, and teacher of the doctrine that the world is made of nāda.

name: Māṭhara
summary: Commentator on the SK named in the colophon of the Māṭhara Vṛtti; his date is disputed.

name: Mathurādāsa Ātā
summary: Disciple of Mādhavadeva, first head (sattrādhikār) at Bārpeṭā by tradition; associated with the Nikā saṃhati.
notes: Saṃhati affiliation to verify.

name: Mathurānātha Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Rahasya commentaries (Māthurī) on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the Dīdhiti and Udayana's works.

name: Sabzang Mati Paṇchen Lodrö Gyaltsen (sa bzang ma ti paN chen blo gros rgyal mtshan)
summary: Disciple of Dolpopa and co-translator, with Jonang Lotsawa Lodrö Pal, of the Jonang revision of the Kālacakra tantra and Vimalaprabhā; also a commentator on the Kālacakra.

name: Matsyendranātha
summary: The first human Nāth after Ādinātha and guru of Gorakṣa; the Kaulajñānanirṇaya calls itself 'brought down' by Macchaghnapāda/Mīnapāda from Candradvīpa and tells how Bhairava as a fisherman recovered the scripture from a fish's belly (KJN 16). Nāth sagas tell how he forgot himself among the women of the Kadalī (or Strī) kingdom and was awakened by Gorakṣa. In the Kathmandu valley he is worshipped as Karuṇāmaya (Buṅga-dyaḥ, Rāto Macchindranāth), brought to end a drought caused by Gorakṣa; Tibetan tradition relates the name to the siddha Lūipa. Abhinavagupta praises 'Macchanda' as a Kaula master (Tantrāloka 1.7).

tradition.text: present in the four ages; Nāth hagiography

realization_account.text: Received the Kaula teaching from Bhairava/Ādinātha (in some Nāth tellings while in the form of a fish, overhearing Śiva teaching Pārvatī); fell into forgetfulness in the Kadalī kingdom and was re-awakened by his disciple Gorakṣa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: HYP 1.5 lists both 'Matsyendra' and 'Mīna', and some traditions distinguish Mīnanātha from Matsyendra (e.g. as father/son); this shard keeps one entry and records the question in dsp:identity-of-matsyendra.
alt_summary: U28 contribution: named second in the HYP's list of Mahāsiddhas (1.5), with Gorakṣa as knower of haṭhavidyā (1.4); the posture matsyendrāsana bears his name (HYP 1.26–27) and HYP 1.18 names 'Matsyendra and other yogins' as authorities on postures.

name: Mauṉa kuru (the silent guru of Tāyumāṉavar)
summary: The silent teacher of Tāyumāṉavar at Tiruchirappalli, praised in his songs as coming in Tirumūlar's line (mūlaṉ marapu), who taught by the instruction 'be still'.

name: Maunappa Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Vīraśaivācārakaustubha.

name: Mauryaputra
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether gods exist.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Māyā
summary: The Buddha's mother, who died seven days after his birth (MN 123; DN 14 as a norm of bodhisattas' mothers).

name: Maya (the asura)
summary: The great asura who, when little of the Kṛta age remained, performed hard austerities to the Sun wishing to know the Vedāṅga of the lights, and received the Sūrya Siddhānta from a person born of the Sun's portion (SS 1.2–9; 12.1–11).

name: Mayanāmatī
summary: Queen-mother in the Bengali Nāth cycle, a disciple of Gorakṣa who received the 'great knowledge' (mahājñāna) and with it power over death; she compels her son Gopīcandra to renounce. One of the few women siddhas of the Nāth tradition.

name: Māyidēva
summary: Author ascribed the Sanskrit Anubhavasūtra on the ṣaṭsthala path.

name: Mazu Daoyi 馬祖道一

realization_account.text: Sitting in meditation to become a buddha, he was asked by Huairang, who polished a tile, 'can polishing a tile make a mirror? can sitting in meditation make a buddha?' and awoke on hearing the instruction (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 5).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Hongzhou school; taught that 'this very mind is buddha', 'neither mind nor buddha' and that 'the ordinary mind is the Way'; his teaching style of shouts, blows and everyday gestures began encounter dialogue; over 130 heirs are recorded.

name: Medhas
summary: The brahmin sage (dvijavarya, MkP 81.9) in whose forest hermitage the Devī Māhātmya is taught to the deposed king Suratha and the merchant Samādhi.

checks.note: MkP 81.9 'dvijavaryasya medhasaḥ' located.

name: Medhātithi
summary: Author of the oldest surviving commentary on Manu, reasoning in the manner of Mīmāṃsā.

checks.note: Confirmed: 9th or early 10th c. (Lingat), probably Kashmir; reasons in the Mīmāṃsā manner (Wikipedia; UT Austin).

name: Medhātithi Kāṇva
summary: Seer of RV 1.12–23, including 1.22.20: 'the wise ever see that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched out in heaven'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 'medhātithiḥ kāṇvaḥ' for 1.12–23; 1.22.20 located.

name: Medhāvin
summary: The son in the father–son dialogue of the Mokṣadharma (12.169), who urges his father to seek the self now because death is always near.

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Medhina

realization_account.text: A tireless farmer taught while working the fields. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 50): By the wisdom of innate awareness and by means stained with afflictions, from the ground, the natural state, the fruit — spontaneous great bliss — is realized.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 50 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A tireless farmer taught while working the fields.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Medhya Kāṇva
summary: Seer of the Vālakhilya hymn RV 8.58: 'one Agni kindled in many ways … one has become all this'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'medhyaḥ kāṇvaḥ'.

name: Meghakumāra
summary: Son of King Śreṇika who became a monk; distressed by being jostled on his first night, he was reminded by Mahāvīra of his past life as an elephant who held up his foot for days to spare a hare (Jñātādharmakathā 1.1).

name: Meghanādāri Sūri
summary: Viśiṣṭādvaita logician before Deśika, author of the Nayadyumaṇi.

name: Meghavijaya
summary: Tapā Gaccha monk-scholar who wrote the Yuktiprabodha against the Adhyātma ('Vāṇārasīya') view.

name: Meghiya
summary: The Buddha's attendant who left to meditate in a mango grove and was overcome by unwholesome thoughts; taught the five things that ripen the liberation of mind (Ud 4.1; AN 9.3).

name: Mekhalā

realization_account.text: The elder of two sisters of Devīkoṭa, mocked in marriage, who took instruction from Kāṇha; when he asked for a fee, the two sisters cut off their heads and offered them, and sang their realization; he restored them; they are linked to the 'headless' Vajrayoginī (Chinnamuṇḍā). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 66): All outer and inner are gathered in mind; without clinging there is equal taste; without striving, the supreme meditation; non-dual great bliss is complete buddhahood.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 66 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). The elder of two sisters of Devīkoṭa, mocked in marriage, who took instruction from Kāṇha; when he asked for a fee, the two sisters cut off their heads and offered them, and sang their realization; he restored them; they are linked to the 'headless' Vajrayoginī (Chinnamuṇḍā).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Mekopa

realization_account.text: A food seller who fed a yogin daily and received instruction; afterwards he wandered the cremation grounds with a terrifying stare. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 43): First realize your own mind from the true guru; then make all appearances undivided; habituated to non-duality, dwell in the cremation ground; having realized equality, practise the observance of madness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 43 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A food seller who fed a yogin daily and received instruction; afterwards he wandered the cremation grounds with a terrifying stare.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. States the order: realization first, the 'mad' observance only after it.

name: Menzan Zuihō 面山瑞方
summary: Tokugawa scholar-monk who revived study of Dōgen's writings and wrote on precepts and zazen.

name: Meruśāstrin
summary: Named in the opening verses of the Jyotsnā as the one at whose urging (abhiyoga) Brahmānanda explained the hidden sense of Gorakṣa's doctrine; the relation is usually taken as teacher and pupil.

name: Merutuṅga (commentator on the Rasādhyāya)
summary: Jain author of a commentary on the Rasādhyāya.

name: Metārya
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether there is another world (rebirth).

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Meton Chenpo (Meton Tsönpo)
summary: One of Marpa's four principal disciples, holder (by one account) of the clear-light instruction.
notes: The allotment 'Ngok — explanation, Tsur — transference, Meton — clear light, Mila — inner heat' is from memory of the Kagyu histories (low).

name: Metteyya
summary: The future Buddha who will arise when human life reaches eighty thousand years (DN 26).

name: Meu Gongdzö Ritrö Chenpo (rme'u dgongs mdzod ri khrod chen po)
summary: Bön master credited with the A-tri system of Dzogchen meditation.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Founder of the Tamil Siddhānta school; author of the Civañāṉa Pōtam; head of the lineage of 'outer' teachers (puṟaccantāṉam).

realization_account.text: Born to a childless Vēḷāḷa couple after they bathed at Tiruveṇkāṭu as Campantar's hymn instructed, and named after its Lord; as a child he was taught by the sage Parañcōti from Kailāsa, who named him Meykaṇṭār, 'he who saw the truth'. He gathered 49 disciples; the learned family priest Aruṇanti, who came to test the child, became his foremost disciple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Meypporuḷ Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.

realization_account.text: A chieftain stabbed by his enemy Muttanātaṉ, who had come disguised as a Śaiva ascetic; dying, he ordered his guard Tattaṉ to escort the assassin safely out, because he wore Śiva's garb.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mhāimbhaṭ
summary: Disciple who gathered the eyewitness memories of Cakradhar into the Līḷācaritra (c. 1278) and compiled the Govindaprabhu-caritra.

name: Mi'an Xianjie 密庵咸傑
summary: Yangqi master in Huqiu's line.

name: Miaodao 妙道
summary: Song nun who awakened under Dahui's instruction and received his confirmation.

name: Miaoye
summary: Ming monk who compiled the Baowang sanmei nianfo zhizhi.

name: Miccaka (Mizhejia 彌遮迦)
summary: Sixth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 6.

name: Mikyö Dorje, the eighth Karmapa
summary: The great scholar Karmapa: author of the Chariot of the Dakpo Kagyu Siddhas (Madhyamaka), the Four-Session Guru Yoga, and compiler of the Kagyu Gurtso; defended the Kagyu view against Gelug critics.

name: Milarepa (Jetsün Mila Shepa Dorje)
alt_names: Mila Shepa Dorje (mi la bzhad pa rdo rje)

tradition.text: 1040–1123 (Tsangnyön Heruka); other Tibetan reckonings 1028/1052–1111/1135

realization_account.text: Having killed thirty-five people through sorcery and destroyed crops with hail, he felt remorse, sought Dharma, and was made by Marpa to build and tear down towers until his evil karma was purified; after empowerment he meditated alone for years, living on nettles until his body turned green; he attained realization through inner heat and Mahāmudrā, displayed miraculous powers (flight; the contest with Naro Bönchung at Kailash), and at death, poisoned by a jealous scholar, showed signs of buddhahood.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great yogin-poet of Tibet: after using sorcery to avenge his family he turned to the Dharma, endured Marpa's ordeals, practised for years in mountain caves wearing only cotton cloth (repa) and sustained by inner heat, and attained buddhahood in one life by the tradition's account; teacher of Gampopa and Rechungpa; his songs are the Hundred Thousand Songs.
notes: Details of the life are from Tsangnyön Heruka's 1488 version; earlier lives differ in details.

name: Milinda
summary: The Indo-Greek king (Menander I) whose questions to Nāgasena form the Milindapañha.

name: Mīnapa

realization_account.text: A fisherman swallowed by a great fish; in its belly on the ocean floor he overheard the god Śiva (Maheśvara) teaching Umā the secret yoga and practised it for twelve years before being freed; his feet sank into rock when he danced. Widely identified with Matsyendranātha of the Nāth tradition (identification disputed). Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 8): The fisherman holding his hook was carried by karma into the ocean; relying on the body of the great fish, he practised the great god's instruction, and his qualities became famed as more than earth and stone could bear.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 8 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A fisherman swallowed by a great fish; in its belly on the ocean floor he overheard the god Śiva (Maheśvara) teaching Umā the secret yoga and practised it for twelve years before being freed; his feet sank into rock when he danced. Widely identified with Matsyendranātha of the Nāth tradition (identification disputed).
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The last line ('ma theg') is read as the weight of his realization sinking into rock (cf. the name Vajrapāda); low certainty on this reading.

name: Mīnarāja
summary: Author of the Vṛddhayavanajātaka, a large versified horā in the Yavana tradition.

name: Mingun Jetavana Sayadaw
summary: Burmese meditation master (U Nārada, 1868–1955) who revived satipaṭṭhāna practice in the early 20th century and taught Mahāsi Sayadaw.

name: Mipham Jamyang Namgyal Gyatso ('ju mi pham)
summary: The great Nyingma scholar of the Rimé era, disciple of Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo and Patrul; he wrote commentaries giving the Nyingma its own scholastic curriculum (Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Bodhicaryāvatāra 9, Guhyagarbha, the Beacon of Certainty, the Gateway to Knowledge), argued with Gelug scholars on Madhyamaka, and taught buddha-nature as the union of luminosity and emptiness.

name: Mīrābāī
summary: Rajput princess of Meṛtā (tradition c. 1498–1547), married into the Sisodia house of Mewar and early widowed, who took Kṛṣṇa as Giridhar Gopāl for her husband, danced with sādhus, survived the poison and the snake sent by the Rāṇā, went to Vṛndāvana and then Dvārakā, and — so tradition says — merged into the image of Raṇchoḍ. The Bhaktamāl praises her for casting off family honour; songs in her name name Raidās as guru.

realization_account.text: Merged bodily into Kṛṣṇa's image at Dvārakā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Raidās as guru is the songs' claim; chronology makes a direct meeting doubtful.

name: Miskīndās
summary: Dādū's younger son, a poet of the Dādū Panth.

name: Mitra Miśra
summary: Author of the Vīramitrodaya.

checks.note: Confirmed: c. 1610–1640, for Vīrasiṃhadeva of Orchha (Wikipedia).

name: Mitra (Pāśupata)
summary: The third of Lakulīśa's four disciples (Liṅga P. 1.24.131 'Mitra'; Kūrma P. 1.51.26 'Mitraka'; Jain lists 'Maitrya').

name: Miyun Yuanwu 密雲圓悟
summary: Late-Ming Linji master at Tiantong who revived the use of shouts and blows; teacher of Feiyin.

name: Moggaliputta Tissa
summary: The elder who, by the Theravāda chronicles and commentaries, presided over the Third Council at Pāṭaliputta under Asoka, purified the Saṅgha, composed the Kathāvatthu and sent missions abroad.

tradition.text: 218 years after the parinibbāna (c. 325 BCE on the tradition's count)

scholarly.text: 3rd c. BCE, if historical; the council is not mentioned in Asoka's inscriptions

notes: Account from the Dīpavaṃsa, Mahāvaṃsa and Samantapāsādikā; U37 owns the Kathāvatthu.
alt_summary: The elder who, according to the Theravāda chronicles and commentaries, presided over the Third Council at Pāṭaliputta under Asoka, expelled holders of wrong views, composed the Kathāvatthu and sent missions to other lands including Mahinda's to Lanka.

name: Mahāmoggallāna
summary: Named in MN 118:1 among the well-known senior disciples present at Sāvatthī.

checks.note: Level not raised (entities are not promoted by the spot-check). By code: every linked id resolves in data/ or these shards; no restricted flag; no modern/psychological/health wording found. Content not read line by line by J.

alt_summary: The left-hand chief disciple, foremost in psychic power; Kolita, Sāriputta's friend, converted with him; the Buddha instructed him against drowsiness (AN 7.61); visits to heavens and hells in the Vimānavatthu and Petavatthu; by the commentarial account killed by bandits shortly before the Buddha's death.

realization_account.text: Attained arahantship seven days after ordination after the Buddha's instruction on drowsiness (AN 7.61, commentarial setting).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Mogharāja
summary: One of the sixteen brahmin students of Bāvarī who questioned the Buddha in the Pārāyanavagga (Snp 5.16).

name: Mogok Sayadaw
summary: Burmese teacher (U Vimala, 1899–1962) whose insight method begins from understanding dependent origination.

name: Moheyan 摩訶衍 (Hwashang Mahāyāna)
summary: Chinese Chan master at the Tibetan court whose teaching of not thinking and not examining was opposed by Kamalaśīla in the Samye debate; the Chinese record is the Dunwu dasheng zhengli jue. (U42 contributes the Chan side; the debate is dsp:sudden-or-gradual, U50.)
notes: Scholars link his teaching to Northern-school lines; the tradition's (Tibetan) accounts say he lost the debate, the Chinese record says he won.

name: Mokchokpa Rinchen Tsöndrü
alt_names: rmog lcog pa rin chen brtson 'grus
summary: Second of the Shangpa 'seven jewels', disciple of Khyungpo Naljor.

name: Mokṣākaragupta
summary: Logician of the Jagaddala monastery, author of the Tarkabhāṣā.

name: Mokuan Shōtō 木庵性瑫
summary: Ingen's Chinese successor as abbot of Manpukuji.

name: Mōḷige Mahādēvi
summary: Wife of Mōḷige Mārayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Mōḷige Mārayya
summary: A king (Kashmir in the tradition's account) who renounced his kingdom and lived in Kalyāṇa by selling bundles of firewood (mōḷige).

name: Vajirañāṇa (King Mongkut)
summary: Siamese prince who spent 27 years as a monk (1824–1851), founded the reformist Dhammayut order, and reigned as King Rāma IV (1851–1868).

name: Moshan Liaoran 末山了然
summary: Tang nun, heir of Gao'an Dayu, the first woman recorded as a Chan master in the Jingde chuandeng lu; asked by Guanxi Zhixian what the master of Moshan is, she answered 'not a male or female form', and he served her three years as gardener.

name: Mu'an Shanqing 睦庵善卿
summary: Compiler of the Chan lexicon Zuting shiyuan (1108).

name: Muchen Könchok Gyaltsen
summary: Ngorchen's disciple and successor, an important transmitter of the Lamdre.

name: Mudaliyāṇḍāṉ
summary: Nephew of Rāmānuja, called his 'triple staff' (tridaṇḍa), entrusted with the administration of the Śrīraṅgam temple.

name: Muddadeva
summary: An ācārya of the Śivayogin lineage from which the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's author descends; named Muddadeva because he gave joy (mud) to all beings (SSM 1.15–16).

name: Muḍumba Narasiṃhasvāmin
summary: Author to whom the Sāṃkhyataruvasanta, a late commentary on the SK, is ascribed.

name: Mugai Nyodai 無外如大
summary: Kamakura-period nun, disciple of Wuxue Zuyuan, founder of the convent Keiaiji in Kyoto; regarded as the first Japanese woman Zen master.

name: Muhammad Mansuruddin
summary: Collector of Bengali folk songs (Hārāmaṇi), a principal preserver of Lalon's and other Bāul songs in print.
notes: A collector and scholar, not a Bāul teacher; recorded because the written transmission of the songs depends on him.

name: Mūka Kavi
summary: The 'mute poet' of Kāñcī who by tradition received speech through Kāmākṣī's grace and poured out the Mūka Pañcaśatī; the Kāñcī Kāmakoṭi tradition counts him among its ācāryas.

realization_account.text: Mute from birth, he became a poet when the Goddess (or a devotee in her presence) gave him her grace.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mūka (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Muktābāī
summary: Youngest of the four siblings; her 'door' abhaṅgas (tāṭīce abhaṅga) coaxed Jñāneśvar out of the hut he had shut himself into after being insulted, teaching that the saint bears insult without anger; the yogī Cāṅgadev became her disciple. Tradition says she vanished in a flash of lightning at Mehūṇ on the Tāpī.

name: Muktananda
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): made the Guru Gītā the daily morning chant of his ashrams (Ganeshpuri recension).

checks.note: Muktananda chose 182 verses of the Guru Gītā as a chant with its own melody.

name: Muktāyakka
summary: The woman śaraṇa who, grieving her brother Ajagaṇṇa, was met by Allama; their exchange on grief, speech and silence is a chapter of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Mukunda Dāsa (Sahajiyā)
summary: Sahajiyā teacher to whom the Amṛtaratnāvalī and Bhṛṅgaratnāvalī are attributed; claimed by Sahajiyās as a disciple of Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja.

name: Mukundarām Cakravartī (Kavikaṅkaṇa)
summary: Bengali poet of the Caṇḍīmaṅgala, the most famous narrative poem of the goddess Caṇḍī.

name: Mummaḍi Kṛṣṇarāja Woḍeyar III
summary: Mahārāja of Mysore under whose patronage the illustrated Śrītattvanidhi, with its section of postures, was compiled; the Mysore palace later hosted T. Krishnamacharya's yoga school under a successor.

name: Muṉaiyaṭuvā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A warrior who fought for the losing side in others' battles for hire and spent the fees on feeding devotees.

realization_account.text: A warrior who fought for the losing side in others' battles for hire and spent the fees on feeding devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Munidatta
summary: Author of the Sanskrit commentary on the Caryāgīti (c. 13th c.?).

name: Munisuvrata
summary: The twentieth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the tortoise. Parents: Sumitra and Padmāvatī. Born at Rājagṛha; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as dark; Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Rāvaṇa lived in his era.

tradition.text: the twentieth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Muṉṟuṟai Araiyaṉār
summary: Jain poet, author of the Paḻamoḻi Nāṉūṟu.

name: Murāri Gupta
summary: Physician of Navadvīpa and companion of Caitanya; author of the earliest Sanskrit biography (kaḍacā).

name: Murāri Miśra
notes: Modern literature numbers several Murāris inconsistently (II/III); low confidence on dating and on the second work.
summary: Mīmāṃsaka whose distinct account of how validity is known (through the after-cognition, anuvyavasāya) made him proverbially the founder of a 'third path'; fragments of his Tripādīnītinayana and (attributed) Aṅgatvanirukti survive.

name: Mūrkka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A gambler who fed devotees with his winnings and dealt harshly with those who would not pay — hence 'the rough one'.

realization_account.text: A gambler who fed devotees with his winnings and dealt harshly with those who would not pay — hence 'the rough one'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Mūrtti Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A merchant who supplied sandal paste to the Madurai temple; when a Jain-favouring usurper stopped the supply he ground his own elbow on the stone; made king by Śiva's will, he ruled with the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa and matted hair as his crown and insignia.

realization_account.text: A merchant who supplied sandal paste to the Madurai temple; when a Jain-favouring usurper stopped the supply he ground his own elbow on the stone; made king by Śiva's will, he ruled with the sacred ash, the rudrākṣa and matted hair as his crown and insignia.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Muruka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who wove flower garlands for Śiva; friend of Campantar, he attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who wove flower garlands for Śiva; friend of Campantar, he attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Musang 無相 (Kim heshang 金和尚)
summary: Korean prince-monk in Sichuan; taught 'no remembering, no thinking, no forgetting' as precepts, samādhi and wisdom, opening his assemblies with drawn-out recitation of the Buddha's name (Lidai fabao ji).

name: Musō Soseki 夢窓疎石
summary: Rinzai master and garden designer, adviser to the Ashikaga, founder of Tenryūji; author of Muchū mondō.

name: Muttusvāmi Dīkṣitar
summary: Karnatic composer and Śrīvidyā initiate whose Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa songs set the Śrīcakra worship to music.
notes: His initiation into Śrīvidyā by a yogin at Kāśī is the tradition's account (not detailed here).
alt_summary: U31 contribution: one of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers, whose Sanskrit kṛtis are also meditations (the Kamalāmbā Navāvaraṇa kṛtis set the Śrīcakra worship in music); music as worship of the deity through nāda.

name: Muyeom 無染
summary: Founder of the Seongjusan school; heir of Magu Baoche.

name: Muzhou Daoming (Chen Zunsu) 睦州道明
summary: Heir of Huangbo who broke Yunmen's leg in a slammed gate, causing his awakening.

name: Myōe
summary: Kegon (Huayan) monk of Kōzan-ji, known for strict precepts, dream records and the 'mantra of light'; after reading the Senchakushū he wrote the Zaijarin (1212) charging Hōnen with discarding the aspiration for awakening.

name: Butsuju Myōzen 佛樹明全
summary: Eisai's disciple who went to China with Dōgen in 1223 and died at Tiantong in 1225.

name: Nabanī Dās Khyāpā Bāul
summary: Birbhum Bāul known to Rabindranath Tagore at Santiniketan; father of Pūrṇa Dās.

name: Nābhādās
summary: Author of the Bhaktamāl (c. 1600), raised as an abandoned child by Agradās and Kīlhadās at Galtā; his garland of devotees crosses sect and caste.

name: Naciketas

realization_account.text: KU 2.3.18: having received this knowledge from Death and the whole rule of yoga, Naciketas attained brahman and became free of stain and death.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Boy who, given to Death by his father, waits three nights in Yama's house and chooses as his third boon the knowledge of what happens after death; refusing all worldly gifts, he receives the teaching of the self and the whole method of yoga and attains brahman (KU 1.1-2.3.18).

checks.note: Text-located: TB 3.11.8.1–6.

Located: KU 1.1.1 to 2.3.18 ('mṛtyuproktāṃ naciketo 'tha labdhvā vidyām etāṃ yogavidhiṃ ca kṛtsnam … brahma prāpto virajo 'bhūd vimṛtyuḥ'). The older ritual form of the story is in TB 3.11.8 (confirmed locally).
Agni 381.1 'yamagītāṃ ... uktā yā nāciketase'.

alt_summary: U02 contribution: in TB 3.11.8 he is given to Death by his father Vājaśravasa, receives three boons and learns the Nāciketa fire by which he conquers re-death — the Brāhmaṇa root of the Kaṭha Upaniṣad.
In U06's texts: the addressee of the Agni Purāṇa's Yama Gītā, which retells the Kaṭha Upaniṣad teaching.

name: Naḍādūr Ammāḷ
summary: Vātsya Varadaguru, celebrated expounder of the Śrībhāṣya at Kāñcī, whose lectures Sudarśana Sūri recorded in the Śrutaprakāśikā; disciple of Engaḷāḻvāṉ and teacher of Ātreya Rāmānuja.

name: The daughter of the nāga king Sāgara
summary: The eight-year-old nāga princess of Lotus ch. 12, whom Mañjuśrī taught in the sea: she offers a jewel to the Buddha, and before Śāriputra's doubt about women's bodies she instantly becomes a male bodhisattva and a buddha in the southern world Vimalā.

name: Nāgabhaṭṭa
summary: Compiler of the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.

name: Nāgabodhi

realization_account.text: A thief who came to rob Nāgārjuna and became his disciple (the 'red-horned thief'); he is counted in the Ārya Guhyasamāja lineage and is said to live on at Śrīparvata. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 76): Dwelling on earth, all is good fortune; gone to the ocean's depths, one is free of poverty; sword in hand, great enjoyment; gone to no particular direction, one meets one's friends.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 76 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A thief who came to rob Nāgārjuna and became his disciple (the 'red-horned thief'); he is counted in the Ārya Guhyasamāja lineage and is said to live on at Śrīparvata.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The images may name siddhis (earth, ocean, sword); uncertain.

name: Nāgadevācārya (Bhaṭobās)
summary: Cakradhar's chosen successor (d. c. 1312), who held the community together after Cakradhar's departure and approved the compilation of the Līḷācaritra.

name: Nāganātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Nāgnāth / Nāgeśnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Āvirhotra.

name: Nāgārjuna

tradition.text: born four hundred years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa (Laṅkāvatāra prophecy); Tibetan histories give him a life of six hundred years

places: Nālandā (ordination and abbacy in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: The Laṅkāvatāra prophesies that a monk named Nāga will destroy the views of existence and non-existence, teach the supreme Mahāyāna and reach the Joyful ground (pramuditā bhūmi) before going to Sukhāvatī. The Chinese Life tells that as a brahmin youth he misused an art of invisibility, narrowly escaped death, renounced, exhausted the available scriptures and received the Mahāyāna sūtras from a great nāga in the nāga palace. Tibetan histories (Bu-ston, Tāranātha) tell that he was ordained at Nālandā, became its abbot, brought the Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 lines back from the nāgas, practised alchemy, advised a Sātavāhana king and at the end gave his head to a prince who severed it with a blade of kuśa grass.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly account: a South Indian monk of c. 150–250 CE connected with the Sātavāhana court; the name was borne also by later authors (a tantric Nāgārjuna and the alchemist tch:nagarjuna-siddha), which the tradition conflates. The 'reasoning corpus' (MMK, VV, ŚS, YṢ, VP) and the RĀ and SL are widely accepted; other attributions are disputed. Laṅkāvatāra prophecy verse number (c. 10.165–166) to check.
summary: Founder of the Madhyamaka: author of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and the other 'reasoning' treatises, of letters to a Sātavāhana king and of hymns, revered in every Mahāyāna tradition as the 'second Buddha' who opened the Perfection of Wisdom teaching of emptiness.
alt_notes: U43 contribution: first of the seven masters of Jōdo Shinshū; the 'chapter on easy practice' of the Daśabhūmikavibhāṣā (T1521 ch. 9) is the Indian root of the easy path (tea:dasabhumika-vibhasa:41b02-06).

Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 14.
alt_summary: Fourteenth patriarch in the Chan list. (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)

name: Nāgārjuna (Jain elder of Valabhī)
summary: Presided over a council at Valabhī contemporary with Skandila's at Mathurā; variant readings of his 'Nāgārjunīya' recension are noted in the commentaries. Not the Buddhist Nāgārjuna.

tradition.text: c. 4th c. CE

name: Nāgārjuna (the siddha)

tradition.text: the Madhyamaka master, who lived some six hundred years

realization_account.text: Ordained at Nālandā, he mastered alchemy, fed the saṅgha in famine by turning iron into gold, received the Prajñāpāramitā from the nāgas, and in the end gave his own head to a prince; the tradition identifies him with the Madhyamaka master and with the author of the Pañcakrama. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 16): One who has not realized should not engage in the (special) conduct: if he does, it is like a kingdom seized by its subjects; one who has realized should not act like one who has not: if he does, it is like an elephant caught in a swamp.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: U44 contribution (the siddha of the eighty-four): No. 16 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). Ordained at Nālandā, he mastered alchemy, fed the saṅgha in famine by turning iron into gold, received the Prajñāpāramitā from the nāgas, and in the end gave his own head to a prince; the tradition identifies him with the Madhyamaka master and with the author of the Pañcakrama.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The unit reads the song as a rule that conduct must match realization.
alt_summary: Named by Ḍalhaṇa as the redactor of the Suśruta Saṃhitā; counted among the twenty-seven siddhas of rasa (Rasaratnasamuccaya 1.4) and cited in the Rasaratnākara (Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.17) as having taught for the sick; alchemical works (Rasendramaṅgala) are attributed to him.
alt_notes: Tibetan and some Indian traditions identify him with the Madhyamaka philosopher (tch:nagarjuna); scholars usually distinguish one or more later Nāgārjunas. Kept separate here.

name: Nāgasena
summary: The monk who answers King Milinda in the Milindapañha (chariot simile, the flame).

name: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Last great Pāṇinian of the classical period; his philosophical works belong to lin:vyakarana (U31).

checks.note: Confirmed: active 1670–1750 (Wellcome authority record).

alt_summary: Pāṇinian grammarian (Laghuśabdenduśekhara, Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā) who also wrote a vṛtti on the Yoga Sūtra.

U31 contribution: the last great classical Pāṇinian philosopher; in the Mañjūṣās and the Sphoṭavāda he systematizes the grammarians' semantics (the three powers of words), identifies the sphoṭa with the madhyamā level of speech, and maps parā, paśyantī, madhyamā and vaikharī onto the root centre, navel, heart and throat.
U09 contribution: the grammarian Nāgeśa of Vārāṇasī, to whom a short vṛtti on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra is ascribed (low confidence).

name: Nagtso Lotsawa Tsultrim Gyalwa
summary: Translator sent to invite Atiśa from Vikramaśīla, who accompanied him and translated several of his works (named in the colophon of the Caryāsaṃgrahapradīpa as the monk translator Tsultrim Gyalwa).
alt_names: nag tsho lo tsā ba tshul khrims rgyal ba

name: Nahuṣa
summary: Ancient king cursed to be a python; he seizes Bhīma and is freed when Yudhiṣṭhira answers his questions on who is a brāhmaṇa (3.173–178).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Nāka Maudgalya
summary: Holds that Vedic study and teaching alone matter, for that is austerity (TU 1.9).

checks.note: Located: TU 1.9.1 ('svādhyāyapravacane eveti nāko maudgalyaḥ | tad dhi tapas tad dhi tapaḥ').

name: Nakkīrar
summary: Poet of the Madurai academy in tradition; author of the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (Tirumuṟai 11). The Tiruviḷaiyāṭal story tells of his dispute with Śiva over a poem.

name: Nakula
summary: Pāṇḍava who, with Sahadeva, blows the conches Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka (1.16).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.16.

name: Nakulamātā
summary: Wife of Nakulapitā, whose counsel to her sick husband is praised in AN 6.16.

name: Nakulapitā
summary: An aged householder of Bhagga told to be 'afflicted in body but not in mind' (SN 22.1); with his wife Nakulamātā foremost among trusting lay followers.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Nalina

realization_account.text: A poor man or prince who was taught to meditate on the lotus; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 40): In the petalled lotus at the crown the moving seed is joy; drawing out the essence is supreme joy; the innate, beyond joy, the unsurpassed, is attained.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 40 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A poor man or prince who was taught to meditate on the lotus; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Refers to the joys of the completion stage (restricted domain); summarized only.

name: Nāmdev
summary: Tailor-caste (śimpī) saint of Paṇḍharpūr (c. 1270–1350), Viṭṭhala's intimate from childhood — the Lord ate his offering — who, after Gorā Kumbhār judged him 'unbaked', took Visobā Khecar as guru and learned to see God everywhere. Companion of Jñāneśvar, he vowed to 'dance in kīrtan and light the lamp of knowledge in the world', carried Viṭṭhala's name to Punjab in Hindi songs, and took samādhi at the temple step (Nāmdev pāyarī).

realization_account.text: Viṭṭhala spoke and ate with him as a child; only after taking a guru did he see the Lord in all things.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Naminanti Aṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who, refused oil by Jains for the temple lamps at Tiruvārūr, lit them with water at Śiva's word, and they burned.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who, refused oil by Jains for the temple lamps at Tiruvārūr, lit them with water at Śiva's word, and they burned.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Naminātha
summary: The twenty-first Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the blue lotus (nīlotpala). Parents: Vijaya and Vaprā. Born at Mithilā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. Not to be confused with the royal sage Nami of Uttarādhyayana 9.

tradition.text: the twenty-first of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Chögyal Namkhai Norbu (nam mkha'i nor bu)
summary: Dzogchen master and scholar who taught Dzogchen internationally (the Dzogchen Community) and wrote on Bön and Zhang Zhung history.

name: Namkhai Nyingpo (nam mkha'i snying po)
summary: One of Padmasambhava's twenty-five disciples, a holder of the Yangdag (Viśuddha) heruka practice.

name: Nammāḻvār
summary: Chief of the Āḻvārs and 'first head of the clan' (kulapati) of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas: author of the Tiruviruttam, Tiruvāciriyam, Periya Tiruvantāti and Tiruvāymoḻi, held to be the four Vedas in Tamil. His hymns teach the Lord's supremacy and accessibility, knowledge-and-love as the Lord's gift, surrender at Tiruvēṅkaṭam with Śrī as mediator, service to the Lord and his devotees, and love-longing in the voice of Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī; the last decads describe the ascent on the path of light and final union.

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

realization_account.text: Born to Kāri and Uṭaiya Naṅkai of a Vellāḷa family at Kurukūr, the child did not cry or feed and repelled the 'śaṭha' wind that makes newborns forget (hence Śaṭhakopa); his parents laid him in a hollow of the tamarind tree at the temple, where he sat silent in absorption for sixteen years. Madhurakavi, following a light from the north, found him and asked: 'If the small is born in the body of the dead, what will it eat and where will it lie?' — the child answered: 'That it will eat, and there it will lie.' He then sang his four works, which Madhurakavi wrote down. Centuries later he appeared to Nāthamuni in vision and gave him the whole Prabandham.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Registry id. U14 references him as the head of the Śrīvaiṣṇava lineage. The 'small/dead' riddle is commonly read as the soul (small) born in matter (dead): it lives on matter's experiences until it knows the Lord. Aṃśa of Viṣvaksena in the tradition's list (moderate). His image-crown Śaṭhāri (caṭāri) bears the Lord's feet (prc:satari).
alt_summary: (U25 owns.) For Viśiṣṭādvaita: the 'first head of the clan' (kulapati) of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas, from whom Nāthamuni received the Prabandham; his Tiruvāymoḻi is the 'Tamil Upaniṣad' (Dramiḍopaniṣad) expounded by the ācāryas, and Deśika's Pādukāsahasra identifies him with the Lord's sandals.

name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Priest of Tirunāraiyūr who, by the tradition's account, recovered the Tēvāram at Chidambaram and arranged the first eleven Tirumuṟai; author of ten works in the eleventh, including the Tiruttoṇṭar Tiruvantāti.

realization_account.text: As a boy he fed the Gaṇeśa (Poḷḷāppiḷḷaiyār) of Tirunāraiyūr, who ate and taught him; guided by that Gaṇeśa he found the hymns in a sealed chamber at Chidambaram, half eaten by termites — what remained was what the Lord wished preserved.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nampiḷḷai
summary: Nampūr Varadarājar, disciple of Nañjīyar, whose lectures on the Tiruvāymoḻi at Śrīraṅgam drew great crowds and were recorded as the Īṭu; called Lokācārya, a title passed to Piḷḷai Lokācārya.

name: Ñāṇamoli Thera
summary: English monk in Sri Lanka (1905–1960) whose translation The Path of Purification (1956) made the Visuddhimagga available in English.

name: Nanda
summary: The Buddha's half-brother, son of Mahāpajāpatī, who went forth reluctantly and was led by the Buddha to overcome his longing (Ud 3.2); foremost in guarding the sense doors.

name: Nanda Vaccha
summary: Named with Kisa Saṅkicca and Makkhali Gosāla as one of the three Ājīvika leaders: 'supremely white' in Pūraṇa's six classes (AN 6.57), the only three the Ājīvikas recognize as having made an end (MN 76), and models of bodily austerity (MN 36).

name: Nanda (Yogācāra master)
summary: One of the ten Indian masters of the Cheng weishi lun, reported as holding that all seeds are newly perfumed and that cognition has only two parts (seeing and seen).

name: Nandaka
summary: The monk who exhorted Mahāpajāpatī's five hundred nuns (MN 146); foremost in exhorting nuns.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Nandapaṇḍita
summary: Commentator on the Viṣṇusmṛti.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: Nandapaṇḍita of Vārāṇasī wrote the Vaijayantī in 1622 (Wikipedia 'Vishnu Smriti'), within the entry's 1580–1630.

name: Nanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet, author of the Rāspañcādhyāyī and a Bhramargīt.

name: Nandi (Nantīcar)
summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Nandi (Nantīcar, Nantitēvar) is the first of the eighteen Siddhars and the channel through whom Śiva's knowledge — including medicine — reached Tirumūlar and the others (TM 67–68).
places: Kāśī — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.
alt_summary: Śiva's chief attendant and doorkeeper at Kailāsa; in Tamil Siddhānta the first human-facing teacher of the inner lineage, and the guru of Tirumūlar.

name: Nandikeśvara
summary: Śiva's attendant Nandin, to whom tradition ascribes a verse commentary on the Māheśvara sūtras (and, separately, works on dance); historical authorship uncertain.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as a traditional attribution: the Kāśikā on the Māheśvara sūtras is ascribed to Nandikeśvara (local reproduction; Indica Today). Historical authorship remains uncertain, as the entry says.

alt_summary: U31 contribution: the name under which the Abhinayadarpaṇa (dance and gesture) and other works on dance and music are transmitted; tradition identifies him with Śiva's attendant Nandin, who taught dance.

name: Nandikeśvara (author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā)
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā defending the wearing of the liṅga.
notes: Distinct from the mythic Nandikeśvara and from the authors on grammar and dance of that name.

name: Nandīśvara
summary: Prābhākara author of the Prābhākaravijaya.

name: Nandīśvara (as named in the Yoga-bhāṣya on 4.3)
summary: Named in the bhāṣya on YS 4.3 as one of those to be cited as an example of dharma removing the obstruction of adharma; nothing more is stated in the passage. Not to be confused with the Nandīśvara of the Prābhākara tradition.
