name: Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo (gyer spungs snang bzher lod po)
summary: Zhang Zhung master of the 8th c. to whom Tapihritsa transmitted the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü, which he set down.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Nañjīyar
summary: Formerly the Advaitin Vedānti Mādhava, converted by Parāśara Bhaṭṭar; renouncer and author of the Oṉpatiṉāyirappaṭi ('Nine Thousand') on the Tiruvāymoḻi; teacher of Nampiḷḷai.

name: Nanpo Shōmyō 南浦紹明 (Daiō kokushi)
summary: Heir of Xutang Zhiyu; first of the Ōtōkan line (Ō-Tō-Kan: Daiō, Daitō, Kanzan) from which all present Rinzai lines descend.

name: Nanquan Puyuan 南泉普願
summary: Heir of Mazu; 'the ordinary mind is the Way'; killed the cat when the monks could not answer; teacher of Zhaozhou.

name: Nantaṉār (Tirunāḷaippōvār)
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Pulaiya (outcaste) labourer who supplied leather and strings for temple drums; at Tiruppuṅkūr Śiva moved the bull Nandi aside so he could see; long saying 'I will go to Tillai tomorrow', he at last reached Chidambaram where, at Śiva's command conveyed to the priests, he passed through fire, rose as a brahmin sage and entered the sanctum, never to be seen again.

realization_account.text: A Pulaiya (outcaste) labourer who supplied leather and strings for temple drums; at Tiruppuṅkūr Śiva moved the bull Nandi aside so he could see; long saying 'I will go to Tillai tomorrow', he at last reached Chidambaram where, at Śiva's command conveyed to the priests, he passed through fire, rose as a brahmin sage and entered the sanctum, never to be seen again.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nānyadeva
summary: King of Mithilā (Karṇāṭa dynasty), author of the Bharatabhāṣya.

name: Nanyang Huizhong 南陽慧忠 (National Teacher Zhong)
summary: Disciple of Huineng and teacher to emperors; taught that the insentient preach the Dharma, criticised 'southern' teachers who held that the body perishes while the mind-nature is eternal, and is said to have originated the circle-figures.

name: Nanyuan Huiyong 南院慧顒
summary: Linji master (d. c. 952).

name: Nanyue Huairang 南嶽懷讓
summary: Disciple of Huineng ('to call it a thing misses the mark'), teacher of Mazu; polished a tile to show that sitting does not make a buddha.

name: Naong Hyegeun 懶翁慧勤
summary: Goryeo master who studied with Pingshan Chulin and the Indian monk Zhikong (Dhyānabhadra).

name: Naracinka Muṉaiyaraiya Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The chieftain who adopted the boy Cuntarar; he honoured every wearer of the ash, giving double gifts even to one whose conduct was unworthy.

realization_account.text: The chieftain who adopted the boy Cuntarar; he honoured every wearer of the ash, giving double gifts even to one whose conduct was unworthy.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nārada

realization_account.text: In a former life the son of a maidservant who served Vedāntin sages, heard Hari's glories, had a vision of the Lord and was told he would see him again only in a later body (BhP 1.5.23-1.6.38); reborn as the celestial sage who wanders singing Hari's names with his vīṇā. BhP 1.3.8 counts him the third avatāra, who 'expounded the Sātvata tantra'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The divine sage and wandering devotee: teacher of Vyāsa (urging him to write the Bhāgavata), initiator of Dhruva with the twelve-syllable mantra, teacher of Prahlāda while still in his mother's womb, pupil of the Kumāras in the Nārada Purāṇa; one of the twelve mahājanas (BhP 6.3.20).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Headers: 8.13 'nāradaḥ kāṇvaḥ'; 9.104–105 'parvatanāradau kāṇvau'. Nāradīya Śikṣā ascription is the text's tradition (local text).
Confirmed as the traditional author of the Nāradasmṛti and the Nāradīya Śikṣā (both held locally).
Located: ChU 7.1.1-3 ('so 'haṃ bhagavo mantravid evāsmi nātmavit'). The epithet 'devarṣi' in the summary is from later tradition and is not in ChU 7.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of paramahamsa, kalisantarana, vasudeva, hayagriva, naradaparivrajaka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.
BhP 6.3.20 (mahājana), 4.8.54 (the twelve-syllable mantra given to Dhruva) located; NP pupil of the Kumāras (1.92) located.

alt_summary: Divine seer; in the Nārāyaṇīya he visits Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī and the White Island, where Nārāyaṇa shows himself and teaches him (12.321–339); he asks Asita Devala about the origin of beings (12.267) and relates the origin of Death (12.248–250); he tells Vālmīki the story of Rāma (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1). 'Among divine seers I am Nārada' (BhG 10.26).
The divine seer (devarṣi) who comes to Sanatkumāra learned in all the sciences yet 'a knower of mantras, not of the self', and in sorrow; he is taught the ladder to bhūman (ChU 7).
The divine seer (devarṣi) cited by Arjuna among those who declare Kṛṣṇa the supreme brahman (BhG 10.13); named by the Lord as his manifestation among the divine seers (10.26).

In the Saṃhitās, Nārada Kāṇva is seer of RV 8.13 and, with Parvata, of the Soma hymns 9.104–105; the Sāmaveda phonetic manual (Nāradīya Śikṣā) is ascribed to Nārada (the Vedic contributions only are recorded here).

U25 contribution: the divine sage to whom the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is attributed ('spoken by Nārada', NBS 84); in NBS 19 his own definition of devotion is that all acts are offered to the Lord and forgetting him is supreme anguish.

The divine sage; in the Nimbārka line he receives the teaching from the four Kumāras (Sanaka and brothers), who received it from Haṃsa (Viṣṇu as swan), and gives it to Nimbārka (Daśaślokī 6). Gauḍīyas hold Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura to be his incarnation.
notes: U05's contribution; the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is covered by U25.
alt_notes: Later traditions attach the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra and other works to a Nārada; this entry records only the Upaniṣadic figure.
Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
U25 contribution only; other units record the Upaniṣadic, epic and Purāṇic Nārada. Identity of the sūtra's author with those figures is the tradition's attribution, not asserted.
Contribution from U08 (Pāñcarātra role); other units record his other roles.

name: Nārada (SN 12.68)
summary: An elder who had seen 'the cessation of becoming is nibbāna' but was not yet an arahant — like one who sees water in a well without a rope (SN 12.68).

name: Narahari Cakravartī
summary: 18th-c. author of the Bhaktiratnākara.

name: Narahari Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Rāja Nighaṇṭu.

name: Narahari Sonār
summary: Goldsmith of Paṇḍharpūr, a devotee of Śiva who would not look at Viṭṭhala; measuring Viṭṭhala's waist blindfolded he felt Śiva's form, and saw Hari and Hara as one.

name: Narahari Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1324–1333 in maṭha lists

scholarly.text: his inscriptions at Śrīkūrmam are dated c. 1264–1293 CE

summary: Disciple of Madhva and his successor after Padmanābha Tīrtha in the Uttarādi line. The tradition says he had served as regent of the Kaliṅga kingdom and brought from its treasury the images of Rāma and Sītā (Mūla Rāma) that Madhva had asked for; inscriptions of his at Śrīkūrmam are used by scholars to date Madhva.
notes: The tradition also credits him with fostering Yakṣagāna — low confidence, not verified.

name: Naraharyānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl; sometimes confused with Tulsīdās's guru Narharidās.

name: Naranārāyaṇa
summary: Koch king (r. c. 1540–1586) at whose court Śaṅkaradeva spent his last years; commissioned the Guṇamālā and defended Śaṅkaradeva against brahmin accusers.

name: Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura
summary: Maithila scholar, author of the Tārābhaktisudhārṇava, a large digest on the worship of Tārā.

name: Narasiṃha Tīrtha (Adamaru)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Adamaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Narasiṃhagupta (Cukhulaka)
summary: Abhinavagupta's father and his first teacher (in grammar), named by Abhinavagupta in the Tantrāloka's closing chapter.

name: Nārāyaṇa
summary: In the Nārāyaṇīya the supreme Lord, also present as the ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa who with Nara performs austerity at Badarī (both born in Dharma's house, 12.332.19); he shows himself to Nārada in the White Island and teaches the fourfold form, his manifestations and the ekāntin dharma (12.321–339).

queries: e-text name search: Nārāyaṇa / Ādi-Nārāyaṇa (as teacher)
checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of mandalabrahmana, paramahamsaparivrajaka, turiyatita, tripadvibhuti-mahanarayana, yogatattva, in the roles the summary gives. Checked: 'sa hovāca nārāyaṇaḥ' (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa 1); Ādi-Nārāyaṇa (Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka, Turīyātīta); Mahāviṣṇu (Tripādvibhūti); Hṛṣīkeśa (Yogatattva 4). A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

checks.note: Located as described.

alt_summary: Viṣṇu as speaker: the Person in the solar orb who teaches Yājñavalkya (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa), Ādi-Nārāyaṇa who answers Brahmā on the paramahaṃsa and the avadhūta (Paramahaṃsaparivrājaka, Turīyātīta), Mahāviṣṇu of the Tripādvibhūti, and Hṛṣīkeśa who teaches Brahmā the Yogatattva.

name: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (author of the Camatkāracintāmaṇi)
summary: Author of the Camatkāracintāmaṇi on house results.

name: Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (Mānameyodaya)
notes: Identification with the author of the Nārāyaṇīyam is traditional; low confidence.
summary: Kerala scholar credited with the first (means-of-knowledge) part of the Mānameyodaya; traditionally identified with Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri of Melpattūr.

name: Nārāyaṇa (author of the Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa)
summary: Author of the Muhūrtamārtaṇḍa (1571).

name: Nārāyaṇa (author of Dīpikās)
summary: Commentator who glossed many Atharvan and minor Upaniṣads (e.g. the Nīlarudra); dates uncertain.

queries: Narayana Dipika Atharvana upanishads date Jacob
checks.note: Existence and works are confirmed: Dīpikās on Atharvan and minor Upaniṣads, in Jacob's 1916 edition and Lubin's Nīlarudra. His dates are unknown, as the entry says; Jacob notes that next to nothing is known of him. He quotes Śaṅkarānanda (wisdomlib), so he is later than Śaṅkarānanda.

name: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍita
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya
summary: Son of Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya and author of the Sumadhvavijaya, the principal life of Madhva, of the Maṇimañjarī and of the Yogadīpikā, a manual of worship and meditation.
notes: Authorship of all three works as named in their colophons in the raw_etexts corpus.

name: Nārāyaṇa (seer of the Puruṣa Sūkta)
summary: The seer of the Puruṣa Sūkta (RV 10.90) and of the Atharvaveda hymn on the making of man (AVŚ 10.2); Vaiṣṇava tradition identifies him with Nārāyaṇa, the Lord.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 10.90 'nārāyaṇaḥ'; AVŚ 10.2 and 19.6 'nārāyaṇaḥ'. Vaiṣṇava identification is the tradition's account.

name: Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha
summary: U09 contribution: author to whom the Sāṃkhyacandrikā on the SK is ascribed; several authors share the name, and identifications are uncertain.
notes: Whether he is the same as the devotional composer Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha is uncertain.
alt_summary: Author of the Bhāṭṭabhāṣāprakāśa.
U25 contribution: a Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha is credited with the Bhakticandrikā on the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra; several authors share the name and the identification is uncertain.

name: Nārāyaṇācārya (author of the Sadācāradīpikā)
summary: Author named in the colophon of the Mādhva conduct manual Sadācāradīpikā; date and identity not established.

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika, author of the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, which explains the Āgama's doctrine of Lord, souls and bonds and defends the Siddhānta's realism; father of Rāmakaṇṭha II.
alt_summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika who wrote the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, defending a dualist reading of the scripture; father of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.

name: Nārāyaṇatīrtha
summary: Author of two commentaries on the Yoga Sūtra, the Yogasiddhāntacandrikā and the Sūtrārthabodhinī; a devotee of Kṛṣṇa who interprets Yoga within Vedānta and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.
notes: Identity with Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha, composer of the Kṛṣṇalīlātaraṅgiṇī, is sometimes asserted — not verified.

name: Narendra
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Narharidās
summary: Tulsīdās's guru, from whom he heard the Rāma story as a boy at Sūkarakhet (Mānas 1.30); the Mānas's opening salutation to the guru as 'Hari in human form' (nara-rūpa hari) is read as a pun on his name.

name: Nāropa

tradition.text: 956–1040 or 1016–1100 (Tibetan histories differ)

scholarly.text: c. 1016–1100 (the later Tibetan reckoning, commonly adopted)

realization_account.text: A great scholar and gatekeeper of Nālandā (or Vikramaśīla) to whom a ḍākinī appeared as an old woman and asked whether he understood the words or the meaning; he left to seek Tilopa, underwent twelve great hardships and received the whole transmission; teacher of Marpa and of the six dharmas. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 20): As a universal monarch with his armies rules the continents and subcontinents, the yogin of the one taste of the innate rules saṃsāra: that is great bliss.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 20 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A great scholar and gatekeeper of Nālandā (or Vikramaśīla) to whom a ḍākinī appeared as an old woman and asked whether he understood the words or the meaning; he left to seek Tilopa, underwent twelve great hardships and received the whole transmission; teacher of Marpa and of the six dharmas.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Narottama Dāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Second-generation leader from Kheturi whose Bengali songs (Prema-bhakti-candrikā, Prārthanā) shaped Gauḍīya practice; organiser of the Kheturi festival that unified the Bengal community.

name: Narsinh Mehta
summary: Nāgar brahmin poet of Junāgaḍh (15th c.), the first great Gujarati poet: taunted by his sister-in-law, he fasted before a Śiva-liṅga in the forest until Śiva led him to see Kṛṣṇa's rāsa; thereafter he sang with low-caste devotees, and Kṛṣṇa rescued him in the Hāramālā, Māmeruṃ and Huṇḍī episodes. Author of 'Vaiṣṇava jana to'.

realization_account.text: Śiva showed him the rāsa-līlā; Kṛṣṇa placed a garland on him before the king.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Naṭanānandanātha
summary: Commentator on the Kāmakalāvilāsa (Cidvallī).

name: Nāthamuni
summary: First ācārya of the Śrīvaiṣṇava lineage (after Nammāḻvār), of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumannārkōyil). The tradition says he recovered and arranged the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham, set its hymns to music for temple recitation, and taught yoga; his works on logic and yoga are lost.

tradition.text: 824–924 CE in one commonly cited traditional reckoning; hagiographies give an extremely long life

realization_account.text: Hearing ten verses of the Tiruvāymoḻi ending 'these ten out of a thousand', he sought the rest at Kurukūr, recited Madhurakavi's Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu twelve thousand times in yogic absorption, and received from Nammāḻvār in vision the whole four thousand hymns and their meaning.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Na Chanshi 那禪師 and Huiman 慧滿
summary: Huike's disciples who carried the four-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra as the essence of mind (Xu gaoseng zhuan juan 16).

name: N. C. Lahiri
summary: Calcutta astronomer-almanac maker whose ayanāṃśa (the Citrāpakṣa, with Spica at 180°) was adopted for the Indian national ephemeris after the Calendar Reform Committee of the 1950s.

name: Nēca Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A weaver who made loincloths and sacred threads for devotees.

realization_account.text: A weaver who made loincloths and sacred threads for devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Niṉṟacīr Neṭumāṟa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. The Pāṇṭiya king, a patron of the Jains, whose burning fever Campantar cured with sacred ash; his hunched back was straightened and he turned Śaiva; he won the battle of Nelvēli.

realization_account.text: The Pāṇṭiya king, a patron of the Jains, whose burning fever Campantar cured with sacred ash; his hunched back was straightened and he turned Śaiva; he won the battle of Nelvēli.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nema Bhārgava
summary: Seer of RV 8.100.1–3, 6–12, in which 'Nema says Indra does not exist — who has seen him? whom shall we praise?', whereupon Indra answers 'here I am, singer, see me' (8.100.3–4).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 1–3, 6–12 Nema Bhārgava, 4–5 Indra — confirmed; 8.100.3–4 located.

name: Nemicandra Siddhāntacakravartin
summary: Digambara master of the karma scriptures ('emperor of the siddhānta') who wrote the Gommaṭasāra, Labdhisāra and Trilokasāra for the minister Cāmuṇḍarāya.
alt_summary: Digambara ācārya of Karnataka, author of the Gommaṭasāra (for the general Cāmuṇḍarāya, who erected the Bāhubali colossus at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa), the Labdhisāra, the Trilokasāra and (by tradition) the Dravyasaṃgraha.
notes: Some scholars assign the Dravyasaṃgraha to a different Nemicandra (Siddhāntideva).

name: Neminātha (Ariṣṭanemi)
summary: The twenty-second Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the conch, son of Samudravijaya and Śivā of the Yādava (Hari) clan, born at Śauryapura, cousin of Kṛṣṇa. On the way to his wedding with Rājīmatī he heard the cries of animals penned for the feast, freed them and renounced; Rājīmatī too became a nun and steadied his brother Rathanemi in his vows (Uttarādhyayana 22). He attained omniscience and nirvāṇa on Mount Girnār (Ujjayanta / Raivataka). His body is described as dark.

tradition.text: the twenty-second Jina, preceding Pārśva by 84,000 years in the traditional chronology

realization_account.text: He renounced on seeing the animals to be killed for his own wedding feast and attained omniscience on Girnār.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Some scholars have argued for a historical core to Nemi; most treat him as legendary.

name: Neten Dangma Lhungyal (gnas brtan ldang ma lhun rgyal)
summary: Recovered the Vima Nyingthig texts concealed by Nyang Tingdzin Zangpo and passed them to Chetsün Senge Wangchuk.

name: Neusurpa Yeshe Bar
summary: Kadam master of the lamrim line, disciple of Gönpawa.

name: Ngawang Lodrö Drakpa (ngag dbang blo gros grags pa)
summary: Twentieth-century Jonang master of Dzamthang and author of the history of the Jonang tradition.

name: Ngendzong Repa
summary: A disciple of Milarepa associated with an early collection of his songs and teachings (the Ngendzong hearing lineage).

name: Ngok Chöku Dorje

realization_account.text: Received from Marpa the explanation (bshad pa) of the tantras; Milarepa came to him with the forged letter.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: One of Marpa's four principal disciples ('the four pillars'), holder of the explanatory lineage of the tantras (especially Hevajra); founder of the Ngok tradition of the Marpa Kagyu.

name: Ngok Lekpai Sherab
summary: Disciple of Atiśa who founded Sangphu Neuthok monastery (1073), later the great Kadam centre of scholastic learning.

name: Ngok Loden Sherab
summary: Translator of the Pramāṇaviniścaya, Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra and the Maitreya texts, founder of the Sangphu scholastic tradition of epistemology and Madhyamaka.
notes: Contribution of U41.
alt_summary: Tibetan translator (1059-1109) who translated the Ratnagotravibhāga with Sajjana and taught it in an 'analytic' tradition reading buddha-nature as emptiness, a non-affirming negation.
alt_notes: works = translation.

name: Ngorchen Könchog Lhündrub
summary: Abbot of Ngor, author of the standard Lamdre manuals Beautiful Ornament of the Three Visions and Beautiful Ornament of the Three Continua.

name: Ngorchen Kunga Zangpo
summary: Founder of Ngor Evaṃ Chöden (1429) and of the Ngor sub-school; great upholder of the Lamdre and of the Vinaya; he travelled three times to Mustang.
alt_names: ngor chen kun dga' bzang po

name: Nidāgha
summary: Disciple of Ṛbhu in the Varāha, Tejobindu, Mahā and Annapūrṇā Upaniṣads; asks about the seven stages (bhūmikā) and about yoga; named among the paramahaṃsas and among rudrākṣa-wearing sages.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of varaha, tejobindu, maha, annapurna, rudraksajabala, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
VP 2.15.4 'tasya śiṣyo nidāgho 'bhūt pulastyatanayaḥ' and 2.15.6 'devikāyās taṭe vīranagaraṃ nāma vai puram' verified.
VP 2.15.4 'tasya śiṣyo nidāgho 'bhūt pulastyatanayaḥ' located.

alt_summary: Son of Pulastya and disciple of Ṛbhu, who lived at Vīranagara on the Devikā; Ṛbhu returns twice in disguise to test and teach him (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16); the recipient of the Ṛbhu Gītā.
Pulastya's son and Ṛbhu's disciple, visited by his teacher twice in disguise and brought to see that there is no difference between 'king' and 'elephant', 'I' and 'you' (VP 2.15-16).

name: Niguma
summary: Kashmiri yoginī (c. 10th–11th c.), in Tibetan accounts Nāropa's sister or consort, who taught Khyungpo Naljor the six dharmas that bear her name and the mahāmudrā of the 'amulet box'; source of the Shangpa Kagyu.
notes: Her 'six dharmas' and the Shangpa details belong mainly to U46.

name: Niguṇa

realization_account.text: A lazy, 'qualityless' son of a householder, taught that his idleness could be the path. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 57): Having shown the experiences like waves on water, enter conduct by means; by the true guru's instruction the concepts of desire and hatred are made into their own nature.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 57 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A lazy, 'qualityless' son of a householder, taught that his idleness could be the path.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Nijaguṇa Śivayōgi
summary: Vīraśaiva yogin and author of the Kannada encyclopaedia Vivekacintāmaṇi and of the songs of the Kaivalya Paddhati.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Bhagavantabhāskara (the Mayūkhas).

checks.note: Confirmed: Kane places him c. 1610–1645; author of the Bhagavantabhāskara (Mayūkhas).

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara
summary: Seventeenth-century Mahārāṣṭrian scholar in Vārāṇasī, famous for his Mahābhārata commentary; in U06 the commentator on the Gaṇeśa Gītā.

checks.note: Confirmed (Deshastha; late 17th c.).
c. 1650-1700, Vārāṇasī; commentary on the Mahābhārata and on the Gaṇeśa Gītā (1693).

alt_summary: Maharashtrian scholar at Vārāṇasī, author of the Bhāratabhāvadīpa, the commentary on the whole Mahābhārata that fixed the vulgate text.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Daivajña
summary: Son of Ananta; author of the Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī (1587), the standard Tājika text; associated by tradition with the court of Akbar.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita
summary: 17th-c. poet and minister at Madurai, grand-nephew of Appayya Dīkṣita, author of the Ānandasāgarastava to Mīnākṣī.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Kriyāsāra, which presents Śrīkaṇṭha's commentary as Vīraśaiva doctrine.
alt_summary: Author of the Sanskrit Vīraśaiva Kriyāsāra.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī
summary: Kerala astronomer (a Somayājin Nambūtiri), author of the Tantrasaṅgraha (1500) and a large commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya; pupil of Dāmodara, son of Parameśvara.

name: Nīlāmbike
summary: Basava's wife and a vacanakāra in whose vacanas Basava appears as her spiritual guide.

name: Nīlamegha
summary: Author of the Tantrayuktivicāra.

name: Niḷobā
summary: 17th–18th c. Vārkarī poet of Pimpaḷner who received Tukārām's grace in a dream after Tukārām's departure; regarded as Tukārām's spiritual successor in one line.

name: Nimbārka (Nimbāditya, Niyamānanda)
summary: Founder of the Dvaitādvaita school; author of the Vedāntapārijātasaurabha and the Daśaślokī; taught natural difference-and-non-difference, Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā as Brahman, and the five means culminating in surrender.

realization_account.text: An incarnation of the Sudarśana discus, born to Aruṇa and Jayantī in the Telugu country; named Nimbārka ('sun on the nimba tree') because he held the sun on a neem tree so that a visiting ascetic could eat before sunset; taught by Nārada on Govardhana.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

tradition.text: a former age (tradition gives very early dates)

scholarly.text: variously 7th–13th c. CE; many place him c. 12th–13th c.

name: Nimi, king of Videha
summary: Speaker: seven tastes, counting alkali (Ca Sū 26.8); in later tradition the author of a lost tantra of eye and head disease.
notes: Speaker ref checked; the lost tantra is recalled only.

name: Sant Niranjan Dass
summary: Head of Dera Sachkhand Ballan under whom the Ravidassia Dharam and the Amritbāṇī were declared (2010).

name: Nirmaḷā
summary: Sister of Cokhāmeḷā and wife of Bankā; a few abhaṅgas.

name: Niṣkriyānandanātha
summary: Krama master named in Anantaśaktipāda's commentary on the Vātūlanāthasūtra as having received instruction from the siddhas of Gandhamādana; the Chummāsaṅketaprakāśa is ascribed to him.

name: Nityānanda (Nitāi, Avadhūta)
summary: Wandering avadhūta from Ekacakrā who joined Caitanya at Navadvīpa and led the mission in Bengal; held to be Balarāma; his wives Vasudhā and Jāhnavā and son Vīrabhadra continued his line (Khaḍadaha).

realization_account.text: Balarāma (Kṛṣṇa's brother) appearing as Caitanya's first expansion; famed for delivering the sinners Jagāi and Mādhāi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Nityanātha
summary: Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): author of the five-part Rasaratnākara, who says he gathered only what he learnt from his guru's mouth and experienced himself (Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.22) and named his work with the claim 'what is elsewhere is here; what is here is nowhere else' (1.25).
alt_summary: U28 contribution: named among the Mahāsiddhas of HYP 1.7; the text says these Siddhas broke the staff of time by the power of haṭha and roam the universe (HYP 1.9).
Siddha named in the Haṭhapradīpikā's list (1.7); a Nityanātha is credited with alchemical and magical works (Rasaratnākara, Kāmaratna) and, in some manuscripts, with the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati.
notes: Whether these are one person is uncertain.

name: Niutou Farong 牛頭法融
summary: Founder of the Oxhead school on Mount Niutou; in the tradition's account visited by Daoxin, after which birds no longer brought him flowers. Credited with the Xinming and the Jueguan lun.

name: Niutou Zhiwei 牛頭智威
summary: Oxhead master in the lineage from Farong.

name: Nivṛttināth
summary: Eldest of the four sibling-saints and Jñāneśvar's guru; initiated into the Nāth path by Gahinīnāth, he passed it to Jñāneśvar and bade him write the Jñāneśvarī and then an independent work (Amṛtānubhava). His own abhaṅgas are few. Samādhi at Tryambakeśvar.

name: Nivṛttināth
summary: Elder brother and guru of Jñāneśvar, initiated in the Nāth line by Gahinīnāth; Jñāneśvar calls himself 'Nivṛtti's servant' (nivṛttidāsu) throughout the Jñāneśvarī. Abhaṅgas are ascribed to him.

tradition.text: 1273–1297 (tradition)

name: Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī (author of the Subodhinī)
summary: Commentator on the Vedāntasāra (Subodhinī). Distinct from Narasiṃha Sarasvatī of the Datta tradition.

name: Nṛsiṃhānandanātha
summary: Bhāskararāya's guru, praised at the opening of the Saubhāgyabhāskara and the Varivasyārahasya as the teacher of the vidyās and mantras.

name: Nṛsiṃhāśrama
summary: 16th-c. Advaitin of the Vivaraṇa line, author of the Vedāntatattvaviveka, the Advaitadīpikā and the Bhedadhikkāra.

name: Nupchen Sangye Yeshe (gnubs chen sangs rgyas ye shes)
summary: Principal early holder of Anuyoga and author of the Samten Migdrön; by tradition he protected the tantric community during Langdarma's persecution by displaying wrathful powers before the king.

tradition.text: disciple of Padmasambhava, living through the persecution

name: Nuliya Candayya
summary: The rope-maker śaraṇa remembered for insisting that kāyaka is not to be interrupted even for worship.

name: Nyabön Kunga Pal (nya dbon kun dga' dpal)
summary: A student of Dolpopa who upheld the other-emptiness teaching and taught widely in central Tibet.

name: Nyak Jñānakumāra (gnyags jñānakumāra)
summary: Translator of the royal period, disciple of Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra, a principal early holder of the Mahāyoga and Anuyoga transmissions and co-translator of the Guhyagarbha.

name: Nyamme Sherab Gyaltsen (mnyam med shes rab rgyal mtshan)
summary: Founder of Menri monastery (1405), the principal seat of Yungdrung Bön monasticism.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Nyanaponika Thera
summary: German-born Sri Lankan monk (1901–1994), co-founder of the Buddhist Publication Society, who trained in the Mahāsi method and presented satipaṭṭhāna as 'bare attention' in The Heart of Buddhist Meditation.

name: Nyang Tingdzin Zangpo (myang ting 'dzin bzang po)
summary: Monk-minister of Trisong Detsen's court and disciple of Vimalamitra who concealed the Vima Nyingthig texts at Zhwa'i Lhakhang; by tradition attained the rainbow body.

name: Nyangral Nyima Özer (nyang ral nyi ma 'od zer)
summary: The first of the five 'king' treasure revealers; revealed the Kagye Deshek Düpa, the Copper Island biography of Padmasambhava, and wrote an early history of the Dharma.

tradition.text: an incarnation of Trisong Detsen

name: Nyoshin
summary: Shinran's grandson (son of Zenran), counted second head of Honganji by Kakunyo's reckoning.

name: Nyoshul Lungtok Tenpai Nyima (smyo shul lung rtogs bstan pa'i nyi ma)
summary: Patrul Rinpoche's principal Dzogchen disciple.

name: Ogyen Trinley Dorje (recognized as seventeenth Karmapa by one party)
summary: One of two claimants recognized as the seventeenth Karmapa (recognized by the Tai Situpa and endorsed by the Dalai Lama); left Tibet in 2000.

name: Orgyen Lingpa (o rgyan gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer of the Pema Kathang (1352) and the Katang Denga (five chronicles).

name: Orgyenpa Rinchen Pal
alt_names: o rgyan pa rin chen dpal
summary: Drukpa master, disciple of Götsangpa, famous for his journey to Oḍḍiyāna and the 'approach and accomplishment of the three vajras' received there; teacher of the 3rd Karmapa, whom (by the tradition's account) he recognized as the rebirth of Karma Pakshi.

name: Ouyi Zhixu
summary: Late-Ming master of Tiantai, Vinaya and Pure Land, one of the four great masters, who made faith, vow and practice (holding the name) the three provisions for birth; ninth patriarch in the later list.

name: Pa-Auk Sayadaw
summary: Burmese abbot of Pa-Auk Forest Monastery (Bhaddanta Āciṇṇa, b. 1934), teacher of the full Visuddhimagga system of calm and insight.

name: Pabongkha Dechen Nyingpo
summary: Influential 20th-c. Gelug teacher whose 1921 lamrim teaching became Liberation in the Palm of Your Hand; his exclusive devotion to a protector deity is controversial within the Gelug.
alt_names: pha bong kha bde chen snying po

name: Pacari

realization_account.text: A pastry-maker who offered his cakes to Avalokiteśvara; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 59): Look nowhere; look in the middle; supreme joy and the joy of cessation are great bliss; having spoken the power of the mantra's secret, the signs of yoga should be made nine(?).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 59 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A pastry-maker who offered his cakes to Avalokiteśvara; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. The last line is not understood.

name: Padampa Sangye (pha dam pa sangs rgyas)

realization_account.text: A siddha who studied with a great number of Indian masters (fifty-four in one account); some Tibetan accounts identify him with earlier Indian figures (low confidence; not recorded here).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: South Indian siddha who made several visits to Tibet (five or seven in different accounts), founded the Pacification (zhi byed) tradition, gave instructions to Machig Labdrön that became the 'father' strand of Chöd, and spent his last years at Dingri, where he gave his Hundred Verses to the people of Dingri.

name: Padmanābha Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1317–1324 in maṭha lists

summary: Disciple of Madhva and first pontiff after him in the line that became the Uttarādi Maṭha; author of the Sattarkadīpāvalī (on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya) and Nyāyaratnāvalī (on the Anuvyākhyāna). In the tradition's account he had been a learned opponent (named Śobhana Bhaṭṭa) before becoming Madhva's disciple.
notes: Former name, pontificate dates and brindāvana location recalled at low confidence.

name: Padmanandi (author of the Pañcaviṃśatikā)
summary: Digambara author of the Padmanandi-pañcaviṃśatikā.

name: Padmapāda
summary: Senior disciple of Śaṅkara, author of the Pañcapādikā, root of the Vivaraṇa school; in the tradition's account named 'lotus-foot' because lotuses sprang up under his feet when he crossed the Gaṅgā at his guru's call, and first head of the Govardhana maṭha at Purī.

name: Padmaprabha
summary: The sixth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the red lotus. Parents: Dhara (Śrīdhara) and Susīmā. Born at Kauśāmbī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as red in colour.

tradition.text: the sixth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Padmaprabha Maladhārideva
summary: Commentator on the Niyamasāra (Tātparyavṛtti).

name: Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche)
summary: The 'Lotus-born', the second Buddha of the Nyingma. Tradition: born from a lotus on Lake Dhanakośa in Oḍḍiyāna, adopted by King Indrabhūti, a renunciant and charnel-ground yogin who received teachings from many masters, attained immortality with Mandāravā in the Māratika cave, was invited to Tibet by Trisong Detsen on Śāntarakṣita's advice, subdued the spirits obstructing Samye, gave the empowerments of the Eight Herukas to his disciples, concealed treasures for future times with Yeshe Tsogyal, and departed for the land of the rākṣasas, where he dwells on the Copper-Coloured Mountain. Scholarly: an 8th-c. Indian tantric master whose brief stay in Tibet is recorded in early sources; his hagiography grows from the 12th c. treasures.

tradition.text: born miraculously; active in Tibet in Trisong Detsen's reign, when Samye was founded (c. 779)

realization_account.text: Attained the vidyādhara level of immortality and the rainbow body of great transference; appears in eight manifestations.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Padmavajra
summary: Author of the Guhyasiddhi, first of the seven siddhi texts; possibly the same as Saroruha(vajra), author of a Hevajra sādhana.

name: Padmāvatī (wife of Jayadeva)
summary: Temple dancer dedicated to Jagannātha and wife of Jayadeva in the hagiographies; the Gīta Govinda calls its poet 'emperor of the dancers at Padmāvatī's feet' (GG 1.2), read by tradition as referring to her.

realization_account.text: Given to Jayadeva by her father at Jagannātha's command; her fidelity was tested when a queen told her falsely that Jayadeva had died, and she fell dead, to be revived by his singing.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Padmāvatī
summary: Woman disciple of Rāmānanda named among the twelve in the Bhaktamāl.
notes: Not the Jain goddess Padmāvatī.

name: Paesi (Pradeśin)
summary: King of Śvetavikā who doubted the soul, tested it by experiments on condemned criminals, and was convinced by Keśin that the soul is distinct from the body (Rājapraśnīya); reborn as the god Sūryābha.
notes: Parallels King Pāyāsi of the Pali Pāyāsi Sutta (DN 23).
alt_summary: King of Seyaviyā in the Jain Rājapraśnīya who held that soul and body are the same and tested it on criminals; converted by the monk Kesi, poisoned by his queen, reborn as the god Sūriyābha.

name: Pāglā Kānāi
summary: Bāul-Fakir singer-poet of Jhenaidah famed for extempore songs and song-debates (kabigān style).

name: Paila
summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Ṛgveda (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.21; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4) and divided it among his own pupils, from whom the Ṛgveda śākhās descend.

checks.note: Located: 'tatrargvedadharaḥ pailaḥ' (Bhāgavata 1.4.21); Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4.8 and 3.4.16 (Paila divides the Ṛgveda-tree, giving Saṃhitās to Indrapramiti and Bāṣkala).

name: Paiṅgala
summary: Disciple who serves Yājñavalkya for twelve years and then asks about kaivalya (Paiṅgala Upaniṣad).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of paingala, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Paiṅgya
summary: Taught 'breath is brahman' with the ordering of the senses (KauU 2.2).

checks.note: Located: KauU 2.2 ('prāṇo brahmeti ha smāha paiṅgyaḥ').

name: Paippalādi
summary: Questioner of Jābāli in the Jābāli Upaniṣad (a descendant or pupil of Pippalāda by name).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabali, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Pakṣadhara Miśra
summary: Mithilā Naiyāyika, also called Jayadeva, author of the Āloka commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi.
notes: Tradition makes him the Mithilā master whom Raghunātha Śiromaṇi challenged (low confidence).

name: Pakudha Kaccāyana
summary: One of the six famous teachers. DN 2 reports his doctrine of seven bodies (kāya) — earth, water, fire, air, pleasure, pain and the soul — unmade, barren, firm as a pillar, unmoving, not affecting one another, so that one who cuts off a head with a sharp sword takes no life: the sword only passes through the space between the seven bodies.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: Doctrine reported_by_opponent. The Pali commentary's report that he avoided cold water is recalled with low confidence. His seven bodies reappear merged with niyati in Ja 545 and in the fourth 'negation' of MN 76.

name: Pālakāpya
summary: The sage of elephant medicine (Hastyāyurveda).

name: Paldarbum
summary: A woman disciple of Milarepa to whom, in the Hundred Thousand Songs, he sings a famous song on meditation using the images of sky, sun and moon, mountain, ocean and mind.

name: Pālkuriki Sōmanātha
summary: Telugu and Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-scholar, author of the Basava Purāṇamu, the Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra and the Vṛṣādhipa Śatakamu.

name: Paltū Sāhib
summary: Sant of Ayodhyā (born near Jalālpur), fierce critic of hypocrisy and exponent of the inner Name and sound; a Sant Mat authority.

name: Pālyakīrti (Śākaṭāyana)
summary: Yāpanīya Jain grammarian who wrote under the name Śākaṭāyana.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: a Yāpanīya Jain grammarian of the 9th c. under Amoghavarṣa (Wisdomlib).

name: Pāmbāṭṭi (Pāmpāṭṭic cittar)
summary: The 'snake-charmer Siddhar', whose songs with the refrain 'dance, O snake!' teach the inner ascent and scorn caste, learning and ritual. The tradition says he was a snake-catcher seeking a jewelled serpent in the hills when a Siddhar (usually Caṭṭaimuṉi) showed him that the true serpent lies coiled within.
places: Caṅkaraṉkōyil — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The meeting with Caṭṭaimuṉi is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Pampa (Ādikavi)
summary: 10th-c. Kannada poet, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjunavijaya.

name: Panaha

realization_account.text: A bootmaker; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 79): Contemplating the meaning of the innate essence, as one contemplates so one realizes; therefore it abides at ease and all one wishes arises freely.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 79 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A bootmaker; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Pañcādhikaraṇa
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher known from the Yuktidīpikā: the organs are elemental (bhautika); the instrument is by nature empty, like a deserted village or dry river bed, its knowledges coming from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from another'; a permanent conveying (ātivāhika) subtle body enters the embryo; knowledge is natural (at the same time as the principles, innate, or flowing) or acquired. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Pañcaśikha
summary: Pupil of Āsuri by whom 'the doctrine was expanded' (SK 70). In the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma he teaches King Janaka (Janadeva) of Mithilā. Sayings ascribed to him are quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 1.4, 1.25, 1.36, 2.13, as identified by Vācaspati Miśra) and in the Tattvakaumudī on SK 2; the Sāṃkhya Sūtra cites his views by name (5.32, 6.68).
notes: Mahābhārata chapter (Śāntiparvan, c. 12.211–212 in the critical edition) recalled, not checked.

checks.note: Located as described.

alt_summary: In the Mokṣadharma, Pañcaśikha 'Kāpileya' (so called because the brāhmaṇī Kapilā nursed him), 'Āsuri's first disciple', comes to Mithilā and so impresses king Janadeva Janaka that he leaves a hundred teachers to follow him (12.211.6–18); he teaches the Sāṃkhya discrimination (12.211–212); Sulabhā refers to Janaka's having learned from him (12.308).
alt_notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Panchen Lobsang Chökyi Gyaltsen
summary: Abbot of Tashi Lhunpo and teacher of the Fifth Dalai Lama, the first to bear the title Panchen Lama (counted as the First or, counting back to Khedrup Je, the Fourth); author of the Gelug Mahāmudrā root text, the Offering to the Spiritual Master and the Easy Path.
alt_names: paṇ chen blo bzang chos kyi rgyal mtshan

name: Panchen Lobsang Yeshe
summary: Second (or Fifth) Panchen Lama, author of the Swift Path lamrim.

name: Panchen Sönam Drakpa
summary: Author of the textbooks of Drepung Loseling and Ganden Shartse colleges; teacher of the Third Dalai Lama.

name: Paṇḍitārādhya (of the five ācāryas)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Śrīśaila pīṭha.

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Mallikārjuna liṅga at Śrīśaila and seat name Sūrya-siṃhāsana: low confidence. Distinct entry from the historical Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya (tch:mallikarjuna-panditaradhya); some accounts connect them.

name: Pāṇḍu
summary: Father of the Pāṇḍavas, named in 'the sons of Pāṇḍu' (1.1, 1.3) and in Arjuna's epithet Pāṇḍava (1.14, 1.20).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.1, 1.3, 1.14, 1.20.

name: Pāṇini
summary: Author of the Aṣṭādhyāyī, the grammar that fixed classical Sanskrit and described the Vedic language; Patañjali calls him 'Dākṣīputra', son of Dākṣī. He names ten predecessors (Āpiśali, Kāśyapa, Gārgya, Gālava, Cākravarmaṇa, Bhāradvāja, Śākaṭāyana, Śākalya, Senaka, Sphoṭāyana).

tradition.text: a sage of old who received the phoneme list from Śiva

realization_account.text: After austerities he received the fourteen phoneme-sūtras from Maheśvara (Śiva), who sounded them on his drum; from them he proclaimed the whole of grammar (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 56–57; Nandikeśvara-kāśikā). A later story (Kathāsaritsāgara) makes him a dull pupil of Varṣa who won Śiva's grace by tapas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

queries: local Aṣṭādhyāyī rules naming predecessors; 'dākṣīputrasya pāṇineḥ' in the Mahābhāṣya
checks.note: The ten predecessors are all text-located in the Aṣṭādhyāyī: Āpiśali 6.1.92, Kāśyapa 1.2.25, Gārgya 7.3.99, Gālava 7.1.74, Cākravarmaṇa 6.1.130, Bhāradvāja 7.2.63, Śākaṭāyana 3.4.111, Śākalya 1.1.16, Senaka 5.4.112 ('gireś ca senakasya' in the eBhāratī Aṣṭādhyāyī; the GRETIL sūtra-text drops 'senakasya', but the Kāśikā glosses 'senakasya ācāryasya matena'), and Sphoṭāyana 6.1.123. The Mahābhāṣya has 'sarve sarvapadādeśā dākṣīputrasya pāṇineḥ'. The tradition's account is at PŚ 56–57 (text-located). The scholarly date of 5th–4th c. BCE is standard; Wikipedia 'Yāska' puts Pāṇini c. 5th c. BCE.

name: Pāñju Śāh
summary: Fakir-Bāul poet of Jhenaidah whose songs of mārephat (gnosis) and the body are widely sung.

name: Paṅkaja

realization_account.text: A brahmin 'born of a lotus' who worshipped Avalokiteśvara and was taught by Nāgārjuna. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 51): As long as one is not held by a guru and does not realize, a wish-fulfilling jewel and a glass bead are the same; held by the guru and by realization, they are as the light of sun and moon to a firefly.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 51 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A brahmin 'born of a lotus' who worshipped Avalokiteśvara and was taught by Nāgārjuna.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Pāragārgya
summary: Number 7 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Parahita
notes: Attribution of D3868 to Parahita from memory; to check.
summary: Kashmiri scholar credited with a commentary on the Śūnyatāsaptati (D3868) and with work on Madhyamaka texts in the 11th century.

name: Paramānanddās
summary: Aṣṭachāp poet of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' longing (Paramānandsāgar).

name: Paramārtha
summary: Indian translator in southern China whose versions of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha and related works founded the Shelun school; he taught a ninth, 'stainless' consciousness (amalavijñāna) identical with suchness, and wrote the Life of Vasubandhu.
notes: Contribution of U41; U39 and U54 also emit this id.
alt_summary: Indian monk (499-569) in southern China who translated Yogācāra and buddha-nature works (Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Foxing lun, and — by attribution — the Awakening of Faith).
Indian translator in China (499–569). This unit records his translation of the Kośa (563–567), of Vasumitra's doxography, of a Saṃmitīya Vinaya treatise, and his Life of Vasubandhu.

Indian Buddhist monk-translator who reached China in 546. Besides Yogācāra works he translated the Sāṃkhya Kārikā with a commentary (Jin qishi lun) and wrote a Life of Vasubandhu that tells of the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa's debate with Buddhamitra.

name: Paramārthasamudgata
summary: The bodhisattva who, in Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7, asks the intent of 'all dharmas lack own-being' and hears the three naturelessnesses and the three turnings.

name: Ṛṣiputra Parameśvara
summary: Kerala scholar credited with the Gopālikā commentary on Maṇḍana's Sphoṭasiddhi.
notes: Several Kerala scholars named Parameśvara are known; the identification needs checking.

name: Parameśvara (of Vaṭaśśeri)
summary: Kerala astronomer who observed for over fifty years and composed the Dṛggaṇita (1431), the Goladīpikā and commentaries on the Āryabhaṭīya and Sūrya Siddhānta.

name: Pāramiti (Pramiti)
summary: Indian monk to whom the Chinese Śūraṅgama Sūtra (T945) is attributed as translator, at Guangzhou in 705; known only from the tradition's account.

tradition.text: translation in 705 CE

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (guru of Meykaṇṭār)
summary: The sage from Kailāsa who, in the tradition's account, taught the child Meykaṇṭār; last of the 'inner' lineage (akaccantāṉam) of Nandi, Sanatkumāra and Satyajñānadarśin.
notes: Distinct from Parañcōti Muṉivar, author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam (tch:parancoti-tiruvilaiyatal).

name: Parañcōti Muṉivar (author of the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam)
summary: Author of the Tamil Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam on Śiva's sixty-four sports at Madurai.

name: Parāśara
summary: Grandson of Vasiṣṭha and father of Vyāsa; the speaker of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa to Maitreya, which he received from Vasiṣṭha and Pulastya after renouncing his rite to burn the rākṣasas (VP 1.1.12-26).

checks.note: Headers: 'parāśaraḥ śāktyaḥ' for 1.65–73. Son of Śakti, grandson of Vasiṣṭha, father of Vyāsa (web); narrator of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa ('śrīparāśara uvāca' in the local text).
Confirmed: the Parāśarasmṛti assigns 'pārāśarāḥ' dharmas to the Kali age (1.24, text-located); he is also named at YājñS 1.5.
Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text

checks.note: VP 1.1.12-26 located: Vasiṣṭha stops Parāśara's rite to burn the rākṣasas (1.1.15-20) and grants a boon (1.1.25).

alt_summary: Parāśara Śāktya, seer of RV 1.65–73 (hymns to Agni). The tradition makes him the son of Śakti and grandson of Vasiṣṭha, father of Vyāsa, and the narrator of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (the Vedic contribution is recorded here).
Seer, father of Vyāsa; he instructs king Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (12.279–287).

For jyotiṣa, the seer who teaches the horā to Maitreya in the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra (tradition's account; the text is a late compilation by scholarly account). Varāhamihira already cites Parāśara among earlier authorities (BJ 12.2 on the mālā and sarpa yogas); the commentators take 'Śaktipūrva' in BJ 7.1 as Parāśara, Śakti's son.
U02 contribution: the sage, father of Vyāsa, to whom the Parāśarasmṛti — the code for the Kali age — is ascribed.
In U06's texts: the sage who instructs King Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.279-287).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).
alt_notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Parāśara (disciple of Ātreya)
summary: One of Ātreya's six disciples, each of whom composed his own tantra and read it to Ātreya and the sages (Ca Sū 1.31-33).
notes: Whether this is the same person as the homonymous sage of other traditions is not settled; kept separate.

name: Parāśara Bhaṭṭar
summary: Son of Kūreśa, named by Rāmānuja in fulfilment of Yāmuna's wish; successor at Śrīraṅgam after Embār; author of the Śrīraṅgarājastava, Śrīguṇaratnakośa, Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa and Aṣṭaślokī; the tradition says he won over the Advaitin Mādhava (Nañjīyar).

checks.note: Confirmed (12th c.).

alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, son of Kūrattāḻvāṉ, author of the Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa on the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

name: Pāraskara
summary: Author by tradition of the White Yajurveda Gṛhyasūtra.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed as the traditional author of the Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra (title of the text).

name: Paraśurāma (Jāmadagnya Bhārgava)
summary: The avatāra-sage, son of Jamadagni and Reṇukā, who in the Śrīvidyā tradition is the chief disciple of Mahādeva and author of the Kalpasūtra, and who in the Tripurā Rahasya receives the teaching of Tripurā from Dattātreya.
notes: PKS colophon (10.85) names Paraśurāma, chief disciple of Mahādeva (checked).

name: Paraśurāma Devācārya
summary: Disciple of Harivyāsadeva associated with the Nimbārka seat at Salemabad (Rajasthan).

name: Pārīkṣi Maudgalya
summary: Speaker: the person and his diseases are born of the self, the conscious principle being the cause (Ca Sū 25.8-9).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Parīkṣit
summary: Grandson of Arjuna, protected in the womb by Kṛṣṇa; cursed to die in seven days, he renounced his kingdom and sat in prāyopaveśa on the Gaṅgā (BhP 1.19), where he heard the Bhāgavata from Śuka; the model hearer (śravaṇa) of the Purāṇa. He also subdued Kali and assigned him five places (BhP 1.17).

checks.note: BhP 1.19.7 (prāyopaveśa on the Gaṅgā) and 1.17.38-40 (Kali's five places) located.

name: Parimēlaḻakar
summary: Author of the most celebrated commentary on the Tirukkuṟaḷ (and on the Paripāṭal); a Vaiṣṇava brahmin of Kāñcīpuram by tradition.
notes: Vaiṣṇava affiliation is traditional; the lineage ids are approximate.

name: Paritoṣa Miśra
summary: Author of the Ajitā commentary on the Tantravārttika.

name: Pārśva (Pārśvanātha)
summary: The twenty-third Tīrthaṅkara, emblem the serpent, son of King Aśvasena and Queen Vāmā of Vārāṇasī. As a prince he rescued a pair of serpents burning in the fire of the ascetic Kamaṭha; reborn as Dharaṇendra and Padmāvatī, they later shielded him with their hoods when Kamaṭha, reborn as the god Meghamālin, assailed his meditation with storm and flood. He taught the fourfold restraint (cāujjāma: non-violence, truth, not stealing, non-possession) and his followers wore garments; he lived a hundred years and attained nirvāṇa on Sammeda Śikhara (Pārasnāth hill). Mahāvīra's parents were followers of his teaching, and his followers (such as Keśin) joined Mahāvīra's community.

tradition.text: nirvāṇa 250 years before Mahāvīra's (traditionally 777 BCE)

scholarly.text: probably historical; c. 9th–7th c. BCE (estimates vary)

realization_account.text: He attained omniscience after 84 days of ascetic practice, following Meghamālin's attack from which Dharaṇendra shielded him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Historicity 'historical' reflects the common scholarly view that Pārśva was a real teacher; the dates are uncertain.

name: Pārśva (Sarvāstivāda elder)
summary: Tenth patriarch in the Chan list, the 'Venerable Side' who vowed never to lie down. (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 10.

tradition.text: Contemporary of King Kaniṣka

realization_account.text: An elder who vowed not to lie down until he had mastered the Tripiṭaka and attained the three knowledges ('the rib elder'); he urged Kaniṣka to convene the Kashmir council.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Sarvāstivāda elder of Gandhāra credited by Xuanzang with prompting the Kashmir council that compiled the Vibhāṣā; distinct from the Jain Tīrthaṅkara Pārśva.

name: Pārśvacandrasūri
summary: 16th-c. founder of the Pārśvacandra Gaccha, author of Gujarati glosses (ṭabo) on the Āgamas.

name: Pārśvadeva
summary: Author of the Saṅgītasamayasāra.

name: Partap Singh (Chachaji Maharaj)
summary: Soamiji's younger brother, associated with the Soamibagh line.

name: Pārthasārathi Miśra
summary: Leading Bhāṭṭa author: the Śāstradīpikā (independent commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra), Nyāyaratnākara (on the Ślokavārttika), Nyāyaratnamālā and Tantraratna. He defined a means of knowledge as a cognition apprehending what was not apprehended, free from defects of cause and from contradicting cognition, and held release to be the end of the threefold bond, without bliss.

name: Pārvatī
summary: Śiva's consort, the questioner in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (her doubt why the supreme Rāma grieved for Sītā, 1.1.13-15) and in the Guru Gītā; in Śākta texts identified with the Goddess who herself teaches (Devī Gītā, Bhagavatī Gītā).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Questioner in AR 1.1.13-15 and in the Guru Gītā.

alt_summary: Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): the Goddess who asks Bhairava about the jīvanmukti hinted at in all the tantras but never disclosed (Rasārṇava 1.6).

name: Pasenadi
summary: King of Kosala and lay follower, questioner in SN 3 and MN 87–90.

name: Paṭācārā
summary: Foremost nun in knowledge of the Vinaya; her verses tell of her liberation at a lamp's going out (Thig 5.10); by the commentarial account she had lost husband, children and parents in a single day; teacher of many nuns (Thig 5.11, 6.1).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Patañcala Kāpya
summary: Man of Madra in whose house Uddālaka studied the sacrifice; through a gandharva possessing his wife they learned of the thread and the inner controller (BAU 3.7.1).

checks.note: Located: BĀU 3.7.1 (and 3.3.1). The Advaita-Śāradā text reads 'patañjala kāpya'; the GRETIL Kāṇva text with Śaṅkara's commentary reads 'patañcala kāpya', as the entry does. The gandharva possessing his wife is Kabandha Ātharvaṇa.

name: Patañjali
alt_names: Śeṣa / Ananta (as whose incarnation he is regarded)

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (incarnation of Śeṣa); identified with the grammarian

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if author of the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra (Maas); the grammarian Patañjali is dated c. 2nd c. BCE

realization_account.text: Regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the serpent of Viṣṇu, who took a human form out of compassion to teach; the bhāṣya's maṅgala verse praises the 'lord of serpents, giver of yoga'. Later tradition credits him with removing the impurities of speech (grammar), mind (yoga) and body (medicine) — Bhoja's introductory verses praise Bhoja for doing the same 'like the lord of serpents'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author (re-teacher) of the Yoga Sūtra. The tradition regards him as Śeṣa incarnate and as the same Patañjali who wrote the grammatical Mahābhāṣya; modern scholarship mostly distinguishes the two and debates whether he also wrote the bhāṣya (the 'Pātañjala Yogaśāstra' hypothesis).
alt_summary: The Tamil tradition counts Patañjali among the eighteen Siddhars and, with Vyāghrapāda, among Nandi's disciples who worshipped at the hall (maṉṟu) of Chidambaram (TM 67); it identifies him with the author of the Yoga Sūtras.
places: Rāmēśvaram — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution. The identification of the Chidambaram sage, the grammarian and the Yoga Sūtra author is the tradition's; scholars keep them apart. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Patañjali (the grammarian)
summary: Author of the Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya. The tradition identifies him with Patañjali of the Yoga Sūtra (tch:patanjali); most scholars distinguish the two. Kept as a separate id so that both accounts stay visible.

tradition.text: an incarnation of the serpent Śeṣa, identical with the author of the Yoga Sūtra

scholarly.text: mid-2nd c. BCE (the Mahābhāṣya refers to sacrificing for Puṣyamitra)

realization_account.text: Tradition regards him as Śeṣa (Ananta) incarnate and as the one who purified speech by grammar, the mind by yoga and the body by medicine (a widely quoted invocatory verse).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: The dating evidence is text-located in the Mahābhāṣya on A 3.2.123: 'iha puṣyamitraṃ yājayāmaḥ' (also 'puṣyamitrasabhā' on 1.1.68). This supports the mid-2nd c. BCE date. The tradition's identification with the Yoga Sūtra author and Śeṣa is correctly labelled as tradition.

name: Patañjali (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: A Sāṃkhya teacher cited by the Yuktidīpikā: mahat arises directly from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from itself'; subtle bodies arise and cease repeatedly (one leads the organs to the womb, another arises at death). Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Whether he is the author of the Yoga Sūtra (tch:patanjali) is disputed.

name: Patrul Rinpoche (dpal sprul o rgyan 'jigs med chos kyi dbang po)
summary: Wandering renunciant master of Kham, speech-incarnation of Jigme Lingpa, famous for simplicity; author of the Words of My Perfect Teacher and the Special Teaching of the Wise and Glorious King; teacher of Mipham and Nyoshul Lungtok.

name: Paṭṭiṉattār (Tiruveṇkāṭar)
summary: Renouncer-poet: a rich merchant of Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam who renounced after his adopted son left him an eyeless needle; his songs on impermanence, the body, women and renunciation are among the most loved in Tamil. Guru of Pattirakiriyār; his samādhi is at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr (Chennai). The tradition treats him as one person with Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār of the eleventh Tirumuṟai; scholars usually distinguish two or more poets.

tradition.text: Cōḻa period

scholarly.text: the Siddhar songs c. 14th–17th c.; Paṭṭiṉattup Piḷḷaiyār c. 10th c.

realization_account.text: Childless, Tiruveṇkāṭar received a boy (Śiva's gift, Marutavāṇaṉ) who went trading and returned with cakes of dung; the angry father broke them and found gems. The boy vanished, leaving a box with an eyeless needle and a palm-leaf: 'even an eyeless needle will not come with you on the final road'. He renounced at once; survived his sister's poisoned cake ('one's own deed burns oneself; the baked cake burns the house'); returned to cremate his mother, singing ten songs; at Ujjain was condemned to the stake, which burst into flame, and the king Bhadragiri became his disciple; at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr, playing with boys who covered him with a basket, he vanished and a liṅga was found in his place.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The story is recalled at moderate confidence from the popular hagiography; details vary between tellings.

name: Paurika
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher who held, according to the Yuktidīpikā (on SK 56), that each puruṣa has its own pradhāna producing its body and the rest; when the pradhāna of the great-bodied one (māhātmyaśarīra) operates, the others operate, and when it ceases, they cease. The Yuktidīpikā rejects this for want of proof. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Pauṣkalāvata
summary: One of Suśruta's fellow students who approached Divodāsa Dhanvantari for the teaching (Su Sū 1.3).
notes: Later commentators cite tantras under some of these names (Aupadhenava, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata) — recalled, not checked.

name: Pavaṇanti
summary: Jain grammarian, author of the Naṉṉūl (c. 13th c.).

name: Pāyāsi

name: P. A. Payutto

name: Pei Xiu 裴休

name: Pema Karpo (the fourth Gyalwang Drukpa)

name: Pema Ledrel Tsal (padma las 'brel rtsal)
summary: Revealer of the Khandro Nyingthig; by tradition the rebirth of Princess Pemasal, and Longchenpa was his rebirth.

name: Pema Lingpa (padma gling pa)
summary: Bhutanese treasure revealer, the fourth 'king' tertön, who by tradition revealed treasures from the Burning Lake holding a lit lamp; his lineages and ritual dances shape Bhutanese Buddhism.

tradition.text: the rebirth of Princess Pemasal and of Longchenpa

name: Dzogchen Pema Rigdzin (rdzogs chen padma rig 'dzin)

name: Periya Nambi

name: Periya Tirumalai Nambi
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna and maternal uncle of Rāmānuja, who taught him the Rāmāyaṇa at Tirupati and brought Govinda (Embār) back to Vaiṣṇavism.

name: Periyāḻvār
summary: Brāhmaṇa priest-gardener of Śrīvilliputtūr, foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ; author of the Tiruppallāṇṭu, which opens the Prabandham and daily worship with a benediction for the Lord's own safety, and of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi, the first Tamil song-cycle of Kṛṣṇa's childhood sung through Yaśodā's eyes.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Summoned when the Pāṇḍya king Vallabhadeva sought to know the supreme truth, he established from the scriptures that Nārāyaṇa is supreme; the purse of gold hung as the prize bent down to him. The Lord appeared on Garuḍa in the sky to see his devotee honoured; fearing the evil eye might fall on the Lord, the Āḻvār sang 'many years, many years' for his safety.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Periyavāccāṉ Piḷḷai

name: Perumiḻalaikkuṟumpa Nāyaṉār

name: Peta Gönkyi

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born in a red lily in a well at Mylapore; at Tirukkōvalūr, by the light the others had kindled, he saw the Lord with Śrī, the golden form, the discus and the conch, and sang the third antāti.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the sword Nandaka in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Phagmodrupa Dorje Gyalpo
alt_names: phag mo gru pa rdo rje rgyal po

name: Phuchungwa Shönu Gyaltsen
summary: One of the 'three brothers' of the Kadam, known for meditation on the sixteen drops of the Book of Kadam.

summary: Teṅkalai author of the Yatīndrapravaṇa Prabhāvam, the life of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, and of commentaries on the rahasya works.

name: Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja

Author of the Chandaḥśāstra, the root text of prosody. The kinship with Pāṇini is a late report (low confidence).

name: Piṅgala (Pāśupata tīrthakara)
summary: Number 12 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Piṅgala (Qingmu 青目)

summary: Author of the commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā translated by Kumārajīva as the Zhong lun; nothing further is known of him.

name: Piṉpaḻagiya Perumāḷ Jīyar
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher to whom the Ārāyirappaṭi Guruparamparāprabhāvam, the chief hagiography of the Āḻvārs and ācāryas, is attributed.

name: Pīpā

alt_summary: Rajput king of Gāgraun who renounced his throne to become Rāmānanda's disciple and wandered with his wife Sītā; a hymn of his stands in the Sikh scripture (context).

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born, not of a womb, in a lotus in the temple tank (poykai) at Tiruveḵkā in Kāñcī. On a night of rain he sheltered in the narrow vestibule of a hermitage at Tirukkōvalūr — room for one to lie; Pūtattāḻvār came and they sat; Pēyāḻvār came and they stood; then a fourth pressed in among them unseen. Poykai lit a lamp with the earth as its bowl and the sea as its ghee and sang the first antāti; in the light the Lord was seen.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Prabhācandra

name: Prabhācandrasūri (Śvetāmbara)

name: Prabhāsa

name: Prabhava
summary: A thief who came to rob Jambū on his wedding night and was converted; Jambū's successor as head of the Śvetāmbara community.

name: Prabhūtaratna

name: Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava

name: Prajñārjuna
summary: Son and disciple of Pradyumnabhaṭṭa in Bhāskara's lineage (Vārttika 1.6-7).

name: Prajñātāra (Bore Duoluo 般若多羅)

name: Prakāśātman

name: Praśastapāda
