name: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali
summary: King of the Pañcālas; asks Śvetaketu the five questions and teaches Gautama Āruṇi the doctrine of the five fires and the two paths, saying this knowledge had never before dwelt with brahmins (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3-10); in ChU 1.8-9 he teaches that space (ākāśa) is the final support of the sāman.

queries: prepared ChU 1.8.1, ChU 1.9.1, ChU 5.3.1, ChU 5.3.7, BĀU 6.2.1
checks.note: Located: ChU 1.8-9 (with Śilaka Śālāvatya and Caikitāyana Dālbhya; ākāśa as the final support), ChU 5.3.1-7 and BĀU 6.2 (the five questions; 'na prāk tvattaḥ purā vidyā brāhmaṇān gacchati'). The Pañcāla assembly is at ChU 5.3.1 and BĀU 6.2.1.

name: Priyādās
summary: Vṛndāvana poet who wrote the Bhaktirasabodhinī (1712), the commentary that turned the Bhaktamāl's allusions into the standard stories of the saints.
notes: Affiliation recalled as Gauḍīya; verify.

name: Pṛthūdakasvāmin
summary: Commentator on the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta and Khaṇḍakhādyaka (864 CE).

name: Pṛthuyaśas
summary: Son of Varāhamihira by tradition; author of the Horāsāra and the Ṣaṭpañcāśikā on interrogation.

name: Pūcalā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A poor brahmin who built a temple in his mind stone by stone and fixed a day for its consecration; the Pallava king, who had fixed the same day for his great stone temple at Kāñcī, was told by Śiva in a dream that he would first attend Pūcalār's consecration, and went to see that temple.

realization_account.text: A poor brahmin who built a temple in his mind stone by stone and fixed a day for its consecration; the Pallava king, who had fixed the same day for his great stone temple at Kāñcī, was told by Śiva in a dream that he would first attend Pūcalār's consecration, and went to see that temple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pudu of Lushan
summary: Yuan monk of Donglin si on Lushan who compiled the Lushan lianzong baojian (1305) to defend the Lotus school and Mao Ziyuan against heterodox White Lotus groups.

name: Puhua 普化
summary: Eccentric companion of Linji who rang a bell in the streets; claimed as founder by the Japanese Fuke school.

name: Puji 普寂
summary: Shenxiu's heir, leader of the Northern school in the capitals; the main target of Shenhui's attacks.

name: Pūjyapāda Devanandin
summary: Digambara ācārya, grammarian and philosopher: author of the Sarvārthasiddhi (which fixed the Digambara Tattvārthasūtra), the Samādhitantra and Iṣṭopadeśa on the self, and the Jainendra grammar.

checks.note: Confirmed: Digambara monk, author of the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa, c. 510–600 CE (Wikipedia).

alt_summary: Digambara teacher; U02 adds only his grammar, the Jainendra-vyākaraṇa.

name: Pukaḻccōḻa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A Cōḻa king whose elephant was cut down by Eṟipattar; later, finding among the heads of slain enemies one with matted hair — a devotee's — he entered the fire in remorse.

realization_account.text: A Cōḻa king whose elephant was cut down by Eṟipattar; later, finding among the heads of slain enemies one with matted hair — a devotee's — he entered the fire in remorse.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pukaḻttuṇai Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A temple priest who kept up worship through a famine; fainting, he let the water-pot fall on the liṅga; Śiva left a gold coin for him on the pedestal each day until the famine ended.

realization_account.text: A temple priest who kept up worship through a famine; fainting, he let the water-pot fall on the liṅga; Śiva left a gold coin for him on the pedestal each day until the famine ended.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Pukkusāti
summary: A clansman who had gone forth for the Buddha without having met him, taught the six elements in a potter's shed (MN 140); he died a non-returner.

name: Pulastiyar
summary: Sage named in Siddha lore as a disciple of Agastya and an authority on medicine.
notes: Recalled at low confidence.

name: Pulippāṇi
summary: Disciple of Bogar who, the tradition says, rode a tiger (puli) and carried water for his guru; associated with Palani, where a line of Pulippāṇi priests traced itself to him; medical works bear his name.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Palani priestly line is recalled at low confidence.

name: Puliśa
summary: The author to whom the Pauliśa Siddhānta is ascribed; known through Varāhamihira and later citations. Historicity unknown.

name: Puming 普明
summary: Author of the alternative 'whitening ox' series of ten oxherding pictures; identity and date uncertain.

name: Puṇḍalīka
summary: The devotee of Paṇḍharpūr whose service to his parents brought Kṛṣṇa to his door; asked to wait, the Lord stood on the brick Puṇḍalīka tossed him and remains there as Viṭṭhala. Vārkarīs chant 'Puṇḍalīka varade Hari Viṭṭhala'.

realization_account.text: Kṛṣṇa himself came to see him because of his devotion to his parents.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Puṇḍarīka
summary: Second kalkin king of Śambhala in the tradition's account, son of Mañjuśrīyaśas, author of the Vimalaprabhā and the Paramārthasevā; historically the Vimalaprabhā dates to c. 1030–1050.

name: Puṇḍarīka
summary: The first gaṇadhara of Ṛṣabha, who (Śvetāmbara tradition) attained liberation on Mount Śatruñjaya, the holiest Śvetāmbara pilgrimage hill (Puṇḍarīkagiri).

name: Puṇḍarīka Viṭṭhala
summary: Karnataka-born musicologist at Mughal-era courts of the north, author of the Ṣaḍrāgacandrodaya and other treatises.

name: Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta
summary: Foremost among Dhamma speakers; explains the seven purifications to Sāriputta with the relay of chariots (MN 24); taught Ānanda (SN 22.83).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Puṇṇa of Sunāparanta
summary: The monk who resolved to live among the fierce people of Sunāparanta with unconditional patience (MN 145; SN 35.88).

name: Puṇyamitra (Buru Miduo 不如蜜多)
summary: Twenty-sixth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 26.

name: Puṇyānanda
summary: A paramahaṃsa teacher of Śrīvidyā, author of the Kāmakalāvilāsa and guru of Amṛtānanda (as the Dīpikā's colophons state).

name: Puṇyarāja
summary: Kashmiri commentator to whom the commentary on the second book of the Vākyapadīya is ascribed.

name: Puṇyatāra
summary: Kashmiri master who recited the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya for Kumārajīva's translation (404); he died before it was finished.

name: Puṇyayaśas (Funa Yeshe 富那夜奢)
summary: Eleventh patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 11.

name: Pūran Sāhib
summary: Kabīr Panth teacher of Burhanpur, author of the Bījak commentary Trijyā that founded the 'pārakh' (discernment) reading of the Bījak.

name: Pūraṇa Kassapa
summary: One of the six famous teachers of the Pali canon, leader of an order. DN 2 reports his doctrine of non-action (akiriya): the one who kills, steals or lies does no evil, and gifts, self-control and truthfulness bring no merit. SN 22.60 and SN 46.56 ascribe to him the view that there is no cause for defilement, purification, knowing or not knowing; AN 6.57 ascribes to him the six classes of birth in which the Ājīvika leaders are 'supremely white'. In the Tamil Maṇimēkalai and Nīlakēci, Pūraṇa is the Ājīvika teacher. Buddhist legend (Dhammapada commentary, Divyāvadāna) says he drowned himself after the Buddha's Twin Miracle.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: All doctrine reported_by_opponent. The commentary's story that he was a slave named 'Full' (pūraṇa) because his birth completed a hundred slaves (Sumaṅgalavilāsinī) is recalled with low confidence.

name: Purāṇa
summary: An elder who, after the First Council, said he would remember the Dhamma and discipline as he had heard them from the Buddha (Cv 11.1.11).

name: Purandara (Cārvāka)
summary: A Cārvāka author quoted by Kamalaśīla: 'the Cārvākas too accept inference as known in the world; what is rejected is inference that some state by transgressing the worldly path' (Tattvasaṅgraha-pañjikā on 1481–82).
notes: Do not confuse with tch:purandara-dasa (the Kannada Haridāsa poet).

name: Purandara Dāsa
summary: U31 contribution: the Haridāsa singer-saint remembered as the 'grandfather' (pitāmaha) of Karṇāṭaka music, who fixed its elementary lessons and made singing the Lord's name the core of practice.

name: Pūrṇa Dās Bāul
summary: Bāul singer of Birbhum who carried Bāul song to world audiences.

name: Pūrṇākṣa Maudgalya
summary: Speaker: three tastes (Ca Sū 26.8).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Pūrṇānanda
summary: Bengali Śākta tantric author (Giri order) of the Śrītattvacintāmaṇi (1577), whose sixth chapter, the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, became the classic description of the six centres and kuṇḍalinī's ascent.
notes: Place of origin low confidence.
alt_summary: Bengali Śākta renunciant of the sixteenth century, author of the Śrītattvacintāmaṇi (1577), whose sixth chapter is the Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa, the classic account of the six centres and the ascent of kuṇḍalinī; also of the Śyāmārahasya on Kālī worship, the Śāktakrama and the Kulavṛtti. Remembered as a disciple of Brahmānanda Giri.

name: Purujit
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army (1.5).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.5.

name: Purūravas (Aila)
summary: King, son of Iḍā, infatuated with the apsaras Urvaśī; his song of disenchantment is the Aila Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.26).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Singer of the Aila Gītā, BhP 11.26.4-24 ('ailaḥ samrāṭ').

name: Puruṣottama (Puruṣottamajī, of the Vallabha line)
summary: The most prolific later Śuddhādvaita scholar: Bhāṣyaprakāśa on the Aṇubhāṣya, Suvarṇasūtra on the Vidvanmaṇḍana, Prasthānaratnākara and many commentaries.

name: Puruṣottama Ṭhākur
summary: Grandson of Śaṅkaradeva and leader of the Puruṣa saṃhati.

name: Puruṣottamācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Nimbārka scholar, author of the Vedāntaratnamañjūṣā on the Daśaślokī and the Śrutyantasuradruma on the Kṛṣṇastavarāja.

name: Puṣpadanta (ācārya)
summary: Pupil of Dharasena and co-author of the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama, of which he wrote the opening (Satprarūpaṇā); the gods are said to have straightened his uneven teeth, hence the name.

name: Puṣpadanta (Apabhraṃśa poet)
summary: 10th-c. Apabhraṃśa poet at the Rāṣṭrakūṭa court of Mānyakheṭa, author of the Mahāpurāṇa, Jasaharacariu and Ṇāyakumāracariu.

name: Puṣpaka
summary: Number 13 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Putali

realization_account.text: A mendicant who carried a painted image (of Hevajra) on his back; identification of Tōh 2292's 'su ta ba' with him is by position. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 78): Everything is the nature of the sugatas; abandoning the wrong paths set up by the intellect and striving on the path of the essence, the fruit of the essence is certain; whoever, from the true guru, has the consecrations together with the innate pervades all with its taste — Vajradhara seals (all) with the unborn.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 78 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A mendicant who carried a painted image (of Hevajra) on his back; identification of Tōh 2292's 'su ta ba' with him is by position.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Pūtattāḻvār
summary: Second of the 'first Āḻvārs'; author of the Iraṇṭām Tiruvantāti, which lights the lamp of love, longing and a melting mind for Nāraṇaṉ.

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born in a flower at Tirukkaṭalmallai; at the Tirukkōvalūr meeting he lit the lamp of love with longing as ghee and his melting mind as wick.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the mace Kaumodakī in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Qingyuan Xingsi 青原行思
summary: Disciple of Huineng who 'did not even practise the holy truths'; teacher of Shitou; ancestor of the Caodong, Yunmen and Fayan houses.

name: Mingjiao Qisong 明教契嵩
summary: Yunmen-house scholar-monk who defended the 28-patriarch lineage and the harmony of Buddhism with Confucianism.

name: Radhaji (Narayani Devi)
summary: Soamiji's wife, revered in the Agra satsang; one account derives the name 'Radhasoami' from 'Radha' and 'Soami'.

name: Rādhāraman Datta
summary: Vaiṣṇava mystic poet of Sylhet (dhāmāil songs of Rādhā's longing), close to the Sahajiyā and Bāul idiom.

name: Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Padārthādarśa (1493/94), a learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: commentator on the Śāradātilaka (Padārthādarśa, 1493/94), whose quotations preserve many lost Āgamas.

name: Rāghavānanda
summary: Rāmānanda's guru in the older Rāmānandī lineage lists, placed in the line descending from Rāmānuja.

name: Rāghavānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Pātañjalarahasya, a gloss on Vācaspati's Tattvavaiśāradī.

name: Rāghavāṅka
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet, nephew and disciple of Harihara, author of the Hariścandra Kāvya, the Siddharāma Cāritra and the Sōmanātha Cāritra.

name: Rāghavendra Tīrtha

tradition.text: entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that Rāghavendra was Prahlāda reborn (through Bāhlīka and Vyāsatīrtha), that he entered his brindāvana alive in 1671, and that he remains present there, answering devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Born Veṅkaṭanātha at Bhuvanagiri, disciple of Sudhīndra Tīrtha, and author of the Parimala on the Nyāyasudhā (hence 'Parimalācārya'), the Bhāvadīpa on the Tattvaprakāśikā, the Tantradīpikā, the Nyāyamuktāvalī, the Candrikāprakāśa, the Bhāṭṭasaṅgraha on Mīmāṃsā, Upaniṣad khaṇḍārthas and the Gītāvivṛti. His brindāvana at Mantrālaya is the tradition's greatest pilgrimage centre.
notes: The claim that he will remain in the brindāvana for 700 years is recalled at low confidence.

name: Raghudeva Nyāyālaṅkāra
summary: Navya-Naiyāyika to whom a set of vāda treatises (Muktivāda, Īśvaravāda, Prāgabhāvavāda, Ākāṅkṣāvāda, Sāmagrīvāda and others) is attributed in their modern edition.

name: Raghunandana
summary: Bengali author of the Smṛtitattva.

checks.note: Confirmed: c. 1510–1580, Bengal (Banglapedia; Wisdomlib).

name: Raghunāth (Sthānakavāsī ācārya)
summary: 18th-c. Sthānakavāsī ācārya in Marwar and the teacher from whom Bhikṣu separated in 1760.

name: Raghunātha Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of Tapana Miśra of Vārāṇasī; lived in Vṛndāvana as a sweet-voiced reciter of the Bhāgavata; wrote no treatise (tradition).

name: Raghunātha Dāsa Gosvāmī
summary: Son of a wealthy landholder of Saptagrāma who renounced home, served Caitanya at Purī under Svarūpa Dāmodara and later lived at Rādhākuṇḍa; poet of the Stavāvalī (Manaḥśikṣā, Vilāpakusumāñjali) and exemplar of renunciation and mañjarī-bhāva.

name: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi
summary: Founder of the Navadvīpa school of Navya-Nyāya; his Dīdhiti on the Tattvacintāmaṇi became the base of later study, and his Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa re-examined the list of categories.
notes: The tradition tells of his defeating Pakṣadhara in debate in Mithilā (low confidence).

name: Raghūttama Tīrtha
summary: Uttarādi Maṭha pontiff called Bhāvabodhācārya after his Bhāvabodha commentaries (e.g. on Madhva's Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya); his brindāvana is at Tirukoilur.

name: Raghuvīra (author of the Kumbhakapaddhati)
summary: Author of the Kumbhakapaddhati, a manual devoted to the kinds of breath-retention.

name: Rahūgaṇa
summary: The king who forced Jaḍa Bharata to carry his palanquin and received from him instruction on the self beyond the body (BhP 5.10-13; the VP 2.13-16 version names the king of Sauvīra).

checks.note: BhP 5.10.1 'sindhusauvīrapateḥ rahūgaṇasya'; VP 2.13.48ff. the Sauvīra king (unnamed) located.

name: Rāhula
summary: The Buddha's son, given the going forth as a boy by Sāriputta (Vin Mv 1.54); instructed in MN 61, 62 and 147; foremost in desire for training.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Rāhula

realization_account.text: An old man despised by his family, taught to meditate on Rāhu swallowing the moon. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 47): The good outer Rāhu devoured the light of the moon non-dually; the drop of the conventional moon is devoured non-dually by the Rāhu of expanse and awareness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 47 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). An old man despised by his family, taught to meditate on Rāhu swallowing the moon.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Rāhulabhadra

realization_account.text: In some Tibetan accounts the brahmin Rāhulabhadra (identified with Saraha) ordained Nāgārjuna at Nālandā; in the Chinese lineage of the Dharma-treasure he follows Kāṇadeva (Āryadeva).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Conflicting placements are both the traditions' accounts; not reconciled here.
summary: Early Madhyamaka poet to whom the Hymn to the Perfection of Wisdom is ascribed; the lineage accounts place him either as Nāgārjuna's teacher (Tibetan) or as a successor of Āryadeva (Chinese patriarch lists).

name: Rāhulata (Luohouluoduo 羅睺羅多)
summary: Sixteenth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 16.

name: Rai Salig Ram (Huzur Maharaj)
summary: Postmaster-General of the North-Western Provinces and Soamiji's leading disciple, who systematized Radhasoami doctrine and led the Agra satsang.

name: Raikva 'with the cart' (sayugvan)
summary: A sage found scratching his sores under a cart, whom King Jānaśruti seeks out; he rebuffs the king's gifts, calling him śūdra, and teaches the saṃvarga ('gatherer') doctrine: wind among the deities and breath among the vital powers absorb all others (ChU 4.1-3).

checks.note: Located: ChU 4.1.3-8 ('sayugvā raikvaḥ'; found 'adhastāc chakaṭasya pāmānaṃ kaṣamāṇam', 4.1.8), 4.2.3 (calls the king śūdra) and the saṃvarga teaching at 4.3.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of subala, in the roles the summary gives. Raikva is the questioner of Subāla khaṇḍas 9, 10, 11 and 15, and is also named in the transmission chain of khaṇḍa 7 (Ghora Āṅgirasa → Raikva → Rāma). A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U04 contribution: asks the questions answered in the Subāla Upaniṣad (in some sections).

name: Raivataka
summary: Named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, naradaparivrajaka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Pāṇḍe Rājamalla
summary: Digambara lay scholar whose Hindi (Ḍhūṇḍhārī) commentary on Amṛtacandra's Samayasāra-kalaśas was the text through which Banārsīdās came to the Samayasāra; author (by tradition) of the Pañcādhyāyī and of the Lāṭīsaṃhitā and Adhyātmakamalamārtaṇḍa.

name: Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma
summary: Later Kashmiri commentator on the Parātrīśikā.

name: Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha (author of the Spandavivṛti)
summary: Kashmiri commentator, a disciple of Utpaladeva, author of the Spandavivṛti (ascribing the kārikās to Kallaṭa) and of the Sarvatobhadra commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā.
notes: Distinct from tch:ramakantha (Rāmakaṇṭha II of the Śaiva Siddhānta).

name: Rājaśekhara
summary: Poet and dramatist of Kanauj, author of the Kāvyamīmāṃsā.

name: Rājendrasūri
summary: Mūrtipūjaka reformer (1827–1906), reviver of the Tristuti Gaccha and compiler of the Abhidhāna Rājendra, a Prakrit–Sanskrit encyclopedia of the canon.

name: Rājeśvar Rām
summary: 20th-century head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi.

name: Rājīmatī (Rājul)
summary: The bride Neminātha left on his wedding day; she became a nun and, sheltering in a cave, recalled his brother Rathanemi to his vows (Uttarādhyayana 22; Daśavaikālika 2).

name: Rajinder Singh
summary: Successor of Darshan Singh; head of Science of Spirituality / Sawan Kirpal Ruhani Mission from 1989.

name: Rajjab
summary: Pathan disciple of Dādū who, on his way to his wedding in the groom's crown, met Dādū and renounced, wearing the crown for life; arranged the Dādū Vāṇī in aṅgas and compiled the Sarbaṅgī anthology.

name: Rāma (Dāśarathi)

tradition.text: Tretā yuga

summary: Prince of Ayodhyā, hero of the Rāmāyaṇa, called 'dharma embodied' (3.37.13); he goes into exile to keep his father's word, teaches Bharata on impermanence (2.105) and kingship (2.100), answers Jābāli that truth is the root of all (2.109), and vows protection to whoever seeks refuge (6.18.33); the Nārāyaṇīya names him among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.78).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of muktika, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
All cited references located (6.18.33 in the local Gita Press text).

Student of Vasiṣṭha (MU), teacher in the Rāma-hṛdaya (AR 1.1.44-52) and the Rāma Gītā (AR 7.5). One precision: the MU says Rāma was 'ūnaṣoḍaśa', not yet sixteen (in his sixteenth year), at the time of his dispassion (1.4.1, 1.7.2).

alt_summary: In U06's texts: the student of Vasiṣṭha in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (whose first book records his dispassion at sixteen); the teacher of Hanumān (Rāma-hṛdaya), Lakṣmaṇa (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.4 and the Rāma Gītā), Śabarī (the nine means of devotion) and Vibhīṣaṇa (Rāmcaritmānas); in the Śiva Gītā the recipient of Śiva's teaching. The Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa presents him as the supreme Brahman.

Rāma, regarded as the supreme Brahman, teaches Hanumān the canon of 108 Upaniṣads and the path to liberation in the Muktikā; the Rāma-Upaniṣads and Upaniṣad Brahmayogin's maṅgala verses make him the goal of every Upaniṣad.

realization_account.text: In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Rāma, after Vasiṣṭha's teaching, rests in the supreme state (Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, opening chapters, e.g. MU 6.5 'rāghava-viśrānti'); the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa instead treats him as the Lord who never lost knowledge.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Rāma Daivajña
summary: Son of Ananta, younger brother of Nīlakaṇṭha; author of the Muhūrtacintāmaṇi (Kāśī, 1600) with his own commentary.

name: Rāma Tīrtha (Kaniyooru)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Kaniyooru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Paramahaṃsa parivrājakācārya named in the colophons of the Yogacintāmaṇi as the guru of its author Śivānanda Sarasvatī.

name: Rāmacandra (Sūri)
summary: Jain monk-poet, disciple of Hemacandra, co-author with Guṇacandra of the Nāṭyadarpaṇa.

name: Rāmacaraṇa Ṭhākura
summary: Mādhavadeva's nephew and author of a verse Guru-carita of Śaṅkaradeva.

name: Rāmatēvar (Irāmatēvar)
summary: Siddhar whose Pūjāviti teaches the worship of the goddess Maṉōṉmaṇi/Vālai at the root; the tradition says he went to Mecca, lived there as 'Yākōpu' and returned, and medical works under that name are ascribed to him.
places: Aḻakar malai (Alagar Kovil) — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Mecca/Yākōpu account is the tradition's, recalled at moderate confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (Rāmakaṇṭha II)
summary: The foremost Kashmirian exegete of the Siddhānta: commentaries on the Mataṅgapārameśvara, Kiraṇa, Sārdhatriśatikālottara, and Sadyojyoti's Nareśvaraparīkṣā, Mokṣakārikā and Paramokṣanirāsakārikā. He argued that mala is a substance removable only by Śiva's power in initiation, that the liberated soul becomes equal to Śiva, and answered the non-dualist Śaivas.
notes: Correction to the unit brief: 'Rāmakaṇṭha II' and 'Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha' are the same person (the Saiddhāntika son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha). He is distinct from Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha, author of the Spandakārikāvivṛti and a Gītā commentary (non-dualist milieu). Some scholars suggest the Śrīkaṇṭha of the Ratnatraya was his teacher (low confidence).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika exegete, son of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, who commented on the Kiraṇa, the Mataṅgapārameśvara and the Sārdhatriśatikālottara, and on works of Sadyojyoti, maintaining that liberation is the soul's becoming equal to Śiva, not identity with him.

name: Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri author credited with the Sarvatobhadra commentary on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.

queries: Rajanaka Ramakantha Sarvatobhadra disciple of Utpaladeva
checks.note: Least-sure item: a Kashmiri author (disciple of Utpaladeva, 10th c.) of the Sarvatobhadra on the Kashmirian Gītā. The entry is right to keep him distinct from the Saiddhāntika Rāmakaṇṭha, though some web sources conflate the two.

notes: Not identified here with the Saiddhāntika Rāmakaṇṭha (tch:ramakantha).

name: Ramakrishna
summary: U23 contribution: priest of Kālī at Dakṣiṇeśvar who practised the tantric disciplines under the Bhairavī Brāhmaṇī and worshipped his wife Sāradā as the Goddess Ṣoḍaśī.

name: Rāmakṛṣṇa Adhvarin
summary: Son of Dharmarāja, author of the Śikhāmaṇi on the Vedāntaparibhāṣā.

name: Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Yuktisnehaprapūraṇī on the tarkapāda of the Śāstradīpikā.

name: Rāmāmātya
summary: Minister at Vijayanagara, author of the Svaramelakalānidhi.

name: Ramana Maharshi
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): recommended the Ṛbhu Gītā, which was read aloud in his presence, and quoted the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā.

checks.note: Ramana often mentioned the Ribhu Gītā and had it read (Sri Ramanasramam editions). His quoting the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha and the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā is noted on the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā page.

name: Rāmānanda
summary: Founder of the Rāmānandī sampradāya, teacher at Vārāṇasī (Pañcagaṅgā ghāṭ). By one tradition a disciple of Rāghavānanda in Rāmānuja's line who founded his own order after being faulted over commensality; by the independent Rāmānandī account, the founder of an order descending from Rāma himself. He taught devotion to Rāma with Sītā through the Rāma mantra, used the vernacular, and — so the Bhaktamāl says — initiated twelve disciples including a weaver (Kabīr), a cobbler (Raidās), a barber (Sena), a Jāṭ farmer (Dhanna), a Rajput king (Pīpā) and women (Padmāvatī, Surasurī).

tradition.text: 1299–1410 (Rāmānandī reckoning)

name: Rāmānanda Rāya
summary: Governor at Vidyānagara (Godāvarī) and author of the drama Jagannāthavallabha, whose dialogue with Caitanya on the goal and means (CC 2.8) rises from varṇāśrama to Rādhā's love.

name: Rāmānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Yogamaṇiprabhā, a vṛtti that follows the bhāṣya; its colophon names him a paramahaṃsa pupil of Govindānanda.

name: Rāmānuja
summary: The principal systematizer of Viśiṣṭādvaita: born at Śrīperumbūdūr, he renounced at Kāñcī, led the Śrīraṅgam temple and community, spent years at Melkote during the Cōḻa persecution, and wrote nine works — the Śrībhāṣya, Vedārthasaṅgraha, Vedāntasāra, Vedāntadīpa, Gītābhāṣya, the three Gadyas and the Nityagrantha.

scholarly.text: 11th–12th c. CE; some scholars doubt the 120-year span and propose c. 1077–1157

realization_account.text: Varadarāja answered his doubts through Tirukkacci Nambi; Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi gave him the secret mantra after eighteen visits, and he proclaimed its meaning to all from the temple tower, accepting hell for himself if others could be saved; he surrendered to Śrī and Raṅganātha on Paṅguni Uttiram, and the Lord's reply is recorded in the Śaraṇāgati Gadya. The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition regards him as an incarnation of Ādiśeṣa (and Lakṣmaṇa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Confirmed; his gloss on 13.4 (Śārīraka sūtras) and his two readings of 18.66, cited in the teaching notes, were located in the local commentary corpus.

alt_summary: Author of a Gītā commentary reading it as teaching bhakti-yoga to Nārāyaṇa, supported by karma- and jñāna-yoga.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Rāmānujācārya (Prābhākara author)
summary: Late Prābhākara author of the Tantrarahasya; distinct from the Vedāntin Rāmānuja.

name: Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Rāmarudrī, a gloss on the Muktāvalī continuing the Dinakarī.

name: Rāmasena (or Nāgasena)
summary: Name under which the Tattvānuśāsana is transmitted (ascription disputed).

name: Rāmasiṃha Muni
summary: Digambara author of the Apabhraṃśa Pāhuḍa Dohā, critic of outer ritual.

name: Rāmatīrtha
summary: Commentator on the Vedāntasāra (Vidvanmanorañjanī) and on the Upadeśasāhasrī. Distinct from the recent Swami Rama Tirtha.

name: Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra
summary: Bengali pandit who compiled the Prāṇatoṣiṇī, a vast compendium of tantric passages (c. 1820).

name: Rāmcaraṇ
summary: Founder of the Shāhpurā Rāmsnehīs, author of the Aṇbhai Vāṇī.

name: Rāmdulāl Pāl (Dulālcānd)
summary: Son of Rāmśaraṇ and Satī Mā, Kartā of the sect and composer of the Bhāber Gīt; under him the sect expanded into Calcutta.

name: Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ
summary: Brahmin of Vāgholī who condemned a Kuṇbī's expounding of scripture and ordered Tukārām's notebooks sunk; after their restoration he became Tukārām's disciple.

name: Rāmeśvara (commentator on the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra)
summary: Author of the Saubhāgyodaya commentary on the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra (usually dated 1831).

name: Rāmī (Rajakinī)
summary: The washerwoman whom the Sahajiyā Caṇḍīdās loved; revered by Sahajiyās as the model female partner, to whom some songs are attributed.

name: Rāmprasād Sen
summary: Bengali Śākta poet-saint of Kumārhaṭṭa (Halisahar), whose songs to Kālī and Umā (the 'Rāmprasādī' songs) created Bengal's devotional Śākta tradition: the devotee as the Mother's child who claims, reproaches and surrenders to her, and who treats Kālī's name as the refuge at death. Patronised by Rājā Kṛṣṇacandra of Nadia, who gave him the title Kavirañjana; author of a Vidyāsundara and a Kālīkīrtana.

realization_account.text: Working as a clerk in Calcutta he filled his account book with songs to the Mother; his employer, moved, sent him home with a stipend. The Mother came in the form of his little daughter to help him mend a fence; he died while immersing Kālī's image in the Ganges, singing.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Biographical legends are from 19th-century Bengali tradition; dates vary by source.

name: Rāmśaraṇ Pāl
summary: Sadgop householder of Ghoshpara, chief disciple of Āulcānd and first Kartā; organized the Kartābhajā community.

name: Raṅgarāmānuja Muni
summary: Viśiṣṭādvaita commentator on the principal Upaniṣads (the Prakāśikās) and on the Śrībhāṣya.

name: Raṅganātha (commentator on the Sūrya Siddhānta)
summary: Author of the Gūḍhārthaprakāśa on the Sūrya Siddhānta (1603).

name: Rangjung Dorje, the third Karmapa
summary: Scholar-yogin who synthesized Mahāmudrā, the Six Yogas and Dzogchen (the Karma Nyingthig); author of the Profound Inner Meaning, the Aspiration Prayer of Mahāmudrā, Distinguishing Consciousness and Wisdom and the Treatise on Buddha-Nature; recognized as a child by Orgyenpa.
alt_summary: Third Karmapa (1284-1339), author of the Treatise on Buddha-Nature and of the Profound Inner Meaning; joined buddha-nature to Mahāmudrā.

name: Rangjung Rigpe Dorje, the sixteenth Karmapa
alt_names: rang byung rig pa'i rdo rje
summary: Karmapa who left Tibet in 1959, founded Rumtek in Sikkim and spread the Karma Kagyu internationally.

name: Rāśīkara
summary: The seventeenth of the eighteen Pāśupata tīrthakaras in the Jain lists (Guṇaratna; Rājaśekhara); the Ratnaṭīkā has the ascetic salute 'the tīrthakaras from Lakulīśa to Rāśīkara', and the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha cites a 'Rāśīkara-bhāṣya'. His identification with Kauṇḍinya is a scholarly suggestion.

name: Ratannāth (Hājī Ratan)
summary: Nāth yogī remembered in Punjab and among Muslims of the north-west as Hājī Ratan; a centre of his cult was at Peshawar.

name: Rathanemi
summary: Brother of Neminātha, a monk who was tempted on seeing Rājīmatī and was brought back to his vows by her rebuke.

name: Ratna Lingpa (ratna gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer who gathered the Old Tantras into the collection from which the Nyingma Gyubum derives.

name: Śāntipa (Ratnākaraśānti)

realization_account.text: A great scholar of Vikramaśīla invited to Siṃhala; returning, he met Koṭali, a peasant digging the mountainside to whom he had once given instruction, and found that Koṭali had realized it while he had not; he then practised twelve years and attained the fruit. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 12): As a child nourished by its mother grows to a wrestler's strength, one of small mind, gradually raised by the guru's instruction, becomes of the great vehicle; as medicines cure the diseases of wind, bile, phlegm and their combination, the guru's instruction burns in an instant the clinging to 'I' and self.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: U44 contribution (the siddha of the eighty-four): No. 12 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A great scholar of Vikramaśīla invited to Siṃhala; returning, he met Koṭali, a peasant digging the mountainside to whom he had once given instruction, and found that Koṭali had realized it while he had not; he then practised twelve years and attained the fruit.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.
alt_summary: Vikramaśīla scholar (by tradition 'gate-keeper' of the eastern gate) and tantric master, counted among the eighty-four mahāsiddhas as Śāntipa; the chief defender of image-less (nirākāra / alīkākāra) Yogācāra and teacher of Atiśa.
U40 contribution: Vikramaśīla master whose Prajñāpāramitopadeśa and Madhyamakālaṃkāropadeśa combine a Yogācāra account of luminous mind with Madhyamaka; classed by some as a Yogācāra-Madhyamaka.

name: Ratnakīrti
summary: Jñānaśrīmitra's pupil at Vikramaśīla, author of concise proofs of momentariness and exclusion and refutations of God and of other mind-streams.

name: Ratnamati
summary: Central Indian monk in Luoyang who translated the Ratnagotravibhāga into Chinese (T1611, 511) and, with Bodhiruci, Vasubandhu's Daśabhūmika commentary.

name: Ratnanandi (Ratnakīrti)
summary: Author of the 15th-c. Bhadrabāhucarita.

name: Ratnaśekhara Sūri
summary: Śvetāmbara author to whom the Guṇasthānakramāroha is ascribed.
notes: Identity with other Ratnaśekharas (e.g. the author of the Sirisirivālakahā) not established.

name: Rātri Bhāradvājī
summary: Named (beside Kuśika Saubhara) as ṛṣikā of the hymn to Night, RV 10.127.

name: Ravaḷobās
summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Ravidās (Raidās)

tradition.text: born 1377 (Ravidāsī reckoning; birth celebrated on Māgh Pūrṇimā) and very long-lived

realization_account.text: Rāmānanda's disciple in the Rāmānandī account; the brahmins who challenged his right to worship were defeated by signs (the image came to his lap; Gaṅgā appeared in his leather-soaking bowl); the queen Jhālī of Chittor and Mīrābāī became his disciples.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Leatherworker (Camār) saint of Banaras, venerated as Guru Ravidās: his songs speak of the city without sorrow (Begampura), of God who raises the lowly, of his own despised caste without shame, and of the unity of self and God. Forty of his hymns are in the Ādi Granth; the Ravidāsī community reveres him as its guru.
notes: Mīrābāī's discipleship rests on her songs naming Raidās as guru (attribution debated).

name: Ravigupta
summary: Author of the Siddhasāra.

name: Raviṣeṇa
summary: Author of the Sanskrit Padmapurāṇa (676–677 CE), the Digambara Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Ṛbhu
summary: Sage of the Advaita dialogues: taught by Varāha after long austerity (Varāha 1–3), he teaches his disciple Nidāgha (Varāha 4–5, Tejobindu 5, Mahā, Annapūrṇā); named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6, Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of varaha, tejobindu, maha, annapurna, jabala, naradaparivrajaka, in the roles the summary gives. Varāha teaches Ṛbhu in chs. 1-3 and Ṛbhu teaches Nidāgha in ch. 4, as the skeleton report says. The e-text has 5 chapters, of which ch. 5 is yoga. A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
VP 2.15.3 'ṛbhur nāmābhavat putro brahmaṇaḥ parameṣṭhinaḥ' and the Nidāgha episode verified; the Śivarahasya's Ṛbhu Gītā confirmed by web sources.
VP 2.15.3 (Ṛbhu, son of Brahmā) and KūP 1.10.13 located.

Mind-born son of Brahmā (KūP 1.10.13 lists him with the Kumāras) who teaches his disciple Nidāgha the non-difference of all selves (VP 2.15-16) - told within Jaḍa Bharata's teaching; the Ṛbhu Gītā (U06) is a separate text.

name: Rechungpa Dorje Drakpa
alt_names: ras chung pa rdo rje grags pa

realization_account.text: Proud of the learning he brought from India, he was humbled by Milarepa's display (sheltering inside a yak horn); Milarepa's Life is framed as told to him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Milarepa's close disciple, called his 'moon-like' son (Gampopa being the 'sun-like'); he went to India and brought back from Tiphupa the teachings of the formless ḍākinīs; source of the Rechung hearing lineage and, by the Drukpa account, of the Six Equal Tastes hidden as treasure.

name: Rendawa Shönu Lodrö
summary: Sakya master of Madhyamaka and Abhidharma, champion of Candrakīrti's Prāsaṅgika in Tibet and principal teacher of Tsongkhapa; critic of the Kālacakra (tradition's account).

name: Rennyo
summary: Eighth head of Honganji who, through his letters (Ofumi), congregational meetings (kō) and the practice of enshrining the six-character name, made the small Honganji the largest Buddhist body in Japan; he taught to rely on Amida single-heartedly in the one great matter of the afterlife and to say the nenbutsu in gratitude, while keeping the laws of the land and respecting other deities; revered as the restorer of Shinshū.

name: Reṇukācārya (Revaṇasiddha)
summary: The first of the five ācāryas: the gaṇa Reṇuka who, cursed for leaping over his fellow gaṇa Dāruka in Śiva's assembly, emerged from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki, taught Agastya the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, and in the tradition founded the Rambhāpurī pīṭha at Bāḷehonnūr.

tradition.text: appears in every yuga; in the Kali age as Revaṇa/Reṇuka

realization_account.text: A pramatha created by Śiva (SSM 2.25–27), sent to earth for overstepping Dāruka (3.66–77), he appeared from the Someśvara liṅga at Kollipāki without human birth (3.83–84; 4.1), taught Agastya, visited Vibhīṣaṇa in Laṅkā, and returned into the liṅga (ch. 21).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Seat: Vīra-siṃhāsana at Rambhāpurī (low confidence on the siṃhāsana name).

name: Revaṇanātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Revaṇnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Camasa. In Karnataka the name Revaṇasiddha also belongs to a Vīraśaiva founder-figure; the relation between the two is unclear.

name: Revata
summary: Named in MN 118:1 among the well-known senior disciples present at Sāvatthī.

name: Rigdzin Chökyi Drakpa
summary: Drikung master and treasure revealer (16th–17th c.) who joined Drikung Mahāmudrā with Dzogchen (the Drikung Yangzab).

name: Rigdzin Gödem (rig 'dzin rgod ldem)
summary: Founder of the Northern Treasures; revealed the Gongpa Zangthal at Zangzang Lhadrak in 1366; named for the vulture-feather-like growths on his head.

name: Rigdzin Kunzang Sherab (rig 'dzin kun bzang shes rab)
summary: Founder of Palyul monastery in Kham (1665).

name: Rigdzin Ngagi Wangpo (rig 'dzin ngag gi dbang po)
summary: Northern Treasure master who re-founded Dorje Drak monastery.

name: Rigpé Yeshe (rig pa'i ye shes), the sage 'Awareness-Wisdom'
summary: The emanation of the Medicine Buddha's mind who teaches the Four Tantras (the tradition's account).

name: Rinchen Zangpo

name: Rohagupta (Ṣaḍulūka)
summary: The sixth schismatic in Śvetāmbara lists, who in debate asserted three categories — soul, non-soul and 'no-soul' (trairāśika) — and would not recant when refuted by his teacher Śrīgupta; the Jain tradition makes him the founder of the Vaiśeṣika system with its six categories.

name: Rolpe Dorje, the fourth Karmapa
summary: Poet and teacher at the Yuan court; by the tradition's account he gave lay vows to the child Tsongkhapa.

name: Romaharṣaṇa

name: Urōmarisi (Romarishi)
summary: Sage counted among the Siddhars in some Tamil lists; works on medicine and wisdom circulate under his name.

name: Romaśā
