name: Rongtön Lhaga

realization_account.text: He told Milarepa that his Dzogchen was such that one who meditates on it by day is awakened by day; Milarepa, overconfident, did not practise and gained nothing, and was sent to Marpa, with whom he had a karmic link.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The Dzogchen teacher who, in the Life of Milarepa, gave Milarepa the Great Perfection before sending him to Marpa, because Milarepa's karma did not suit it.

name: Rongtön Sheja Kunrig
summary: Sakya scholar, founder of Nalendra monastery (1436), author of commentaries on the Maitreya texts and Madhyamaka; teacher of Gorampa and Shākya Chokden.
alt_names: rong ston shes bya kun rig

name: Rongzom Chökyi Zangpo (rong zom chos kyi bzang po)
summary: The greatest early Nyingma scholar, translator and commentator on the Guhyagarbha, author of Entering the Way of the Great Vehicle; counted with Longchenpa and Mipham among the 'three omniscient ones' of the Nyingma.

name: Ṛṣabha (Ṛṣabhanātha, Ādinātha)
summary: The first Tīrthaṅkara of this era, emblem the bull, son of the last patriarch (kulakara) Nābhi and Marudevī, born at Ayodhyā (Vinītā). As first king he taught humanity the arts of livelihood — arms, writing, agriculture, learning, trade and crafts — writing (the Brāhmī script) to his daughter Brāhmī and arithmetic to Sundarī, then renounced, fasted for about a year until Prince Śreyāṃsa offered him sugarcane juice (remembered on Akṣaya Tṛtīyā), attained omniscience and taught the dharma; he reached nirvāṇa on Mount Aṣṭāpada. His sons were the world-emperor Bharata and Bāhubali. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa also knows him as a renouncer-avatāra.

tradition.text: lived in the third age (suṣamā-duḥṣamā) of this descending half-cycle; his lifespan is given as 8,400,000 pūrvas

realization_account.text: After renouncing kingship he undertook a long fast; he attained omniscience (kevala-jñāna) under a banyan tree and preached in the first samavasaraṇa of this era; his mother Marudevī, seeing his glory, became the first soul of this era to reach liberation (Śvetāmbara account).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Śvetāmbara account makes Marudevī the first liberated soul of this era; Digambara accounts differ on her.

checks.note: BhP 1.3.13 (eighth avatāra, son of Nābhi and Merudevī), 5.5.1, 5.6.9 located.

alt_summary: In the Bhāgavata an avatāra of Viṣṇu and avadhūta-teacher; the same figure the Jains honour as the first Tīrthaṅkara. BhP 5.6.9 adds that a king named Arhat of Koṅka, Veṅka and Kuṭaka, imitating him, will spread a heterodox path in Kali (a polemical report).

name: Ṛṣabheśvara
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Not to be confused with the Jain Ṛṣabha.

name: Rudra (Kerala commentator)
summary: Author of the Vivaraṇa commentary on the Bṛhajjātaka preserved in Kerala manuscripts.

name: Rudraṭa
summary: Author of a Kāvyālaṅkāra in sixteen chapters, counting ten rasas (with śānta and preyas).

name: Tiantong Rujing 天童如淨
summary: Caodong abbot of Tiantong and Dōgen's teacher; in Dōgen's account he taught that sitting is 'body and mind dropping off' and that just sitting suffices.

name: Rūpa Bhavānī
summary: 17th-century Kashmiri Śaiva yoginī and poet in the line of Lal Ded, revered as a saint; her vākhs teach inner realization of Śiva.

tradition.text: 1621-1721 CE (traditional dates)

name: Rūpa Gosvāmī
summary: Formerly Dabir Khās, minister of Sultan Husain Shah of Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Prayāga (CC 2.19); settled in Vṛndāvana; the chief theorist of Gauḍīya devotion: Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, Ujjvalanīlamaṇi, Laghubhāgavatāmṛta, Upadeśāmṛta, dramas and hymns.

name: Rūpa Kavirāja
summary: Gauḍīya teacher who taught that in rāgānugā practice the rules of vaidhī bhakti may be abandoned; condemned by Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and remembered in Gauḍīya accounts as a deviant close to Sahajiyā views.

name: Rūpcand Pāṇḍe
summary: Digambara scholar at Agra who taught Banārsīdās and his friends the Gommaṭasāra and the guṇasthānas (1635).

name: Ruyyaka
summary: Kashmiri author of the Alaṅkārasarvasva.

name: Ryōchū
summary: Benchō's successor, third patriarch of Jōdo-shū, who spread the Chinzei line in Kamakura and wrote commentaries on Shandao and the Senchakushū.

name: Ryōe Dōkō
summary: Jōdo monk who compiled Hōnen's collected words (1274–75).

name: Ryōgen
summary: Tendai abbot who restored Mt Hiei, teacher of Genshin; a work on the nine grades of birth is ascribed to him.

name: Taigu Ryōkan 大愚良寛
summary: Sōtō hermit-poet and calligrapher who lived as a mendicant in Echigo.

name: Ryōnen Genso 了然元總
summary: Ōbaku nun and poet who, refused admission because of her beauty, is said to have scarred her face; later abbess.
notes: The face-scarring episode is recorded as the tradition's account; restricted-type austerity, summary only.

name: Ryōnin

realization_account.text: In 1117, in samādhi, Amida revealed to him the interfusing nenbutsu (Yūzū nenbutsu engi).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Tendai monk of Ōhara, master of shōmyō chant, founder of the Yūzū nenbutsu: he enrolled nobles and commoners — and, in the tradition's account, gods — in a register of nenbutsu practitioners whose recitations interpenetrate.

name: Ryūkan
summary: Hōnen's disciple associated with the 'many-calling' teaching (tanengi), exiled in the Karoku persecution of 1227; Shinran commended his writings.

name: Śabarasvāmin

realization_account.text: A late popular verse makes Śabarasvāmin, a brāhmaṇa, the father by wives of the four varṇas of Varāhamihira, King Vikramāditya, Bhartṛhari and others; another story says he lived disguised as a śabara (forest-dweller). These are legends, not Mīmāṃsā doctrine.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Legend details are from memory (low confidence).
summary: Author of the Śābarabhāṣya, the earliest surviving commentary on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra and the base text of both later schools.

name: Śabarī
summary: A forest woman of low birth, disciple of the sage Mataṅga, who waited for Rāma; he teaches her that gender, caste and stage of life are no cause of devotion and gives her the nine means of devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.10).

checks.note: Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: AR 3.10.20-43. Her guru, the sage Mataṅga, is named in the Gita Press gloss on 3.10.13 (the verse itself says 'guru').

realization_account.text: After guiding Rāma to Sugrīva she entered the fire before him and, freed of all bonds made by ignorance, attained liberation by Rāma's grace (AR 3.10.39-42).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: An aged female ascetic (śramaṇī) of the Śabara people who served the sages of Mataṅga's hermitage, receives Rāma and ascends to the heavenly worlds (Rāmāyaṇa 3.73–74).

name: Sabbakāmī
summary: The most senior elder (by tradition a pupil of Ānanda) who judged the ten points at the Second Council (Cv 12).

name: Saccidānanda Bābā
summary: Scribe who wrote down the Jñāneśvarī at Nevāse as Jñāneśvar spoke it; tradition says Jñāneśvar restored him to life.

name: Sachen Kunga Nyingpo
summary: First of the five founding masters of the Sakya; son of Khön Könchok Gyalpo; at twelve he received Parting from the Four Attachments from Mañjuśrī in a vision; he received the Lamdre from Zhangtön Chöbar, and later the tradition says Virūpa appeared to him and gave him the Lamdre directly (the 'short lineage'); he wrote eleven commentaries on the Vajra Verses.
alt_names: sa chen kun dga' snying po

realization_account.text: Received the four lines of Parting from the Four Attachments from Mañjuśrī at twelve; later Virūpa appeared to him in visions over a month and transmitted the Lamdre and many instructions.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Śacī Paulomī
summary: Indra's consort, ṛṣikā of RV 10.159, in which she praises herself as victorious.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'paulomī śacī', deity 'śacī (ātmānaṃ tuṣṭāva)'.

name: Ṣaḍakṣaradēva
summary: Seventeenth-century Kannada Vīraśaiva poet of campū works including the Rājaśēkharavilāsa and the Vṛṣabhēndravijaya.

name: Sadānanda (Yogīndra)
summary: Author of the Vedāntasāra.

name: Sadānanda Śarmā
summary: Author of the Rasataraṅgiṇī, a modern textbook of rasa medicine.

name: Sadāparibhūta
summary: The 'Never-Disparaging' bodhisattva of Lotus ch. 20, a past life of Śākyamuni, who bowed to everyone saying 'I do not disparage you, for you will all become buddhas' and was beaten for it.

name: Sadāprarudita
summary: The 'Ever-Weeping' bodhisattva of Aṣṭasāhasrikā ch. 30-31, who searches for the perfection of wisdom, sells his own flesh and blood to honor the teacher Dharmodgata, and is tested by Śakra; model of devotion to the spiritual friend.

name: Sadāśiva Brahmendra
places: Tamil country, Kāveri region (samādhi shrine at Nerur by tradition)
summary: Advaita avadhūta and composer of Sanskrit songs remembered in South Indian tradition; author of the Yogasudhākara on the Yoga Sūtra.
notes: Tradition makes him a pupil of Paramaśivendra Sarasvatī and credits him with further works (Brahma Sūtra vṛtti, Ātmavidyāvilāsa) — not verified here.
alt_summary: Avadhūta and poet of the Kāverī region (c. 17th–18th c.), author of the Ātmavidyāvilāsa, a Brahmasūtra commentary (Brahmatattvaprakāśikā), a Yoga Sūtra commentary and Sanskrit songs; remembered as a jīvanmukta who wandered naked and silent.

name: Saddālaputra
summary: A potter of Polāsapura, formerly a lay follower of Gośāla, converted by Mahāvīra's argument about his pots (if effort were nothing, why punish a man who smashes them?) (Upāsakadaśā 7).

name: Saddālaputta
summary: A wealthy Ājīvika potter of Polāsapura, lay follower of Gosāla, who became a follower of Mahāvīra after being asked who makes his pots (Uvāsagadasāo 7).

name: Ṣaḍguruśiṣya
summary: Commentator on the Sarvānukramaṇī (Vedārthadīpikā) and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Sukhapradā).

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed: author of the Vedārthadīpikā on the Sarvānukramaṇī (12th c.) and the Sukhapradā on the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (published).

name: Sadhnā the butcher
summary: Muslim butcher devotee whose hymn in the Ādi Granth is among the bhagat-bāṇī; named by Ravidās among those the Lord saved.

name: Sadyojyoti
summary: The earliest Siddhānta author whose works survive: philosophical treatises proving the soul and the Lord against Buddhists and others, and defining liberation as the soul's equality with Śiva; commentaries on the Svāyambhuva and (reportedly) the Raurava.
notes: Names his teacher as Ugrajyoti (moderate confidence). A commentary on the Raurava(sūtrasaṅgraha) is reported but not treated here (gap).
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue: commentaries). Doctrine is U18's.
alt_summary: Kashmirian theologian of the Śaiva Siddhānta, the earliest datable exegete of its scriptures; he commented on the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha and wrote short doctrinal treatises (the Nareśvaraparīkṣā, Mokṣakārikā, Bhogakārikā and others).

name: Sahadeva
summary: Pāṇḍava who, with Nakula, blows the conches Sughoṣa and Maṇipuṣpaka (1.16).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.16.

name: Sahajavajra
summary: Disciple of Maitrīpa, author of the Tattvadaśakaṭīkā on 'mahāmudrā joined with the pāramitā view'.

name: Sahajayoginīcintā
summary: Yoginī author of the Vyaktabhāvānugatatattvasiddhi.

name: Sahajobāī
summary: Woman Sant, disciple of Caraṇdās, author of the Sahaj Prakāś, famous for placing the guru above Hari.

name: Sāhib Kaul
summary: 17th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar-poet: a commentary on the Śiva Sūtra, the Devīnāmavilāsa, and works of Śrīvidyā ritual (Śrīvidyānityapaddhati).

name: Śaibya
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army, 'bull among men' (1.5).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.5.

name: Śaibya Satyakāma
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks what world the one who meditates on Om until death wins (PrU 5); distinct from Satyakāma Jābāla.

checks.note: Located: PrU 1.1 and 5.1 (asks about meditation on Om until death).

name: Saichō
summary: Founder of Japanese Tendai (767-822), who defended the Lotus's one vehicle and universal buddha-nature against Tokuitsu.
notes: Owned by U55 (Tendai); this entry contributes the debate with Tokuitsu.

name: Sain (Sen) the barber
summary: Barber devotee counted among Rāmānanda's disciples, remembered for Hari taking his place in service to the king; a hymn in the Ādi Granth.

name: Sajjana
summary: Kashmiri paṇḍita who taught the Maitreya texts to Ngok Loden Sherab and Tsen Kawoche, source of the Tibetan 'analytic' and 'meditative' transmissions of the Maitreya teachings.

name: Sakalakīrti (Bhaṭṭāraka)
summary: 15th-c. Digambara bhaṭṭāraka of the Balātkāra gaṇa in Gujarat and Rajasthan, prolific author of Sanskrit purāṇas and caritras (Mahāvīrapurāṇa and others).

name: Sakalēśa Mādarasa
summary: A chieftain-poet among the śaraṇas.

name: Śākalya
summary: The teacher credited with the Padapāṭha of the Ṛgveda and eponym of the Śākala recension; cited by Yāska and Pāṇini. Tradition sometimes identifies him with Vidagdha Śākalya, Yājñavalkya's questioner on the number of the gods in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.9) — an identification scholars dispute.

queries: Sakalya padapatha cited by Yaska and Panini; Vidagdha Sakalya Brhadaranyaka
checks.note: Confirmed: author of the Ṛgveda Padapāṭha, named by Yāska and Pāṇini; Vidagdha Śākalya questions Yājñavalkya in BĀU 3.9 — some sources identify the two, as the entry reports, with scholarly doubt.

Cited by Pāṇini (1.1.16 'sambuddhau śākalyasyetāv anārṣe'; 8.3.19 'lopaḥ śākalyasya') and in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (3.2.1 'prāṇo vaṃśa iti sthaviraḥ śākalyaḥ'). The Padapāṭha authorship is standard (U01 checked the Padapāṭha).

alt_summary: Author of the word-by-word text (padapāṭha) of the Ṛgveda, cited by Pāṇini (e.g. 1.1.16) and the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. Some Purāṇic accounts identify him with Vidagdha Śākalya, Yājñavalkya's opponent (tch:vidagdha-sakalya).

name: Sakara (Sāgara)

realization_account.text: A prince born from a lotus (Dowman's 'lotus child'); identification of Tōh 2292's 'pa ga ra' with him is by position. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 74): Beings tormented by suffering were given a rain of desirable things; so at the great place of suchness, pressing the nāga king of awareness, the rain of secret-mantra awareness fell on the fortunate male and female vidyādharas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 74 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A prince born from a lotus (Dowman's 'lotus child'); identification of Tōh 2292's 'pa ga ra' with him is by position.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Śākaṭāyana (Pālyakīrti)
summary: Yāpanīya ācārya and grammarian at the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Amoghavarṣa I, author of the Śabdānuśāsana with the Amoghavṛtti and of the Strīnirvāṇa- and Kevalibhukti-prakaraṇas.

checks.note: Text-located: A 3.4.111 'laṅaḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva'; Nir 1.12 'nāmāny ākhyātajānīti śākaṭāyanaḥ'.

alt_summary: Pre-Pāṇinian grammarian cited by Yāska and Pāṇini (e.g. 3.4.111); author of the thesis that all nouns derive from verbs (Nirukta 1.12). Distinct from the Jain grammarian Pālyakīrti who took his name.

name: Śākāyanya
summary: Sage who teaches King Bṛhadratha the knowledge of the self in the Maitrī Upaniṣad, relaying what Prajāpati taught the Vālakhilyas.

evidence: text:sources_raw/prepared/maitri-upanisad/segments.jsonl (eBhāratī Ebharati-9566, Cowell's Bibliotheca Indica recension and numbering)
checks.note: Located: MaiU 1.2 (comes to Bṛhadratha), 2.1-3 (relays the teaching of Maitri and Prajāpati to the Vālakhilyas) and 6.29-30.
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of maitreya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U04 contribution: his teaching to Bṛhadratha is recapitulated in Maitreya Upaniṣad 1.

name: Śakti (son of Vasiṣṭha)
summary: Vasiṣṭha's son, father of Parāśara, to whom Vasiṣṭha teaches yoga in the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā (as recalled).

name: Śākunteya
summary: A brahmin speaker: two tastes, the eliminating and the pacifying (Ca Sū 26.8).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Sakya Paṇḍita Kunga Gyaltsen
summary: Fourth of the five Sakya founders, the most learned Tibetan of his age in the five sciences; trained under Drakpa Gyaltsen and the Kashmiri paṇḍita Śākyaśrībhadra; author of the Treasury of Valid Reasoning, the Discrimination of the Three Vows, Clarifying the Sage's Intent, the Gateway to Learning and the Treasury of Good Sayings; debated and defeated the Hindu scholar Harinanda (tradition's account); went to the Mongol prince Köden in 1244–47 and died at Liangzhou.
alt_names: sa skya paṇḍi ta kun dga' rgyal mtshan
alt_summary: Sakya hierarch whose Treasury of Reasoning re-established Dharmakīrti's denial of real universals in Tibetan epistemology.
notes: Contribution of U41 (pramāṇa side); U47 owns.

name: Ngawang Kunga Tegchen Palbar, 41st Sakya Trizin
summary: Throne-holder of the Sakya from 1959 to 2017, teacher of the Lamdre in exile and worldwide.

name: Śākyabuddhi
summary: Devendrabuddhi's pupil and author of a sub-commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika; Tibetan scholastics group him with Devendrabuddhi as commentators who follow the words closely (classification recalled).

name: Śākyamitra
summary: Commentator on the Tattvasaṃgraha (Kosalālaṃkāra) and member of the Ārya Guhyasamāja circle (Pañcakrama chapter traditions).

name: Śākyaśrībhadra
summary: Kashmiri mahāpaṇḍita who came to Tibet in 1204 and fully ordained Sakya Paṇḍita, teaching him Indian epistemology and the sciences.
notes: U44 also references this id; Sakya contribution.
alt_summary: Kashmiri master who came to Tibet in 1204 and began the 'Kashmiri paṇḍita' Mūlasarvāstivāda ordination lineage, transmitted in the Sakya and other schools.
The Kashmiri paṇḍita (1127/1140s–1225) who went to Tibet in 1204 after the destruction of Vikramaśīla, giving ordination and Kālacakra transmissions.

name: Śālikanātha Miśra
notes: Direct discipleship of Prabhākara is traditional.
summary: Principal systematizer of the Prābhākara school: author of the Prakaraṇapañcikā and of the Ṛjuvimalā and Dīpaśikhā on Prabhākara's works.

name: Śālinātha
summary: Author of the Rasamañjarī.

name: Śalipa

realization_account.text: A low-caste man terrified by the howling of wolves (jackals) near the cremation ground where he lived; a monk taught him to meditate on all sounds as the howl, and through the fear itself he realized. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 21): Skilled painters paint a very terrifying image; seeing it they themselves grow afraid; examined, it is an unestablished image that appears.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 21 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A low-caste man terrified by the howling of wolves (jackals) near the cremation ground where he lived; a monk taught him to meditate on all sounds as the howl, and through the fear itself he realized.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Tōh 2292 spells the name like Śavari; its position (21) and the song's theme of fear fit Abhayadatta's Śalipa.

name: Samādhi (the merchant)
summary: A merchant cast out by his greedy family who still could not stop worrying about them; with Suratha he heard the Devī Māhātmya, and asked the Goddess not for wealth but for the knowledge that frees from attachment, which she granted (DM 13).

checks.note: MkP 81 (the merchant) and 93 (his boon of knowledge) located.

name: Samagāra Haraḷayya
summary: The cobbler śaraṇa whose son's marriage to the daughter of the brāhmaṇa Madhuvarasa precipitated the orthodox reaction and the upheaval at Kalyāṇa; both fathers were put to death by the king's order in the tradition's account.

name: Sāmanta Candraśekhara
summary: Odia astronomer who, with naked-eye instruments of his own making, corrected planetary constants within the siddhānta framework in the Siddhāntadarpaṇa.

name: Samantabhadra

tradition.text: often placed in the 2nd c. CE

realization_account.text: The image of Candraprabha emerged from the liṅga at Vārāṇasī as he sang the hymn to the eighth Tīrthaṅkara.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Digambara poet-philosopher who first set out many-sidedness and the sevenfold predication systematically in the Āptamīmāṃsā, and wrote the Svayambhūstotra, Yuktyanuśāsana and (by tradition) the Ratnakaraṇḍaśrāvakācāra. The tradition tells that he was afflicted by an insatiable hunger (bhasmaka), took leave of monkhood to cure it, and at Vārāṇasī caused the image of Candraprabha to appear from a Śiva-liṅga while reciting his hymn.
alt_summary: The bodhisattva of practice and vows: at the end of the Gaṇḍavyūha Sudhana enters his body and his vows of good conduct (Bhadracarī) conclude the text; in Lotus ch. 28 he rides a six-tusked white elephant to protect those who keep the sūtra; in Nyingma, Samantabhadra is also the name of the primordial buddha (a distinct usage).

name: Samantabhadra (Kun tu bzang po), the primordial buddha
summary: In the Nyingma and Bön the dharmakāya primordial buddha, depicted naked and sky-blue in union with Samantabhadrī: the ground recognized as itself. He is the teacher of the Kunjed Gyalpo and the Seventeen Tantras and speaks the Aspiration of Samantabhadra. Distinct from the bodhisattva Samantabhadra of the sūtras (tch:samantabhadra).
alt_names: the Primordial Protector (gdod ma'i mgon po)

realization_account.text: Primordially liberated by recognizing the ground-appearances as his own display, 'without doing even an instant of virtue', and so never entering saṃsāra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Samarasiṃha
summary: Author of one of the earliest Sanskrit Tājika works (1274).

name: Samartha Rāmdās
summary: Marathi saint (1608–1681/82), born Nārāyaṇ Ṭhosar at Jāmb, who fled his wedding at the word 'sāvadhān' ('beware'), spent twelve years in austerity and Rāma-japa at Ṭākaḷī near Nāsik and twelve years on pilgrimage, then founded maṭhs and Māruti temples, taught the Dāsbodh and Manāce Śloka and, in Marathi tradition, guided Śivājī.

realization_account.text: Rāma and Hanumān appeared to him as a boy; Rāma initiated him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The extent of his relation to Śivājī is debated by historians.

name: Sāmaśravas
summary: Yājñavalkya's pupil, told to drive home Janaka's thousand cows (BAU 3.1.2).

checks.note: Located: BĀU 3.1.2 ('svam eva brahmacāriṇam uvācaitāḥ somyodaja sāmaśravā3 iti').

name: Śamathadeva
summary: Compiler of the Upāyikā, which gives in full the sūtras quoted in the Kośa.

name: Sambhavanātha
summary: The third Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the horse. Parents: Jitāri and Senā. Born at Śrāvastī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the third of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Śambhu Bhaṭṭa
summary: Pupil of Khaṇḍadeva; author of the Prabhāvalī on the Bhāṭṭadīpikā.

name: Śambhunātha
summary: Abhinavagupta's teacher in the Kaula form of the Trika, from Jālandhara; the Tantrāloka credits him with the teaching of the seven ānandas of the breath (TĀ 5.52) and with the Kula ritual of ch. 29.
notes: Teacher-name Sumati(nātha) from TĀ ch. 1 as quoted in Jayaratha (low confidence on the relationship).

name: Sambhūtavijaya
summary: Elder who with Bhadrabāhu succeeded Yaśobhadra; teacher of Sthūlabhadra.

name: Samprati
summary: Maurya king, grandson of Aśoka, converted by Suhastin, who (Śvetāmbara tradition) spread Jainism beyond Magadha and built many temples.

name: Śāṃśapāyana
summary: Disciple of Romaharṣaṇa and maker of one of the root Purāṇa-saṃhitās (VP 3.6.17-18); absent from the Bhāgavata's list of six paurāṇikas, which names Trayyāruṇi, Kaśyapa, Sāvarṇi, Akṛtavraṇa, Vaiśampāyana and Hārīta instead (BhP 12.7.5).

checks.note: VP 3.6.17-18 located; absent from BhP 12.7.5 as stated.

name: Samudra

realization_account.text: A pearl-diver; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 83): Realizing the unborn but lacking experience is like an ogress carrying a child in her hand; not separated from experience and the natural state, that too is like an elephant entering a pond.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 83 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A pearl-diver; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Whether the second image is praise or warning is unclear.

name: Saṃvanana Āṅgirasa
summary: Seer of RV 10.191, the closing hymn of concord.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'saṃvanana āṅgirasaḥ'.

name: Saṃvartaka
summary: Named first among the paramahaṃsas who live with unmanifest marks and conduct (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, bhiksuka, naradaparivrajaka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Samyeong Yujeong 四溟惟政
summary: Hyujeong's heir, monk-soldier and envoy to Japan.

name: Sanaka
summary: Eldest of the four mind-born sons of Brahmā (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra), whose question on separating mind from the guṇas occasions the Haṃsa Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.13).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: BhP 11.13.16 'putrā hiraṇyagarbhasya mānasāḥ sanakādayaḥ'.

alt_summary: U23 contribution: named by Lakṣmīdhara as author of one of the five Śubhāgamas that teach the Vedic Samaya way.

name: Śāṇakavāsin
summary: Disciple of Ānanda and teacher of Upagupta in the Sarvāstivāda succession of masters.

name: Sanandana
summary: Named by the Sāṃkhya Sūtra (6.69): 'the (owner–owned relation of puruṣa and prakṛti) is caused by the subtle body, says the teacher Sanandana'. Gauḍapāda (on SK 1, 43) names Sanaka, Sanandana (Sananda), Sanātana and Sanatkumāra among Brahmā's sons, in whom the dispositions arose naturally at sixteen.
notes: Whether the SS's teacher is the Kumāra of Purāṇic lore is not stated in the text.
alt_summary: U23 contribution: named by Lakṣmīdhara as author of one of the five Śubhāgamas that teach the Vedic Samaya way.

name: Sanātan Dās Bāul
summary: Bankura Bāul master (Khayerbuni ākhṛā), respected as a sādhaka-singer of the older style.

name: Sanātana Gosvāmī
summary: Rūpa's elder brother, formerly Sākar Mallik, minister at Gauḍa; taught by Caitanya at Vārāṇasī for two months (CC 2.20–24); author of the Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta and the Vaiṣṇavatoṣaṇī; associated with the Haribhaktivilāsa.

name: Sanatkumāra
summary: Teacher of Nārada in ChU 7: leads him from name to plenitude (bhūman) and shows him 'the far shore beyond darkness'; 'they call him Skanda' (ChU 7.26.2).

checks.note: Located: ChU 7.1.1 and 7.26.2 ('bhagavān sanatkumāraḥ … taṃ skanda ity ācakṣate').
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of kalagnirudra, atharvasikha, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.

Existence and roles confirmed (KūP 1.10.13-14; 1.1.17; NP 1.92.5; BhP 6.3.20). But 'eldest of the four Kumāras' is not supported: BhP 3.12.4 lists Sanaka, Sananda, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra (Sanatkumāra last), VP 1.7.9 speaks of 'Sanandana and the others', and KūP 1.10.13 lists Sananda first. The claim should be dropped or sourced (Phase D).

alt_summary: Eldest of the four Kumāras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra), mind-born sons of Brahmā who refused to procreate and remained celibate knowers (VP 1.7; KūP 1.10.13-14); the first avatāra in BhP 1.3.6; with his brothers he instructs Nārada in the Nārada Purāṇa; the first Upapurāṇa bears his name (KūP 1.1.17).
Mind-born sage who, in the Vṛtra Gītā, teaches the greatness of Viṣṇu and the six colours of living beings (12.271).
U23 contribution: named by Lakṣmīdhara as author of one of the five Śubhāgamas that teach the Vedic Samaya way.
U04 contribution: asks Kālāgnirudra about the tripuṇḍra (Kālāgnirudra) and, with Pippalāda and Aṅgiras, asks Atharvan about the first meditation (Atharvaśikhā).
notes: U05's contribution; his teaching in Chāndogya 7 is covered by U03.

name: Sanatsujāta
summary: An ever-youthful sage (kumāra) summoned by Vidura's thought, who teaches Dhṛtarāṣṭra that heedlessness is death and heedfulness immortality, and describes the brāhmaṇa, silence, the virtues and the shining Brahman seen by yogins (5.41–45).

checks.note: This was on the skeleton's least-sure list. The local e-text of the Haṃsa reads 'sanatsujāta uvāca', which confirms the entry for this recension. The Adyar 1920 edition (Muktabodha M00107, with Brahmayogin's commentary) reads 'sanatkumāra uvāca', and Brahmayogin's commentary also names Sanatkumāra. The attribution to Sanatsujāta therefore holds only for the e-text recension. The entry hedges with 'in this recension', which is correct; a reviewer may wish to add the variant.
Located as described; his status as Brahmā's mind-born son is not checked, as the entry itself notes.

notes: The tradition counts him among Brahmā's mind-born sons (not checked here).
alt_summary: One of Brahmā's mind-born sons; in this recension of the Haṃsa Upaniṣad he teaches Gautama the haṃsa-vidyā that Śiva told Pārvatī.

name: Śāṇavāsa (Shangna Hexiu 商那和修)
summary: Third patriarch in the Chan list, successor of Ānanda.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 3.

name: Śāṇḍilya
summary: Named author of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā: all this is brahman; the self within the heart, smaller than a grain and greater than the worlds, is brahman, which 'I shall attain on departing' (ChU 3.14.1-4).
notes: The same teaching appears in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.3 (moderate). Later works (Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra, Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad) are attributed to a Śāṇḍilya; identity not asserted here.

checks.note: Text-located: the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā at ŚB 10.6.3.1–2 (= ChU 3.14), and Śāṇḍilya in the Agnicayana vaṃśa at ŚB 10.6.5.9.

Located: ChU 3.14.4 ('iti ha smāha śāṇḍilyaḥ'). The note's parallel ŚB 10.6.3 is confirmed in the GRETIL Mādhyandina ŚB: 10.6.3.1-2 has 'satyaṃ brahmety upāsīta … kratumayo 'yaṃ puruṣaḥ … manomayaṃ prāṇaśarīraṃ bhārūpam …'.
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of sandilya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U25 contribution: the sage to whom the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra is attributed; in the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (NBS 18) his definition of devotion is love 'not opposed to delight in the self'; in the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra he holds that devotion bears on both the Lord and the self (as recalled).
U04 contribution: disciple of Atharvan in the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad, who, not finding brahmavidyā in the four Vedas, asks for it.

The authority of the fire-altar books of the Śatapatha (6–10), whose meditation on the self 'made of mind, with breath for body, of the form of light', smaller than a grain yet greater than the worlds, is the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā (ŚB 10.6.3; ChU 3.14). The Bhakti Sūtra ascribed to a Śāṇḍilya (U25) is a separate, much later attribution.
Sage who relates the Jayākhya's teaching to other sages; a Pāñcarātra account quoted by Śaṅkara (BSBh 2.2.45) says he took up this teaching after not finding the highest good in the four Vedas.
alt_notes: U25 contribution only; identity with the Upaniṣadic Śāṇḍilya (ChU 3.14) and with the Pāñcarātra Śāṇḍilya is the tradition's, not asserted here.
Contribution from U08.

name: Saṅgamāditya
summary: Descendant of the Tryambaka siddhas (son of the fifteenth, who married a brāhmaṇa woman) who came wandering to Kashmir; great-great-grandfather of Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.115-119).

name: Saṅgārava
summary: A brahmin taught the water similes for the hindrances (SN 46.55).

name: Saṅghabhadra

tradition.text: Contemporary of Vasubandhu (Xuanzang)

realization_account.text: Xuanzang relates that he spent twelve years composing a refutation of the Kośa and set out to debate Vasubandhu, who declined; Saṅghabhadra died before they met and Vasubandhu renamed his work Nyāyānusāra.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great Kashmiri Vaibhāṣika who defended orthodoxy against Vasubandhu's Sautrāntika criticisms in the Nyāyānusāra, developing new formulations (e.g. on the activity of dharmas).

name: Saṅghadāsagaṇi
summary: Author of the Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya; a Saṅghadāsagaṇi is also author of the Vasudevahiṇḍī (whether the same person is uncertain).

name: Saṅghamittā
summary: Daughter of Emperor Asoka and a bhikkhunī who, by the chronicles, brought the bhikkhunī ordination and a branch of the Bodhi tree to Laṅkā.

tradition.text: 3rd c. BCE, in the reign of Devānampiya Tissa

notes: Known from the Dīpavaṃsa and Mahāvaṃsa (not in the canon).

name: Saṅghanandi (Sengqie Nanti 僧伽難提)
summary: Seventeenth patriarch in the Chan list.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 17.

name: Saṅghapāla (Sengqiepoluo 僧伽婆羅)
summary: Monk from Funan who translated the Vimuttimagga and other texts into Chinese at the Liang court in the early 6th century.

name: Sangye Lingpa (sangs rgyas gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer of the Lama Gongdü (1364).

name: Rigongpa Sangye Nyentön
alt_names: ri gong pa sangs rgyas gnyan ston
summary: Fourth of the Shangpa 'seven jewels'.

name: Sangye Tönpa Tsöndrü Senge
alt_names: sangs rgyas ston pa brtson 'grus seng ge
summary: Fifth of the Shangpa 'seven jewels' (counting Vajradhara and Niguma), after whom the Shangpa spread through several disciples.
notes: The counting of the 'seven jewels' (Vajradhara, Niguma, Khyungpo Naljor, Mokchokpa, Kyergangpa, Nyentön, Sangye Tönpa) is from memory.

name: Sañjaya

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Dhṛtarāṣṭra's charioteer and counsellor, given divine sight by Vyāsa to see and report the battle (6.2); he narrates the Gītā to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and says he heard it 'by the grace of Vyāsa' directly from Kṛṣṇa (18.75).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Divine sight granted by Vyāsa (6.2.10) and "vyāsaprasādāt" (18.75) located.

alt_summary: The narrator of the Gītā's frame, reporting the scene on the battlefield to Dhṛtarāṣṭra in answer to his question (1.2 onward; 1.24, 1.47, 2.1, 2.9–10).
Narrator to Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the showing of the universal form (11.9–14), of Arjuna's trembling homage (11.35) and of Kṛṣṇa's resuming his gentle form (11.50).

name: Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta
summary: One of the six famous teachers, the type of the 'eel-wriggler'. DN 2 reports that asked whether there is another world, spontaneously born beings, fruit of deeds or a Tathāgata after death, he refused every alternative ('I do not say it is so, nor thus, nor otherwise, nor not so, nor not not so'); King Ajātasattu calls him the most foolish of the six. The Vinaya tells of the wanderer Sañjaya of Rājagaha, teacher of Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who left him with 250 wanderers for the Buddha, whereupon hot blood gushed from Sañjaya's mouth.

scholarly.text: c. 5th c. BCE (contemporary of the Buddha and Mahāvīra)

notes: The Vinaya (Mv 1.23) says only 'Sañjaya the wanderer'; the identification with Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta of DN 2 is the commentaries' and is questioned by some scholars. Do not confuse with tch:sanjaya (the Mahābhārata's narrator).

name: Śaṅkara (Ādi Śaṅkarācārya)

tradition.text: 788–820 CE in the commonest traditional reckoning; 509–477 BCE in the Kāñcī and Dvārakā maṭha reckonings

scholarly.text: c. 700–750 CE (Hacker, Nakamura); other scholars up to c. 800

places: Kedāranātha or Kāñcī (death, by differing accounts)

realization_account.text: The Śaṅkaradigvijaya tells that Śaṅkara, an only son of Śivaguru and Āryāmbā, obtained his mother's consent to renounce when a crocodile seized him in the river; that Govinda initiated him; that Vyāsa appeared to him at Kāśī and extended his life from sixteen to thirty-two years; and that he ascended the Sarvajña-pīṭha in Kashmir.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Scholarly consensus (Hacker, Mayeda, Ingalls) accepts the BSBh, the principal Upaniṣad commentaries, the Gītā commentary and the Upadeśasāhasrī; most prakaraṇas and stotras are doubted.
summary: The systematizer of Advaita Vedānta: commentator on the Brahma Sūtras, the principal Upaniṣads and the Gītā, author of the Upadeśasāhasrī; in the tradition's account a child renunciant from Kālaṭi who studied under Govinda, debated Maṇḍana Miśra, founded the four āmnāya maṭhas and the Daśanāmī order, revived Vedic dharma and died at thirty-two.

checks.note: Text-located: BSBh 3.4.20 (GRETIL) cites the Jābāla ('brahmacaryaṃ parisamāpya gṛhī bhavet … pravrajet'), and BSBh 3.4.17 quotes 'brahmacaryād eva pravrajet'. A Nṛsiṃhapūrvatāpanīya-bhāṣya under Śaṅkara's name exists locally (eBhāratī). Its authenticity is questioned by scholars, as the entry says; that was not checked further.
Works and characterization confirmed; the two minor commentaries are traditionally credited to him and their authorship is disputed.

alt_summary: Author of the oldest extant Gītā commentary, which reads the Gītā as teaching liberation by knowledge of the self with renunciation, action serving to purify the mind; also credited with commentaries on the Sanatsujātīya and the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

U23 contribution: in the Śrīvidyā tradition's account Śaṅkara is the author of the Saundaryalaharī, the Triśatī-bhāṣya and hymns to the Goddess, an upāsaka of Śrīvidyā in the line of Gauḍapāda, and the one who installed Śrīcakras at Śṛṅgeri (Śāradā) and Kāñcī (Kāmākṣī) and placed Śrīcakras in the earrings of Akhilāṇḍeśvarī at Tiruvāṉaikkā; scholars doubt the ascriptions.
U28 contribution: the Yogatārāvalī, a short rājayoga poem on nādānusandhāna and the mindless state, is ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya; scholars do not accept the attribution.

U04 contribution: cites the Jābāla (4) for renunciation directly from studentship (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 3.4.20); a commentary on the Nṛsiṃhatāpanī is attributed to him (questioned by scholars). The Daśanāmī tradition traces its four maṭhas to him (Maṭhāmnāya).

(Yoga unit contribution) The Pātañjalayogaśāstravivaraṇa, a sub-commentary on the Yoga-bhāṣya, is ascribed in its colophons to Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, pupil of Govinda; whether this is the Advaita teacher is disputed.
U31 contribution: tradition ascribes to Śaṅkara the Prapañcasāra, a manual of mantra-śāstra (the ascription is doubted by scholars).
alt_notes: U05's contribution only (Gītā and epic works).

name: Śaṅkara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Son of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa; author of the Mīmāṃsābālaprakāśa and a critique of Appayya's Vidhirasāyana.

name: Śaṅkara Miśra
summary: Mithilā scholar, author of the Upaskāra on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra (the standard commentary until Candrānanda's was recovered) and of the Vādivinoda.

name: Śaṅkaradeva
summary: Founder of the Ekaśaraṇa Dharma (tradition 1449–1568), of the Śiromaṇi Bhuyan family of Bardowā; orphaned and raised by his grandmother, he studied under Mahendra Kandali, made two long pilgrimages, preached exclusive devotion to Kṛṣṇa through the name, converted Mādhavadeva, and — persecuted in the Ahom kingdom — continued under the Koch kings Naranārāyaṇa and Cilarāi. Poet of the Kīrtana-ghoṣā, bargīts and aṅkīyā nāṭs; called the Mahāpuruṣa.

scholarly.text: c. 1449–1568 (the traditional span of 119 years is sometimes questioned)

realization_account.text: Recognised as the Mahāpuruṣa; Assamese hagiographies tell of a meeting with Caitanya at Purī (not found in Bengali sources).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Śaṅkarānanda
summary: 14th-c. Advaitin saluted as guru in the opening verse of the Pañcadaśī; author of the Ātmapurāṇa and of Upaniṣad and Gītā commentaries.

queries: Shankarananda Advaita teacher of Vidyaranya Upanishad dipika commentary
checks.note: This was on the skeleton's least-sure list. Śaṅkarānanda, c. 13th-14th c., wrote Upaniṣad-dīpikās and the Ātmapurāṇa and was a pupil of Ānandātman. Sources call him the guru of Sāyaṇa and, in tradition, of Vidyāraṇya. The entry's 'c. 14th c.' is compatible.

alt_summary: Advaitin commentator (Dīpikās) on many Upaniṣads including Atharvan ones; tradition makes him a teacher of Vidyāraṇya.

name: Śaṅkaranandana
summary: Kashmiri Buddhist logician, known as 'the brahmin', author of works on exclusion and necessary connection and of a commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika.

name: Śaṅkarasvāmin
summary: Pupil of Dignāga (Chinese tradition) and author of the Nyāyapraveśa, the primer of East Asian logic.

name: Sāṅkṛti
summary: U28 contribution: the sage who wanders the earth seeking yoga and receives it from Dattātreya in the Dattātreyayogaśāstra; at the end he attains all powers by Dattātreya's grace (DYŚ 148).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of darsana, avadhuta, aksi, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: Sage who questions Dattātreya in the Darśana and Avadhūta Upaniṣads and visits the sun's world in the Akṣi Upaniṣad; at the end of the Darśana he abides fearless in the Self.

name: Ṣaṇmukhasvāmi
summary: A later Vīraśaiva ascetic and vacanakāra.

name: Sansheng Huiran 三聖慧然
summary: Disciple of Linji named as compiler of the Linji lu.

name: Santājī Jagnāḍe
summary: Oil-presser (Telī) companion of Tukārām who wrote down his abhaṅgas and sang with him.

name: Santāna
summary: Number 16 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Śāntarakṣita
alt_names: Khenpo Bodhisattva (mkhan po bo dhi sa twa)

tradition.text: invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen; with Padmasambhava founded Samye

realization_account.text: Invited to Tibet, he taught the ten virtues and dependent origination; when local spirits obstructed the work he advised the king to invite Padmasambhava; he consecrated Samye, ordained the first seven Tibetan monks and, foreseeing a dispute over the view, left instructions that his student Kamalaśīla be invited to answer it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Abbot of Nālandā who synthesized Madhyamaka, Yogācāra and Dharmakīrti's epistemology (Madhyamakālaṃkāra, Tattvasaṅgraha), founded Samye and ordained the first Tibetan monks.
alt_summary: Nālandā abbot and founder of Yogācāra-Madhyamaka, who also wrote the Tattvasaṃgraha — the great Dharmakīrtian critique of rival systems — and a commentary on the Vādanyāya.

For the Nyingma, the first of the 'abbot, master and king' (mkhan slob chos gsum): the Nālandā abbot who ordained the first seven Tibetan monks, founded Samye with Padmasambhava and Trisong Detsen, and advised the king to invite Padmasambhava.
Nālandā abbot (8th c.). This unit records that he ordained the first Tibetan monks at Samye according to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, the origin of the 'lower Vinaya' lineage.
notes: Contribution of U41 (pramāṇa side).

name: Śāntideva

realization_account.text: A prince who, on the eve of his coronation, saw Mañjuśrī seated on the throne in a dream and renounced; at Nālandā he seemed only to eat, sleep and relieve himself ('Bhusuku'); asked to recite before the assembly, he taught the Bodhicaryāvatāra and at the verse 'when neither being nor non-being remains before the mind' (9.34) rose into the sky and vanished, while his voice continued; the Śikṣāsamuccaya was later found in his cell (Bu-ston; Tāranātha; a Nepalese Sanskrit hagiography).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Hagiographical details from memory (moderate). Scholarly: an earlier shorter recension of the BCA survives in Dunhuang.
summary: Nālandā monk-poet, author of the Bodhicaryāvatāra and the Śikṣāsamuccaya, the classic Indian manuals of the bodhisattva's awakening mind, patience, exchange of self and other and wisdom.

name: Śāntinātha
summary: The sixteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the deer (antelope). Parents: Viśvasena and Acirā. Born at Hastināpura; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. He was also the fifth world-emperor (cakravartin) before renouncing; in a previous life as King Megharatha he offered his own flesh to save a pigeon from a hawk. He is invoked for peace (śānti) and widely worshipped.

summary: Tang master of Muzhou (Zhejiang) called 'the later Shandao', who taught children to recite by paying them a coin per recitation and led large recitation assemblies; fifth patriarch in the Fozu tongji list.
notes: The coin episode is widely told; recalled, moderate.

name: Sharawa Yönten Drak
summary: Kadam master, disciple of Potowa, renowned for his teaching of the Abhidharma and mind training; teacher of Chekawa, who studied with him for years after seeking out the teaching of the Eight Verses.
alt_names: sha ra ba yon tan grags

name: Shardza Tashi Gyaltsen (shar rdza bkra shis rgyal mtshan)
summary: Bön Dzogchen master and prolific author of Kham (history of Bön, Dzogchen manuals), who by tradition attained the rainbow body at his death.

realization_account.text: His body shrank and dissolved into light at death (rainbow body).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Shechen Gyaltsap Gyurme Pema Namgyal (zhe chen rgyal tshab 'gyur med pad+ma rnam rgyal)
notes: Catalogue holds works under his name (OpenPecha P000010, P000011, P000159, P000160).
summary: Nyingma master of Shechen, student of Mipham and teacher of Dilgo Khyentse, author of collected advice, praises and commentaries.

name: Shenchen Luga (gshen chen klu dga')
summary: Principal Bön treasure revealer (discoveries of 1017), from whose disciples descend the great Bön families (Dru, Zhu, Pa).
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Shengan Shixian
summary: Qing monk famed for his Exhortation to Arouse the Mind of Awakening (Quan fa putixin wen), which joins bodhicitta to recitation; eleventh patriarch in the later list.

name: Shengchang
summary: Song monk of Hangzhou who formed the Jingxing she (Society of Pure Conduct) of officials and monks modelled on Huiyuan's, writing out the Huayan chapter on pure conduct in his blood; last of the seven patriarchs in the Fozu tongji and fourth successor in the Lebang wenlei.

name: Heze Shenhui 荷澤神會
summary: Disciple of Huineng who at the Huatai assembly (732) and in Luoyang attacked the Northern school as collateral and gradual and proclaimed Huineng the true Sixth Patriarch; raised funds for the state by ordinations during the An Lushan rebellion; in 796 an imperial commission recognised him as seventh patriarch. In the Zongbao Platform Sūtra Huineng calls him a mere 'follower of intellectual understanding'.

name: Shenxiu 神秀 (Datong)
summary: Senior disciple of Hongren and founder of the Northern school; invited to the court by Empress Wu (701) and honoured as 'Dharma lord of the two capitals'. In the Platform Sūtra he writes the verse 'the body is the bodhi tree, the mind like a bright mirror's stand; wipe it constantly' and later sends Zhicheng to Huineng, praising Huineng's 'wisdom without a teacher'.

name: Sherab Jungne
summary: Disciple of Jigten Sumgön who compiled his vajra statements as the Gongchig ('Single Intent').

name: Jetsün Sherab Senge
summary: Disciple of Tsongkhapa who founded the Lower Tantric College (Gyümé) in 1433 to transmit the Guhyasamāja.

name: Shinbutsu
summary: Shinran's leading disciple in Takada (Shimotsuke), head of the Takada community from which the Takada branch descends.

name: Shinchi Kakushin 心地覺心 (Hottō kokushi)
summary: Studied under Wumen Huikai and brought the Wumen guan to Japan (1254); regarded by the Fuke school as its founder in Japan.

name: Shinkyō
summary: Ippen's successor who organised the itinerant followers into the Ji-shū order and wrote its regulations.

name: Shinran

realization_account.text: After twenty years as a hall monk on Mt Hiei he secluded himself in the Rokkakudō for a hundred days; on the ninety-fifth dawn Prince Shōtoku (Kannon) appeared in a dream, and he went to Hōnen (Eshinni's letters; Godenshō). He 'abandoned the miscellaneous practices and took refuge in the primal vow' in 1201 (Kyōgyōshinshō postscript).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Hōnen's disciple who, laicised and exiled to Echigo in 1207, called himself 'Gutoku' (foolish bald-head), neither monk nor layman, married Eshinni and taught in the Kantō for some twenty years before returning to Kyoto to write. His Kyōgyōshinshō presents teaching, practice, shinjin and realization as Amida's gift; shinjin is the true cause; the evil person is the true object of the vow. Founder (in the tradition's reckoning) of Jōdo Shinshū; he himself said he had not a single disciple.

name: Shishuang Chuyuan (Ciming) 石霜楚圓
summary: Linji master, teacher of both Yangqi and Huanglong.

name: Shishuang Qingzhu 石霜慶諸
summary: Master who asked 'how do you step forward from the top of a hundred-foot pole?' (Wumenguan case 46).

name: Shitou Xiqian 石頭希遷
summary: Heir of Qingyuan in Hunan, author of the Cantongqi; with Mazu one of the 'two great masters' of the later 8th c. — 'Jiangxi is ruled by Daji, Hunan by Shitou'.

name: Shiv Dayal Singh (Soamiji Maharaj)

realization_account.text: He practised surat-śabd yoga in a back room for some fifteen years before opening satsang to the public in 1861.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Khatri of Agra who, after years of inner practice, opened public satsang on Basant Pañcamī 1861 and founded Radhasoami; his discourses and poems are the Sār Bachan.

name: Shōgei
summary: Chinzei scholar who systematised the school's doctrine and its fivefold transmission (gojū sōden).

name: Shōju Rōjin (Dōkyō Etan) 道鏡慧端
summary: Hermit master of the Ōtōkan line who humbled Hakuin after his first awakening and deepened his practice.

name: Shōkai
summary: Ippen's disciple (and, by some accounts, younger brother) who compiled the Ippen Hijiri-e (1299).

name: Shōkū
summary: Hōnen's disciple (who helped compile the Senchakushū), founder of the Seizan line.

name: Shönu Gyalchok
summary: Compiler (with Könchok Gyaltsen) of the anthology Mind Training: The Great Collection.

name: Shōtatsu
summary: Seizan monk of Dazaifu, Ippen's teacher.

name: Shoushan Shengnian 首山省念
summary: Linji master; the 'bamboo staff' case (Wumenguan 43).

name: Shūhō Myōchō 宗峰妙超 (Daitō kokushi)
summary: Heir of Nanpo, founder of Daitokuji; said to have lived twenty years among beggars under Kyoto's Gojō bridge after awakening.

name: Shunjō
summary: Chion-in abbot to whom the compilation of the 48-scroll illustrated biography of Hōnen is traditionally ascribed.

name: T. G. Siddappārādhya
summary: Twentieth-century author of a Vīraśaiva commentary on the Bhagavad Gītā (1965).

name: Siddha Kṛṣṇadāsa Bābā (of Govardhana)
summary: 18th-c. Braj renunciate associated with manuals (guṭikā/paddhati) of meditative service in the eightfold daily play and the siddha-praṇālī tradition.

name: Siddhanañjeśa Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Sanskrit Śivasiddhāntacandrikā, of the Pūvalli Pañcavarṇa Bṛhanmaṭha.

name: Siddhanātha Śivācārya
summary: Father of Śivayogi Śivācārya, praised as 'crest-jewel of the Vīraśaivas' and a determiner of Śiva-siddhānta (SSM 1.17–20).

name: Siddharāma
summary: Siddharāma (Siddharāmēśvara) of Sonnalige, the builder of tanks and temples for Mallikārjuna who, in the tradition's account, was challenged by Allama, received liṅga-initiation from Cennabasava and joined the śaraṇas; vacanas signed Kapilasiddhamallikārjuna.

realization_account.text: A karmayogin devoted to Mallikārjuna of Śrīśaila, he was met at Sonnalige by Allama, who mocked his works; he went to Kalyāṇa, received liṅga-initiation and later attained union at Sonnalige.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The Tattvapradīpikā's introduction calls the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's author a member of the lineage of Siddharāma, 'born from the glance of Revaṇasiddha' (e-text M00207).

name: Siddhārth Gautam Rām
summary: Present head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi (from 1978, as commonly reported), a disciple of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām.

name: Siddhasena Divākara

tradition.text: contemporary of Vikramāditya of Ujjain

realization_account.text: Pārśvanātha's image emerged from the liṅga at the Mahākāla temple when he recited his hymn (legend).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Logician-poet revered by both sects: author of the Prakrit Sanmatitarka on the standpoints and of hymns (dvātriṃśikās); the Nyāyāvatāra and Kalyāṇamandira are ascribed to him (disputed). He held that in the omniscient knowledge and perception are one. The tradition tells that he proposed rendering the Prakrit scriptures into Sanskrit, was sent into twelve years' exile for it, and during it made Pārśva's image appear at the Mahākāla temple of Ujjain, converting king Vikramāditya.

name: Siddhasena (as horā author)
summary: Horā author named by Varāhamihira among those who taught longevity (BJ 7.7); not to be assumed identical with the Jain logician Siddhasena Divākara.
notes: Known only from citations in Varāhamihira and his commentators.

name: Siddhasenagaṇi
summary: Śvetāmbara commentator on the Tattvārthasūtra and its bhāṣya.
notes: Distinct from Siddhasena Divākara.

name: Sigāla
summary: A young householder worshipping the six directions, taught the lay discipline (DN 31).

name: Śikhaṇḍin
summary: Great chariot-warrior of the Pāṇḍava side who blows his conch (1.17). (The epic's account of Śikhaṇḍin's sex change is not in these verses; gender left 'unknown'.)
notes: The Gītā uses the masculine; the epic tells that Śikhaṇḍin was born female. Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.17.

name: Sikhī
summary: The second of the seven Buddhas of DN 14 (thirty-one aeons ago).

name: Śikhidhvaja
summary: King of Mālava who renounced his kingdom for forest austerities but found no peace until his wife Cūḍālā, disguised as Kumbha, taught him that renunciation of everything includes renunciation of the mind that renounces.

checks.note: See Cūḍālā; śikhidhvajapravrajyā 6.88, sarvatyāga 6.96.

realization_account.text: After giving up even his ascetic's belongings and his body-identification he entered a long samādhi, awoke liberated and returned to rule with Cūḍālā.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Śikṣānanda
summary: Khotanese monk (652-710) who translated the 80-fascicle Avataṃsaka (695-699) and the seven-fascicle Laṅkāvatāra; the Kṣitigarbha Pūrvapraṇidhāna Sūtra is attributed to him.

name: Śīlabhadra
summary: Abbot of Nālandā, pupil of Dharmapāla, who taught Xuanzang the Yogācārabhūmi; Xuanzang reports that he was cured of a painful illness after being told in a dream to await a Chinese monk.

name: Śilaka Śālāvatya
summary: One of three experts on the udgītha who discuss the support of the sāman (ChU 1.8).

checks.note: Located: ChU 1.8.1-8.

name: Śīlāṅka
summary: U33 contribution: Śvetāmbara commentator on the Ācārāṅga and Sūtrakṛtāṅga, whose commentary derives the 363 rival views and explains the ajñānika maxim 'ignorance is better'.
alt_summary: 9th-c. Śvetāmbara commentator on the Ācārāṅga and Sūtrakṛtāṅga; a Śīlāṅka also wrote the Cauppannamahāpurisacariya (identity debated).

name: Ṣimānanda Dīkṣita
alt_names: Kṣemānanda (identification suggested by the e-text's editor, uncertain)
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana on the Tattvasamāsa; by his own account son of Raghunandana, a Kānyakubja brahmin living at Iṣṭikāpura.

name: Sīmandhara
summary: One of the twenty 'living' (viharamāna) Tīrthaṅkaras now teaching in the Mahāvideha region, where liberation is always possible. Digambaras hold that Kundakunda travelled to him to hear the teaching; he is also the focus of devotion in the Kanji Swami movement.

name: Siṃhabhūpāla
summary: Recherla king and author of the Saṅgītasudhākara commentary on the Saṅgītaratnākara (and of the Rasārṇavasudhākara on dramaturgy).

name: Siṃhasūri Gaṇi (Vādikṣamāśramaṇa)
summary: Śvetāmbara commentator on Mallavādin's Nayacakra.

name: Siṃhatilaka Sūri
summary: Śvetāmbara author of works on the Sūrimantra and the Vardhamāna-vidyā.

name: Siṅgirāja
summary: Kannada poet of the Amala Basavarāja Cāritra.

name: Sirāj Sāṃi
summary: Fakir (a palanquin-bearer by some accounts) who was Lalon's guru; named in the signature (bhaṇitā) of Lalon's songs.

name: Ciṟuttoṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. General of the Pallava king who led the capture of Vātāpi; retiring to serve devotees, he was visited by Śiva as a Bhairava ascetic who asked for a meal cooked from an only son of five; he and his wife Veṇkāṭṭu Naṅkai cooked their son Cīrāḷaṉ; the ascetic bade them call the boy to eat with him, and the boy came running, alive.

realization_account.text: General of the Pallava king who led the capture of Vātāpi; retiring to serve devotees, he was visited by Śiva as a Bhairava ascetic who asked for a meal cooked from an only son of five; he and his wife Veṇkāṭṭu Naṅkai cooked their son Cīrāḷaṉ; the ascetic bade them call the boy to eat with him, and the boy came running, alive.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Sītā
summary: Daughter of Janaka of Mithilā and Rāma's wife; the Rāmāyaṇa's exemplar of the devoted wife, taught by Anasūyā (2.117–119).

checks.note: Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: AR 1.1.32-43 ('rāmaṃ viddhi paraṃ brahma ...').

alt_summary: In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa she instructs Hanumān (1.1.31-43): Rāma is the non-dual Brahman and she is primal nature (mūlaprakṛti), the agent of all the deeds superimposed on him.

name: Śītalanātha
summary: The tenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the śrīvatsa mark in Śvetāmbara lists (a wish-fulfilling tree in some Digambara lists; low confidence). Parents: Dṛḍharatha and Nandā. Born at Bhadrilapura (Bhaddilapura); attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the tenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha
summary: Author of the Mahānayaprakāśa on the Krama in Old Kashmiri with a Sanskrit commentary.

name: Situ Paṇchen Chökyi Jungne (the eighth Tai Situpa)
alt_names: si tu paN chen chos kyi 'byung gnas
summary: Scholar of grammar, medicine and art, editor of the Derge Kangyur (1733), founder of Palpung; revived the Karma Kagyu and favoured the shentong reading.

name: Śiva
summary: In U06's texts: speaker of the Īśvara Gītā (to the sages), the Śiva Gītā (to Rāma), the Guru Gītā (to Pārvatī) and the Rudra Gītā (to the Pracetās); narrator of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa to Pārvatī; in the Mokṣopāya he teaches Vasiṣṭha the true worship of the divine as consciousness (MU 6.31-46).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of yogasikha, yogakundali, tejobindu, maitreya, sukarahasya, hamsa, jabala, muktika, in the roles the summary gives. Speaker-roles checked: Hiraṇyagarbha asks Maheśvara (Yogaśikhā 1); padmaja asks Śaṅkara (Yogakuṇḍalī 3); Kumāra and Śiva (Tejobindu 2-4); Mahādeva teaches Maitreya (Maitreya 2); the tāraka given at Kāśī (Muktikā 1.19-21) and at Avimukta (Jābāla 1). A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
All cited references located.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Speaker of the Īśvara Gītā (KP 2.1-11), Śiva Gītā, Guru Gītā and Rudra Gītā (BhP 4.24.33-79); verified in each local text.

alt_summary: U23 contribution: as Bhairava / Parameśvara he reveals the Śrīvidyā tantras to the Goddess (Vāmakeśvara, Yoginīhṛdaya, Tantrarāja, Jñānārṇava); as Kāmeśvara he is Lalitā's consort; he is one of the twelve great worshippers of the vidyā.
Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): as Bhairava he answers the Goddess in the Rasārṇava; mercury is 'equal to me, born from my limbs, the rasa of my body' (Rasārṇava 1.36).
Named by Kṛṣṇa, as Śaṅkara, among his manifestations: 'of the Rudras I am Śaṅkara' (Bhagavad Gītā 10.23).

In the epic, Śiva teaches Umā dharma (13.126–134), is named as the proclaimer of the Pāśupata knowledge (12.337.62), grants Arjuna the Pāśupata weapon after testing him as a hunter (3.38–41), and is praised with a thousand names (13.14–17); 'among the Rudras I am Śaṃkara' (BhG 10.23); Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).

Śiva/Maheśvara as speaker: teaches Brahmā the Yogaśikhā and Yogakuṇḍalī ch.3, teaches Kumāra in the Tejobindu, Maitreya in the Maitreya, Śuka in the Śukarahasya, and Pārvatī the haṃsa-vidyā reported in the Haṃsa; whispers the tāraka to the dying at Kāśī (Muktikā 1.19–21, Jābāla 1).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Śivabhūti (Sahasramalla)
summary: In the Śvetāmbara account the founder of the Boṭika (Digambara) schism at Rathavīrapura 609 years after the nirvāṇa: when his teacher Āryakṛṣṇa tore up a precious blanket the king had given him, he declared that the Jinakalpa nakedness was the true path and went naked; his sister Uttarā, told that women may not go naked, kept her clothes — hence the Boṭikas deny liberation to women.

realization_account.text: This is the Śvetāmbara (opponent's) account of the origin of the Digambaras; the Digambaras do not accept it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Śivacandra Vidyārṇava Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: Bengali Śākta pandit and guru, author of the Tantratattva (translated as 'Principles of Tantra'), and teacher of Sir John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), through whom many Kaula and Kālī texts were printed.

name: Śivadāsa Sena
summary: Bengali commentator; author of the Carakatattvapradīpikā.

name: Śivāditya
summary: Author of the Saptapadārthī, which expounds the categories as seven (adding absence) and fuses Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika.

name: Śivagaṇaprasādi Mahādēvayya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Śivāgrayogin
summary: Sixteenth-century bilingual Siddhānta scholar of the Tamil country who wrote in Sanskrit (the Śaivaparibhāṣā; a commentary on the Sanskrit Śivajñānabodha) and in Tamil (a commentary on the Civañāṉa Cittiyār).
alt_summary: Late Saiddhāntika author of the Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣā and ritual works.

name: Śivakoṭyācārya (of the Vaḍḍārādhane)
summary: The traditional author of the Kannada Vaḍḍārādhane; authorship uncertain.

name: Śivakumāra Svāmi (Siddhagaṅgā)
summary: Head of the Siddhagaṅgā maṭha, known for dāsōha — daily free feeding and schooling of thousands of children of every background.

name: Śivānanda (author of the Ṛjuvimarśinī)
summary: Commentator on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (Ṛjuvimarśinī). Not the 20th-c. Swami Sivananda.

name: Śivānanda Sarasvatī (author of the Yogacintāmaṇi)
summary: A Daśanāmī (Sarasvatī) renouncer, pupil of Rāmacandra Sadānanda Sarasvatī (colophons), who compiled the Yogacintāmaṇi, an anthology of yoga citations with his own commentary.
notes: Not Swami Sivananda of Rishikesh (tch:sivananda).

name: Śivarām (Kīnārām's Vaiṣṇava guru)
summary: Vaiṣṇava ascetic who gave Kīnārām his first initiation (tradition).

name: Śivārya (Śivakoṭi)
summary: Author of the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā, who names his teachers and calls himself a 'hand-eater'; often placed by scholars in the Yāpanīya milieu.
alt_summary: Author of the Bhagavatī Ārādhanā on the four propitiations and the good death.

name: Sivavākkiyar (Civavākkiyar)
summary: The most iconoclastic Siddhar poet: his Civavākkiyam mocks stone images, temple ritual, pilgrimage, Vedic recitation and caste, locates the Lord within, and in one famous verse denies the rebirth of the dead. His name is explained as 'he whose (first) utterance was Śiva'.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition identifies him with Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār in his Śaiva phase; others reject the identification. Not in the popular list of eighteen, but in other lists and in every Siddhar anthology.

name: Śivayogi Śivācārya
summary: Compiler of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, son of the Vīraśaiva ācārya Siddhanātha in the line of Muddadeva (SSM 1.13–24), who composed it from the Āgamas 'from Kāmika to Vātula' and the Śaiva Purāṇas without contradicting the Vedic path (1.25–27).

scholarly.text: debated: placed variously between the 12th and 15th c.

notes: The Tattvapradīpikā places him in the lineage of Siddharāma; the SSM colophon also styles the composition Reṇukācārya's.
alt_summary: Author of the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, presenting Reṇukācārya's teaching to Agastya on the 101 sthalas.

name: Śivopādhyāya
summary: 18th-century Kashmiri commentator who completed the commentary on the Vijñāna Bhairava from v. 24, where Kṣemarāja's breaks off.

name: Skanda / Guha
summary: Named by the Lord as his manifestation among generals (senānī) (BhG 10.24).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of aksamalika, skanda, jabali, in the roles the summary gives. The Jābāli transmission (Īśāna → Ṣaḍānana → Jābāli) is located in the e-text. A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: Son of Śiva: teaches Prajāpati the rosary (Akṣamālikā); the Skanda Upaniṣad is his declaration of the identity of jīva and Śiva; in the Jābāli his line (Īśāna → Ṣaḍānana → Jābāli) transmits the Paśupati teaching.
U23 contribution: one of the twelve great worshippers of Śrīvidyā.

name: Skandasvāmin
summary: Author of an early Ṛgveda commentary (partly surviving) and, with Maheśvara, a commentary on the Nirukta.
notes: Reported as teacher of Harisvāmin, commentator on the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (low confidence).

queries: Skandasvamin Rigveda commentary Narayana Udgitha Harisvamin pupil 7th century Nirukta tika Mahesvara
Harisvamin Satapatha Brahmana commentary Skandasvamin his teacher
checks.note: Confirmed: c. 625 CE (son of Bhartṛdhruva of Valabhī); Ṛgveda commentary; Nirukta commentary with Maheśvara (Sarup ed.); guru of Harisvāmin, commentator on the Śatapatha — the low-confidence note is confirmed.

Low-confidence entry confirmed: the Ṛgveda commentator (c. 625 CE; confirmed by U01), whose Nirukta commentary was continued by Maheśvara (Sarup's edition). Wisdomlib's 1060–1350 date for the joint ṭīkā most likely reflects Maheśvara's part.

alt_summary: Commentator on the Ṛgveda and the Nirukta.

name: Skandhila
summary: Author of the Abhidharmāvatāra, a concise Vaibhāṣika manual.

name: Skandila
summary: Presided over the council (vācanā) at Mathurā (c. 827–840 years after the nirvāṇa) that restored the canon after a famine; the 'Māthurī' recension.

tradition.text: c. 4th c. CE

name: Saubhāgbhāī (Sobhāgbhāī) of Sāyalā
summary: Close disciple of Śrīmad Rājacandra, for whom (with others) the Ātmasiddhi was written.

name: Soḍhala
summary: Author of the Gadanigraha.

name: Sokuhi Nyoitsu 即非如一
summary: Chinese Ōbaku master and calligrapher, founder of Fukujuji.

name: Somā
summary: A nun who answered Māra's taunt about women's 'two-finger wisdom' (SN 5.2; Thig 3.8).

name: Somadatta
summary: Named in chapters 1–3 only through his son, Saumadatti (1.8).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.8.

name: Somadeva (author of the Rasendracūḍāmaṇi)
summary: Author of the Rasendracūḍāmaṇi.

name: Somadeva Sūri
summary: Digambara author of the Yaśastilaka (959) including its Upāsakādhyayana, and of the Nītivākyāmṛta.
notes: Distinct from tch:somadeva-rasa (another unit's alchemist).
alt_summary: Author of the Yaśastilaka (959 CE) and the political treatise Nītivākyāmṛta.

name: Somānanda
summary: Founder of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy with the Śivadṛṣṭi; he traced his descent from the mind-born siddhas of Durvāsas' Tryambaka line (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-122). Teacher of Utpaladeva; also wrote a (lost) commentary on the Parātrīśikā cited by Abhinavagupta.

realization_account.text: Heir of a line of siddhas born of the mind of Durvāsas, descended through the fifteenth who married, whose son came to Kashmir.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Somanātha Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Mayūkhamālikā on the Śāstradīpikā.

name: Somanātha (zla ba mgon po), the Kashmiri paṇḍita
alt_names: kha che zla ba mgon po
summary: Kashmiri paṇḍita who brought the Kālacakra teaching to Tibet in the 11th century and, with the translator Dro Lotsawa Sherab Drak, stands at the head of the Dro transmission from which the Jonang lineage derives.

name: Somanātha (author of the Rāgavibodha)
summary: Author of the Rāgavibodha (1609).

name: Somaśambhu
summary: Abbot of a Śaiva monastery in central India (the Golagī maṭha tradition is usually named — moderate confidence), author of the most influential Siddhānta ritual manual, the Somaśambhupaddhati (Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī), completed 1095/96.
alt_summary: Author of the Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī (Somaśambhupaddhati, 1095/96), the most influential manual of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual, covering daily worship, initiation, consecration and funeral rites.

name: Someśvara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Nyāyasudhā ('Rāṇaka') on the Tantravārttika.

name: Someśvara III
summary: Western Cālukya king, author of the Mānasollāsa (1131 CE).

name: Soṇa Koḷivisa
summary: A monk whose feet bled from over-exertion, taught by the simile of the lute (AN 6.55; Vin Mv 5.1); foremost in energy.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Sönam Gyatso, Third Dalai Lama
summary: Received the title 'Dalai' from the Mongol ruler Altan Khan in 1578 (applied retrospectively to his two predecessors); spread the Gelug among the Mongols; author of the Essence of Refined Gold.

name: Sönam Tsemo
summary: Second of the five Sakya founders, Sachen's son; scholar of the tantras and author of the General Presentation of the Tantra Classes; the tradition says he departed without leaving his body.
alt_names: slob dpon bsod nams rtse mo

name: Songyuan Chongyue 松源崇嶽
summary: Yangqi master in Huqiu's line; 'why does the person of great strength not lift his legs?' (Wumenguan 20).

name: Sopāndev
summary: Third of the four siblings, disciple of Nivṛttināth; a few abhaṅgas survive under his name; samādhi at Sāsvaḍ.

name: Soyrābāī
summary: Wife of Cokhāmeḷā, poet of abhaṅgas that question bodily impurity and celebrate oneness in devotion.

name: Sphoṭāyana
summary: A grammarian named once by Pāṇini (6.1.123); later tradition, reading his name, makes him the originator of the sphoṭa doctrine.
notes: The link with the sphoṭa doctrine is a later traditional inference from the name.

name: Sphujidhvaja
summary: Author of the versified Yavanajātaka (269/270 CE by Pingree's reading).

name: Śraddhā Kāmāyanī
summary: The ṛṣikā of the hymn to Faith (RV 10.151).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Sāyaṇa's attributes and introduction: 'kāmagotrajā śraddhā nāmarṣikā … śraddhā kāmāyanī' (DharmicData header garbled for this hymn).

name: Śreṇika (Bimbisāra)
summary: King of Magadha at Rājagṛha, a hearer of Mahāvīra, who (because of his faith) will be the first Tīrthaṅkara, Padmanābha, of the next ascending half-cycle, though he first suffers in hell for past deeds.

name: Śreyāṃsanātha
summary: The eleventh Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the rhinoceros. Parents: Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu(-śrī) (low confidence). Born at Siṃhapurī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. The first vāsudeva, Tripṛṣṭha, lived in his time.

tradition.text: the eleventh of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Sri Aurobindo
summary: U01 contribution: author of The Secret of the Veda, a symbolic-psychological reading of the Ṛgveda.

queries: The Secret of the Veda Sri Aurobindo Arya
checks.note: Confirmed: author of The Secret of the Veda (Arya, 1914–1920); dates 1872–1950 are standard.
Confirmed.

alt_summary: Author of the Essays on the Gita (1916–20).
notes: U05's contribution only; his lineage is owned by U52.

name: Śrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Disciple of Keśava Kāśmīrin; author of the Yugalaśataka, Braj verses on the divine couple.

name: Śrī Śaṅkuka
summary: Commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra, known through Abhinavagupta's report: rasa is the stable emotion inferred (anumita) in the actor, who is taken as Rāma like a painted horse taken as a horse (citraturaga-nyāya).
notes: Known only through opponents' reports.

name: Śrī Siṃha
summary: Master of the instruction series who, by tradition, was born in China (or Khotan), studied with Mañjuśrīmitra, divided the instruction series into outer, inner, secret and innermost secret cycles, and taught Jñānasūtra, Vimalamitra, Padmasambhava and Vairocana; co-translator of the Kunjed Gyalpo according to its colophon.

name: Sri Yukteswar (on the yugas)
summary: In The Holy Science (1894) proposed a 24,000-year cycle of ascending and descending yugas, holding that the conventional reckoning of the Kali age was mistaken.

name: Śrīdhara Ayyāvāḷ
summary: Tamil Smārta saint of Tiruviśanallūr, remembered with Bodhendra as a founder of the South Indian nāma-bhajana tradition.

name: Śrīdhara Svāmin
summary: The most influential commentator on the Bhāgavata and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (and on the Gītā, Subodhinī), a renunciant whose non-dualism is devotional (Narasiṃha-bhakti); later Vaiṣṇava schools build on or argue with his readings.

checks.note: Confirmed, including the c. 1350–1450 date.
Web: Bhāvārthadīpikā composed mid-14th to mid-15th c.; commentaries on the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and Gītā; the entry's c. 1350-1450 is right.

alt_summary: Commentator on the Bhāgavata (Bhāvārthadīpikā), the Gītā (Subodhinī) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, blending non-dualism with devotion; Caitanya insisted on respect for him (CC 3.7).
Advaita commentator who emphasizes devotion; author of the Subodhinī on the Gītā (and of the Bhāvārthadīpikā on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa).
Advaita renunciant (associated with Purī) whose commentaries on the Bhāgavata (Bhāvārthadīpikā), the Gītā (Subodhinī) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa combine non-dualism with devotion.

name: Śrīdhara
summary: Bengali author of the Nyāyakandalī on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, dated 991 CE in its colophon. (Distinct from Śrīdhara Svāmin, the Bhāgavata commentator.)

name: Śrīgupta
summary: Madhyamaka author of the Tattvāvatāravṛtti; in the Tibetan lineage the teacher of Jñānagarbha.

name: Śrīharṣa
summary: Poet and dialectician, author of the Khaṇḍanakhaṇḍakhādya and of the mahākāvya Naiṣadhīyacarita; demolished the Nyāya definitions in defence of Advaita.

name: Śrīkalaśa
summary: Named by Devasena's Darśanasāra as the Śvetāmbara monk who founded the Yāpanīya saṅgha at Kalyāṇa (the Digambara polemical account; low confidence).

name: Śrīkaṇṭha Śivācārya
summary: Author of the Śaiva Brahmasūtrabhāṣya: Śiva with his cit-śakti is Brahman; souls and world are his body; Veda and Śivāgama are equal; liberation is equality with Śiva.

tradition.text: Vīraśaiva authors place him before Śaṅkara

name: Śrīkaṇṭha (author of the Ratnatraya)
summary: Saiddhāntika author of the Ratnatraya on Śiva, Śakti and bindu, commented on by Aghoraśiva.
notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (Śrīkaṇṭhabhāṣya, Śivādvaita). Possibly the Śrīkaṇṭha named as a teacher of Rāmakaṇṭha (low confidence).

name: Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa
summary: Son of Mahādevabhaṭṭa, from whom Bhāskara received the Śiva Sūtra teaching (Vārttika 1.8).
notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (Śaiva Vedānta) and tch:srikanthanatha (mythic).

name: Śrīkaṇṭhadatta
summary: Pupil of Vijayarakṣita who completed the Madhukośa.

name: Śrīkaṇṭha(nātha)
summary: The form of Śiva who, wandering on Mount Kailāsa when the Śaiva secrets had been lost at the start of the Kali age, descended for grace and commanded the sage Durvāsas to keep the scripture from being cut off (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.107-110).

realization_account.text: A form of Śiva himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Distinct from tch:srikantha (the Śaiva Vedāntin) and tch:srikanthabhatta (Bhāskara's teacher).

name: Śrīkumāra
summary: Commentator (Tātparyadīpikā) on Bhoja's Tattvaprakāśa.

name: Śrīlāta
summary: Sautrāntika master whose lost Vibhāṣā is known through Saṅghabhadra's refutations; he taught a 'subsidiary element' (anudhātu) carrying the potential of past actions (low confidence on the term).

name: Śrīmad Rājacandra

realization_account.text: Memory of former lives (jātismaraṇa) at seven; later accounts in his letters of self-realization (samyagdarśana).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Gujarati jeweller, poet and lay teacher (1867–1901), author of the Ātmasiddhi, the Apūrva Avasara and the Mokṣamāḷā; he taught a non-sectarian path of self-realization under a true teacher and was a guide of M. K. Gandhi. The tradition says he recalled past lives from the age of seven, was a prodigy of memory (śatāvadhāna), and attained self-realization; his followers later formed several ashrams (e.g. Agas, Dharampur).
notes: Affinity with the Adhyātma current (he taught from the Samayasāra and Banārsīdās's Nāṭaka) rather than formal membership.

name: Śrīmālā
