summary: Queen of Ayodhyā, daughter of king Prasenajit and Mallikā, who in the Śrīmālā sūtra teaches the one vehicle and the tathāgatagarbha with the Buddha's confirmation; she receives the prediction that she will become the buddha Samantaprabha.

realization_account.text: Predicted to buddhahood as Samantaprabha (Śrīmālā ch. 1)
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (as a figure of the sūtras)

name: Śrīnivāsa Ācārya
summary: Second-generation leader who, with Narottama and Śyāmānanda, carried the Gosvāmīs' books from Vṛndāvana to Bengal; the tradition says they were stolen at Viṣṇupur and recovered when King Vīra Hāmvīra became his disciple.

name: Śrīnivāsa Dīkṣita
notes: Self-description checked in sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/gretil_devanAgarI/1_sanskr/4_rellit/vaisn/srinivasamakhi_vedantadesika_dasavidhahetunirupana.md (GRETIL, input by U. Hüsken) (DHN 1.15–20). Date not established here.
summary: Vaikhānasa scholar ('Śrīnivāsamakhin', titled Vedāntadeśika), of the Kauśika lineage, son of Govindācārya and devotee of Veṅkaṭeśa, author of the Tātparyacintāmaṇi commentary containing the Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa.

name: Śrīnivāsa (author of the Haṭharatnāvalī)
summary: Author of the Haṭharatnāvalī, a 17th-c. manual that engages critically with the Haṭhapradīpikā (eight cleansing acts instead of six; the unity of the four yogas).
notes: Title 'mahāyogīndra' and South Indian origin are low-confidence recollections.

name: Śrīnivāsācārya (of the Nimbārka school)
summary: Direct disciple of Nimbārka (tradition) and author of the Vedāntakaustubha, the classical commentary on Nimbārka's Brahma Sūtra commentary.

name: Śrīnivāsa Tīrtha
summary: Mādhva commentator, author of the Ṛgarthoddhāra on the Ṛgveda hymns covered by Madhva's Ṛgbhāṣya.

name: Śrīnivāsadāsa
summary: Author of the Yatīndramatadīpikā, the standard short manual of Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.

name: Śrīpādarāja
summary: Ascetic of Mulbagal (monastic name Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Tīrtha), teacher of Vyāsatīrtha in the śāstras, author of the Vāgvajra on the Nyāyasudhā, and, in the tradition, the 'grandfather' of the Kannada Haridāsa movement, composing songs with the signature Raṅgaviṭhala.

name: Śrīpati Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Śrīkarabhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtras, the Vīraśaiva Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita: Śiva and soul, both qualified by Śakti, are non-dual; liberation is liṅgāṅga-sāmarasya.
alt_summary: Author of the Śrīkarabhāṣya, the Vīraśaiva commentary on the Brahmasūtra that names the doctrine Śakti-viśiṣṭādvaita (philosophy owned by U16; this entry records the Vīraśaiva lineage link).
11th-century author of the Siddhāntaśekhara, the Jyotiṣaratnamālā on muhūrta and a manual (paddhati) of nativities with his method of house division.

name: Śrīvallabha
summary: Author of the Nyāyalīlāvatī, an independent Vaiśeṣika treatise. (Distinct from Vallabha of the Puṣṭimārga.)

name: Śrīvāsa Ṭhākura
summary: Navadvīpa devotee in whose courtyard the nightly kīrtanas were held; identified with Nārada; one of the Pañca-tattva.

name: Śrutasāgara Sūri
summary: Digambara commentator of the 16th c. (Tattvārthavṛtti, commentary on the Aṣṭapāhuḍa).

name: Sthiramati

realization_account.text: Tāranātha tells that in a former life he was a pigeon who heard Vasubandhu recite the abhidharma daily, and was reborn human as a result.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great commentator of Valabhī whose Sanskrit commentaries on the Thirty Verses and the Madhyāntavibhāga are the classic Indian explanations of Yogācāra; in East Asian doxography the representative of the view that the seen and seeing parts of cognition are imagined, only the self-witnessing part real.

name: Sthūlabhadra
summary: Son of the Nanda minister Śakaṭāla, who lived twelve years with the courtesan Kośā, renounced, and later spent a rainy season in her house without falling (celebrated as the model of chastity). He presided over the council at Pāṭaliputra after the famine; he learned the fourteen Pūrvas from Bhadrabāhu, but after he displayed a magical power (turning into a lion before his sisters) Bhadrabāhu taught him the last four as text only, without their meaning — the beginning of the loss of the Pūrvas.

realization_account.text: Invoked in the auspicious verse 'maṅgalaṃ sthūlabhadrādyā' after Mahāvīra and Gautama (Śvetāmbara form).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Subha Todeyyaputta
summary: A young brahmin who asked why beings are inferior and superior (MN 135).

name: Śubhacandra (author of the Jñānārṇava)

tradition.text: time of king Muñja/Bhoja of Dhārā

summary: Digambara ācārya, author of the Jñānārṇava on meditation. The tradition tells that he and his brother Bhartṛhari were princes who renounced; Bhartṛhari became a yogin who gained an alchemical elixir, and Śubhacandra showed him that self-knowledge, not the elixir, is the true attainment — the Jñānārṇava being written for his instruction.
notes: Distinct from Bhaṭṭāraka Śubhacandra (16th c.).

name: Subhadda the wanderer
summary: The last person ordained by the Buddha, taught that ascetics are found only where the eightfold path is found (DN 16).

name: Subhadrā
summary: Mother of Saubhadra; named only through her son's metronymic (1.6, 1.18).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6, 1.18.

name: Subhagānandanātha
summary: Author of the Manoramā commentary on the Tantrarāja up to paṭala 22; styled in its colophons 'Prapañcasāra-siṃharāja-prakāśa'.

name: Śubhagupta
alt_names: Kalyāṇarakṣita (back-translation of the Tibetan dge srung)
summary: Buddhist logician who, unusually, defended external objects against Yogācāra, while otherwise following Dharmakīrti (omniscience, exclusion, refutation of God and the Veda).

name: Śubhakarasiṃha
summary: Indian master (637–735) who brought the Mahāvairocana Sūtra to China and translated it with Yixing (724).

name: Subhūti
summary: Disciple of the Buddha, foremost of those who dwell in peace (araṇāvihārin); in the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras he teaches the perfection of wisdom through the Buddha's power and is the Buddha's interlocutor in the Vajracchedikā, where he weeps on hearing it.

realization_account.text: An arhat declared foremost in dwelling without conflict; in the Vajracchedikā §9 he says he does not think 'I am an arhat free of passion'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (as a figure of the sūtras)

alt_summary: Anāthapiṇḍika's brother, foremost in dwelling without conflict and in being worthy of gifts; his verse opens the Theragāthā (Thag 1.1).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Sucandra
summary: King of Śambhala who requested the Kālacakra from the Buddha at Dhānyakaṭaka and wrote it down as the Mūlatantra (the tradition's account); regarded as an emanation of Vajrapāṇi.

name: Sucarita Miśra
summary: Author of the Kāśikā commentary on the Ślokavārttika.

name: Sudarśana Sūri
summary: Author of the Śrutaprakāśikā on the Śrībhāṣya; the tradition says he perished when Śrīraṅgam was sacked and that Vedānta Deśika saved his manuscript and his sons.

tradition.text: died in the sack of Śrīraṅgam (c. 1323)

name: Suddhodana
summary: The Buddha's father, a Sakyan chief of Kapilavatthu, at whose request the rule on parental consent for going forth was made (Vin Mv 1.54).

name: Sudhākara Dvivedī
summary: Benares scholar who edited the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta and other siddhāntas and wrote the Gaṇakataraṅgiṇī on the lives of Indian astronomers.

name: Sudhana
summary: The merchant's son of the Gaṇḍavyūha who, sent by Mañjuśrī, visits over fifty spiritual friends, enters Maitreya's tower and merges with Samantabhadra; model of the seeker in one life (Huayan: the fifty-three stages).

name: Sudharman
summary: The fifth gaṇadhara, whose doubt was whether beings are reborn in the same kind; the only gaṇadhara besides Gautama to survive Mahāvīra, he became head of the community, and the Śvetāmbara Aṅgas are his recension, addressed to his pupil Jambū ('I have heard, O long-lived one…'). All later Śvetāmbara monks trace their descent to him.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience twelve years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa and liberation eight years later (Śvetāmbara account; moderate confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Sudhīndra Tīrtha
summary: Successor of Vijayīndra Tīrtha and the teacher who gave renunciation to Rāghavendra Tīrtha.

name: Sudinna Kalandaputta
summary: The monk on whose account the first pārājika rule was laid down (Vin Pār 1).

name: Suhastin
summary: Pupil of Sthūlabhadra who converted the Maurya king Samprati, grandson of Aśoka, a great patron of Jainism; the Kalpa Sūtra's list of gaṇas and kulas descends largely from his pupils.

name: Śuka

realization_account.text: Born liberated and absorbed in Brahman, he was drawn by the qualities of Hari to learn the Bhāgavata from his father (BhP 1.7.9-11); an avadhūta wandering naked whom women did not notice as a man (BhP 1.4.5); he recited the Bhāgavata to Parīkṣit in seven days and ended with the non-dual instruction 'I am Brahman, the supreme abode' (BhP 12.5.11).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Vyāsa's son, the paramahaṃsa narrator of the Bhāgavata to King Parīkṣit on the bank of the Gaṅgā; one of the twelve 'great ones' (mahājana) who know the dharma of devotion (BhP 6.3.20, 'vaiyāsaki').

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of sukarahasya, rudrahrdaya, varaha, bhiksuka, yajnavalkya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.
BhP 6.3.20 'vaiyāsakiḥ' among the twelve and the Bhāgavata frame located.

alt_summary: Son of Vyāsa, instructed by his father (12.224–247) and by Janaka at Mithilā (12.312–313); he rises by yoga from the peak of Kailāsa into the sky and attains the highest state, while Vyāsa grieves after him (12.318–320).

Son of Vyāsa: receives the great sayings from Śiva at his initiation (Śukarahasya), asks about Rudra (Rudrahṛdaya); model of the 'bird's path' of immediate liberation (Varāha 4.34–37) and named among paramahaṃsas (Bhikṣuka, Yājñavalkya).
Son and disciple of Vyāsa; in the Advaita guru-paramparā the teacher of Gauḍapāda (tradition), and a model of the born-free renunciant.
U23 contribution: named by Lakṣmīdhara as author of one of the five Śubhāgamas that teach the Vedic Samaya way.
notes: U05's contribution; his role as reciter of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa is covered by U07. The Janaka who teaches Śuka is referenced by the registry id tch:janaka without asserting identity with the Upaniṣadic king.

name: Sukeśā Bhāradvāja
summary: One of the six seekers devoted to brahman who come to Pippalāda with fuel in hand; he asks about the person of sixteen parts (PrU 6).

checks.note: Located: PrU 1.1 (listed among the six) and 6.1 (asks about the person of sixteen parts).

name: Sukhānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples named in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Sukhasiddhi
summary: Yoginī of Kashmir who, per the Shangpa account, became a siddha late in life under Virūpa; named in Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa (Tōh 2330) as the source of the instructions on the intermediate state and transference.

name: Sulabhā
summary: A female mendicant (bhikṣukī) practising the dharma of yoga who wanders the earth alone; doubting king Janaka's liberation, she enters his mind by yoga ('sattva by sattva', 12.308.16) and answers his rebuke with a discourse showing that his attachments remain (12.308).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Sūle Saṅkavva
summary: A courtesan who became a śaraṇa and vacanakāra.

name: Sumaṅgala (author of the Vibhāvinī)
summary: Pupil of Sāriputta, author of the Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī-ṭīkā on the Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha.

name: Sumantu
summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Atharvaveda ('the fierce sage of the Atharvāṅgirasas', Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.22).

checks.note: Located: 'atharvāṅgirasām āsīt sumantur dāruṇo muniḥ' (Bhāgavata 1.4.22) — the entry's quotation 'the fierce sage of the Atharvāṅgirasas' is exact.

name: Sumati ('Jaḍa')
summary: Son of a Bhārgava brahmin who behaved like a dullard (jaḍa) because he remembered past births; he told his father how beings are born, die, travel to Yama and suffer in hell (MkP 10-15), the account the wise birds relate to Jaimini.

checks.note: MkP 10.8-9 'sumatir nāma ... brāhmaṇo bhārgavaḥ kaścit sutam āha ... jaḍarūpiṇam' located.

name: Sumatinātha
summary: The fifth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the curlew (krauñca) in Śvetāmbara lists; the ruddy goose (cakravāka) in Digambara lists. Parents: Megharatha (Megha) and Maṅgalā. Born at Ayodhyā; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara.

tradition.text: the fifth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.
alt_summary: Kaula teacher praised in the Tantrāloka as the one whose wisdom dispelled Śambhunātha's darkness; Abhinavagupta's teacher's teacher.

name: Sumatiśīla
summary: Commentator on Vasubandhu's Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa (Tibetan).

name: Sumtön Yeshe Zung (sum ston ye shes gzungs)
summary: Principal disciple of Yuthok the Younger, through whom the Yuthok Nyingthig and the Four Tantras lineage were passed on.

name: Śunaḥśepa
summary: Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti, later adopted as Devarāta Vaiśvāmitra, seer of RV 1.24–30, including the prayer that Varuṇa loosen the upper, middle and lower fetters so that we may be sinless before Aditi (1.24.15). His rescue from being sacrificed is told in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa narrative (7.13–18) is cited from memory.

checks.note: Headers: 'ājīgartiḥ śunaḥśepaḥ sa kṛtrimo vaiśvāmitro devarātaḥ' for 1.24–30 (the adoption as Devarāta Vaiśvāmitra is in the header itself). Aitareya Brāhmaṇa narrative (7.13–18) not re-checked.
Text-located: AB 7.13–18 (sold by Ajīgarta Sauyavasi, freed by praising the gods, taken into Viśvāmitra's line).

alt_summary: The boy sold by his father Ajīgarta to be sacrificed in place of Rohita, freed by praising the gods, and adopted by Viśvāmitra (AB 7.13–18).

name: Sundaradeva
summary: A brāhmaṇa of Kāśī of the Kāśyapa gotra, son of Govindadeva and grandson of Viśvanāthadeva (colophon of the Haṭhatattvakaumudī), author of two large haṭha compendia, the Haṭhatattvakaumudī and the Haṭhasaṅketacandrikā; the colophon calls him also a physician (devavaidya, variant).

name: Cuntarāṉantar (Sundarānandar)
summary: Siddhar associated with Madurai: the Siddhar shrine in the Mīṉākṣī temple is linked by tradition with him and with Śiva's sport as the 'all-powerful Siddhar' (ellām valla cittar) who made the stone elephant eat sugarcane.
places: Madurai — samādhi in the popular list

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: The link between the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal episode and this Siddhar is recalled at low confidence. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Sundarapāṇḍya
summary: Early author to whom later commentators attribute the three verses quoted at the end of Śaṅkara's BSBh 1.1.4 (that once 'I am the existent Brahman' is known, there is nothing further to be done, and the knower-status lasts only until the self is known).

name: Sundardās (the younger)
summary: Dādū's learned disciple, a Khaṇḍelvāl Vaiśya of Dausa who studied Sanskrit at Banaras; the most scholarly Sant poet, author of Jñān Samudra and Sundar Vilās, joining Sant bhakti with yoga and Advaita.

name: Sundarī
summary: Daughter of Ṛṣabha, to whom he taught arithmetic; she became a nun (Śvetāmbara accounts tell of her long austerities before Bharata allowed her to renounce).

name: Sunlun Sayadaw

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that he attained arahantship through his own vigorous practice.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Burmese farmer who became a monk (U Kawi, 1878–1952) and, with little scriptural learning, developed a vigorous method of mindfulness of breathing and touch.

name: Śūnyasamādhipāda
summary: Author of the Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi.

name: Supārśvanātha
summary: The seventh Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the svastika. Parents: Pratiṣṭha and Pṛthvī. Born at Vārāṇasī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. Images often show him under a canopy of five serpent hoods.

tradition.text: the seventh of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Surapāla
summary: Author of the Vṛkṣāyurveda.

name: Surasurānanda
summary: One of Rāmānanda's twelve disciples; the Vaiṣṇavamatābjabhāskara is framed as Rāmānanda's answers to his questions.

name: Surasurī
summary: Wife of Surasurānanda, counted among Rāmānanda's twelve disciples in the Bhaktamāl.

name: Surat Gopāl
summary: Disciple of Kabīr to whom the Kabīr Chaurā line of Varanasi traces its succession of mahants.

name: Suratha
summary: A king of the Caitra line, deposed by enemies and ministers; after hearing the Devī Māhātmya he worshipped the Goddess for three years and received his kingdom back and the boon of becoming Sāvarṇi, the eighth Manu (DM 13; MkP 93.17).

checks.note: MkP 81.3 ('caitravaṃśasamudbhavaḥ suratho nāma') and 93.17 (to be Sāvarṇi Manu) located.

name: Sūrdās
summary: Blind Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of Kṛṣṇa's childhood and the gopīs' love and separation (Sūrsāgar); foremost of the aṣṭachāp.

realization_account.text: The Caurāsī Vārtā says Sūrdās, blind from birth, lived at Gaughāṭ near Agra singing songs of humility (dainya) until Vallabha initiated him and told him to sing Kṛṣṇa's play instead; he then sang at Śrīnāthjī's temple.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Puṣṭimārga)

notes: Registry id; primary owner U26/U27. Scholarly account: the sectarian link rests on Vallabhan sources only.

name: Surendra Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff of the Kumbhakonam maṭha who, in the tradition's account, received Vijayīndra Tīrtha from Vyāsatīrtha as his successor.

name: Sureśvara
notes: Identity with Maṇḍana: the tradition's account (Śaṅkaradigvijaya). Most modern scholars (Hiriyanna, Kuppuswami Sastri) hold them distinct because their doctrines differ (e.g. on prasaṅkhyāna and on works).
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara, author of the Naiṣkarmyasiddhi and of the Vārttikas on Śaṅkara's Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Taittirīya commentaries; exponent of the semblance theory (ābhāsa-vāda) and of knowledge alone as liberating; in the tradition's account first head of Śṛṅgeri and identical with Maṇḍana Miśra after his defeat in debate.

name: Sūrya (as revealer of jyotiṣa)
summary: The Sun as the source of astronomical knowledge: he taught the Sūrya Siddhānta to the asura Maya through a person born of his own portion (SS 1.4–9); he granted Varāhamihira a boon at Kāpitthaka (BJ 28.9); in horā he is the self (ātman) of the Kālapuruṣa (BJ 2.1) and the lord of planets to whom Parāśara bows (BPHS 1.6).

name: Sūryā Sāvitrī
summary: Daughter of Savitṛ, the ṛṣikā of the wedding hymn RV 10.85, which opens 'by truth the earth is upheld' and distinguishes the pressed soma from the soma the brahmins know.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Headers: 10.85 'sāvitrī sūryā ṛṣikā'; AVŚ 14.1 'sūryā sāvitrī'. 10.85.1 and 3–4 located.

name: Suśruta
summary: The student who put the questions to Divodāsa Dhanvantari on behalf of his fellows, who asked that surgery be made the root of the teaching (Su Sū 1.10-14); the Suśruta Saṃhitā is addressed to him ('vatsa Suśruta').
notes: Later tradition makes him a son of Viśvāmitra (recalled, not checked).

name: Suvidhinātha (Puṣpadanta)
summary: The ninth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the makara (crocodile / sea-monster). Parents: Sugrīva and Rāmā. Born at Kākandī; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. His body is described as white. Not to be confused with the Digambara author Puṣpadanta (tch:puspadanta-acarya).

tradition.text: the ninth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Suzuki Shōsan 鈴木正三
summary: Former samurai turned monk who taught fierce 'guardian-king Zen', death contemplation and work in each occupation as buddha-practice.

name: Svāmī Haridās
summary: Singer-saint of Vṛndāvana (16th c.), founder of the Haridāsī (Sakhī) sampradāya, who sang the eternal pair's play in the Kelimāl; at his singing in Nidhivan the image of Bāṅke Bihārī appeared. Revered as Tānsen's teacher; the Emperor Akbar is said to have visited him in disguise to hear him. His tradition holds him to be the sakhī Lalitā.

tradition.text: 16th c. (dates vary between accounts)

realization_account.text: Bāṅke Bihārī manifested before him; he is Lalitā sakhī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The guru Āśudhīra is given in the Nimbārkī account; the independent Haridāsī account differs.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: the Vṛndāvana singer-saint remembered as the master of dhrupad and, by tradition, the teacher of Tānsen.

name: Svāmi Kārttikeya
summary: Author of the Prakrit Kārttikeyānuprekṣā on the twelve reflections.
alt_summary: Author of the Kārttikeyānuprekṣā on the twelve reflections; date and identity uncertain.

name: Svapneśvara
summary: Author of the standard commentary (bhāṣya) on the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra.

name: Svarūpa Dāmodara
summary: Caitanya's intimate secretary at Purī, whose notebook (kaḍacā) is quoted in the Caitanya Caritāmṛta's opening verses.

name: Svāti Tirunāḷ
summary: Mahārāja of Travancore and composer of devotional songs in several languages and styles.

name: Svātmārāma

tradition.text: in the succession of Matsyendra and Gorakṣa

realization_account.text: He says he knows haṭhavidyā through the grace (prasāda) of Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the other Siddhas, and offers the 'lamp of haṭha' out of compassion to those lost in the darkness of many doctrines (HYP 1.3–4).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Compiler of the Haṭhapradīpikā (c. 1450), who gathered verses from some twenty earlier haṭha and rājayoga texts into a single four-part system taught 'solely for the sake of rājayoga'. He salutes his guru as 'Nātha' (HYP 1.2); the tradition places him in Gorakṣa's line. Nothing reliable is known of his life.
notes: HYP 1.2 'praṇamya śrīguruṃ nātham' — whether 'Nātha' names a specific guru is not settled.
alt_summary: U21 contribution: author of the Haṭhapradīpikā, who bows to the Nātha guru and places himself after Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the siddhas (HYP 1.2–9).

name: Svayambhūdeva
summary: 9th-c. Apabhraṃśa poet, author of the Paumacariu and Riṭṭhaṇemicariu.

name: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya
summary: Son of Uddālaka Āruṇi; returns proud after twelve years of Vedic study and is taught being and tat tvam asi (ChU 6); cannot answer Pravāhaṇa Jaivali's five questions (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3); sent to Citra (KauU 1.1).

checks.note: Located: ChU 6.1.2 (goes to study at twelve and returns at twenty-four, 'mahāmanā anūcānamānī stabdhaḥ'); ChU 5.3.1 and BĀU 6.2.1 (the Pañcāla assembly); KauU 1.1 (sent to Citra).
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, bhiksuka, naradaparivrajaka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U04 contribution: named among the paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka; Nāradaparivrājaka 3.86).

name: Śvetāśvatara

realization_account.text: SU 6.21: by tapas and the grace of God (devaprasāda) he knew brahman.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The sage named at SU 6.21: by the power of austerity and by God's grace he knew brahman and declared it to the renunciants beyond the stages of life (atyāśramin).
notes: The name may be that of a Vedic school; historicity is unknown.

checks.note: Located: ŚU 6.21 ('tapaḥprabhāvād devaprasādāc ca brahma ha śvetāśvataro 'tha vidvān | atyāśramibhyaḥ … provāca'). That the name may be a school's, and that historicity is unknown, fit the Wikipedia account.

name: Śyāmā Śāstrī
summary: Karnatic composer of Tañjāvūr devoted to the Goddess Kāmākṣī (Bangāru Kāmākṣī), whose songs are addressed almost entirely to her.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: eldest of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers, whose songs to the Goddess Kāmākṣī make music a form of devotion.

name: Śyāmānanda
summary: Second-generation leader who spread Gauḍīya devotion in Odisha.

name: Śyāmārya (Ārya Śyāma)
summary: Elder credited with the Prajñāpanā, the fourth Upāṅga.

name: Śyāvāśva Ātreya
summary: Seer of RV 5.81 to Savitṛ, which opens 'the inspired yoke their mind and yoke their thoughts' (5.81.1).
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: 'śyāvāśva ātreyaḥ', deity Savitṛ.

name: Syūmaraśmi
summary: A sage who, entering a sacrificial cow, challenges Kapila's exclamation at the Vedas (12.260–262).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Tāḍaka
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 37.
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Taego Bou 太古普愚
summary: Goryeo master who received Linji (Yangqi) transmission from Shiwu Qinggong in China (1348); regarded as reviver of the Jogye lineage and eponym of the Taego order.

name: Taklung Thangpa Tashi Pal
alt_names: stag lung thang pa bkra shis dpal
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa, founder of Taklung monastery (1180) and of the Taklung Kagyu.

name: Taktsang Lotsawa Sherab Rinchen
summary: Sakya scholar and translator who criticised Tsongkhapa's Madhyamaka for 'eighteen great burdens of contradiction' (tradition's name for the charges); answered by the Gelug scholar Jamyang Shepa among others.

name: Takuan Sōhō 澤庵宗彭
summary: Daitokuji abbot and adviser to the shogun; wrote on immovable wisdom for swordsmen.

name: Takujū Kosen 卓洲胡僊
summary: Founder of the Takujū branch of the Hakuin kōan curriculum.

name: Tāṇḍavarāya Svāmī
summary: Author of the Tamil Advaita classic Kaivalya Navanītam.

name: Tandhepa

realization_account.text: A gambler who lost everything and was taught that the three realms are as empty as his purse. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 33): As the many recollections and awarenesses are exhausted and cease in the non-conceptual expanse, so all phenomena of appearance and existence are exhausted and cease in the expanse of emptiness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 33 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A gambler who lost everything and was taught that the three realms are as empty as his purse.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Identification with Abhayadatta's Tandhepa is by position only (low).

name: Tanlin 曇林
summary: Disciple of Bodhidharma who recorded the Two Entrances with a preface.

name: Tanluan

scholarly.text: c. 476–c. 542 (some sources place his death after 554)

realization_account.text: After falling ill while commenting on the Mahāsaṃnipāta he sought Daoist longevity; meeting Bodhiruci in Luoyang he was given the Contemplation Sūtra, burned his Daoist texts and devoted himself to the Pure Land (Xu gaoseng zhuan; Shōshinge).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Northern Wei master trained in the Four Treatises (Sanlun) who wrote the Commentary on Vasubandhu's Rebirth Treatise, the first systematic Pure Land theology: the easy path is to be born by the power of Amitābha's vow (other-power); birth there is the 'birth of non-birth'; ten continuous recitations outweigh heavy karma; merit is transferred for going and returning. Third of the seven Shinshū masters.

name: Tānsen
summary: Court musician of Akbar (d. 1589), remembered as Svāmī Haridās's disciple in dhrupad.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: the court musician of Akbar, remembered as the greatest singer of dhrupad; tradition makes him a pupil of Svāmī Haridās and credits his singing with miraculous effects (lamps lit by Dīpak rāga).

realization_account.text: Stories of lamps lit and rain brought by his rāgas.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tantipa

realization_account.text: An old weaver neglected by his family, living in a hut behind their house; Jālandhara, passing, taught him to see his weaving as the path, and he attained realization in old age. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 13): Worldly weavers weave all their threads into cloth; by my guru's instruction all phenomena are woven: the emptiness of the five gnoses is the thread, the instruction the comb, wisdom the frame, and they are woven into the dharmakāya in which space and awareness are not two.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 13 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). An old weaver neglected by his family, living in a hut behind their house; Jālandhara, passing, taught him to see his weaving as the path, and he attained realization in old age.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Taṇṭiyaṭikaḷ
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. Born blind, he dug out the silted temple tank at Tiruvārūr guided by ropes and stakes, mocked by Jains; Śiva gave him sight and the Jains lost theirs (the account adds that they left the town).

realization_account.text: Born blind, he dug out the silted temple tank at Tiruvārūr guided by ropes and stakes, mocked by Jains; Śiva gave him sight and the Jains lost theirs (the account adds that they left the town).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tantrī
summary: Siddha-poet of the Caryāgīti: poet of Caryāgīti 25 (lost in the Sanskrit manuscript; known from the Tibetan); possibly Tantipa the weaver.
notes: Song numbers recalled from the standard edition (Shastri/Kvaerne); not read locally.

name: Tapihritsa (ta pi hri tsa)
summary: Zhang Zhung master of the Nyengyü lineage who attained the rainbow body and later appeared as a boy to Gyerpung Nangzher Löpo to transmit the Oral Transmission; visualized as a naked, crystal-white figure in guru yoga.

realization_account.text: Attained the rainbow body; returned as an emanation to teach.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Taponitya Pauruśiṣṭi
summary: Holds that austerity (tapas) is what matters (TU 1.9).

checks.note: Located: TU 1.9.1 ('tapa iti taponityaḥ pauruśiṣṭiḥ').

name: Tapussa and Bhallika
summary: Two merchants who offered the newly awakened Buddha food and became the first lay followers, taking the two refuges (Vin Mv 1.4).
notes: Two persons in one entry, as the texts always pair them.

name: Tāraṇa Svāmī
summary: Founder of the aniconic Tāraṇapantha in Bundelkhand (1448–1515), who taught the inner nature of the soul and veneration of scripture instead of images.

name: Tāranātha (Jetsün Kunga Nyingpo, rje btsun kun dga' snying po)

realization_account.text: Regarded as the rebirth of Kunga Drolchok; after his death he was recognized as reborn in Mongolia as Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great reviver of the Jonang: recognized as the rebirth of Kunga Drolchok, he received the Kālacakra, the Shangpa instructions and, from the Indian yogin Buddhaguptanātha, the seven instruction lineages; wrote on other-emptiness (The Essence of Other-Emptiness, Twenty-one Differences), on Kālacakra practice (Meaningful to Behold), and histories of Indian Buddhism and of the Tārā tantra; and founded Takten Phuntsok Ling (1615). Soon after his death his seats were converted to Gelug.
alt_summary: Jonang master (1575–1634); this unit records his History of Buddhism in India with its accounts of the councils and schools.

name: Tāyumāṉavar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint (early 18th c.) whose songs join Siddhānta and Vedānta in a 'harmony' (camaracam), extol the silent guru and stillness (cummā iruttal), honour the Siddhars, and pray that all beings be happy. Named after Śiva as 'He who became the mother' at the Tiruchirappalli rock temple.

realization_account.text: An accountant-minister at the Nāyak court of Tiruchirappalli, he met the silent guru (Mauṉa kuru) of Tirumūlar's line, who told him 'be still' (cummā iru); he later left the court, married at his guru's bidding, and after his wife's death lived as a renouncer until his samādhi near Rāmanātapuram.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Biographical details recalled at moderate–low confidence. Not post-1800, so not flagged recent.

name: Lopön Tenzin Namdak (slob dpon bstan 'dzin rnam dag)
summary: Bön scholar and Dzogchen master who re-established Bön monastic education in exile (Dolanji, Triten Norbutse) and taught the Zhang Zhung Nyengyü widely.
notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Tēraiyar
summary: Physician-Siddhar, disciple of Agastya, to whom many Siddha medical works are ascribed. The tradition tells that he cured a king by drawing a frog out of his skull with a bowl of water — hence his name ('frog-man').

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

notes: Frog story and works recalled at low confidence.

name: Terdak Lingpa Gyurme Dorje (gter bdag gling pa 'gyur med rdo rje)
summary: Founder of Mindroling (1676), treasure revealer and compiler of the Nyingma kama; teacher of the Fifth Dalai Lama.

name: Tertön Sogyal Lerab Lingpa (gter ston bsod rgyal las rab gling pa)
summary: Treasure revealer, teacher of the Thirteenth Dalai Lama.

name: Tetsugen Dōkō 鐵眼道光
summary: Japanese Ōbaku monk who produced the woodblock edition of the complete canon (1669–1681), twice diverting the funds to famine relief first.

name: Tettsū Gikai 徹通義介
summary: Third abbot of Eiheiji, teacher of Keizan.

name: Thaganapa

realization_account.text: A compulsive liar taught by a monk to meditate that all appearances are a lie; he realized emptiness through his own habit. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 19): As water in the ear is drawn out by water, so, meditating on the false appearances of existence as false, one sees the truth.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 19 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A compulsive liar taught by a monk to meditate that all appearances are a lie; he realized emptiness through his own habit.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Thakar Singh
summary: Disciple of Kirpal Singh who led a separate line after 1976.

name: Thangtong Gyalpo

scholarly.text: 14th–15th c.; the long life-span is the tradition's

summary: Yogin, engineer and holder of the Shangpa (and of a Niguma lineage received by vision), famous for building iron-chain bridges, for founding Tibetan opera by tradition, and for the Avalokiteśvara practice 'Benefit of Beings Pervading Space'.

name: Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu
summary: American forest monk (Geoffrey DeGraff, b. 1949), pupil of Ajahn Fuang, abbot of Metta Forest Monastery and translator of Ajahn Lee, Ajahn Mun and much of the Pali canon.

name: Thekchok Dorje, the fourteenth Karmapa
summary: Karmapa of the Rimé era, teacher and student of Jamgön Kongtrul and Jamyang Khyentse Wangpo.

name: Thongwa Dönden, the sixth Karmapa
summary: Karmapa who compiled Kagyu liturgies and rituals.

name: Thöpa Bhadra (thod pa bha dra)
summary: Indian yogin who became Machig Labdrön's consort; their union is presented in her biography as foretold.

name: Thuken Lobsang Chökyi Nyima
summary: Gelug scholar of Amdo, author of the Crystal Mirror of Tenets.

name: Tianhuang Daowu 天皇道悟
summary: Heir of Shitou (also studied with Mazu), ancestor via Longtan of Deshan and Xuefeng.

name: Tianru Weize
summary: Yuan Linji master, disciple of Zhongfeng Mingben, whose Jingtu huowen persuades Chan practitioners to recite Amitābha's name.

name: Tiantai Deshao 天台德韶
summary: Heir of Fayan and National Teacher of Wuyue; helped recover Tiantai texts from Korea.

name: Tilopa

tradition.text: 988–1069 (Tibetan histories)

realization_account.text: A brahmin who served as a royal priest, then became a monk and yogin; lived as a sesame pounder and as servant to a courtesan in Bengal; by the Tibetan account received the four instruction lineages from Caryāpa, Nāgārjuna, Lavapa and Sukhasiddhi and directly from Vajradhara; guru of Nāropa. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 22): A bird on the slope of Mount Meru appears golden by the mountain's nature; the wise, realizing the unborn, let go of things: great bliss.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 22 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A brahmin who served as a royal priest, then became a monk and yogin; lived as a sesame pounder and as servant to a courtesan in Bengal; by the Tibetan account received the four instruction lineages from Caryāpa, Nāgārjuna, Lavapa and Sukhasiddhi and directly from Vajradhara; guru of Nāropa.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Tiphupa

realization_account.text: Darma Dode's consciousness entered a pigeon, then a dead brahmin boy's body; the boy revived and became the yogin Tiphupa ('the pigeon one').
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Indian yogin who, by the Kagyu account, was the rebirth (through transference) of Marpa's son Darma Dode; he taught Rechungpa in India.

name: Tirukkacci Nambi
summary: Non-brahmin devotee who served Varadarāja at Kāñcī by fanning him; the tradition says the Lord spoke through him the six sayings that settled Rāmānuja's doubts.

realization_account.text: Varadarāja conversed with him directly and answered Rāmānuja's questions through him with six sayings.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirukkōṭṭiyūr Nambi
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna who, after making Rāmānuja come to him eighteen times, taught him the secret meaning of the tirumantra and the carama-śloka.

name: Tirukkuṟipputtoṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A washerman who washed devotees' clothes; Śiva as a poor ascetic left a garment that had to be dry by evening, rain fell, and he began to dash his head against the washing stone — Śiva's hand stopped him.

realization_account.text: A washerman who washed devotees' clothes; Śiva as a poor ascetic left a garment that had to be dry by evening, rain fell, and he began to dash his head against the washing stone — Śiva's hand stopped him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirukkurukaippirāṉ Piḷḷāṉ
summary: Disciple (and adopted son, in tradition) of Rāmānuja who, at his direction, wrote the first commentary on the Tiruvāymoḻi, the Ārāyirappaṭi ('Six Thousand'); a link in the teacher-line the Vaṭakalai follow.

name: Tirumālai Āṇḍāṉ
summary: Disciple of Yāmuna who taught Rāmānuja the meaning of the Tiruvāymoḻi.

name: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār
summary: Author of the Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti and the Tiruccanta Viruttam; the Āḻvār who, in the tradition's account, first studied the Buddhist, Jain and Śaiva doctrines and then found refuge in Nārāyaṇa; his verses insist that Nārāyaṇa created Brahmā and Brahmā Śiva.

tradition.text: born in the Dvāpara age and said to have lived some 4,700 years (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born to the sage Bhārgava as a limbless form, abandoned, quickened by the Lord and raised by a woodcutter's family; he passed through the Śākya, Jain and Śaiva teachings before Pēyāḻvār turned him to Viṣṇu. When the Pallava king banished his disciple Kaṇikaṇṇaṉ from Kāñcī, the Āḻvār told the Lord of Tiruveḵkā to roll up his serpent-bed and come too; the Lord did, and returned when they returned — hence 'the Lord who did as he was told' (coṉṉa vaṇṇam ceyta perumāḷ). He cast his writings into the Kāvēri and only two floated back against the current. At Kuṭantai the reclining Lord began to rise when the Āḻvār asked him to speak.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the discus Sudarśana in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tirumāḷikaittēvar
summary: First of the nine poets of the Tiruvicaippā (Tirumuṟai 9).

name: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār
summary: Chieftain of Tiruvāli-Tirunakari in the Cōḻa country, from the Kaḷḷar community, who turned from robbery to become the most prolific Āḻvār: author of the Periya Tirumoḻi, Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam, Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam, Tiruveḻukkūṟṟirukkai and the two Maṭals (held to be the six aṅgas of the Tamil Veda). He sang some eighty sacred sites, the saving name Nārāyaṇa, and love-longing as Parakāla-nāyakī.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla)

realization_account.text: A commander under the Cōḻa, he loved Kumudavalli, who would marry him only if he took the Vaiṣṇava marks and fed a thousand and eight devotees daily. To keep the vow he turned to robbing travellers, and waylaid a bridal party that was the Lord and Lakṣmī in disguise. Unable to pull the ring from the bridegroom's toe, he demanded the spell that held it; the Lord whispered into his ear the eight-syllable mantra, and he burst into the hymn of the name. He spent his wealth on the walls of Śrīraṅgam — by one story melting down a golden image taken from a Buddhist shrine at Nāgapaṭṭinam — and is credited with beginning the festival of reciting the Tiruvāymoḻi at Śrīraṅgam.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the bow Śārṅga in the tradition's list (moderate). The Nāgapaṭṭinam image story is the hagiographies' and is recorded here as such.

name: Tirumūlar
summary: Author of the Tirumantiram, one of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and counted among the eighteen Tamil Siddhars.
alt_names: Cuntaraṉātar (his name before entering Mūlaṉ's body, per the Periya Purāṇam)

tradition.text: lived 3,000 years in yoga

places: Chidambaram — samādhi in the popular list

realization_account.text: A yogī-disciple of Nandi from Kailāsa, travelling south to meet Agastya, found the herdsman Mūlaṉ dead at Cāttaṉūr with his cows grieving; he entered Mūlaṉ's body by yogic power to console them, later found his own body gone by Śiva's will, and sat in yoga under a pipal tree at Tiruvāvaṭuturai, singing one verse a year for three thousand years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: In the Tamil Siddha tradition Tirumūlar heads many lists of the eighteen Siddhars; his Tirumantiram is their root text for eightfold yoga, the eight great powers and the perfecting of the body ('I nourished the body and so nourished the life', TM 724). Later Siddhar works (Tirumūla nāyaṉār ñāṉam, medical treatises) circulate under his name.
notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the full entry. TM 69 names his seven (or eight) disciples, among them Kālāṅki and Kañcamalaiyaṉ. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Tirunīlakaṇṭa Yāḻppāṇa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A bard (pāṇar) who accompanied Campantar's hymns on the yāḻ (harp) with his wife Mataṅkacūḷāmaṇiyār; he entered Śiva's light at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A bard (pāṇar) who accompanied Campantar's hymns on the yāḻ (harp) with his wife Mataṅkacūḷāmaṇiyār; he entered Śiva's light at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirunīlakaṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A potter of Tillai who, reproached by his wife for his infidelity, vowed 'by Tirunīlakaṇṭam' never to touch her and kept the vow into old age; when Śiva as a yogī's begging bowl left in his keeping vanished, the couple had to bathe holding hands to prove their word — they held a stick between them, the vow was revealed, and they rose from the water young again.

realization_account.text: A potter of Tillai who, reproached by his wife for his infidelity, vowed 'by Tirunīlakaṇṭam' never to touch her and kept the vow into old age; when Śiva as a yogī's begging bowl left in his keeping vanished, the couple had to bathe holding hands to prove their word — they held a stick between them, the vow was revealed, and they rose from the water young again.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tirunīlanakka Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin priest whose wife blew away a spider that fell on the liṅga; he rebuked her for defiling it, and Śiva showed him blisters everywhere on his body except where she had blown. He attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.

realization_account.text: A brahmin priest whose wife blew away a spider that fell on the liṅga; he rebuked her for defiling it, and Śiva showed him blisters everywhere on his body except where she had blown. He attained Śiva at Campantar's wedding.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār
summary: Bard of the pāṇar community, held untouchable, who sang to Raṅganātha from across the Kāvēri until the priest Lokasāraṅga was commanded to carry him on his shoulders into the sanctum; there he sang the ten verses of Amalaṉātipirāṉ, describing the Lord from feet to face, and entered the Lord.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Raised in a family of pāṇar bards at Uṟaiyūr, he would not set foot on the holy island and sang from the far bank. When Lokasāraṅga Muni, going for water for the Lord, found him in his way and struck him, the Lord bled and commanded the priest to carry the Āḻvār in on his shoulders. Seeing the Lord from feet to face, he sang that his eyes would see nothing else, and merged into the image.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the Śrīvatsa mark in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tiruttakkatēvar
summary: Jain monk-poet, author of the Cīvakacintāmaṇi (c. 9th–10th c.); tradition makes him a Cōḻa prince.

name: Tiruvaḷḷuvar
summary: Author of the Tirukkuṟaḷ. His affiliation is contested (Jain, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Buddhist, non-sectarian); the Jain tradition identifies him with Elācārya/Kundakunda; Tamil Śaivas honour him as Tiruvaḷḷuva Nāyaṉār.

tradition.text: Sangam age; Tamil Nadu's Tiruvaḷḷuvar era begins 31 BCE

scholarly.text: c. 5th–6th c. CE (range proposed: 300 BCE–6th c. CE)

realization_account.text: Later legends make him a weaver of Mayilāppūr with a devoted wife Vācuki, and a son of the brahmin Pakavaṉ and the Pulaiya woman Āti (from the late Kapilar Akaval — low confidence); his Kuṟaḷ was the only work the academy's plank would bear.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: lineages records the traditions that have claimed him, not an established affiliation.
alt_summary: The Siddha tradition counts Tiruvaḷḷuvar among the Siddhars and ascribes to him works such as the Tiruvaḷḷuvar ñāṉam on kāya-siddhi, muppu and vāci; the medicine chapter of the Kuṟaḷ (941–950) is the classical statement of the three humours.
alt_notes: U22 contribution; U18 owns the entry and the Kuṟaḷ affiliation dispute.

name: Tiruvaraṅga Perumāḷ Araiyar
summary: Son (or kinsman) of Yāmuna and temple singer (araiyar) of Śrīraṅgam, one of Rāmānuja's five teachers.

name: Tiruvaraṅgattu Amudaṉār
summary: Śrīraṅgam temple functionary who became Rāmānuja's devotee through Kūreśa and composed the Irāmāṉuca Nūṟṟantāti.

name: Tiruvāymoḻi Piḷḷai
summary: Teacher of Maṇavāḷa Māmuni, who restored the worship at Āḻvār Tirunagari and handed on the Īṭu and Piḷḷai Lokācārya's works.

name: Tīsaṭa
summary: Author of the Cikitsākalikā.

name: Tittiri
summary: Eponym of the Taittirīya school. The Purāṇa derives the name from Vaiśampāyana's pupils who became partridges (tittiri) to take up the disgorged Yajus (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.13); the grammatical tradition derives it from a teacher named Tittiri (Pāṇini 4.3.102).
notes: The Pāṇini sūtra number is recalled from memory (moderate).

checks.note: Both derivations located: Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.13 'jagṛhus tittirā bhūtvā taittirīyās tu te tataḥ'; Pāṇini 4.3.102 'tittirivaratantukhaṇḍikokhāc chaṇ' with the gloss 'tittiriṇā proktam …' — the sūtra number recalled from memory is correct.
Low-confidence entry confirmed: A 4.3.102 derives 'Taittirīya' from Tittiri (text-located by U01). The Purāṇic partridge story is recorded as the tradition's alternative.

alt_summary: Eponym of the Taittirīya school; the Purāṇas instead derive the name from partridges (tittiri).

name: Ṭoḍarmal
summary: Digambara lay scholar of Jaipur (c. 1719–1767), leading figure of the Digambara Terāpantha, author of the Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka and of the Hindi commentary Samyagjñānacandrikā on the Gommaṭasāra; the tradition says he was executed at Jaipur as a result of sectarian hostility.
alt_summary: Paṇḍit of Jaipur (18th c.), leading lay scholar of the Digambara Terāpantha, author of the Mokṣamārga Prakāśaka and Hindi commentaries on the Gommaṭasāra.

name: Tōrei Enji 東嶺圓慈
summary: Hakuin's leading disciple and systematiser; author of the Shūmon mujintō ron.

name: Tokden Jampal Gyatso
summary: Tsongkhapa's retreat disciple to whom, in the Gelug account, the oral Mahāmudrā lineage was first entrusted.

name: Gyalse Tokmé Zangpo
summary: Sakya-trained monk famed as a living bodhisattva, author of the Thirty-Seven Practices of Bodhisattvas and of a commentary on the Seven Points of Mind Training; held both Sakya and Kadam lineages.
alt_names: rgyal sras thogs med bzang po

name: Tokuitsu
summary: Japanese Hossō monk (c. 780-842) who debated Saichō on whether the one vehicle or the three vehicles are final and whether all beings have buddha-nature (the 'three-one' controversy).

name: Tōlāmoḻittēvar
summary: Jain poet, author of the Cūḷāmaṇi.

name: Tönpa Shenrab Miwoche (ston pa gshen rab mi bo che)
summary: Founder of Yungdrung Bön. Tradition: a fully enlightened teacher who descended from the heavens and was born prince of Ölmo Lungring in Tagzig; he taught Bön, pursued into Tibet the demon Khyapa Lagring who had stolen his horses, taught there and returned; his deeds are told in the Dodü, the Zermig and the Zijid.

tradition.text: born in 16,017 BCE by a traditional Bön reckoning

notes: Optional (Bön).

name: Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga
summary: Fifteenth-century Vīraśaiva ascetic of Yeḍiyūr whose Ṣaṭsthalajñānasārāmṛta renewed the vacana tradition; teacher of a line of renunciant (virakta) masters.

name: Toṇṭadārya
summary: A renunciant Vīraśaiva teacher (parivrājakācārya) to whom the Kaivalyasāra's exposition of the 101 sthalas is ascribed.
notes: Relation to Toṇṭada Siddhaliṅga (tch:tontada-siddhalinga) not settled here.

name: Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār
summary: Garland-maker of Śrīraṅgam whose name means 'dust of the feet of the Lord's servants'; author of the Tirumālai and the dawn-awakening Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci. After a fall into a courtesan's household he was restored by the Lord's grace and taught that the name is sweeter than Indra's kingdom and that devotees of any birth are to be honoured.

tradition.text: early Kali age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: A brāhmaṇa devoted to making garlands for Raṅganātha, he was infatuated with the courtesan Dēvadēvi and lost all his wealth. The Lord, in the guise of a servant, sent her a golden vessel of the temple in Vipranārāyaṇa's name; he was arrested for its theft until the Lord revealed the truth in a dream to the king. Humbled, he returned to service and named himself dust of the feet of the devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the garland Vanamālā in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tönyön Samdrub (thod smyon bsam grub)
summary: A son (in some accounts a grandson) of Machig Labdrön, holder of the family lineage of Chöd.

name: Toṭaka (Toṭakācārya)
notes: Not to be confused with Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna), the 13th-c. commentator.
summary: Disciple of Śaṅkara, author (tradition) of the Toṭakāṣṭaka in praise of his guru and the Śrutisārasamuddharaṇa; in the tradition's account a devoted servant (called Giri) whose realization came through the guru's grace, first head of Jyotirmaṭh.

name: Touzi Yiqing 投子義青
summary: Reviver of the Caodong line, received its transmission by proxy through Fushan Fayuan.

name: Trilocana
summary: Naiyāyika named by Vācaspati Miśra as his teacher ('following the path led by my teacher Trilocana', Tātparyaṭīkā on NS 1.1.4); his works are known only from citations.

name: Trilocanaśiva
summary: Twelfth-century South Indian Saiddhāntika, author of the Siddhāntasārāvalī and the Prāyaścittasamuccaya (and reportedly a commentary on the Somaśambhupaddhati — low confidence).
alt_summary: South Indian Saiddhāntika author of the Siddhāntasārāvalī, a verse digest of ritual.

name: Trinley Thaye Dorje (recognized as seventeenth Karmapa by one party)
summary: One of two claimants recognized as the seventeenth Karmapa (recognized by the Shamarpa).

name: Tripiṭakamala
summary: Author of the Nayatrayapradīpa (c. 10th–11th c.?) setting out the superiority of the mantra way.

name: Tripurāntaka (Pāśupata)
summary: Pāśupata ascetic eulogised in the Cintra praśasti of 1287 CE for his foundations at Somanātha; the inscription traces his line to one of Lakulīśa's disciples (details to be checked).

name: Triśaṅku
summary: Seer whose declaration after realization, beginning 'I am the mover of the tree', is recorded as 'the Veda-recitation of Triśaṅku' (TU 1.10).

checks.note: Located: TU 1.10.1 ('iti triśaṅkor vedānuvacanam').

name: Triśikhi
summary: A brāhmaṇa who goes to Āditya's world with questions on body, self and liberation (Triśikhibrāhmaṇa).

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of trisikhibrahmana, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Trisong Detsen (khri srong lde btsan)
summary: Tibetan emperor (reigned c. 755-797) who invited Śāntarakṣita, Padmasambhava and Vimalamitra, founded Samye and made Buddhism the state religion; for the Nyingma an emanation of Mañjuśrī and a principal disciple and treasure recipient of Padmasambhava.

tradition.text: emanation of Mañjuśrī

name: Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya
summary: An Advaita scholar who, in the tradition's account, debated Madhva for many days at Viṣṇumaṅgala (Kasaragod) and became his disciple. He wrote the Tattvapradīpa, the first commentary on Madhva's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, and the Vāyustuti praising Vāyu's three avatāras; his son Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya wrote the Sumadhvavijaya.

name: Tryambakāditya
summary: Mind-born son of Durvāsas who received the Śaiva secrets, went to a cave named Tryambaka and in turn created a mind-born son; fourteen such siddhas followed (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.111-114). The lineage was known as Tryambaka, 'Terambā' in the local language (7.121).

name: Tsangnyön Heruka Sangye Gyaltsen
alt_names: gtsang smyon he ru ka sangs rgyas rgyal mtshan
summary: The 'madman of Tsang', a Kagyu yogin who compiled and printed the Life and the Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa (1488) and the Life of Marpa.

name: Tsangpa Gyare Yeshe Dorje (the first Gyalwang Drukpa)
alt_names: gtsang pa rgya ras ye shes rdo rje

realization_account.text: At Namdruk he heard thunder and saw nine dragons rise into the sky, and named his lineage Drukpa, 'of the Dragon'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Drukpa Kagyu at Ralung (1180) and Druk (1189); disciple of Lingje Repa; rediscoverer (by the tradition's account) of the Six Equal Tastes hidden by Rechungpa; the first of the Gyalwang Drukpa incarnations.

name: Tsarchen Losal Gyatso
summary: Founder of the Tshar sub-school; revived the Lamdre Lobshé as a secret explanation for close disciples and the 'thirteen golden dharmas' of the Sakya.
alt_names: tshar chen blo gsal rgya mtsho

name: Tselé Natsok Rangdröl
alt_names: rtse le sna tshogs rang grol
summary: Kagyu and Nyingma master of the 17th c., author of the Lamp of Mahāmudrā and of works joining Mahāmudrā and Dzogchen.

name: Tsongkhapa Lobsang Drakpa
summary: Founder of the Gelug. Born in Tsongkha (Amdo), he trained with teachers of all schools — Rendawa above all in Madhyamaka — did long retreats with eight disciples at Wölkha, and through the visionary Umapa and then directly communicated with Mañjuśrī; the tradition says his realization of emptiness came while reading Buddhapālita's commentary after a dream of Nāgārjuna and his disciples. He wrote the Great Treatises on the Stages of the Path and of Mantra, founded the Great Prayer Festival at Lhasa and Ganden monastery (1409), and restored monastic discipline.
alt_names: tsong kha pa blo bzang grags pa

realization_account.text: Regarded as an emanation of Mañjuśrī; after years of dialogue with Mañjuśrī through Umapa and then directly, he dreamt of Nāgārjuna and his five disciples, one of whom, Buddhapālita, touched his head with a text; next day, reading Buddhapālita's commentary, he gained complete certainty about the view (Praise of Dependent Origination closes with this gratitude).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: U41 also contributes to tch:tsongkhapa; this is the owner's entry.
alt_summary: Founder of the Gelug school; his Essence of Eloquence and treatise on mind and the store-consciousness are the Tibetan reference expositions of Cittamātra.
alt_notes: Contribution of U41; U47 owns.

name: Tsurtön Wangi Dorje
alt_names: mtshur ston dbang gi rdo rje
summary: One of Marpa's four principal disciples, holder of the Guhyasamāja transmission and (by one account) of transference.

name: Tukaḍojī Mahārāj
summary: Vidarbha kīrtankār and bhajan poet (1909–1968), author of the Grāmgītā on village uplift through devotion.

name: Tukārām
summary: Kuṇbī grocer of Dehu (1608–1650 by the usual tradition) who, ruined by famine and bereavement, turned wholly to Viṭṭhala; initiated in a dream by Bābājī Caitanya with the mantra 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'. His abhaṅgas — thrown into the Indrāyaṇī at the order of the brahmin Rāmeśvar Bhaṭṭ and restored after thirteen days — became the Tukārām Gāthā. He is 'the pinnacle' of the Vārkarī temple; tradition says he departed bodily for Vaikuṇṭha (Tukārām Bīj).

tradition.text: 1608–1650 (Śaka 1530–1571); some accounts give 1598 for his birth

realization_account.text: Initiated in a dream; Viṭṭhala restored his drowned abhaṅgas; at the end he ascended to Vaikuṇṭha in his body.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Tulādhāra
summary: A merchant of Vārāṇasī who teaches the ascetic Jājali that the eternal dharma is friendliness and non-injury to all beings (12.253–256).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Tulku Urgyen Rinpoche (sprul sku o rgyan)
summary: Holder of the Chokling Tersar and Dzogchen teacher in Nepal.

name: Tulku Zangpo Drakpa (sprul sku bzang po grags pa)
summary: Treasure revealer of the Prayer in Seven Chapters (14th c.; low confidence).

name: Ācārya Tulsī
summary: Ninth ācārya of the Terāpanth (1914–1997), founder of the Aṇuvrata movement of 'small vows' for all people (1949), of the samaṇ/samaṇī order and of the Jain Vishva Bharati; directed the Lāḍnūn edition of the Āgamas.

name: Tulsī Sāhib of Hāthras

tradition.text: he said he had been Tulsīdās in a former birth

summary: Sant of Hāthras, author of the Ghaṭ Rāmāyaṇ, whose teaching of the inner regions and sound current directly preceded Radhasoami; Soamiji's family were among his followers.
notes: Whether Tulsī Sāhib was Soamiji's guru is disputed within Sant Mat.

name: Tulsīdās
summary: Poet-saint of Rāma (c. 1532–1623; tradition 1497–1623), a brahmin abandoned at birth and raised by sādhus, disciple of Narharidās. Turned to Rāma, by tradition, by his wife Ratnāvalī's rebuke, he lived at Ayodhyā, Citrakūṭ and Vārāṇasī (Assi ghāṭ), where Hanumān led him to the vision of Rāma. He wrote the Rāmcaritmānas (from 1574), the Vinaya Patrikā, Kavitāvalī, Gītāvalī, Dohāvalī and other works; the Hanumān Cālīsā is traditionally his. The Bhaktamāl calls him Vālmīki reborn for the Kali age.

tradition.text: born Saṃvat 1554 (1497), died Saṃvat 1680 (1623)

realization_account.text: Hanumān, met through a ghost's guidance, showed him Rāma at Citrakūṭ; Śiva approved the Mānas at Vārāṇasī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Author of the Rāmcaritmānas passages (local Gita Press text).

alt_summary: In U06's texts: author of the Rāmcaritmānas passages known as the Lakṣmaṇa Gītā and the Vibhīṣaṇa Gītā; he drew on the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (Śiva-Pārvatī frame, Śabarī's nine devotions).

name: Tumburu
summary: The gandharva singer paired with Nārada, named among the authorities of music (ŚR 1.1.16).

name: Tura Kāvaṣeya
summary: Near the head of the final teacher-line of the BAU, receiving from Prajāpati (BAU 6.5.4).

checks.note: Text-located: ŚB 10.6.5.9 '… turāt kāvaṣeyāt, turaḥ kāvaṣeyaḥ prajāpateḥ, prajāpatir brahmaṇaḥ …'.
Located: BĀU 6.5.4 ('turāt kāvaṣeyāt turaḥ kāvaṣeyaḥ prajāpateḥ').

alt_summary: The first human link in the Agnicayana lineage of ŚB 10.6.5.9, who received it from Prajāpati, who received it from Brahman the self-existent.

name: Turaimaṅkalam Śivaprakāśar
summary: Tamil Vīraśaiva poet who rendered the Prabhuliṅgalīle into Tamil.

name: Turugāhi Rāmaṇṇa
summary: A cowherd śaraṇa and vacanakāra.

name: Tyāgarāja
summary: Telugu singer-saint of Tiruvaiyāru (1767–1847), devotee of Rāma, composer of some seven hundred surviving kṛtis and two musical dramas; he declined the Tanjore court's patronage ('Is wealth happiness, or service near Rāma?') and is said to have taken sannyāsa before death.
notes: Born before 1800; not flagged recent.
alt_summary: U31 contribution: in his songs on nāda Tyāgarāja teaches that nāda is the body of the Lord and that music joined to devotion (nādopāsanā) is a way to liberation, echoing the Saṅgītaratnākara; one of the three great Karṇāṭaka composers.

name: Sayagyi U Ba Khin
summary: Burmese government official (Accountant-General) and lay meditation teacher (1899–1971), pupil of Saya Thetgyi, who founded the International Meditation Centre in Rangoon (1952) and taught Goenka.

name: Sayadaw U Paṇḍita
summary: Senior Mahāsi-tradition teacher (1921–2016), abbot of Paṇḍitārāma, Yangon, known for rigorous retreats; author of In This Very Life.

name: Ubbirī
summary: A nun who mourned her daughter Jīvā until told that 84,000 Jīvās had been burned in that charnel ground (Thig 3.5).

name: Ubhaya Bhāratī
summary: Wife of Maṇḍana Miśra who, in the tradition's account, judged the debate between Śaṅkara and her husband by the fading of the garlands they wore, then herself debated Śaṅkara; venerated as Sarasvatī (Śāradā), associated with the Śāradā shrine at Śṛṅgeri.
notes: Known only from hagiography.
alt_summary: Wife of Maṇḍana Miśra in Śaṅkara's hagiographies, learned in the śāstras, who acts as judge of the debate between Maṇḍana and Śaṅkara and is presented as an incarnation of Sarasvatī.

name: Udaṅka Śaulbāyana
summary: One of the teachers whose view Janaka reports to Yājñavalkya: brahman is breath (BAU 4.1.3); Yājñavalkya says he taught only its abode, not its support.

checks.note: Located: BĀU 4.1.3 (Udaṅka Śaulbāyana: prāṇa is brahman).

name: Udayana

tradition.text: Lakṣaṇāvalī dated Śaka 906 = 984 CE by its own closing verse

summary: Called simply 'the Ācārya' by later Naiyāyikas; the great defender of Īśvara (Nyāyakusumāñjali) and of the self against the Buddhists (Ātmatattvaviveka), commentator on Vācaspati (Pariśuddhi) and on Praśastapāda (Kiraṇāvalī), author of the Lakṣaṇāvalī. He joined Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika and is regarded as the bridge between old and new Nyāya.
notes: Hagiographic tradition (low confidence): denied entry to the Jagannātha temple at Puri, he is said to have addressed the Lord: 'Drunk with lordship you disregard me; when the Buddhists come, your existence depends on me.'

name: Udbhaṭa
summary: Kashmiri poetician of Jayāpīḍa's court (Kāvyālaṅkārasārasaṅgraha); also named as an early commentator on the Nāṭyaśāstra (ŚR 1.1.19).

name: Uddaka Rāmaputta
summary: A teacher of the bodhisatta who taught the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception realised by his father Rāma (MN 26, MN 36).
notes: Known only through Buddhist texts; the text distinguishes Rāma, who had attained it, from Uddaka.

name: Uddālaka Āruṇi
summary: Brahmin teacher of the Gautama clan, father of Śvetaketu: teaches the doctrine of being (sat) with the refrain tat tvam asi (ChU 6); questions Yājñavalkya on the thread and the inner controller (BAU 3.7); goes as a pupil to Pravāhaṇa Jaivali (BAU 6.2; ChU 5.3), to Aśvapati Kaikeya (ChU 5.11) and to Citra (KauU 1.1).
notes: ChU 3.11.4 says his father taught him the honey-doctrine as the eldest son.

checks.note: Text-located: ŚB 11.4.1.1 'uddālako hāruṇiḥ udīcyān vṛto dhāvayāṃ cakāra …'; Svaidāyana Śaunaka answers him and Uddālaka becomes his pupil ('samitpāṇiḥ praticakrama', 11.4.1.9). In the vaṃśa: 'yājñavalkya uddālakāt' (14.9.4.33).

queries: prepared BĀU 3.7.1, BĀU 6.3.7, ChU 3.11.4, ChU 5.11.2, ChU 6.8.1, KauU 1.1
checks.note: Located: BĀU 3.7.1 (studied in Madra), 6.3.7 (teaches Yājñavalkya); ChU 3.11.4 (taught by his father as eldest son), 5.11.2 (goes with the householders to Aśvapati), 6.1–6.16 (teaches Śvetaketu); KauU 1.1 (Āruṇi, called Gautama, goes to Citra). He is addressed as Gautama in BĀU 6.2.4 and ChU 5.3.6.
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of aruni, jabala, bhiksuka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: U02 contribution: in ŚB 11.4.1 he challenges and is defeated by Svaidāyana Śaunaka in a brahmodya; teacher of Yājñavalkya in the vaṃśas.
U04 contribution: tradition identifies him with the Āruṇi who goes to Prajāpati's world to learn renunciation (Āruṇi Upaniṣad); named among paramahaṃsas (Jābāla 6; Bhikṣuka).

name: Uddhava
summary: Kṛṣṇa's cousin, counsellor and devotee; recipient of the Uddhava Gītā. Earlier Kṛṣṇa sent him to Vraja, where he learned from the gopīs' love (Bhāgavata 10.46-47). At the end of the teaching he departs for Badarikāśrama (11.29).

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: Recipient of the Uddhava Gītā (BhP 11.6.40-11.29); sent to Vraja in BhP 10.47, where he wishes to be a creeper touched by the gopīs' feet (10.47.61).
BhP 10.47.34-36, 10.47.61 and the Uddhava Gītā (11.14-15) located.

realization_account.text: Having heard the teaching, Uddhava, freed of doubt, went to Badarikāśrama to live it out (Bhāgavata 11.29).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Kṛṣṇa's friend and counsellor, sent to Vraja with Kṛṣṇa's message to the gopīs, whose love in separation he came to revere (BhP 10.46-47); later the recipient of the Uddhava Gītā (BhP 11.7-29, owned by U06).

name: Uddyotakara
summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika, written to remove the 'ignorance created by bad reasoners' — Dignāga and others, as Vācaspati glosses. The colophon of his work calls him a Pāśupata teacher.
notes: The Pāśupata affiliation rests on the colophon as usually reported (moderate confidence).
alt_summary: Author of the Nyāyavārttika; the colophon of that work calls him 'Pāśupatācārya', a sign of the link between Nyāya and the Pāśupatas (this unit's contribution; the full entry belongs to the Nyāya unit).

name: Udhili

realization_account.text: A man who wished to fly like the birds; he gained the power of flight. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 71): Following after others, yogins go astray; do not let go of unrelated habits(?); do not abide anywhere; it is not something to be sought elsewhere.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 71 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A man who wished to fly like the birds; he gained the power of flight.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292. Two lines are uncertain.

name: Uditācārya
summary: Pāśupata teacher of the Mathurā pillar inscription of 380 CE, described as tenth in succession from Kuśika; he installed two liṅgas named after his teachers (Kapileśvara and Upamiteśvara) in a teachers' shrine.

name: Ugrāditya
summary: Jain author of the Kalyāṇakāraka, an Āyurveda without meat, alcohol or honey.

name: Ugrajyoti
summary: Named by Sadyojyoti as his teacher; no work of his survives.

name: Ugraśravas Sauti

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Lomaharṣaṇa, the bard who retells the Mahābhārata, as heard at Janamejaya's sacrifice, to the sages assembled for Śaunaka's twelve-year sacrifice in the Naimiṣa forest (1.1).

evidence: local:DharmicData MBh CE 1.1.1 (lomaharṣaṇaputra ugraśravāḥ ... naimiṣāraṇye śaunakasya kulapater dvādaśavārṣike satre)
checks.note: Located as entered.
BhP 12.7.6 (the Sūta learned all the saṃhitās), 1.2.1 ('raumaharṣaṇiḥ'), 1.4.1 (Śaunaka questions the Sūta) located.

alt_summary: Son of Romaharṣaṇa, the Sūta who recites the Bhāgavata and other Purāṇas to Śaunaka and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest (having heard the Bhāgavata from Śuka at Parīkṣit's assembly); he learned all four root saṃhitās (BhP 12.7.6).

name: Ulūka (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. 'Ulūka' is also a name of the Vaiśeṣika founder Kaṇāda; no identity is implied.

name: Umā (Pārvatī)
summary: Śiva's consort, who questions him on dharma and herself expounds the dharma of women in the Anuśāsana (13.126–134).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Umā Haimavatī
summary: The very beautiful woman who appears to Indra in the sky where the yakṣa vanished and tells him it was brahman, in whose victory the gods had been glorifying themselves (Kena 3.12-4.1).
notes: Later Śākta and Śaiva readers identify her with the Goddess Umā/Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat.

checks.note: Located: Kena 3.12 ('striyam ājagāma bahuśobhamānām umāṃ haimavatīm') and 4.1 ('brahmeti hovāca'). The same passage is in JUB 4.20-21 (DCS). The later Śākta/Śaiva identification is correctly marked as later reading.

name: Umānandanātha
summary: Disciple of Bhāskararāya, author of the Nityotsava, the standard manual expanding the Paraśurāma Kalpasūtra.

name: Umapa Pawo Dorje
summary: Yogin who had visions of Mañjuśrī and, in the Gelug account, served as Tsongkhapa's intermediary in questioning Mañjuśrī on the view.

name: Umāpati Civācāriyār
summary: Chidambaram priest (Tillai dīkṣitar) turned disciple of Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar; author of eight of the fourteen Meykaṇṭa Śāstras (Civappirakācam, Tiruvaruṭpayaṉ, Viṉāveṇpā, Poṟṟippahṟoṭai, Koṭikkavi, Neñcuviṭu Tūtu, Uṇmai Neṟi Viḷakkam [disputed], Caṅkaṟpa Nirākaraṇam), of the Sanskrit Pauṣkarabhāṣya and Śataratnasaṅgraha, and of Tamil purāṇas of Chidambaram and the saints.

realization_account.text: Excluded by the Tillai priests, he lived at Koṟṟavaṉkuṭi; when the festival flag would not rise he sang the Koṭikkavi and it rose. Naṭarāja is said to have sent him a verse-letter ordering liberation for the outcaste Peṟṟāṉ Cāmpāṉ, and he granted release even to a thorn bush.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Contribution from U08 (Sanskrit Āgama works); Tamil works are U18's.
alt_summary: Cidambaram Saiddhāntika who wrote in Tamil and Sanskrit; in Sanskrit he commented on the Pauṣkarāgama's jñānapāda and compiled the Śataratnasaṅgraha of Āgama verses.

name: Umāsvāti
summary: Author of the Tattvārthasūtra, the first Sanskrit summa of Jain doctrine, accepted by both sects. The Śvetāmbaras know him as Umāsvāti, son of Svāti and Umā, of the Uccairnāgara branch, who also wrote the bhāṣya and the Praśamarati; the Digambaras as Umāsvāmin (also called Gṛdhrapiccha), in Kundakunda's line.
notes: His Praśamarati (Śvetāmbara) is not given a separate entry here (gap).

name: Umbeka
notes: Identification with Bhavabhūti is traditional and disputed; being Kumārila's direct pupil is also traditional.
summary: Early commentator on the Ślokavārttika (Tātparyaṭīkā) and on Maṇḍana's Bhāvanāviveka; tradition identifies him with the dramatist Bhavabhūti.

name: Upagupta
summary: Fourth patriarch in the Chan list. (U42 contributes the Chan patriarchal role only.)
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 4.

tradition.text: A hundred years after the parinirvāṇa, teacher of King Aśoka (Aśokāvadāna)

realization_account.text: He subdued Māra and made him display the Buddha's form; he taught Aśoka; a cave was filled with the tally-sticks of those he led to arhatship.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Master of Mathurā, fourth in the Sarvāstivāda succession after Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda and Śāṇakavāsin, and a hero of the Aśokāvadāna.

name: Upaka
summary: An Ājīvika ascetic who met the newly awakened Buddha on the road to Benares and did not accept his claim (MN 26; Vin Mv 1.6).

name: Upaka the Ājīvaka
summary: The first person the newly awakened Buddha met on the road from Gayā; told of the Buddha's awakening he said 'may it be so' and went another way (MN 26; Vinaya Mv 1.6). The Therīgāthā verses of Cāpā tell of her husband Kāḷa, formerly an ascetic with a staff, who left her to go forth; the commentary identifies him with Upaka.

name: Upakosala Kāmalāyana
summary: Pupil of Satyakāma who tended his teacher's fires for twelve years; the fires themselves taught him 'breath is brahman, ka is brahman, kha is brahman' before his teacher taught him the person in the eye (ChU 4.10-15).

checks.note: Located: ChU 4.10.1 (twelve years tending the fires), 4.10.4 (the fires' teaching) and 4.14–4.15.

name: Upāli
summary: The Sakyan princes' barber who went forth with them and was ordained before them; foremost in knowledge of the Vinaya; questioned by Mahākassapa on the discipline at the First Council (Cv 11.1.7).
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Upāli the householder
summary: A wealthy lay follower of the Nigaṇṭhas who, sent to refute the Buddha, became his follower (MN 56).

name: Upāli Thera (of Ayutthaya)
summary: Siamese elder who led the mission of 1753 that restored higher ordination in Kandy; the borān meditation manuals of Sri Lanka are associated with this mission.

name: Upamanyu
summary: The Śaiva sage who, having won Śiva's favour as a child through austerity, gives Kṛṣṇa Pāśupata initiation and teaches him Śaiva doctrine, worship, the pañcākṣara and yoga in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā (ŚiP 7.2) and in LiP 1.107.

checks.note: Located as described.
ŚiP 7.2.12.2 and 7.2.37.5 (Upamanyu teaches Kṛṣṇa) located; LiP 1.107 Upamanyu story located locally (1.107.2) and confirmed on the web (the milk story).

alt_summary: A sage devoted to Śiva who teaches Kṛṣṇa the thousand names of Śiva first revealed by Taṇḍi (13.14–17).

name: Upaniṣad Brahmayogin

tradition.text: 18th c.

summary: Advaitin renouncer of Kāñcīpuram who wrote commentaries on all 108 Muktikā Upaniṣads; his maṅgala verses open each text in the South Indian printed collection used here.

queries: Upanishad Brahmayogin Kanchipuram 18th century Ramachandrendra commentaries 108 Upanishads
checks.note: This was on the skeleton's least-sure list; it is confirmed. The initiation name was Rāmacandrendra Sarasvatī, so the '(?)' in alt_names can be dropped; he was also called Upaniṣad-brahmendra and Upaniṣad-brahman. He was initiated by Vāsudevendra Sarasvatī at Kāñcīpuram and founded the Upaniṣad Brahmendra maṭha. He is dated to the mid-18th century, and his Muktikā commentary was completed in 1751, which fits '18th c.'. He commented on all 108 Muktikā Upaniṣads.

alt_summary: 18th-c. Advaitin of Kāñcī who wrote commentaries on all 108 Upaniṣads of the Muktikā canon.

name: Uparicara Vasu
summary: A king devoted to Nārāyaṇa who performed a horse sacrifice without slaughter; when he sided with the gods that 'aja' in the injunction means a goat, he fell, and was restored by his devotion (12.322–324).

evidence: local:DharmicData MBh CE 12.323.3-14 (rājoparicaro vasuḥ; aśvamedha without paśughāta), 12.324.3-12 (aja dispute)
checks.note: Located as described.

name: Upaśānta
summary: Commentator on the Abhidharmahṛdaya.

name: Upasena (author of the Saddhammapajjotikā)
summary: Author of the commentary on the Niddesa.

name: Upasīva
summary: One of the sixteen brahmin students of Bāvarī who questioned the Buddha in the Pārāyanavagga (Snp 5.7).

name: Upatissa (author of the Vimuttimagga)
summary: The elder named as author of the Vimuttimagga, a manual of the path earlier than the Visuddhimagga; nothing else is known of him with certainty.
notes: Dhammapāla's sub-commentary identifies some anonymous views cited in the Visuddhimagga as Upatissa's (as remembered; not checked).

name: Upavarṣa
notes: Whether Upavarṣa is the same as the Vṛttikāra quoted by Śabara, or as Bodhāyana (the Vṛttikāra of Rāmānuja's tradition), is disputed.
summary: Called 'the revered (bhagavān) Upavarṣa' by Śabara, who cites his view that the word 'gauḥ' is simply the letters g, au and ḥ; Śaṅkara (BSBh 3.3.53) reports that Upavarṣa in the first treatise deferred the proof of the self to the Śārīraka.
alt_notes: Some later tradition identifies him with Bodhāyana the vṛttikāra; the Kathāsaritsāgara makes him a grammarian of Pāṭaliputra (low confidence).
alt_summary: Ancient commentator on the Mīmāṃsā (and, by Śaṅkara's report, the one who deferred discussion of the self to the Śārīraka); Śaṅkara calls him 'bhagavān Upavarṣa' (BSBh 1.3.28; 3.3.53).

name: Upendra Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Puttige maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Uppalavaṇṇā
summary: Foremost nun in psychic power; verses at Thig 11.1; answers Māra in SN 5.5.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Uriliṅgadēva
summary: A śaraṇa teacher whose disciple and successor Uriliṅgapeddi came from the margins of society.

name: Uriliṅgapeddi
summary: A former thief of low-caste birth who became Uriliṅgadēva's disciple, successor and a vacanakāra.

name: Uruttirapacupati Nāyaṉār
