summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A brahmin who stood in a tank day and night reciting the Śrī Rudram until Śiva granted him release.

realization_account.text: A brahmin who stood in a tank day and night reciting the Śrī Rudram until Śiva granted him release.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Uruvela Kassapa
summary: Leader of a thousand matted-hair fire-worshipping ascetics at Uruvelā, converted with his brothers Nadī Kassapa and Gayā Kassapa; they heard the Fire Sermon at Gayāsīsa (Vin Mv 1.15–21).

name: Urvaśī
summary: The apsaras whose dialogue with King Purūravas forms RV 10.95; ṛṣikā of her verses.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header: Purūravas Aila seer; Urvaśī ṛṣikā of vv. 2, 4–5, 7, 11, 13, 15–16, 18.

name: Uśanas (Śukra)
summary: Named by the Lord as his manifestation among the seer-poets: 'the seer Uśanas' (BhG 10.37).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Located as described.

alt_summary: Preceptor of the asuras, who questions Vṛtra (12.270); 'among poets I am Uśanas' (BhG 10.37).

name: Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa
summary: Asks Yājñavalkya to explain the brahman that is immediate and direct, the self within all (BAU 3.4, as Uṣasta); in ChU 1.10-11 he survives a famine among the Kurus by eating an elephant-keeper's leftover beans but refuses the leftover water, and then instructs priests on the deities of the chant.
notes: Identity of the BAU Uṣasta and the ChU Uṣasti is assumed from the shared patronymic (moderate).

queries: Ushasti Chakrayana Chandogya 1.10 Ushasta Chakrayana Brihadaranyaka 3.4 same person
checks.note: Both figures are located: Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa at BĀU 3.4.1-2 and Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa at ChU 1.10-11 (the ibhya's kulmāṣa beans; teaches the priests). No external source was found that identifies the two; Wikipedia's 'Ushasta' page treats the BĀU figure. The identity rests only on the shared patronymic, as the entry itself says (moderate).

name: Utpala Vaiṣṇava
notes: Quotations noted in the introduction to the JS edition (local e-text).
summary: Kashmirian Vaiṣṇava author of the Spandapradīpikā, a commentary on the Spandakārikā that quotes Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (the Jayākhya, the Ahirbudhnya), furnishing an early date-limit for them.
alt_summary: A Kashmiri Vaiṣṇava (Pāñcarātra) scholar who wrote the Spandapradīpikā, a commentary on the Spandakārikā ascribing it to Kallaṭa - an instance of Vaiṣṇava engagement with Spanda.

name: Utpaladeva
summary: Son of Udayākara (ĪPK 4.18) and disciple of Somānanda; systematized the Pratyabhijñā in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā with a short and a long commentary, wrote the Siddhitrayī and the devotional hymns of the Śivastotrāvalī.

realization_account.text: His hymns present devotion as the relish of an identity with Śiva already recognized.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Uttamaujas
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army, 'valiant' (1.6).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6.

name: Uttamūr Vīrarāghavācārya
summary: 20th-century Vaṭakalai scholar and editor-commentator of Viśiṣṭādvaita works (post-1800; recorded as recent).

name: Uvaṭa
summary: Son of Vajraṭa of Ānandapura; wrote at Avantī under King Bhoja a commentary (Mantrabhāṣya) on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and a commentary on the Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya.

queries: Uvata son of Vajrata Anandapura Avanti Bhoja
checks.note: Confirmed in every detail: son of Vajraṭa of Ānandapura; wrote at Avantī in Bhoja's reign; Vājasaneyi-saṃhitā-bhāṣya and Ṛkprātiśākhya-bhāṣya; 11th c.
Confirmed: son of Vajraṭa; commentaries on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and on the Ṛgveda and Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhyas; at Bhoja's court in the mid-11th c. (Wikipedia).

alt_summary: Commentator on the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā and on the Ṛgveda and Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhyas.

name: Uyyakkoṇḍār
summary: Disciple of Nāthamuni and teacher of Maṇakkāl Nambi; the tradition says he preferred the Lord's service to learning yoga.

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tirukkaṭavūr
summary: Author of the Tirukkaḷiṟṟuppaṭiyār (c. 1177), a commentary in verse on the Tiruvuntiyār; in the teaching line of the Tiruviyalūr author (through Āḷuṭaiya Tēvanāyaṉār — low confidence).

name: Uyyavanta Tēvanāyaṉār of Tiruviyalūr
summary: Author of the Tiruvuntiyār (c. 1147), earliest of the Meykaṇṭa Śāstras.

name: Vācaspati Miśra

scholarly.text: 9th or 10th c. CE (Nyāyasūcīnibandha dated 898 of an era read as Vikrama = 841 CE or Śaka = 976 CE)

summary: Polymath of Mithilā who commented on every Vedic school; for Nyāya he wrote the Tātparyaṭīkā — rescuing Uddyotakara's 'aged cows' from the mire of bad commentaries — and the Nyāyasūcīnibandha, which fixed the sūtra text. He reads 'avyapadeśya' and 'vyavasāyātmaka' in NS 1.1.4 as indeterminate and determinate perception, following his teacher Trilocana.
notes: His non-Nyāya works belong to U09, U10, U12 and U13.
alt_summary: (Yoga unit contribution) Author of the Tattvavaiśāradī, the standard sub-commentary on Vyāsa's Yoga-bhāṣya; a polymath who also commented on Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Mīmāṃsā and Advaita texts.
U09 contribution: author of the Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, the standard later commentary on the SK; the Yuktidīpikā's colophon also names him, an ascription scholars reject.
Polymath of Mithilā who commented on the works of six schools; his Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara's BSBh founded the Bhāmatī line of Advaita, and his lost Tattvasamīkṣā commented on Maṇḍana's Brahmasiddhi.
Polymath commentator; for Mīmāṃsā he wrote the Nyāyakaṇikā on Maṇḍana's Vidhiviveka and the Tattvabindu on sentence meaning (defending abhihitānvaya).

name: Vacchagotta
summary: A wanderer who repeatedly questioned the Buddha on the self and the undeclared (MN 71–73; SN 44.7–11); he went forth and became an arahant (MN 73).

name: Vāddhali
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). The reading of the name in the e-text is uncertain.

name: Vādībhasiṃha
summary: Author of the Kṣatracūḍāmaṇi and Gadyacintāmaṇi on Jīvandhara.

name: Vādidevasūri
summary: Śvetāmbara logician of Gujarat, author of the Pramāṇanayatattvāloka and Syādvādaratnākara; the tradition tells of his debate victory over the Digambara Kumudacandra at Siddharāja's court (1125).

name: Vādikesari Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Jīyar
summary: Teṅkalai commentator credited with the Paṉṉīrāyirappaṭi ('Twelve Thousand') on the Tiruvāymoḻi.

name: Vādirāja Tīrtha

tradition.text: the tradition gives him 120 years, 1480–1600

realization_account.text: The tradition regards Vādirāja as a ṛju soul — one of the class destined for the highest offices — and as a future Vāyu (bhāvi-samīra).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Pontiff of the Sode maṭha (Uḍupi), worshipper of Hayagrīva, poet and polemicist: author of the Yuktimallikā, the Tīrthaprabandha, the Rukmiṇīśavijaya and a commentary on the Mahābhārata, and of Kannada songs signed 'Hayavadana'. The tradition credits him with making the Uḍupi paryāya of Kṛṣṇa worship a two-year turn.
notes: The 1522 start of the two-year paryāya and the 'bhāvi-samīra' belief are recalled at moderate/low confidence.

name: Vāgbhaṭa
summary: Author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, 'son of Siṃhagupta, lord of physicians' (colophons), who made a verse 'heart' of the eight-limbed medicine from the scattered tantras of Agniveśa and the others (AHS Sū 1.3-5). He opens with homage to the unprecedented physician who destroyed the diseases of passion, and ends by asking readers to take what is well said without partisanship.
notes: Buddhist affiliation is a scholarly inference from AHS Sū 1.1 and 2.21-22. Some later authors distinguish an elder Vāgbhaṭa (Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha). The Rasaratnasamuccaya's author also calls himself son of Siṃhagupta.

name: The eight Vāgdevatās (Vaśinī and the others)
summary: The eight goddesses of speech — Vaśinī, Kāmeśvarī, Modinī, Vimalā, Aruṇā, Jayinī, Sarveśvarī and Kaulinī — who composed the Lalitā Sahasranāma at the Goddess's command and preside over the eight-cornered enclosure of the Śrīcakra; the Saundaryalaharī (17) makes them givers of poetic speech.
notes: Names as in PKS 3.20 (checked).

name: Vāgīśvarakīrti
summary: Vikramaśīla 'gatekeeper' (11th c.), author of the Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa and of works on the Guhyasamāja and consecration.

name: Vaidehī
summary: Queen of Magadha, mother of Ajātaśatru, whose plea for a land without sorrow occasions the Contemplation Sūtra.
notes: U43 contribution: the sūtra calls her an ordinary being (fanfu) of feeble mind (T365 341c23); Shandao reads her as the model of the ordinary person for whom the sūtra was taught; at the end she attains the acceptance of non-arising (T365 346a27-b01).

name: Vaidyanātha Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Jātakapārijāta.

name: Vairocana the translator (Pagor Vairocana)
summary: One of the first seven Tibetan monks; sent to India, he received the mind and space series from Śrī Siṃha, translated the five early mind-series scriptures and (with Śrī Siṃha) the Kunjed Gyalpo; exiled through court intrigue to Gyalmo Rong, he taught Yudra Nyingpo there.
alt_names: ba go ra bai ro tsa na
alt_summary: In Sowa Rigpa's account the translator who brought the Four Tantras from India (via Kashmir) and taught them to Yuthok the Elder and to King Trisong Detsen before they were concealed as treasure.

name: Vaiśampāyana

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Vyāsa's disciple who recites the Mahābhārata to king Janamejaya during the snake sacrifice; the narrator of the Nārāyaṇīya to Janamejaya.

checks.note: Located: 27 branches (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.1), teacher of Yājñavalkya, Taittirīyas as partridges (3.5.13). Narrator of the Mahābhārata to Janamejaya — standard (Vaiśampāyana article).
Confirmed: A 4.3.104 lists Vaiśampāyana's pupils (U01). The Purāṇic quarrel with Yājñavalkya is the tradition's account.
Narrator of the Nārāyaṇīya passages to Janamejaya, as entered.

alt_summary: Vyāsa's pupil who received the Yajurveda and made twenty-seven branches of it (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.1); teacher of Yājñavalkya, whose disgorged Yajus the other pupils took up as partridges (tittiri) — hence the Taittirīyas; narrator of the Mahābhārata to Janamejaya.
Teacher of the Black Yajurveda and, in the Purāṇic story, the teacher with whom Yājñavalkya quarrelled.

name: Vaiśravaṇa (Vālakhilya)
summary: Questioner in the Pāśupatabrahma Upaniṣad, called a son of Brahmā and a Vālakhilya; not the Kubera of the Purāṇas as far as the text says.

checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of pasupatabrahma, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Vaitaraṇa
summary: One of Suśruta's fellow students who approached Divodāsa Dhanvantari for the teaching (Su Sū 1.3).
notes: Later commentators cite tantras under some of these names (Aupadhenava, Aurabhra, Pauṣkalāvata) — recalled, not checked.

name: Vājapyāyana
summary: Ancient grammarian cited in Kātyāyana's vārttikas and the Mahābhāṣya (on P 1.2.64) as holding that a word denotes the universal form (ākṛti).

name: Vājaśravasa (father of Naciketas)
alt_names: Uśan (some read uśan in KU 1.1.1 as a name)
summary: Naciketas's father, who in the Viśvajit sacrifice gives away all his possessions, offering worn-out cows; in anger he gives his son to Death (KU 1.1.1-4). Yama calls him Auddālaki Āruṇi (KU 1.1.11) and Naciketas calls him Gautama (KU 1.1.10).
notes: Whether he is the Uddālaka Āruṇi of ChU/BAU is not settled; KU 1.1.11 calls him Auddālaki ('son of Uddālaka').

checks.note: Located: KU 1.1.1 ('uśan ha vai vājaśravasaḥ sarvavedasaṃ dadau'), 1.1.10 (Naciketas calls him 'gautama') and 1.1.11 (Yama calls him 'auddālakir āruṇiḥ'). The older TB 3.11.8 has the same opening and 'gautama-kumāram'. 'Viśvajit' is from Śaṅkara's gloss, not the text. The entry correctly leaves his identity with Uddālaka open.

name: Vajirā
summary: A nun who answered Māra with the chariot simile: 'a being' is a convention for the heap of aggregates (SN 5.10).

name: Vajrabodhi
summary: South Indian master (671–741) who brought the Tattvasaṃgraha (Vajraśekhara) tradition to China; teacher of Amoghavajra.

name: Vajradhara
summary: The 'holder of the vajra', the primordial or sixth buddha in whose form the Buddha teaches the tantras; the ultimate source of the tantric lineages and the form in which the guru is to be seen (Gurupañcāśikā 22).

name: Vajragarbha (bodhisattva of the Daśabhūmika)
summary: The bodhisattva who, empowered by the buddhas, expounds the ten grounds in the Daśabhūmika.
alt_summary: U44 contribution: in the Hevajra the bodhisattva who questions the Buddha; the Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā, one of the three 'bodhisattva commentaries' of the Kālacakra circle, is ascribed to him.

name: Vajrapāṇi (the Indian master)
summary: Disciple of Maitrīpa (b. 1017), who taught mahāmudrā in Nepal and Tibet and translated Saraha's Queen Dohā with Asu (colophon of Tōh 2264).
notes: Distinct from the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.

name: Vajrasattva (Dorje Sempa)
summary: In the Dzogchen transmission the sambhogakāya through whom the teaching passes from Samantabhadra to Garab Dorje; the interlocutor of the Kunjed Gyalpo ('sems dpa' rdo rje'); the deity of purification in the preliminaries (the hundred-syllable mantra).

name: Vajrasvāmin
summary: The last to know ten Pūrvas (daśapūrvin) in the Śvetāmbara account; famous child-renouncer and wonder-worker who (the stories say) carried the saṅgha through a famine by magical power.

tradition.text: c. 1st c. CE

name: Vāc Āmbhṛṇī
summary: Vāc, daughter of the seer Ambhṛṇa, the ṛṣikā of RV 10.125, in which Speech proclaims herself the queen and self of all, moving with the gods, the power by which beings eat, see, breathe and hear, who makes whom she loves a brahman and a seer.

realization_account.text: The Anukramaṇī gives the deity of her hymn as 'ātman', the seer praising herself as the self of all; later commentary (Sāyaṇa) presents her as a knower of Brahman who spoke from identity with it.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Sāyaṇa's characterization recalled with moderate confidence.

checks.note: Header: 'vāg āmbhṛṇī', deity ātmā.

name: Vakkali
summary: A monk devoted to gazing at the Buddha's body, told 'whoever sees the Dhamma sees me' (SN 22.87); foremost in faith.
notes: AN 1 Etadaggavagga (the 'foremost' lists)

name: Välivita Saraṇaṅkara
summary: Sri Lankan monk (1698–1778) who led the 18th-century revival and, after higher ordination was restored by Siamese monks in 1753, became the first Saṅgharāja of the Siyam Nikāya.

name: Vallabhācārya (Śrī Vallabha, Mahāprabhujī)
summary: Founder of Śuddhādvaita and the Puṣṭimārga; author of the Aṇubhāṣya, Tattvārthadīpanibandha, Subodhinī and the sixteen short works; established the worship of Śrīnāthjī at Govardhana and taught the brahmasambandha initiation.

realization_account.text: Born at Campāraṇya to the Telugu Brahmin Lakṣmaṇa Bhaṭṭa and Illammā; won a debate at the Vijayanagara court and was honoured as ācārya; travelled India three times (the 84 'seats', baiṭhak, mark where he expounded the Bhāgavata); at midnight on Śrāvaṇa śukla ekādaśī at Gokul, Kṛṣṇa appeared and gave him the brahmasambandha, and the next day he initiated Dāmodaradās Harsānī; at the end he took renunciation and entered the Ganges at Kāśī (1531), leaving the Śikṣāślokī as his last instruction.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Least-sure item: founder of the Puṣṭimārga; his reading of the Gītā is in the first section (Śāstrārtha-prakaraṇa) of the Tattvārthadīpanibandha. Traditional dates 1479–1531 as entered.

alt_summary: Founder of the Puṣṭimārga; counts the Gītā among the four authorities and expounds its meaning in the first section of his Tattvārthadīpanibandha.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Vālmīki

tradition.text: Tretā yuga, contemporary of Rāma

summary: The first poet (ādikavi), author of the Rāmāyaṇa; told Rāma's story by Nārada (1.1), he utters the first śloka in grief at a hunter's killing of a krauñca bird (1.2.15–18) and teaches the poem to Kuśa and Lava.

checks.note: Located as described.
MU 1.1: Brahmā grants Bharadvāja a boon and sends him to his teacher Vālmīki (1.1.7-11), who tells the Mokṣopāya (1.1.5 'bharadvājāya'). The entry's summary fits.

alt_summary: In U06's texts: the traditional author of the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha / Mokṣopāya, who opens it by telling Bharadvāja that Brahmā sent him to complete a Rāmāyaṇa of liberation (MU 1.1).
Counted among the eighteen Siddhars in the popular Tamil list, with a samādhi place at Eṭṭukkuṭi.
places: Eṭṭukkuṭi — samādhi in the popular list
notes: U22 contribution; whether the list intends the epic poet or a Tamil namesake is not settled. Counted in the popular list of the eighteen Siddhars (see cpt:eighteen-siddhars); the samādhi place given follows that list and is recalled at low confidence.

name: Vālmīki (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. No identification with the poet of the Rāmāyaṇa is implied.

name: Vāmadeva

realization_account.text: AU 2.1.5-6: while still in the womb he knew the births of the gods; knowing thus, on the body's breaking he rose up and became immortal.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The Ṛgvedic seer who, seeing that he was brahman, declared 'I was Manu, I was the sun' (BAU 1.4.10) and who, lying in the womb, knew all the births of the gods (AU 2.1.5, quoting RV 4.27.1).

checks.note: Headers: 'vāmadevo gautamaḥ' for book 4; 4.26.1–3 speaker Vāmadeva or Indra, deity Indra or ātman — as the entry says; citations at BĀU 1.4.10 and the Aitareya Upaniṣad located.
Located: BĀU 1.4.10 ('ṛṣir vāmadevaḥ pratipede 'haṃ manur abhavaṃ sūryaś ca', = RV 4.26.1) and AU 2.1.5 ('garbhe nu san … vāmadeva evam uvāca', = RV 4.27.1). Both RV verses were located in DCS.
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of varaha, bhiksuka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

alt_summary: Vāmadeva Gautama, seer of Ṛgveda book 4. His verses 'I was Manu and I the Sun' (4.26.1) and 'while still in the womb I knew all the births of the gods' (4.27.1) are cited in the Upaniṣads as the words of one who realized himself as all (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.10; Aitareya 2.5).
U04 contribution: model of the 'ant's path' of gradual liberation through births (Varāha 4.38–42) and named among the paramahaṃsas (Bhikṣuka).
Author of the Janmamaraṇavicāra on birth and death.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). The Anukramaṇī allows Indra (or the self, ātman) as speaker/deity of 4.26.1–3.

name: Vāmadeva (in the Amanaska)
summary: The sage to whom Īśvara teaches the mindless yoga in the Amanaska (recalled).

name: Vāmana (the poetician)
summary: Author of the Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra, holding that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry; distinct from Vāmana co-author of the Kāśikā.

name: Vāmana (co-author of the Kāśikā)
summary: Co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti; distinct from Vāmana the theorist of poetics.

checks.note: Confirmed: co-author of the Kāśikāvṛtti, 7th c. CE.

name: Vāmaṉa Muṉivar
summary: 14th-c. Tamil Jain monk, author of the Mērumantara Purāṇam and of the Samayadivākaram commentary on the Nīlakēci.

name: Vāmana Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Shirur maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Vāmanadatta
summary: Author of the Svabodhodayamañjarī.

name: Vāmaśakti

scholarly.text: 12th c. (inscriptions name more than one Vāmaśakti)

summary: Kālāmukha pontiff of the Kōḍiya-maṭha at Balligāve, praised in 12th-c. inscriptions for learning and influence (details to be checked).

name: Vanacandra
summary: Hita Harivaṃśa's son and successor at the Rādhāvallabha temple.

name: Vaṅgasena
summary: Author of a large Cikitsāsārasaṅgraha.

name: Vaṅgīsa

name: Vappa

name: Varadarāja (Kṛṣṇadāsa)
summary: Author of a second Śivasūtravārttika, following Kṣemarāja.

name: Varadarāja (grammarian)
summary: Pupil of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita; author of the Laghu- and Madhya-siddhāntakaumudī.

checks.note: Confirmed: 17th-c. pupil of Bhaṭṭoji; wrote the Madhya-, Laghu- and Sāra-siddhāntakaumudī (Wikipedia).

name: Varadarāja (commentator on the Nayaviveka)
summary: Author of the Nayavivekadīpikā on Bhavanātha's Nayaviveka.

name: Varadarāja
summary: Author of the Tārkikarakṣā, a Nyāya manual with auto-commentary.

name: Varāha (the Boar avatāra)
summary: Viṣṇu's boar form, who appears to Ṛbhu after twelve divine years of austerity and teaches him the 96 tattvas and non-dual knowledge (Varāha 1–3).

queries: e-text name search: Varāha (the Boar avatāra)
checks.note: Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of varaha, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.

name: Varāhamihira
summary: The great compiler of all three branches of jyotiṣa: Pañcasiddhāntikā (siddhānta), Bṛhajjātaka and Laghujātaka (horā), Bṛhat Saṃhitā (saṃhitā), and works on marriage and royal expeditions (Yogayātrā). Son and pupil of Ādityadāsa, of Avanti, he received a boon from the Sun at Kāpitthaka and composed his horā after studying the views of the seers (BJ 28.9); he bows to the former promulgators (BJ 28.10) and honours the Yavanas (BS 2.14). Tradition counts him among the 'nine jewels' of Vikramāditya's court (scholarly account: a later legend).

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE; Pañcasiddhāntikā epoch 505; death 587 by a late report

realization_account.text: Received a boon of grace from the Sun (savitṛ-labdha-vara-prasāda) at Kāpitthaka.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vardhamāna Upādhyāya
summary: Son of Gaṅgeśa; wrote Prakāśa commentaries on Udayana's works (Kusumāñjali, Kiraṇāvalī) and on his father's Tattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Vareṇya
summary: The king to whom Gajānana teaches the Gaṇeśa Gītā; in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa Gaṇeśa had been born in his house.

queries: Gajanana born to King Varenya Pushpika Ganesha Purana
checks.note: In the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa the Gajānana avatāra is born as the son of Vareṇya and Puṣpikā and raised by Parāśara; the Gaṇeśa Gītā is his teaching to Vareṇya.

name: Varṣāditya
summary: Son of Saṅgamāditya in Somānanda's lineage (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.119).

name: Vārṣagaṇya
alt_names: Vṛṣagaṇa (a related name in the Yuktidīpikā and in the Chinese Life of Vasubandhu)
summary: Early Sāṃkhya teacher. The Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 3.53) cites him by name: there is no difference at the root, since there is no difference of form, separation or kind. The Yuktidīpikā (on SK 22) reports his views that mahat arises directly from pradhāna and that the subtle elements are cumulative; it lists him among the teachers before Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71). Some scholars ascribe the Ṣaṣṭitantra to him.

name: Vārṣyāyaṇi
summary: Teacher cited by Yāska for the six modifications of being: is born, exists, changes, grows, declines, perishes (Nirukta 1.2).

checks.note: Text-located: Nir 1.2 'ṣaḍ bhāvavikārā bhavantīti vārṣyāyaṇiḥ'.

name: Varuṇa
summary: Father and teacher of Bhṛgu in Taittirīya 3, who sets him to seek brahman by tapas.

Located: TU 3.1.1 (the definition 'yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante …') and 3.2–3.5.

alt_summary: The god Varuṇa as father-teacher of Bhṛgu: gives the definition of brahman as that from which beings are born, by which they live and into which they enter, and sends him to seek it by tapas (TU 3.1).
Named by Kṛṣṇa among his manifestations ('of the water-dwellers I am Varuṇa'), and by Arjuna in his praise of the Lord (Bhagavad Gītā 10.29, 11.39).

name: Varuṇaśiva
summary: Author of the Varuṇapaddhati, a Siddhānta ritual manual.

name: Vasantarāja
summary: Author of the Vasantarāja Śākuna on augury.

name: Vāseṭṭha
summary: A young brahmin who, with Bhāradvāja, asked whether one is a brahmin by birth or by deeds (MN 98 / Snp 3.9) and questioned the Buddha on union with Brahmā (DN 13); in DN 27 a Vāseṭṭha is a novice.
notes: The Vāseṭṭhas of DN 13, DN 27 and MN 98 may not be the same person.

name: Vasiṣṭha
summary: In U06's texts: the family priest of the Ikṣvākus who, at Viśvāmitra's request, teaches the despondent young Rāma the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha / Mokṣopāya; within it he recounts his own learning from Brahmā, from the crow Bhuśuṇḍa and from Śiva.

checks.note: Headers: 'maitrāvaruṇir vasiṣṭhaḥ' for book 7 (7.33.10–14 Vasiṣṭha's sons as seers with Vasiṣṭha as deity); 7.33.11 birth from Mitra-Varuṇa and Urvaśī; 7.18 Sudās; seer of 10.137.7. Parāśara as grandson through Śakti confirmed by web sources.
Confirmed as the traditional author of the extant Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra; he is also named among the lawgivers at YājñS 1.5 (text-located).
Epic role located; Rāmāyaṇa preceptor role consistent with the text.

queries: role located in the local text
evidence: local:sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/vedAnta/valmiki/ and unknown_Anandabodhendra/ (Yogavāsiṣṭha vulgate with Tātparyaprakāśa, Nirṇaya Sāgara ed.; Muktabodha M00335-M00339, M00345)
checks.note: Teacher of Rāma throughout the Mokṣopāya / Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

alt_summary: Vasiṣṭha Maitrāvaruṇi, seer of Ṛgveda book 7: the hymns to Varuṇa in which he searches his conscience (7.86–89), the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya verse (7.59.12), the account of his birth from Mitra-Varuṇa and Urvaśī, 'born from mind' (7.33.11), and the victory of King Sudās in the Battle of the Ten Kings (7.18, 7.33). The tradition makes him the Ikṣvāku family priest and teacher of Rāma, rival and finally acknowledger of Viśvāmitra.

Ancient seer, family priest of the Ikṣvākus; in the Mokṣadharma he teaches Karāla Janaka the Sāṃkhya-Yoga doctrine of the 24 principles, the 25th and the 26th (12.291–296); in the Rāmāyaṇa he is Rāma's preceptor.
U28 contribution: the teacher of the Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā's yoga, and named in HYP 1.18 with 'the munis' as an authority on postures (as distinct from Matsyendra and 'the yogins').
U23 contribution: named by Lakṣmīdhara as author of one of the five Śubhāgamas that teach the Vedic Samaya way.
One of the promulgators of jyotiṣa: the Vāsiṣṭha Siddhānta (summarized in the Pañcasiddhāntikā) and a Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā on muhūrta are ascribed to him.
U02 contribution: the Vedic seer to whom the Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra is ascribed.

realization_account.text: Varuṇa took Vasiṣṭha into his boat and made him a seer by his powers (RV 7.88.3–4).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Ṛgveda)

notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). Parāśara is his grandson (through Śakti) in the tradition; 'students' here records that line of descent.
alt_notes: His teaching in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is covered by U06.

name: Vasu (commentator on the Śataśāstra)
summary: Author of the commentary on Āryadeva's verses in the Bai lun translated by Kumārajīva; otherwise unknown.

name: Vasubandhu

tradition.text: died aged 80 at Ayodhyā (Paramārtha's Life)

scholarly.text: c. 4th–5th c. CE; E. Frauwallner proposed two Vasubandhus (an elder Yogācāra, a younger Kośa author) — a thesis now mostly abandoned but still cited

realization_account.text: A master of Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika who wrote the Abhidharmakośa and scorned the Mahāyāna, he was brought to it when Asaṅga, feigning illness, had him hear the Akṣayamatinirdeśa and Daśabhūmika; repenting, he wished to cut out his tongue, but Asaṅga told him to use that tongue to teach the Mahāyāna instead.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu, T2049; Tibetan histories)

summary: Author of the Abhidharmakośa and, after his conversion by Asaṅga, of the Twenty and Thirty Verses, the Three Natures and commentaries on the Maitreya texts; honoured in East Asia as the second patriarch of Yogācāra and in Tibet as one of the 'six ornaments'.
notes: U38 owns the Abhidharma side of this entry; U41 contributes the Yogācāra works and account.
alt_summary: Author of the Abhidharmakośa and its bhāṣya, the classic summary of Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika Abhidharma with Sautrāntika criticisms; in its ninth chapter he refutes the Vātsīputrīya person and the non-Buddhist self. (This unit contributes the Abhidharma side; the Yogācāra works belong to U41.)
alt_notes: U43 contribution: known in East Asian Pure Land as Tianqin 天親 / Seshin 世親; the Rebirth Treatise (T1524) is attributed to him; second of the seven masters of Jōdo Shinshū.

name: Vasubandhu (Posu Pantou 婆修盤頭), twenty-first Chan patriarch
summary: Twenty-first patriarch in the Chan list; the Chan biography (an ascetic who ate one meal a day) does not match the Yogācāra author (tch:vasubandhu), so a separate entry is kept.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 21.

name: Vāsudeva Dīkṣita
summary: Author of the Adhvaramīmāṃsākutūhalavṛtti on the whole Mīmāṃsā Sūtra.

name: Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma
summary: Navadvīpa scholar who, on the tradition's account, studied in Mithilā and brought the Tattvacintāmaṇi to Navadvīpa (by memory, since copying was not permitted); teacher of Raghunātha Śiromaṇi in the same account; later a court scholar at Puri, where the Gauḍīya hagiographies place his meeting with Caitanya.
notes: Most details are the tradition's account (low confidence).

name: Vāsudevāśrama
summary: Author of the Yatidharmaprakāśa, a digest of the renouncer's rules.

checks.note: Confirmed as the author of the Yatidharmaprakāśa (Olivelle 1976-77). The entry gives no dates.

name: Vasugupta
summary: The Kashmiri teacher to whom the Śiva Sūtras were revealed and from whom the Spanda tradition descends; Kṣemarāja also makes him the author of the Spandakārikā.

realization_account.text: Paramaśiva, wishing the secret tradition not to be cut off, favoured him in a dream and told him of a secret on a great rock on Mahādeva mountain; on waking he found the rock, which turned over at the touch of his hand, and received the sūtras (Kṣemarāja). In Bhāskara's account the sūtras appeared to him 'by a siddha's command'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vasumitra

tradition.text: Presided over the council of Kaniṣka in Kashmir (Xuanzang)

summary: One of the four great masters of the Vibhāṣā, who held that dharmas are called past, present and future according to their state (avasthā) — the view Vasubandhu judged the best (AK 5.26). The tradition also credits a Vasumitra with the Prakaraṇapāda and the Samayabhedoparacanacakra; scholars usually distinguish several Vasumitras.
notes: Homonyms: scholars distinguish the Vibhāṣā master, the author of the Prakaraṇapāda and the doxographer; the tradition often identifies them. One id is used here with that caveat.

name: Vasumitra (Posumiduo 婆須蜜多), seventh Chan patriarch
summary: Seventh patriarch in the Chan list. Not to be merged automatically with the Sarvāstivāda master Vasumitra (tch:vasumitra); scholars think the Chan list borrowed names from Sarvāstivāda lineage lists.
notes: Position in the Chan list of 28 Indian patriarchs as given in the Platform Sūtra (Zongbao ed., T2008, read locally at prepared ref 13.11) and the Jingde chuandeng lu juan 1–3. The list goes back to the Baolin zhuan (801); scholars regard the Chan biographies of these figures as legendary. Number 7.

name: Vasunandi
summary: Commentator on the Mūlācāra (Ācāravṛtti) and author of a Śrāvakācāra (c. 11th–12th c.).
alt_summary: Digambara author of a śrāvakācāra and of commentaries (on the Āptamīmāṃsā and Mūlācāra).

name: Vāsupūjya
summary: The twelfth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the buffalo. Parents: Vasupūjya and Jayā. Born at Campā; attained nirvāṇa at Campā. The only Tīrthaṅkara to attain nirvāṇa at Campā; his body is described as red; Śvetāmbara accounts say he did not marry or rule.

tradition.text: the twelfth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Vasurāta
summary: Named by the commentators as Bhartṛhari's teacher in grammar.
notes: Known only from commentarial report (Puṇyarāja on the closing verses of VP 2, from memory).

name: Vaṭakku Tiruvīti Piḷḷai
summary: Disciple of Nampiḷḷai who wrote down his teacher's lectures as the Īṭu Muppattāṟāyirappaṭi; father of Piḷḷai Lokācārya and Aḻagiya Maṇavāḷa Perumāḷ Nāyaṉār.

name: The Vātaraśana munis (seven wind-girdled sages)
summary: The seven 'wind-girdled' silent sages to whom the verses of the Keśin hymn (RV 10.136) are ascribed one each: Jūti, Vātajūti, Viprajūti, Vṛṣāṇaka, Karikrata, Etaśa and Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked). A group entry.

checks.note: Header: '1 jūtiḥ, 2 vātajūtiḥ, 3 viprajūtiḥ, 4 vṛṣāṇakaḥ, 5 karikrataḥ, 6 etaśaḥ, 7 ṛṣyaśṛṅgaḥ (ete vātaraśanā munayaḥ)' — list confirmed.

name: Vaṭeśvara
summary: Author of the Vaṭeśvarasiddhānta (904 CE), defender of the Āryabhaṭa school.

name: Vātsīputra
summary: Eponymous founder of the Vātsīputrīya, the first Pudgalavāda school; Chinese sources make him a disciple in the line of Śāriputra and Rāhula (low confidence).

name: Vātsya (redactor of the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā)
summary: In the Kāśyapa Saṃhitā's own account, restored the lost tantra of Vṛddha Jīvaka.

name: Vātsyāyana
summary: Author of the Nyāyabhāṣya, the first extant commentary on the Nyāya Sūtra; criticized by Dignāga. Not to be identified (on the scholarly account) with Vātsyāyana Mallanāga of the Kāmasūtra.

name: Vātsyāyana Mallanāga
summary: Author of the Kāmasūtra; distinct from Vātsyāyana Pakṣilasvāmin of the Nyāyabhāṣya (tch:vatsyayana).

checks.note: Author of the Kāmasūtra (text held locally). The 'c. 3rd c. CE' date was not confirmed by a scholarly page (the search found only 1st–6th c. ranges). His distinction from Vātsyāyana Pakṣilasvāmin is standard.

name: Vaṭṭagāmaṇī Abhaya
summary: King of Laṅkā in whose reign, by the chronicles, the Tipiṭaka and its commentary were written down at the Āloka-vihāra (Aluvihāra) for fear of their loss.

name: Vaṭṭakera
summary: Author of the Mūlācāra; some Digambaras identify him with Kundakunda.
alt_summary: Name under which the Mūlācāra is transmitted.

name: Vāyilā Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. He worshipped Śiva in a temple built within his mind, with love as the offering.

realization_account.text: He worshipped Śiva in a temple built within his mind, with love as the offering.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vāyorvida (the royal sage)
summary: The royal sage who praised vāyu as the upholder of body and world, 'the lord Vāyu himself' (Ca Sū 12.8, 12.10); six tastes defined by qualities (Sū 26.8); in Sū 25.12-13 (as Vāryovida) he holds that beings and diseases arise from rasa (water).
notes: Refs checked against the DCS e-text of the Caraka Saṃhitā.

name: Vāyubhūti
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether the soul is other than the body. Brother of Indrabhūti.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Vedānta Deśika
summary: Veṅkaṭanātha of Tūppul near Kāñcī, poet, logician and theologian; the Vaṭakalai regard him as their doctrinal source. He wrote over a hundred works in Sanskrit, Maṇipravāḷa and Tamil — the Rahasyatrayasāra, Tattvamuktākalāpa, Śatadūṣaṇī, Nyāyasiddhāñjana, Nyāyapariśuddhi, Seśvaramīmāṃsā, Pādukāsahasra, Saṅkalpasūryodaya and many hymns — and lived through the sack of Śrīraṅgam.

realization_account.text: The tradition holds him an incarnation of the bell of Veṅkaṭeśvara; the titles Vedāntācārya and Sarvatantrasvatantra were conferred on him by Raṅganātha and Raṅganāyakī; Hayagrīva, whose mantra he received from Garuḍa, granted him knowledge; he declined royal patronage.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

checks.note: Both works confirmed.

notes: Contribution from U08.
alt_summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (Veṅkaṭanātha) whose Pāñcarātrarakṣā defends and expounds the Pāñcarātra.
Author of the Tātparyacandrikā on Rāmānuja's Gītābhāṣya.
For Mīmāṃsā: author of the Seśvaramīmāṃsā, a theistic commentary on the Mīmāṃsā Sūtra, and the Mīmāṃsāpādukā.
alt_notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Vena Bhārgava
summary: Seer of the Vena hymn RV 10.123; in the Atharvaveda (2.1) and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (32.8) Vena is the seer who 'saw that highest, hidden in secret, in which all becomes one nest'.
notes: Seer attributions follow the Sarvānukramaṇī as printed in the hymn headers of the local Ṛgveda text (checked).

checks.note: Header 10.123 'veno bhārgavaḥ'; AVŚ 2.1 seer Vena (brahma, ātmā); VS 32.8 'venas tat paśyan nihitaṃ guhā sat …' located.

name: Veṇābāī
summary: Young widow of Miraj who became Rāmdās's disciple and a mahant of the order (17th c.).

name: Veṅkaṭamādhava
summary: Author of the Ṛgarthadīpikā, a concise commentary on the whole Ṛgveda.

checks.note: Confirmed: author of the Ṛgarthadīpikā; dated between Skandasvāmin and Sāyaṇa, 10th–12th c. (debated).

name: Veṅkaṭamakhin
summary: Tanjore scholar, author of the Caturdaṇḍīprakāśikā and its seventy-two mela scheme; son of Govinda Dīkṣita.

name: Veṅkaṭeśa Daivajña
summary: Author of the Sarvārthacintāmaṇi.

name: Vessabhū
summary: The third of the seven Buddhas of DN 14 (thirty-one aeons ago).

name: Vibhīṣaṇa
summary: Rāvaṇa's righteous brother who took refuge with Rāma; the Rāmcaritmānas's 'chariot of dharma' teaching is addressed to him.

checks.note: Located as described.

queries: role located in the local text
checks.note: RCM Laṅkā, before dohā 80.

alt_summary: Rāvaṇa's brother who leaves him and takes refuge with Rāma; Rāma accepts him with the vow to protect all who seek refuge (6.18.33).

name: Vibhūticandra
summary: Indian master of the six-branch yoga (c. 1200) who fled to Nepal and Tibet after the fall of the monasteries; source of a six-branch lineage.

name: Vicakhnu
summary: A king who, pitying the animals at a sacrifice, proclaims non-violence as the highest dharma (12.257).

checks.note: Located as described.

name: Vidagdha Śākalya
summary: The last and most aggressive challenger at Janaka's court: questions Yājñavalkya on the number of gods and the persons and their abodes; unable to answer the question about the person of the Upaniṣads, his head shatters (BAU 3.9). In BAU 4.1.7 he holds that brahman is the heart.

checks.note: Text-located: ŚB 11.6.3.3–11 (the questions 'kati devāḥ'; his death and the stolen bones).
Located: BĀU 3.9.1-26 (his head shatters, 3.9.26) and 4.1.7 ('hṛdayaṃ vai brahma').

alt_summary: Yājñavalkya's opponent at Janaka's court, who asks 'how many gods?' and loses his head (ŚB 11.6.3; BĀU 3.9).

name: Videgha Māthava
summary: King who carried Agni Vaiśvānara in his mouth eastward to the Sadānīrā with his priest Gotama Rāhūgaṇa (ŚB 1.4.1.10–17).

checks.note: Text-located: ŚB 1.4.1.10–17 (with Gotama Rāhūgaṇa; the Sadānīrā boundary).

name: Vidura

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: An embodiment of Dharma; his death by yoga, entering Yudhiṣṭhira, is narrated at 15.33.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Half-brother of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Pāṇḍu, born of a śūdra woman; Dharma incarnate through Māṇḍavya's curse (1.100.28). He counsels Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Viduranīti, 5.33–40) and, declaring that as one born of a śūdra womb he will not speak beyond this, calls Sanatsujāta to teach the higher knowledge (5.41.5); consoles him after the war (11.2–7); dies in the forest by entering Yudhiṣṭhira's body limb by limb and breath by breath (15.33.25).

evidence: local:DharmicData MBh CE 1.100.28 (dharmo vidurarūpeṇa śāpāt ... māṇḍavyasya), 5.41.5, 15.33.25
checks.note: Every cited reference located, including the Māṇḍavya curse at 1.100.28.

name: Vidyādhirāja Tīrtha
summary: Jayatīrtha's successor; the tradition dates the later division of the lines (towards the Uttarādi, Rāghavendra and Vyāsarāja maṭhas) from his disciples.

name: Vidyāguru
summary: Number 18 of the eighteen avatāras / tīrthakaras of Śiva worshipped by the Śaiva (Pāśupata-Naiyāyika) ascetics according to the Jain doxographers Guṇaratna (Tarkarahasyadīpikā) and Rājaśekhara (Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 1348). Nothing else is recorded.
notes: Known only from the Jain lists; not to be conflated with the Vedic/Purāṇic sage of the same name.

name: Vidyānanda
summary: Digambara logician, author of the Tattvārthaślokavārttika, the Aṣṭasahasrī on the Āptamīmāṃsā and the Āptaparīkṣā, defending the omniscient teacher and refuting the creator God.

name: Vidyānanda (author of the Artharatnāvalī)
summary: Commentator on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (Artharatnāvalī).

name: Vidyāpati
summary: Maithili court poet of Mithila (c. 1352–1448) whose songs of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (and of Śiva) Caitanya relished.

name: Vidyāraṇya
notes: Identity with the minister Mādhava is the tradition's; scholars debate it.
summary: Pontiff of Śṛṅgeri (d. 1386), author of the Pañcadaśī, the Jīvanmuktiviveka, the Vivaraṇaprameyasaṅgraha and the Anubhūtiprakāśa; in the tradition identified with Mādhava, minister of the founders of Vijayanagara and brother of Sāyaṇa, and so credited with the Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha and the Śaṅkaradigvijaya.

checks.note: Low-confidence entry confirmed. Tradition identifies Mādhava (the author of the Parāśaramādhavīya and Kāla-mādhavīya, elder brother of Sāyaṇa) with Vidyāraṇya; some scholars contest this (Wikipedia). The entry states it as debated.
Confirmed: the Jīvanmuktiviveka treats vividiṣā- and vidvat-saṃnyāsa, and vāsanākṣaya, manonāśa and tattvajñāna, drawing on the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads and the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

queries: Vidyaranya Jivanmuktiviveka Yoga Vasistha vasanakshaya manonasha
checks.note: The Jīvanmuktiviveka builds its account of vāsanākṣaya and manonāśa on quotations from the (Laghu) Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

alt_notes: The identification of Mādhava with the monk Vidyāraṇya is traditional and disputed; registry id used.
alt_summary: For Mīmāṃsā: Mādhava, minister and family preceptor of King Bukka of Vijayanagara, composed the Jaiminīya-nyāya-mālā with its prose Vistara, a verse digest of all the adhikaraṇas.
The Mādhavācārya to whom the Kālamādhava on the right times of rites is ascribed; the tradition identifies him with Vidyāraṇya.
U04 contribution: the Jīvanmuktiviveka builds its account of the knower's renunciation and liberation while living on the Saṃnyāsa Upaniṣads and the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

In U06's context: his Jīvanmuktiviveka builds its account of liberation while living largely on quotations from the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (e.g. the weakening of latent tendencies and the dissolution of mind).
U02 contribution: tradition identifies the Vijayanagara scholar-minister Mādhava, author of the Parāśaramādhavīya and Kālanirṇaya, with Vidyāraṇya after renunciation; the identification is debated.

name: Vidyāraṇya Yati (author of the Śrīvidyārṇava)
summary: The renunciant to whom the Śrīvidyārṇava Tantra is ascribed; tradition sometimes identifies him with Mādhava Vidyāraṇya of Śṛṅgeri (tch:vidyaranya), which scholars doubt.

name: Ācārya Vidyāsāgara
summary: Digambara ācārya (1946–2024), initiator of a very large order of naked monks and of āryikās, poet in Hindi and Sanskrit (Mūkamāṭī).

name: Vidyāśaṅkara (Vidyātīrtha)
summary: Śṛṅgeri pontiff of the 14th c., remembered in the Śṛṅgeri tradition as Vidyāraṇya's teacher; the Vidyāśaṅkara temple at Śṛṅgeri commemorates him.

name: Vijayadhvaja Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff of the Pejavara maṭha (Uḍupi) and author of the Padaratnāvalī, the standard Mādhva commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

name: Vijayarakṣita
summary: Began the Madhukośa commentary on the Mādhava Nidāna.

name: Vijayīndra Tīrtha
summary: Pontiff at Kumbhakonam, trained by Vyāsatīrtha; a prolific polemicist (the tradition credits him with over a hundred works) who answered Appayya Dīkṣita's critiques of Madhva and commented on the Nyāyāmṛta.

name: Vijñānabhikṣu

scholarly.text: second half of the 16th c. CE

summary: (Yoga unit contribution) Vedāntin of 'non-separation' (avibhāga) who commented on Yoga, Sāṃkhya and the Brahma Sūtra. In the Yogavārttika he reads Yoga theistically, calls the bhāṣya 'the essence of all the Veda', argues for the mutual reflection of consciousness and buddhi (YV 1.7), gives his own account of the samprajñāta samādhis (YV 1.17) and holds that knowledge of the Supreme Lord is the swift cause of liberation (YV 1.51).
alt_summary: Commentator who revived Sāṃkhya-Yoga in a theistic, Vedānta-reconciling form: his Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra, his manual Sāṃkhyasāra, and his Yogavārttika on the Yoga Bhāṣya; he also wrote a Vedānta commentary on the Brahma Sūtra (Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya).

16th-c. Vārāṇasī scholar; in his Vijñānāmṛtabhāṣya he interprets the Brahma Sūtras as non-separation (avibhāga) of souls and prakṛti from Brahman — a difference-and-non-difference Vedānta integrating Sāṃkhya-Yoga and rejecting Śaṅkara's māyāvāda (which he calls a crypto-Buddhism, citing the Padma Purāṇa).

name: Vijñāneśvara
summary: Author of the Mitākṣarā at the court of Vikramāditya VI of Kalyāṇa.

name: Vikarṇa
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the leaders of his (the Kaurava) army (1.8).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.8.

name: Vikhanas

realization_account.text: Vikhanas is Nārāyaṇa himself (or the four-faced Brahmā born from him), so that his Sūtra is the first and best of sūtras.

summary: Founding sage of the Vaikhānasas and author of their Sūtra; the tradition identifies him with Brahmā born of Nārāyaṇa, or with Nārāyaṇa himself, and salutes him as the one 'whose father is Nārāyaṇa, whose mother is Haripriyā, whose disciples are Bhṛgu and the other sages' (Kriyādhikāra 1.1).

name: Vilāsavajra
summary: Author of the Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti (8th c.?).

name: Vimalakīrti
summary: The Licchavi householder of Vaiśālī, a bodhisattva of inconceivable skillful means who lives as a layman, visits gambling halls and brothels to teach, feigns illness to draw the Buddha's disciples, and answers Mañjuśrī's question on non-duality with silence; he comes from Akṣobhya's world Abhirati.

realization_account.text: Had served past buddhas, obtained the acceptance of dharmas, eloquence and dhāraṇī (Vimalakīrti 2.1)

name: Vimalamitra
summary: Indian paṇḍita invited to Tibet under Trisong Detsen; he translated the Guhyagarbha and mind-series texts and taught the Heart-essence (Vima Nyingthig) to the king and to Nyang Tingdzin Zangpo, then went to Wutaishan in China. Author of the Simultaneous Entry meditation text in the Tengyur (Tōh 3910).

tradition.text: 8th c.; remains in a body of light at Wutaishan and returns to Tibet every hundred years

realization_account.text: Attained the great transference rainbow body ('ja' lus 'pho ba chen po).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Vimalānanda Svāmī
summary: Commentator on the Karpūrādistotra (Hymn to Kālī) whose commentary Avalon translated.
notes: Date not recalled (probably 19th c.).

name: Vimalanātha
summary: The thirteenth Tīrthaṅkara of the present descending half-cycle (avasarpiṇī). Emblem (lāñchana): the boar. Parents: Kṛtavarman and Śyāmā. Born at Kāmpilya; attained nirvāṇa at Sammeda Śikhara. The Tamil Mērumantara Purāṇam makes Meru and Mandara his gaṇadharas.

tradition.text: the thirteenth of the twenty-four Jinas of this era (tradition's chronology of immense lifespans and intervals)

notes: Parents, birthplaces and emblems follow the common Śvetāmbara lists (e.g. Hemacandra); Digambara lists agree in most points and differ in some emblems and names.

name: Vimalaprabodha
summary: Author of Nepalese Kubjikā ritual works (Paścimārcanapaddhati, Mahārahasyasaṃpradāya) preserved in the Muktabodha collection.

name: Vimalaśiva
notes: From the Muktabodha catalogue description (sources_raw/raw_etexts/mixed/mukta/muktabodha_metadata.json (Muktabodha catalogue descriptions)).
summary: Saiddhāntika author of the Vimalāvatī on ritual, who took a lifelong vow of residence in Vārāṇasī.

name: Vimalasūri
summary: Author of the Prakrit Paumacariya, the earliest Jain Rāmāyaṇa; his sectarian affiliation is debated (some see Yāpanīya features).

name: Vimuktātman
summary: Author of the Iṣṭasiddhi, defending indescribable ignorance and the self as pure experience.

name: Ārya Vimuktisena
summary: Early commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra; classed by Tibetan doxographers among the Yogācāra-Svātantrika.

name: Vīṇāpa

realization_account.text: A prince devoted to playing the vīṇā; his guru taught him to meditate on the sound of the lute without discursive thought, and through sound he realized the unborn. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 11): Examining with devotion and diligence the sound to which one has grown habituated in error, examining sound as unborn, Vīṇāpa realized selflessness.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 11 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). A prince devoted to playing the vīṇā; his guru taught him to meditate on the sound of the lute without discursive thought, and through sound he realized the unborn.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Vinayavijaya
summary: Śvetāmbara monk, fellow-student of Yaśovijaya, author of the Lokaprakāśa and of the Śrīpāla-rāsa completed by Yaśovijaya.
alt_summary: 17th-c. Tapā Gaccha monk, author of the Kalpasūtra-Subodhikā (1639) and the cosmological Lokaprakāśa; companion of Yaśovijaya.

name: Vindhyavāsin
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher whose distinctive views the Yuktidīpikā records: from mahat arise six non-specifics (ahaṃkāra and the five subtle elements); the organs are eleven and all-pervading; the functions of saṅkalpa, abhimāna and adhyavasāya are one; there is no subtle body — birth is the organs' functioning at the seed-place and death its abandonment; even the supreme sage's knowledge is acquired, not innate. Kumārila reports that he did not accept an intermediate body. Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu tells that the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa, pupil of Vṛṣagaṇa, defeated Vasubandhu's teacher Buddhamitra in debate before a king at Ayodhyā.
notes: Kumārila's report (Ślokavārttika, Ātmavāda section) and the Chinese biography details are recalled, not checked.

name: Vinītadeva
summary: Nālandā commentator on Dharmakīrti's shorter treatises and on Vasubandhu's Twenty and Thirty Verses.
alt_summary: Commentator on Dharmakīrti and on Vinaya texts; author of the summary of the eighteen schools in four groups followed in Tibet.

name: Vipassī
summary: The first of the seven Buddhas of DN 14, ninety-one aeons ago, whose life is narrated as the model of a bodhisatta's career.

name: Vīrabhadra (Vīracandra)
summary: Son of Nityānanda and leader of his line at Khaḍadaha.
alt_summary: A monk of Mahāvīra's time to whom tradition ascribes several Prakīrṇakas (Catuḥśaraṇa, Bhaktaparijñā, and others).

name: Viṟaṉmiṇṭa Nāyaṉār
summary: One of the sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs. A devotee who declared Cuntarar and even the Lord 'outside' the fold when Cuntarar passed the assembled devotees at Tiruvārūr without honouring them; this led Śiva to give Cuntarar the first line of the Tiruttoṇṭattokai.

name: Vīrasena
summary: Digambara ācārya of the Pañcastūpa lineage who wrote the Dhavalā on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama (816 CE) and began the Jayadhavalā; teacher of Jinasena.

name: Virāṭa
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army (1.4); blows his conch (1.17).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.4, 1.17.

name: Virocana
summary: Lord of the asuras who studies with Prajāpati alongside Indra, concludes that the body is the self and teaches the asuras this 'doctrine of the asuras' (ChU 8.8.4-5).

checks.note: Located: ChU 8.7.2 and 8.8.4-5 ('asurāṇāṃ hy eṣopaniṣat').

name: Virūpa
alt_names: Śrī Dharmapāla (monastic name, per Tibetan accounts)
Dharmapāla (monastic name, in the tradition's account)

realization_account.text: A monk-scholar (at Nālandā or Somapura) who recited the Vajravārāhī (or Cakrasaṃvara) mantra for twelve years without a sign and threw his rosary into the latrine; that night Nairātmyā appeared and gave him consecration; he ate pigeons and drank wine and was expelled, walked across the Ganges, stopped the sun to go on drinking without paying, and subdued non-Buddhist shrines; his Hevajra teaching is the source of the Sakya Path and Result. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 3): Within mahāmudrā, rest that innate, beyond thought and reasoning, in its own selfless state; it does not fall into annihilation, being self-known in experience; it does not fall into permanence, being without clinging: it is union.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: U44 contribution (the siddha of the eighty-four): No. 3 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.
alt_summary: Indian mahāsiddha revered by the Sakya as the source of the Path with its Result: the tradition tells that, after years of fruitless practice at Nālandā, he was given the four empowerments by the goddess Nairātmyā in her maṇḍala and spoke the Vajra Verses; also known for stopping the sun and for his dohās.

U28 contribution: a Virūpākṣa is named among the Mahāsiddhas of HYP 1.5, and the Amṛtasiddhi is ascribed in its transmission to Virūpākṣa, commonly identified with the Buddhist mahāsiddha Virūpa; the identifications are not settled.
alt_notes: U44 also defines tch:virupa; this is the Sakya contribution.

name: Virūpākṣanātha
summary: Author of the Virūpākṣapañcāśikā, probably South Indian.

name: Visākhā Migāramātā
summary: Foremost laywoman donor, builder of the Pubbārāma at Sāvatthī; the uposatha teaching of AN 3.70 was addressed to her.

name: Visākha (lay follower)
summary: The lay follower, former husband of Dhammadinnā, who questioned her in MN 44.

name: Viṣṇu Tīrtha (Sode)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Sode maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa. He was Madhva's younger brother; the tradition also derives the Subrahmaṇya maṭha from him and remembers his austerities.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Viṣṇucitta (Engaḷāḻvāṉ)

Priest of King Sudās in book 3; the tradition makes him the rival of Vasiṣṭha and, in the epics, a king who became a brahmarṣi through tapas.

Royal sage who takes the young Rāma to protect his sacrifice and teaches him (Bālakāṇḍa); in the Āpaddharma, during a famine, he takes a dog's haunch from an outcaste, arguing the case for survival (12.139).

realization_account.text: Born a kṣatriya king (son of Gādhi), he attained the status of brahmarṣi by long tapas and was at last acknowledged by Vasiṣṭha (Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla-kāṇḍa).

summary: Mahānubhāva poet (late 13th – 14th c.), author of one of the seven classic Mahānubhāva poems.

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin

name: Viśvanātha Cakravartin

name: Viśvanātha Kavirāja
summary: Orissan poet-theorist, author of the Sāhityadarpaṇa, who defined poetry as a sentence whose soul is rasa and called rasa the twin of tasting Brahman.

name: Viśvārādhya

name: Vitapāda

name: Viṭṭhal Vipul
summary: Successor of Svāmī Haridās in the ascetic line.

name: Viṭṭhalanātha (Gusāṃījī)
summary: Vallabha's younger son and the organiser of the Puṣṭimārga: completed the Aṇubhāṣya, wrote the Vidvanmaṇḍana and Śṛṅgārarasamaṇḍana, elaborated the eightfold daily service (aṣṭayāma sevā), founded the aṣṭachāp of eight poet-singers and emphasised Rādhā (Svāminī); his seven sons founded the seven 'houses'.

summary: Father of Nivṛttināth, Jñāneśvar, Sopāndev and Muktābāī: a brahmin of Āpegāv who took sannyāsa at Kāśī, returned to household life at his guru's command, and was outcast with his family; he and his wife Rukmiṇībāī are said to have given up their lives at Prayāga as expiation so that their children might be accepted.

name: Vivekananda
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): he often quoted the Avadhūta Gītā and the Aṣṭāvakra Gītā; Ramakrishna is remembered as having had him read the Aṣṭāvakra Saṃhitā.

name: Vopadeva

alt_summary: U25 contribution: compiler of the Muktāphala, an arrangement of Bhāgavata verses under the themes of devotion, commented on by Hemādri.

name: Vṛddha Jīvaka

name: Vṛnda

name: Vṛṣabhadeva
summary: Author of the Paddhati, a sub-commentary on the Vṛtti to the first book of the Vākyapadīya.

name: Vṛtra

name: the Vṛttikāra (cited by Śabara)

summary: U31 contribution: the ancient grammarian credited with the lost Saṃgraha (said to have had a hundred thousand verses), which Bhartṛhari says declined before Patañjali; in the Mahābhāṣya he holds that a word denotes the individual substance (dravya), against Vājapyāyana's universal.

checks.note: Confirmed: the Vikṛtivallī is 'ascribed to Vyāḍi'; Vyāḍi known as an ancient grammarian (low confidence in the entry is now supported).
Low-confidence entry confirmed. The Mahābhāṣya praises 'dākṣāyaṇasya saṅgrahasya kṛtiḥ' (on 2.3.66) and cites Vyāḍi's view (on 1.2.64). The Vikṛtivallī is ascribed to Vyāḍi (Dharmawiki).

alt_summary: Ancient grammarian; the Vikṛtivallī on the eight modified recitations is ascribed to him.
Early grammarian, author by tradition of the lost Saṃgraha cited by Patañjali; the Vikṛtivallī on the modified recitations is also ascribed to him (low confidence).
notes: Ascription of the Vikṛtivallī recalled with low confidence.

name: Vyāḍi (the rasa-siddha)
summary: Counted among the twenty-seven siddhas of rasa (Rasaratnasamuccaya 1.3) and, as 'Vyāli', among those liberated in life (SDS Raseśvara 12).
notes: Relation to the grammarian Vyāḍi (tch:vyadi) not established; kept separate.

name: Vyāghrapāda (Viyākkiramar, Puliyūr muṉi)
summary: The 'tiger-footed' sage who with Patañjali worshipped the Dance at Chidambaram (Puliyūr); named in TM 67 among Nandi's eight disciples.

name: Vyakta
summary: One of the eleven gaṇadharas (chief disciples) of Mahāvīra, originally a learned brāhmaṇa who came to debate him at Madhyamā Pāvā and was converted when Mahāvīra resolved his hidden doubt — his doubt was whether the elements (and all things) are real or empty.

realization_account.text: Attained omniscience and liberation before or soon after Mahāvīra, according to the Śvetāmbara lists.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: The doubts are those of the gaṇadharavāda in the Viśeṣāvaśyaka Bhāṣya (moderate confidence on the pairing of each doubt with each name).

name: Vyāli

realization_account.text: An alchemist who sought the elixir of immortality; a courtesan found it for him; low certainty. Realization song in Tōh 2292 (no. 84): Seeing the true guru one sees reality; meditating in the openness of the sky is the supreme solitude; fully realizing phenomena there is nothing adverse; drinking the milk of the sky one lives.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: No. 84 of the eighty-four siddhas (Tōh 2292 order). An alchemist who sought the elixir of immortality; a courtesan found it for him; low certainty.
notes: Life from Abhayadatta's Caturaśītisiddhapravṛtti recalled from memory (not read locally); the song is read locally in Tōh 2292.

name: Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: Presented as a seer who knows past, present and future, able to grant divine sight and to foresee the war's outcome; identified with the earlier Apāntaratamas (12.337.54).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Parāśara and Satyavatī, in the tradition the arranger of the Vedas and author of the Mahābhārata; grandfather of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas; gives Sañjaya divine sight, teaches his son Śuka (12.224–247), and tells that in a former birth he was Apāntaratamas, the Veda-teacher born of Nārāyaṇa's word, reborn in Vasiṣṭha's line (12.337.38–54). The Gītā names him among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13) and 'among sages I am Vyāsa' (10.37).

checks.note: Fidelity checker F (bhagavad-gita ch10-12): this unit's contribution checked against the Sanskrit of the cited verses; no change needed.
Tradition's account located: Bhāgavata 1.4.19–22 and Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4.6–10 (divides the Veda in the Dvāpara; Paila Ṛg, Vaiśampāyana Yajus, Jaimini Sāma, Sumantu Atharva, Romaharṣaṇa itihāsa-purāṇa).
Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of sukarahasya, rudrahrdaya, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Roles located; the Apāntaratamas identification is at 12.337.54. Semi-legendary historicity and tradition dating as entered.

checks.note: Traditional author of the Bhāgavata, Kūrma and Devī Bhāgavata Purāṇas as the entry states. Vyāsa speaks the Kūrma's Vyāsa Gītā (2.12 ff.) and narrates the Devī Gītā.

Tradition's account located: VP 3.6.15-16 (Purāṇa-saṃhitā to Romaharṣaṇa), KūP 1.11.279-280 (eighteen by Vyāsa, Upapurāṇas by his disciples), VP 3.4.8-9 (Paila, Vaiśampāyana, Jaimini, Sumantu), BhP 12.7.5-7.

alt_summary: Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, son of Parāśara, called Veda-vyāsa, 'arranger of the Veda': seeing the decline of the ages, he divided the one Veda into four for the continuity of the sacrifice and taught the Ṛg to Paila, the Sāma to Jaimini, the Yajus to Vaiśampāyana and the Atharva to Sumantu, who branched them into śākhās through their pupils (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.4.19–23; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.4).

(Yoga unit contribution) For the Yoga tradition, the author of the Yogabhāṣya, the oldest commentary on the Yoga Sūtra. Vijñānabhikṣu calls him Vedavyāsa and Bādarāyaṇa and says he spoke 'the essence of all the Veda under the guise of the Yoga-bhāṣya'; Nārāyaṇatīrtha also names the bhāṣyakāra Bādarāyaṇa. Modern scholars doubt the identification; several ascribe the bhāṣya to Patañjali himself.
Cited by Arjuna among the seers who declare Kṛṣṇa supreme (BhG 10.13); named by the Lord as his manifestation among sages (munis) (10.37).

In the Purāṇic tradition the compiler of the eighteen Purāṇas (and Upapurāṇas through his disciples, KūP 1.1.280), who gave the Purāṇa-saṃhitā to his sūta disciple Romaharṣaṇa (VP 3.6.15-16) and the Bhāgavata to his son Śuka.

In U06's texts: the traditional author of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Uddhava and Kapila Gītās), the Devī Bhāgavata (Devī Gītā), the Kūrma Purāṇa and, as part of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa; the speaker of the Vyāsa Gītā.

In the Vedānta tradition, author of the Brahma Sūtras (as Bādarāyaṇa) and of the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas; in the Advaita guru-paramparā, son and disciple of Parāśara and teacher of his son Śuka; the Śaṅkaradigvijaya has him appear to Śaṅkara at Kāśī, test his commentary and extend his life.
notes: U01 contribution: Vyāsa as divider of the Veda. Other units contribute Vyāsa as author of the Mahābhārata, Brahma Sūtras (as Bādarāyaṇa in some traditions) and Purāṇas.

name: Vyāsa Rāmācārya
summary: Mādhva scholar who wrote the Nyāyāmṛta-taraṅgiṇī defending Vyāsatīrtha's Nyāyāmṛta against Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi.
notes: A story that he first studied Advaita under Madhusūdana before refuting him circulates in modern accounts — low confidence, not verified.

name: Vyāsatīrtha

realization_account.text: The tradition regards Vyāsatīrtha as a rebirth of Prahlāda (after Bāhlīka of the Mahābhārata), later reborn as Rāghavendra; it tells that he sat on the Vijayanagara throne to avert an inauspicious conjunction (kuhu-yoga) that threatened the king, and that he installed 732 images of Hanumān.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The foremost dialectician of Dvaita and rājaguru of the Vijayanagara court (under Kṛṣṇadevarāya). His Nyāyāmṛta, Tarkatāṇḍava and Tātparyacandrikā ('the three of Vyāsa') attack Advaita, Navya-Nyāya and rival readings of the Brahmasūtras; the Nyāyāmṛta drew Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi in reply. A composer of Kannada songs, he was the teacher of the Haridāsas Purandara Dāsa and Kanaka Dāsa, and of Vijayīndra Tīrtha. His brindāvana is at Nava Brindāvana near Hampi.

name: Vyomaśiva

scholarly.text: c. 10th c. CE (some place him earlier)

summary: Author of the Vyomavatī, the oldest extant commentary on the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha; a Śaiva ācārya.

name: Wang Rixiu
summary: Song lay scholar of Longshu who abandoned an official career for recitation, compiled a collated edition of the Larger Sūtra (T364) and wrote the popular Longshu jingtu wen; said to have died standing while reciting.

name: Wangchuk Dorje, the ninth Karmapa
summary: Author of the three classic Karma Kagyu Mahāmudrā manuals: the Ocean of Definitive Meaning, Dispelling the Darkness of Ignorance and Pointing Out the Dharmakāya.

name: Wangxi 王錫
summary: Compiler of the Chinese record of Moheyan's replies.

name: Wansong Xingxiu 萬松行秀
summary: Caodong master in the north (Jin/Yuan) who commented on Hongzhi's verses in the Book of Equanimity; teacher of Yelü Chucai.

name: Webu Sayadaw
summary: Burmese forest monk (1896–1977) renowned for his attainments and for teaching simple, continuous awareness of the breath at the nostrils; admired by U Ba Khin.

name: Wei Jing 魏靜
summary: Compiler of the Yongjia ji.

name: Wei Yuan
summary: Qing scholar who compiled the Larger Sūtra into a conflated version and grouped the Samantabhadra chapter with the three Pure Land sūtras as 'four sūtras' (as recalled).
notes: Contribution to the Pure Land canon recalled; low confidence.

name: Wŏnch'ŭk
summary: Silla Korean monk in Chang'an who studied with Xuanzang but, integrating Paramārtha's teachings, differed from Kuiji; his Saṃdhinirmocana commentary was translated into Tibetan.

name: Wumen Huikai 無門慧開
summary: Compiler of the Gateless Barrier; said to have worked on 'wu' for six years and awakened on hearing the drum for the midday meal.

name: Wuxue Zuyuan 無學祖元 (Mugaku Sogen)
summary: Chinese master (heir of Wuzhun) invited by Hōjō Tokimune; founded Engakuji (1282).

name: Wuzhu 無住

name: Wuzhun Shifan 無準師範
summary: Abbot of Jingshan, teacher of Enni Ben'en and of several Chinese masters who went to Japan.

name: Wuzhuo Miaozong 無著妙總
summary: Song nun, recognised as one of Dahui's Dharma heirs; she later taught as abbess.

name: Wuzu Fayan 五祖法演
summary: Yangqi master at Mount Wuzu who used Zhaozhou's 'wu' as a single-word barrier and posed 'Qiannü and her soul separated' (Wumenguan 35).

name: Xianglin Chengyuan 香林澄遠
summary: Heir of Yunmen in Sichuan; ancestor of Xuedou.

name: Xiangmo Zang 降魔藏
summary: Northern-school disciple of Shenxiu.

name: Xitang Zhizang 西堂智藏
summary: Heir of Mazu; teacher of the Korean founders Doui, Hongcheok and Hyecheol.

summary: Huanglong-branch master at Mount Tiantai who gave Eisai the Linji transmission (1191).

name: Xuansha Shibei 玄沙師備
summary: Heir of Xuefeng; 'the whole ten-direction world is one bright pearl'.

name: Xuanzang

notes: Contribution of U41.
alt_summary: Chinese pilgrim and translator (602-664) who studied at Nālandā and translated the 600-fascicle Mahāprajñāpāramitā, the Heart Sūtra (649), the Saṃdhinirmocana (647), the Vimalakīrti (650), the Bhaiṣajyaguru (650) and the Yogācārabhūmi; founder of the Faxiang tradition with Kuiji.

Chinese pilgrim and translator (602–664). This unit records his translations of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma (the seven books, the Mahāvibhāṣā in 200 fascicles, the Kośa, the Nyāyānusāra), Vasumitra's doxography, and his record of the schools in India.

name: Xuedou Chongxian 雪竇重顯
summary: Yunmen-house poet-master whose verses on a hundred cases formed the core of the Blue Cliff Record.

name: Xuefeng Yicun 雪峰義存
summary: Heir of Deshan in Fujian with a huge community; ancestor of the Yunmen and Fayan houses.

name: Xueyan Zuqin 雪巖祖欽
summary: Yangqi master; 'small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening' (Changuan cejin); teacher of Gaofeng.

name: Xutang Zhiyu 虛堂智愚
summary: Yangqi master whose Japanese heir Nanpo Shōmyō began the Ōtōkan line.

name: Xuyun 虛雲
summary: Modern Chinese master who restored many monasteries (including Huineng's Nanhua) and is said to have held transmission in all five houses.

name: Yādavaprakāśa
summary: Advaita-leaning teacher of Kāñcīpuram under whom Rāmānuja first studied; taught svābhāvika bhedābheda (Brahman itself becomes Īśvara, souls and matter). His Brahma Sūtra commentary is lost; the Yatidharmasamuccaya and the lexicon Vaijayantī are attributed to him.

realization_account.text: Śrīvaiṣṇava hagiography (Guruparamparāprabhāva) says he disagreed with Rāmānuja's readings, plotted against him on a pilgrimage, and later became his disciple as the renouncer Govinda Jīyar.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Śrīvaiṣṇava)

tradition.text: 11th c.

checks.note: Confirmed as Rāmānuja's first teacher in tradition, a Bhedābheda Vedāntin, and author of the Yatidharmasamuccaya (ed. Olivelle 1995). On the text's date (11th vs 12th c.) see the check of src:yatidharmasamuccaya.

alt_summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin, remembered in Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition as Rāmānuja's first teacher, later a tridaṇḍin renouncer; author of the Yatidharmasamuccaya on renouncers' rules.

Kāñcī teacher of bhedābheda Vedānta under whom Rāmānuja first studied; the tradition says they disagreed over Upaniṣadic readings and that he later became Rāmānuja's disciple as the renouncer Govinda Jīyar. (U16 owns his entry; this is U14's contribution.)

name: Yadu
summary: Ancestor-king of the Yādavas who questions a carefree young avadhūta brāhmaṇa about the source of his peace and hears of his twenty-four teachers (Bhāgavata 11.7.25-11.9.33).

name: Yājñavalkya

realization_account.text: BAU 6.5.3 says the white Yajus formulas come from the sun (Āditya) and are proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya; later Purāṇic accounts elaborate that he received them from the sun (not recorded here in detail).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The central teacher of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: he teaches Maitreyī that the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon (BAU 2.4, 4.5), defeats the brahmins at Janaka's court (BAU 3) and teaches Janaka on light, dream, sleep, death and karma (BAU 4.3-4). BAU 6.5.3 names him Vājasaneya, through whom the white Yajus formulas received from the sun are proclaimed.
notes: Teacher of the mantha rite lineage: Uddālaka Āruṇi taught it to his pupil Yājñavalkya (BAU 6.3.7, moderate on the kaṇḍikā). The Yājñavalkya Smṛti and Yoga-Yājñavalkya are later works attributed to him (owned by other units).

queries: Yajnavalkya son of Brahmarata Vaisampayana vomited Yajus Surya horse
checks.note: Located in Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5.7–29 (expiation offer, disgorged Yajus, breath-control, the Sun as horse, ayātayāma Yajus, Vājins). Son of Brahmarāta (Viṣṇu Purāṇa; Devarāta elsewhere) — confirmed by web.

U02's claims are all text-located: the beef remark (ŚB 3.1.2.21), the Agnihotra with Janaka (11.3.1, 11.6.2), the defeat of Vidagdha Śākalya (11.6.3), and the White Yajus from the Sun (14.9.4.33, 'ādityānīmāni śuklāni yajūṃṣi vājasaneyena yājñavalkyenākhyāyante'). The ŚB 1–5, 11–14 vs 6–10 division is given in Wikipedia. The Smṛti is set in Mithilā (YājñS 1.1–2).

queries: prepared BĀU 2.4.1, BĀU 3.1.2, BĀU 4.3.1, BĀU 6.3.7, BĀU 6.5.3
checks.note: Located as the central teacher of BĀU 2.4, 3.1–3.9, 4.1–4.5. His pupil Sāmaśravas is at 3.1.2. BĀU 6.3.7 has 'uddālaka āruṇir vājasaneyāya yājñavalkyāyāntevāsina uktvā', and 6.5.3 has 'ādityānīmāni śuklāni yajūṃṣi vājasaneyena yājñavalkyenākhyāyante'. Historicity and the later works attributed to him are outside a text check.

Text-located: the name occurs in the e-text of jabala, yajnavalkya, mandalabrahmana, paingala, tarasara, bhiksuka, in the roles the summary gives.  A mythic or textual figure, so there is no historical dating to check.
Located as described.

alt_summary: U02 contribution: the authority of ŚB books 1–5 and 11–14, where he answers Janaka on the Agnihotra (11.3.1, 11.6.2), defeats Vidagdha Śākalya on the number of gods (11.6.3) and says he eats beef 'if it is tender' (3.1.2.21); tradition also makes him the lawgiver of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, which scholars date many centuries later.

Son of Brahmarāta, pupil of Vaiśampāyana. Told to give back what he had learned after offering to perform an expiation alone, he disgorged the Yajus; then, devoted to breath-control, he praised the Sun as the door of liberation and received from the Sun, in the form of a horse (vājin), Yajus unknown to his teacher — the White Yajurveda of the Vājasaneyins (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.5).

In the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306) Yājñavalkya teaches king Daivarāti Janaka the evolution of the principles, the guṇas, yoga and dissolution, tells how he won the Yajus teaching from the Sun by austerity (12.306.3–22), and relates his answers to the Gandharva Viśvāvasu (12.306.27); he declares that knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (12.306.85).

U04 contribution: in the minor Upaniṣads Yājñavalkya teaches Bṛhaspati, Atri and Janaka on Avimukta, the tāraka and renunciation 'on the very day one becomes dispassionate' (Jābāla, Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad), is taught by the Person in the sun (Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa), teaches Paiṅgala, and is named among the kuṭīcaka renouncers (Bhikṣuka).

U28 contribution: the Dattātreyayogaśāstra names Yājñavalkya as the authority of the eight-limbed yoga (DYŚ 26), and the Yoga Yājñavalkya presents him teaching that yoga to Gārgī; the Jyotsnā quotes 'Yājñavalkya' on the qualifications of the yoga student.

tradition.text: the Vedic sage of Janaka's court; the Smṛti presents the same sage teaching in Mithilā

scholarly.text: the Vedic teacher c. 8th–6th c. BCE (if historical); the Yājñavalkyasmṛti c. 3rd–5th c. CE

Lord of the dead; in the Sāvitrī episode he takes Satyavat's life and, pleased by Sāvitrī's words, returns it (3.281); in the Jāpaka story he appears with Kāla and Mṛtyu (12.192–193).

name: Yāmunācārya

realization_account.text: As a boy he defeated the court scholar and won half a kingdom, hence 'Āḷavantār' ('he who came to rule'); Maṇakkāl Nambi led him to renounce it.
