name: Yangshan Huiji 仰山慧寂
summary: Heir of Guishan and co-founder of the Guiyang house; received and burned the book of 97 circle-figures, having understood them.

name: Yaoshan Weiyan 藥山惟儼
summary: Heir of Shitou; asked what he thought while sitting, answered 'thinking of not-thinking… non-thinking' (Jingde chuandeng lu juan 14).

name: Yasa
summary: A wealthy young man of Benares who went forth after hearing the Buddha's gradual talk; his parents became the first lay followers taking the three refuges (Vin Mv 1.7–8).

name: Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta
summary: The elder who objected to the ten points of the Vajjian monks and called the Second Council at Vesālī (Cv 12).

tradition.text: a century after the parinibbāna

realization_account.text: Finding the Vajjiputtaka monks of Vesālī accepting gold and silver, he objected, was expelled by them, and gathered the elders (Revata, Sabbakāmī and others) for the council that rejected the ten points.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The monk who, according to the Vinaya accounts, called the Second Council at Vaiśālī a century after the parinirvāṇa.

name: Yāska
summary: Author of the Nirukta, the etymological commentary on the Vedic word-lists (Nighaṇṭu). He defends the meaningfulness of the mantras against Kautsa (Nirukta 1.15–16), teaches that the seers had direct vision of dharma (1.20), that one who recites the Veda without knowing its meaning is a post bearing a load (1.18), and that because of the deity's greatness the one Self is praised in many ways (7.4).

scholarly.text: c. 6th–5th century BCE (before Pāṇini, low confidence)

notes: U01 contribution (Yāska as interpreter of the Saṃhitās); U02 owns the Nirukta.

checks.note: Confirmed: author of the Nirukta; modern scholars place him c. 7th–5th c. BCE, before Pāṇini (entry: c. 6th–5th c. BCE — within range). Loci 1.15–16, 1.18, 1.20, 7.4 (one Self praised in many ways) located.

Wikipedia: modern scholars place Yāska in the 7th–5th c. BCE, before Pāṇini, which agrees with the entry (600–400 BCE). The named predecessors (Śākaṭāyana, Gārgya, Aupamanyava, Aurṇavābha, Śākapūṇi, Kautsa) are text-located in the Nirukta (1.12, 2.11, 12.1, 7.4, 1.15).

alt_summary: Author of the Nirukta, the Vedāṅga of etymology; he reports the views of Nairuktas, Aitihāsikas, Yājñikas and grammarians and of many named predecessors (Śākaṭāyana, Gārgya, Aupamanyava, Aurṇavābha, Śākapūṇi, Kautsa and others).

name: Yaśobhadra
summary: Successor of Śayyambhava; teacher of both Sambhūtavijaya and Bhadrabāhu.

name: Rāhulamātā
summary: The bodhisatta's wife and mother of Rāhula, called 'Rāhula's mother' in the Vinaya (Mv 1.54); the name Yasodharā is commentarial.

name: Yaśodhara (rasa author)
summary: Author of the Rasaprakāśasudhākara.

name: Yaśomitra
summary: Author of the Sphuṭārthā, the only complete Sanskrit commentary on the Kośa and bhāṣya, written from a Sautrāntika standpoint.

name: Yaśovijaya
summary: Śvetāmbara (Tapā Gaccha) monk-scholar ('Nyāyaviśārada', 'Upādhyāya') who studied Navya-Nyāya at Vārāṇasī and wrote over a hundred works in Sanskrit, Prakrit and Gujarati: on logic and standpoints (Jaina Tarkabhāṣā, Nayopadeśa, Jñānabindu), on adhyātma and yoga (Adhyātmasāra, Adhyātmopaniṣad, Jñānasāra, a commentary on the Yoga Sūtra, dvātriṃśikās), and a critique of Banārsīdās's Adhyātma circle. The tradition tells that he met Ānandaghana and praised him in eight verses.

name: Yativṛṣabha
summary: Author of the cūrṇi-sūtras on the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa and (by tradition) of the Tiloyapaṇṇatti.
alt_summary: Digambara author of the Tiloyapaṇṇatti and of cūrṇi-sūtras on the Kaṣāyapāhuḍa.

name: Yavanācārya ('the Yavana teacher')
summary: The teacher or teachers called 'the Yavanas' whom Varāhamihira cites on longevity (BJ 7.1), royal yogas (BJ 11.1) and the count of nābhasa yogas (BJ 12.1), and whom he says are honoured like seers (BS 2.14).

name: Yavaneśvara
summary: The 'lord of the Yavanas' who, by the Yavanajātaka's own closing account (as read by Pingree), rendered a Greek horoscopic text into Sanskrit prose in 149/150 CE.

name: Yelpa Yeshe Tsek
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa, founder of the Yelpa Kagyu.

name: Yelü Chucai 耶律楚材
summary: Khitan statesman under Chinggis Khan and lay disciple of Wansong, who asked for the Congrong lu and wrote its preface.

name: Yeshe De
summary: Tibetan translator (late 8th-early 9th c.) who, with Indian scholars such as Jinamitra, Surendrabodhi and Dānaśīla, translated a large part of the Mahāyāna sūtras into Tibetan.

name: Yeshe Dorje, the eleventh Karmapa
summary: Short-lived Karmapa who also held Nyingma treasure teachings.

name: Lha Lama Yeshe Ö
summary: King-monk of Gugé (Ngari) who, to restore pure Buddhism, sent young Tibetans to Kashmir and invited Indian masters; the tradition tells that, captured by the Garlok, he refused to be ransomed and asked that the gold be used to invite Atiśa.

name: Yeshe Tsogyal (ye shes mtsho rgyal)
summary: Tibetan noblewoman who became Padmasambhava's consort and principal disciple; she compiled and concealed his teachings as treasures, received the Khandro Nyingthig lineage, and is revered as a fully enlightened ḍākinī (the Queen of Great Bliss of the Longchen Nyingthig).

realization_account.text: Attained buddhahood in one life and departed without leaving a body.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

tradition.text: 8th c.

scholarly.text: 8th c. (her full hagiography is a 17th-c. treasure)

name: Yifu 義福
summary: Shenxiu's heir in Chang'an.

name: Yijing
summary: Chinese pilgrim who studied at Nālandā and translated much of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya; his record describes the four nikāyas of India.
alt_summary: Chinese pilgrim-monk (635-713) who translated the Golden Light (703), the Diamond and the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, and described Indian monastic life.

name: Yilé Kyé (yid las skyes), the sage 'Born from Mind'
summary: The emanation of the Medicine Buddha's speech who requests the Four Tantras and records them (the tradition's account).

name: Yinguang
summary: Modern Chinese master whose letters spread Pure Land practice among lay people: faithfully fulfil one's social duties, avoid evil and do good, believe in cause and effect, and hold the name with faith and vow; established Lingyan shan as a recitation monastery; counted the thirteenth patriarch.

name: Yogarāja
summary: Disciple of Kṣemarāja; author of the commentary (Vivṛti) on the Paramārthasāra.

name: Yogīndu

scholarly.text: c. 6th c. CE (some: up to the 10th c.)

summary: Digambara mystic poet in Apabhraṃśa, author of the Paramātmaprakāśa and the Yogasāra, teaching that the soul in its essence is the supreme self.

name: Yōkan
summary: Sanron monk of Tōdaiji lineage and abbot of Zenrin-ji who practised and taught exclusive recitation (Ōjō jūin); tradition says Amida turned to look back at him as he circumambulated (the 'looking-back Amida' of Eikandō).

name: Yongjia Xuanjue 永嘉玄覺
summary: Tiantai-trained monk said to have been confirmed by Huineng after one night ('the one-night guest'); credited with the Zhengdao ge and the Yongjia ji.

name: Yongming Yanshou

realization_account.text: Tradition says he drew lots before an image, choosing between meditation and the myriad good practices, and drew the latter seven times; he recited the name 100,000 times daily (Song biographies, as recalled).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Fayan Chan master of Hangzhou whose Wanshan tonggui ji defends recitation and all good practices alongside Chan; counted the sixth Pure Land patriarch in the Fozu tongji. The 'four alternatives' on Chan and Pure Land ('with Chan and with Pure Land, like a tiger with horns') are traditionally ascribed to him but are not found in the Wanshan tonggui ji (checked locally) and appear only in later sources.
notes: Shared with U42 (Chan).
alt_summary: Heir of Deshao; compiled the Zongjing lu harmonising Chan and the teachings and advocated combining Chan with Pure Land practice; counted as a Pure Land patriarch.

name: Yongzin Yeshe Gyaltsen
summary: Tutor of the Eighth Dalai Lama, prolific author on lamrim, mind and Mahāmudrā in the Ganden oral lineage.

name: Khetsün Yönten Gyatso (mkhas btsun yon tan rgya mtsho) of Jonang
summary: Abbot of Jonang before Dolpopa and Dolpopa's principal teacher of the Kālacakra six-branch yoga.

name: Yoshishige no Yasutane
summary: Heian literatus, organiser of the Kangaku-e (society joining students and Hiei monks in Lotus lecture and nenbutsu), compiler of the Nihon ōjō gokuraku ki; later took the tonsure as Jakushin.

name: Youxi Chuandeng
summary: Ming Tiantai master of Youxi (Tiantai shan) who explained birth in the Pure Land as the birth of non-birth in ten Tiantai gates.

name: Yuan Hongdao
summary: Late-Ming literatus of the Gong'an school who turned from Chan to Pure Land and wrote the Xifang helun.

name: Yuanjue Zongyan 圓覺宗演
summary: Editor of the 1120 edition of the Linji lu.

name: Yuanwu Keqin 圜悟克勤
summary: Author of the Blue Cliff Record lectures; teacher of Dahui and Huqiu.

name: Yudhāmanyu
summary: Named by Duryodhana among the heroes of the Pāṇḍava army, 'valiant' (1.6).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.6.

name: Yudhiṣṭhira (Dharmarāja)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Eldest Pāṇḍava, son of Dharma; answers the Yakṣa (3.297) and Nahuṣa (3.177), defends acting righteously without seeking its fruit against Draupadī (3.32.4), wishes to renounce after the war and is persuaded to rule (12.7–36), receives Bhīṣma's instruction, and at the end refuses to enter heaven without the dog who was devoted to him (17.3).

checks.note: Located as described.

alt_summary: King, son of Kuntī, who blows the conch Anantavijaya (1.16).
notes: Linked in BhG ch. 1–3 at 1.16.

name: Yudra Nyingpo (g.yu sgra snying po)
summary: Vairocana's disciple from Gyalmo Rong, who with Vimalamitra translated the thirteen later mind-series scriptures.

name: Yūkimuṉi
summary: Physician-Siddhar to whom the Yūki vaittiya cintāmaṇi, a standard work on the classification of diseases, is ascribed.

scholarly.text: undetermined; Siddhar works are usually placed after c. 1400

name: Yuien
summary: Shinran's disciple of Kawada (Hitachi), generally regarded as the compiler of the Tannishō.

name: Yumo Mikyö Dorje (yu mo mi bskyod rdo rje)
summary: Eleventh-century Tibetan Kālacakra master, counted by the Jonang as the first Tibetan in their lineage of the six-branch yoga; a student of the Kashmiri paṇḍita Somanātha; the Four Clear Lamps are attributed to him.

name: Lama Yungtön Trogyal
summary: The sorcerer (a Nyingma mantrin) from whom, in the Life of Milarepa, the young Milarepa learned the destructive magic he used against his relatives.

name: Yunju Daoying 雲居道膺
summary: Heir of Dongshan through whom the Caodong line continued.

name: Yunmen Wenyan 雲門文偃

realization_account.text: When Muzhou slammed his gate on Yunmen's leg, breaking it, Yunmen awoke (tradition's account; Biyan lu case 6 commentary).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of the Yunmen house in Guangdong; heir of Xuefeng; known for one-word answers ('every day is a good day', 'a dried shit-stick').

name: Yunqi Zhuhong
summary: Late-Ming reviver of monastic discipline at Yunqi si who joined Chan and Pure Land, taught recitation of the name as the principal practice for all, promoted releasing living beings and lay self-examination ledgers, and wrote the Amitābha Sūtra commentary; eighth patriarch in the later Pure Land list; one of the four great masters of the late Ming.
notes: Shared with U42.
alt_summary: Ming reformer who combined Chan with Pure Land recitation ('who is it that recites the Buddha's name?') and compiled the Changuan cejin; counted a Pure Land patriarch.

name: Yunyan Tansheng 雲巖曇晟
summary: Heir of Yaoshan and teacher of Dongshan; 'just this is it'.

name: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Elder (g.yu thog rnying ma yon tan mgon po)

scholarly.text: historicity doubted; the figure may be a later projection of the Younger

realization_account.text: An emanation of the Medicine Buddha; lived 125 years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: In the tradition's account the chief physician of King Trisong Detsen, who travelled to India and elsewhere to study, received the Four Tantras from Vairocana and lived to a great age; regarded as an emanation of the Medicine Buddha. Scholars question his historicity.

name: Yuthok Yönten Gönpo the Younger (g.yu thog gsar ma yon tan mgon po)
summary: Twelfth-century physician, in the tradition's account the thirteenth-generation descendant of the Elder, who revised the Four Tantras into their present form (in the scholarly account, compiled them) and is the source of the Yuthok Nyingthig, the physicians' spiritual practice.

name: Öndör Gegeen Zanabazar, the first Jebtsundamba Khutughtu

realization_account.text: Recognized as the rebirth of Tāranātha.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Mongolian lama and artist, first of the Jebtsundamba incarnations; in the tradition's account the rebirth of Tāranātha, which links the Jonang line of incarnation to Mongolia.

name: Zanning 贊寧
summary: Author of the Song gaoseng zhuan (988).

name: Zarawa Kalden Yeshe Senge
summary: Disciple of Phagmodrupa associated with the founding of the Yazang Kagyu.

name: Zenran
summary: Shinran's son, sent to the Kantō, who claimed to have received a secret teaching from his father at night and disparaged the eighteenth vow as a 'withered flower'; Shinran disowned him in 1256 (letters).

name: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal
alt_names: zhabs drung ngag dbang rnam rgyal
summary: Drukpa hierarch recognized by one party as Pema Karpo's rebirth; after the succession dispute he went to Bhutan (1616), unified it, and founded the Southern Drukpa state tradition.

name: Zhangtön Chöbar
summary: Master from whom Sachen Kunga Nyingpo received the full Lamdre over four years, with instructions to keep it secret for eighteen years (tradition's account).

name: Zhangtön Tashi Dorje (zhang ston bkra shis rdo rje)
summary: Heart-essence master who recovered further Nyingthig texts and transmitted the Seventeen Tantras.

name: Zhaozhou Congshen 趙州從諗
summary: Heir of Nanquan who taught for forty years in old age; famed for his 'wu' to 'does a dog have buddha-nature?', 'the cypress in front of the hall', 'wash your bowl', 'have some tea'.

name: Zhenxie Qingliao 真歇清了
summary: Caodong master in the Song, ancestor of Rujing's line; scholars suggest he may be among those Dahui criticised for 'silent illumination'.

name: Zhiju 智炬
summary: Compiler of the Baolin zhuan (801).

name: Zhipan
summary: Southern Song Tiantai historian whose Fozu tongji lists seven patriarchs of the Lotus society.

name: Zhishen 智詵
summary: Hongren's disciple in Sichuan, founder of the Jingzhong line.

name: Zhongfeng Mingben 中峰明本
summary: Yuan master and hermit who advocated huatou practice and joint Chan–Pure Land practice.

name: Zhu Fonian
summary: Chinese translator who rendered into Chinese the texts recited by Buddhayaśas, Dharmanandi and others.

name: Zhuoan Deguang 拙庵德光
summary: Heir of Dahui who sent a certificate of transmission to Dainichi Nōnin's envoys (1189).

name: Zibo Zhenke 紫柏真可
summary: Ming master who initiated the Jiaxing canon; died in prison.

name: Zongbao 宗寶
summary: Yuan-dynasty monk of Guangzhou who edited the standard edition of the Platform Sūtra (1291).

name: Guifeng Zongmi 圭峰宗密
summary: Fifth Huayan patriarch who considered himself an heir of Shenhui's Heze line; classified the Chan schools, taught sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation and the mind's 'empty and calm knowing', and criticised Hongzhou. (Owned by U54; U42 contributes the Chan role.)

name: Mixian Zongshao 彌衍宗紹
summary: Disciple who compiled the Wumen guan.

name: Zongxiao
summary: Southern Song Tiantai monk who compiled the Lebang wenlei (1200), the first to name a line of Lotus-school patriarchs.

name: Zonkaku
summary: Kakunyo's son and the most learned early Shinshū scholar (Rokuyōshō, the first commentary on the Kyōgyōshinshō); twice disowned by his father.

name: Zurkhar Lodrö Gyalpo (zur mkhar blo gros rgyal po)
summary: Physician-scholar of the Zur school, author of the Oral Instructions of the Ancestors (mes po'i zhal lung), who also examined the question whether the Four Tantras is the Buddha's word.

name: Zurkhar Nyamnyi Dorje (zur mkhar mnyam nyid rdo rje)
summary: Founder of the Zur school of Tibetan medicine.

name: Zurpoche Shākya Jungne (zur po che shAkya 'byung gnas)
summary: First of the 'three Zur' who organized the Nyingma kama (Mahāyoga and Anuyoga) transmission and founded Ugpalung.
